hello → SHA-256 2cf24dba… (64 hex chars), MD5 5d41402a… (32). Lengths identify algorithms at a glance: 40 SHA-1, 64 SHA-256, 128 SHA-512. Use SHA-256 for integrity checks and fingerprints; MD5 only for legacy manifest compatibility — never for passwords (use bcrypt/argon2 server-side). Flip one letter (hallo) and the avalanche effect rewrites the whole digest. Compare side by side in the hash generator, step up to keyed HMAC in the HMAC tool, and encrypt (not just hash) secrets with the AES encryptor. Guide: hash comparison.

Seeding test DBs: how many UUIDs without collisions

v4 UUIDs carry 122 random bits — you can mint millions per second for fixtures with effectively zero collision risk (birthday math needs ~2.7 quintillion for 50% odds). Practical flow: generate 10,000 in bulk, bulk-copy into seed scripts, dedupe on insert as belt-and-braces. Prefer UUIDs over auto-increment IDs in test data to avoid order-dependent flakes; prefer random-string only for human-readable codes, never for unguessable tokens. Bulk mint in the UUID generator. Seeding guide: UUID seeding.

Regex flags g/i/m/s and capture groups that actually capture

Two thirds of regex pain is flags, not patterns. g finds all matches (d+ pulls 42 from “Order 42”), i ignores case, m makes ^/$ per-line for 4000-line logs, s lets . cross newlines. Named groups ((?<year>d{4})-(?<month>d{2})) beat numbered ones for 2024-05-01 extraction; non-capturing (?:…) keeps indexes stable. Greedy .* backtracks catastrophically on large inputs — prefer lazy .*? or explicit classes. Our regex tester highlights matches with per-flag control and runs catastrophic patterns in a worker with timeouts instead of freezing your tab. Flags lab: capture groups guide.

JWT expiry without trust: exp, skew and alg:none

Decoding shows claims; verification proves them — do both, in that order. Check exp against now (allow ~30s clock skew, sync NTP), confirm aud is your service and iss your IdP, and reject alg:none unconditionally — unsigned tokens must never authorize. exp: 1717252800 two hours past means expired, full stop, regardless of a valid-looking signature from the wrong key. Paste into the JWT decoder (redact emails before screenshotting), convert timestamps in the timestamp converter. Expiry guide: JWT checks.

Why café becomes caf%C3%A9 (and spaces become %20)

URLs allow a small ASCII set; everything else percent-encodes as UTF-8 bytes — é is two bytes, hence %C3%A9. Spaces encode as %20 in paths but + in form bodies (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) — the most common encoding bug in form posts. Encode &, = and # inside values or they split your query; never double-encode (%2520). URLs over ~2000 chars risk proxy truncation — POST the payload instead. Encode and parse safely with the URL encoder and URL parser. Encoding guide: URL encoding.

Try it now: paste a broken API reply into the free JSON formatter — line errors, offline, nothing uploads and fix it in seconds.

Limits and honest notes

Local tools inspect; they do not execute. Decoded JWTs are unverified until your backend checks signatures against the IdP keys. Hash comparisons catch corruption, not malice without a trusted channel. Regex testers validate patterns, not intent — a matching pattern can still be the wrong pattern. And no formatter fixes a 500 status: client-side validation narrows the suspect list, server logs close the case.

General guidance only. Never paste production secrets into any web tool you have not audited — ours runs locally, but verify in DevTools Network tab.

faqs.question: How do I debug a JSON API error locally?
faqs.answer: Paste the payload into a local formatter for line:column errors — a missing comma at 1:18 beats staring at 10,000 lines. Fix trailing commas, quotes and comments, decode nested Base64/JWT layers one at a time, and verify token expiry and audience separately.

faqs.question: When should I use URL-safe Base64?
faqs.answer: For tokens, query params, filenames and slugs, where it uses -_ without padding. Standard Base64 (+/ with =) belongs in MIME, email and data URLs. Mixing modes across a boundary is the classic midnight outage — standardize per side.

faqs.question: Is MD5 ever acceptable?
faqs.answer: Only for legacy checksum compatibility, never for passwords or security. Use SHA-256 for integrity fingerprints, keyed HMAC for origin proof, and slow bcrypt/argon2 for password storage server-side.

faqs.question: Does decoding a JWT verify it?
faqs.answer: No. Decoding displays claims; your backend must verify the signature against IdP keys and exp, aud and algorithm checks on every request. Reject alg:none unconditionally — unsigned tokens authorize nothing.

faqs.question: Why does my regex freeze the tab?
faqs.answer: Catastrophic backtracking: nested quantifiers like (a+)+$ explode exponentially on non-matches. Prefer lazy quantifiers and explicit classes, anchor patterns, and test in runners that isolate execution in workers with timeouts.

title: Why JSON.parse Fails: Trailing Commas and Quotes
description: Fix JSON.parse errors fast: position to line:column, trailing commas, comments, quotes + 500KB-scale validation. Free local formatter.
keywords: why json parse fails trailing commas single quotes
html:
Unexpected token } in JSON at position 412. No line number, no context, just a position to count by hand. Every developer meets this error monthly; the fix takes seconds once you know the three causes that produce 90% of failures: trailing commas, comments, and single quotes. This guide teaches reading the error, fixing each cause, and validating at scale — with the line:column pinpointing that turns counting into clicking.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. Validate in the JSON formatter; its tree view navigates large responses and its YAML view converts configs.

Read the error: position → line:column

V8 reports a character offset, not a location. Pasting into the formatter translates position 412 to line 18, column 7 with the offending token highlighted — and names the cause class. The 500KB API reply that defeats eyeballing submits instantly; collapse completed subtrees to isolate the broken branch. For recurring feeds, validate on a schedule and diff against the last green payload — most production JSON breaks come from upstream schema drift, not your code.

Three causes, three fixes (with examples)

CauseBrokenFixed
Trailing comma{"a": 1,}{"a": 1} — minify to confirm
Comments{// x
"a": 1}		Strip all comments (JSONC ≠ JSON)
Single quotes{'a': 1}Double-quote keys + strings
Duplicate keys{"a":1,"a":2}Dedupe — last wins silently

After fixing, minify and re-pretty-print: a clean round-trip proves validity better than any single check. Payloads over 10MB should split before pasting — oversized dumps hang tabs in every tool, not just ours.

At scale: 500KB replies, duplicate keys, minify math

Large API responses fail differently: truncated transfers (compare Content-Length), duplicated keys across merged objects (last-wins silently corrupts), and encoding mismatches (BOM prefixes break strict parsers — strip \uFEFF). Minified output runs ~20% smaller than pretty-printed — meaningful at 500KB over metered connections. Keep a known-good sample response per endpoint; when parse fails, diff structure first (added field? renamed key?) and syntax second. For config files, consider YAML source with JSON build output — humans edit YAML, machines consume JSON, and the converter bridges them.

General guidance only. Validate untrusted payloads before processing — malformed JSON is also a classic injection vector; parse strictly, never eval.

faqs.question: Why does JSON.parse fail on trailing commas?
faqs.answer: Strict JSON forbids them, unlike JavaScript literals where they are tolerated. Delete the comma and paste into the formatter, which translates positions like 412 into line 18 column 7 with highlighting. Minify and re-pretty-print afterward, since a clean round-trip proves validity better than any single check.

faqs.question: Can JSON have comments?
faqs.answer: No — JSONC with comments is a different format that strict parsers reject. Strip all comments before parsing, since even one line breaks validation. Configs needing comments should live as YAML source with JSON build output, where humans edit YAML, machines consume JSON, and the converter bridges them.

faqs.question: How do I find the error in a 500KB file?
faqs.answer: Paste into a formatter for line:column pinpointing with the offending token highlighted, then collapse subtrees to isolate the broken branch. Diff against the last known-good payload to spot upstream schema drift, truncated transfers or renamed keys. For recurring feeds, validate on a schedule rather than eyeballing.

faqs.question: What do duplicate JSON keys do?
faqs.answer: Last value wins silently with no error but wrong data, since parsers keep the final occurrence. Dedupe keys and use validators that flag them explicitly. Across merged objects, duplicated keys corrupt results invisibly, so compare Content-Length for truncation and strip BOM prefixes that break strict parsers.

faqs.question: Should I minify JSON?
faqs.answer: For transport, yes — minified output runs about 20% smaller than pretty-printed, which matters at 500KB over metered connections. Pretty-print for debugging readability. A clean minify-pretty round-trip proves validity, while payloads over 10MB should split before pasting to avoid hanging tabs in every tool during development.

title: Base64 URL-Safe vs Standard: Padding and Modes
description: Base64 standard vs URL-safe: alphabet table, padding rules, 33% size math, UTF-8 step + JWT segment link. Free mode-toggle encoder.
html:
Auth broke at midnight: tokens generated with + and / sailed through tests, then shattered in production URLs — and became space, slash split the path, padding got stripped by a proxy. The fix was three characters of alphabet swap: URL-safe Base64. Standard vs URL-safe is the most common encoding bug in this space, and it hides until deployment. This guide maps both alphabets, padding rules, size math and the JWT connection.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. Encode in the Base64 tool (mode toggle); inspect tokens in the JWT decoder.

Two alphabets: +/= vs -_ (no pad)

Standard (RFC 4648)URL-safe
Chars 62–63+ /- _
Padding= requiredOmitted
Safe in URLsNo (space/path splits)Yes
Safe in email/MIMEYes (76-char wrap)Decoders may choke
Example (fa fb fc)+vv8-vv8

Rule: standard for MIME, email and data-URLs; URL-safe for tokens, query params, filenames and slugs. Mixing modes (URL-safe encode, standard decode) is the midnight-outage pattern — standardize per boundary and document which side owns encoding.

Size math: 33% overhead, UTF-8 first

Base64 inflates ~33%: every 3 bytes become 4 characters. Budget it: a 3MB binary becomes 4MB of text — fine for tokens, fatal for “embed the video in JSON” designs. UTF-8 encodes first: café → bytes 63 61 66 C3 A9 → Y2Fmw6k=; emoji cost 4 bytes each, so “🎉” alone becomes 8 characters. Forgetting the UTF-8 step produces mojibake that decodes “successfully” into garbage — always encode text as UTF-8 bytes, decode bytes as UTF-8 text. The 76-character mail wrap is transport-only; strip whitespace before decoding stored values.

JWT segments are Base64URL (and why padding vanishes)

Every JWT is three Base64URL segments joined by dots — header, payload, signature. No padding, -_ alphabet, always. So exp: 1717252800 rides inside segment two, and decoding it needs a URL-safe decoder (standard decoders reject unpadded input or misread -_). Workflow: decode segments in the Base64 tool with URL-safe mode, then hand the full token to the JWT decoder for claim inspection — and remember decoding ≠ verifying (see expiry checks).

General guidance only. Base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone can decode it. Never put secrets in tokens or URLs.

faqs.question: When do I use URL-safe Base64?
faqs.answer: For tokens, query params, filenames and slugs using dash-underscore without padding. Standard with plus-slash and equals serves MIME, email and data URLs with 76-character wrap. Mixing modes causes midnight outages, so standardize per boundary and document which side owns encoding for reliability across production and staging environments.

faqs.question: Why did my token break in a URL?
faqs.answer: Standard and became space and slash split the path, while proxies stripped padding unexpectedly. Re-encode URL-safe with dash-underscore and no padding, or percent-encode the standard output. Test with production URLs containing and and slash, since single-word test data hides the bug until deployment across different gateways and browsers.

faqs.question: How much bigger is Base64?
faqs.answer: About 33% overhead since every three bytes become four characters, so a 3MB binary becomes 4MB of text. Budget carefully since embedding video in JSON turns fatal quickly. Remember UTF-8 encodes first — café becomes Y2Fmw6k= and emoji cost four bytes each — then strip whitespace before decoding.

faqs.question: Is Base64 encryption?
faqs.answer: No — encoding is trivially reversible by anyone, unlike encryption with keys. Never put secrets in tokens or URLs since decoding requires no permission. For example, exp 1717252800 rides visibly inside JWT segment two. Encrypt separately with proper tools and treat encoded values as public text.

faqs.question: Why does JWT use no padding?
faqs.answer: JWT segments are Base64URL by specification with dash-underscore alphabet and padding omitted always. Three dot-joined segments carry header, payload and signature, so standard decoders reject unpadded input or misread characters. Use a URL-safe decoder mode, then hand the full token to the JWT decoder for reliable claim inspection workflows.

title: SHA-256 vs MD5: When to Use Which Hash
description: SHA-256 vs MD5 with digest-length table, avalanche demos, hash-vs-HMAC-vs-AES ladder + password hashing warning. Free compare tool.
html:
“Just MD5 it, it's only a checksum.” Six months later that checksum guarded password resets. Hash choice is a security decision wearing a utility costume: MD5 for legacy manifests, SHA-256 for integrity, bcrypt for passwords — and the wrong pick fails silently for years. This guide gives digest lengths that identify algorithms on sight, the avalanche intuition, and the hash-vs-HMAC-vs-encryption ladder, with hello worked through every level.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. Compare in the hash generator; step up keyed hashing in HMAC; encrypt secrets with AES.

Digest lengths identify algorithms on sight

AlgorithmHex lengthhello startsUse for
MD5325d41402a…Legacy checks only
SHA-140aaf4c61d…Legacy (git internals)
SHA-256642cf24dba…Integrity, fingerprints
SHA-5121289b71d224…High-assurance digests

Count the hex: 32/40/64/128 tells you the algorithm before any label does. Case varies by tool (uppercase manifests vs lowercase APIs) — normalize before comparing, and compare full strings, never prefixes.

Avalanche: hello vs hallo rewrites everything

Flip one letter and the digest scrambles completely — hello and hallo share no recognizable prefix. That avalanche is the security property: no partial credit for close guesses. It also kills two folk practices: leet substitutions (a→4) barely change crack time because attackers normalize them, and truncated digests (“first 8 chars match!”) prove nothing. Test both inputs side by side in the hash generator to build the intuition permanently.

The ladder: hash vs HMAC vs AES (when to climb)

  • Hash (SHA-256): fingerprinting downloads, cache keys, dedupe. Anyone can recompute — proves integrity against accidents, not attackers.
  • HMAC: hash and secret key — proves the message came from a key holder. Webhooks, API signatures. Step up in the HMAC tool.
  • AES encryption: reversible secrecy for stored/transmitted data. Passwords get bcrypt/argon2 instead (slow by design). Encrypt in the AES tool.

Passwords are the classic misplacement: fast hashes (even SHA-256) fall to GPUs in hours; password hashing must be slow (bcrypt cost factors) and salted per user. If your login table uses MD5/SHA, migrating to argon2 outranks every feature on the roadmap.

General guidance only, not a security audit. Hash choices for regulated data need professional review — this page builds intuition, not compliance.

faqs.question: When is MD5 acceptable?
faqs.answer: Only legacy checksum compatibility, never for passwords or security decisions. Six months after just-MD5-it thinking, checksums often guard password resets and fail silently for years. Use SHA-256 for integrity and fingerprints, bcrypt or argon2 slow salted hashes for passwords, and migrate MD5 login tables immediately.

faqs.question: How do I tell hash algorithms apart?
faqs.answer: Count hex chars: 32 means MD5 starting 5d41402a, 40 means SHA-1, 64 means SHA-256 starting 2cf24dba, and 128 means SHA-512. Case varies between uppercase manifests and lowercase APIs, so normalize before comparing. Always compare full strings, never prefixes, since truncated matches prove nothing for reliable identification across tools.

faqs.question: Do leet substitutions strengthen passwords?
faqs.answer: Barely, since attackers normalize a-to-4 automatically and avalanche gives no partial credit for close guesses. Length and randomness dominate crack time, not substitutions. Test hello versus hallo side by side in the hash generator — one flipped letter scrambles the digest completely without recognizable prefixes.

faqs.question: Hash vs HMAC vs encryption?
faqs.answer: Hash with SHA-256 proves integrity for downloads, cache keys and dedupe against accidents, not attackers. HMAC adds a secret key to prove keyed origin for webhooks and API signatures. Encryption with AES provides reversible secrecy, while passwords need slow salted bcrypt or argon2 instead of fast hashes.

faqs.question: Why did half my digest match?
faqs.answer: Truncated comparisons prove nothing because avalanche means close inputs like hello and hallo share no prefix structure. First-eight-char matches show coincidence, not integrity. Always compare full digests after normalizing case, and test both inputs side by side to build lasting avalanche intuition for secure verification workflows.

title: Seed Test Databases With UUIDs: Math and Workflow
description: Generate 10,000 UUIDs for seed data, understand v4 collision odds, and choose committed fixtures or deterministic v5 IDs for stable tests.
html:
A test suite failed for the third time in a week because test B assumed the user created by test A still had ID 7. The database had been reseeded, the auto-increment counter had moved, and the assumption collapsed. Switching the fixtures to UUIDs removed the dependency on insertion order. Random identifiers decouple tests from sequence, but they introduce a second question that is easy to miss: should the same test run produce the same IDs every time? The answer depends on whether you are protecting isolation or protecting a snapshot.

The wider developer toolkit guide covers the surrounding debugging workflow. Generate IDs in the UUIDs tab of the random number and UUID studio, then format the resulting fixtures in the JSON formatter.

122 random bits, and what the collision odds mean

An RFC 4122 version 4 UUID contains 128 bits, of which 122 are random; six bits are fixed for the version and variant. The birthday approximation for the chance of at least one duplicate among n IDs is about n² divided by twice 2¹²². For 10,000 IDs that is roughly 9.4 × 10⁻³⁰, close to 10⁻²⁹. Reaching a 50% chance would take about 2.7 quintillion IDs. At a million IDs per second, that is tens of thousands of years, which is why the risk is negligible at practical scale. Negligible is not the same as impossible, so the honest phrasing is low risk rather than collision-proof.

Worked example: 10,000 user fixtures. The probability of any duplicate is about one in 10²⁹, far below the chance of a hardware fault corrupting the seed file. A unique index on the ID column still costs almost nothing and catches a duplicated row from a bad import or a copy-paste error. Deduplication is belt and braces, not a sign that the math is shaky.

The formula grows with the square of the number of IDs, which is why the odds stay tiny for test-sized sets and become interesting only at astronomical scale. A million IDs still sit near 10⁻²⁵. The practical lesson is not to memorize the exponent but to stop treating uniqueness as a scheduling problem: generate the IDs, enforce a unique constraint, and spend the saved attention on the test logic.

The browser tool caps a run at 500 UUIDs. Ten thousand IDs therefore means 20 runs of 500, or a script or database function that does it in one statement. The tool has no 10,000-in-one-click mode, and requesting a larger number silently produces 500 rather than an error; the result header tells you how many were generated, so check it. Practical generation options include crypto.randomUUID() in browsers and Node, uuid.uuid4() in Python, gen_random_uuid() in PostgreSQL, UUID() in MySQL and NEWID() in SQL Server. The versions differ: MySQL's UUID() returns a time-based version 1 value, while NEWID() is random. Check the version digit when the distinction matters.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const ids = Array.from({ length: 10000 }, () => randomUUID());

Write those IDs to a fixture file or insert them in a transaction; do not regenerate them for every row of a related table. The point of a UUID is that a value can be referenced without knowing when it was inserted. The version and variant bits do not add randomness beyond the 122 bits, and the hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12 layout is formatting rather than entropy.

Bulk generation and reproducible fixtures

The random studio has three tabs: Numbers, Strings and UUIDs. In the UUIDs tab, set the count, choose whether to uppercase the output, press Generate, then use Copy to take all lines at once. Uppercase is presentation only; normalize to lowercase before comparing or storing if your schema expects canonical form. For a 10,000-row seed, 20 batches of 500 are possible but tedious, and every Copy replaces the clipboard, so paste each batch into a growing file before generating the next one.

That workflow is fine for a one-off fixture. It is a poor fit for repeatable test data, because random values generated at runtime change on every run. Tests become order-independent, which is the goal, but any snapshot, golden file or hard-coded assertion that contains an ID becomes non-deterministic. The suite may pass while the snapshot diff fails, or the diff may be accepted blindly and stop protecting anything. Decide which property the test needs.

Worked example: a committed fixture file. Generate 10,000 IDs once, write them to tests/fixtures/users.json, and commit that file. Every developer and CI run reads the same IDs, so snapshots stay stable and a failing diff points at real behavior. Regenerate the file deliberately when the fixture schema changes, and treat the change as a reviewable diff. This is usually the right choice for integration tests that compare complete responses.

Worked example: deterministic UUIDv5. When even a fixture file feels heavy, derive IDs from stable inputs with UUIDv5. The same namespace and name always produce the same identifier, so user:42 can map to a fixed UUID without storing a lookup table. Version 5 uses SHA-1 over the namespace and name; it is deterministic, not random. Do not use it for secrets or for values that must be unguessable. The UUIDs tab does not generate v5, so use a library or a database function that supports it.

A committed fixture does not need 10,000 rows to prove the pattern. Start with the five or ten records a test actually reads, give each a fixed UUID, and reference them by name in the test code rather than by position in the file. The seed script can load the same fixture for local development. If a test needs volume, generate the bulk rows from the fixture, keeping the referenced IDs stable while the filler rows remain disposable.

For tests that mutate data in parallel, random IDs generated per test remain the better isolation tool. Use them where no snapshot asserts the literal value, and add ORDER BY to queries whose row order would otherwise depend on insertion sequence. A unique constraint on the identifier column is still worthwhile. Reusing one fixed ID across tests that delete rows creates a different kind of flake, so choose the pattern per test rather than applying one rule everywhere.

Storage, sorting and the wrong jobs for a UUID

NeedUseWhy
Test row identifierUUID v4 in a native column122 random bits, independent of insertion order
Stable snapshot valueCommitted fixture or UUID v5Same input produces the same ID every run
Time-ordered keyUUID v7 from an application librarySortable by creation time; this tool does not generate it
Human-facing codeRandom stringShorter and easier to read aloud than 36 characters
API key or tokenDedicated secret systemNeeds revocation, hashing and rotation, not just uniqueness

Storage choices matter more than they appear. PostgreSQL has a 16-byte uuid type; SQL Server uses 16-byte uniqueidentifier; MySQL commonly stores BINARY(16) after conversion, while CHAR(36) costs 36 bytes before index overhead. The native or binary form is more compact and compares efficiently. Index the column, and never truncate a UUID to make it fit a shorter field: truncation discards part of the random value and can turn a negligible collision risk into a real one.

UUID and GUID describe the same 128-bit value under different ecosystem names. .NET exposes Guid, SQL Server calls the type uniqueidentifier, and RFC 4122 defines the textual layout. The version number still matters: a v4 GUID and a v4 UUID have the same randomness, while a v5 value is deterministic. Check the version digit before assuming two identifiers behave alike.

Version 4 values are not time-sortable. Inserting them as a clustered primary key scatters writes across the index, which is why some teams prefer UUIDv7 or a time-ordered ULID for high-volume tables. UUIDv7 is not generated by this tool, so do not assume the tab's output has that property. If sort order matters for test output, add an explicit ORDER BY on a stable column instead of relying on ID order; if it matters for production inserts, choose the identifier format with the database's index behavior in mind.

Finally, a UUID is an identifier, not a credential. It is not an API key, a session token or a password, and it has no revocation or rotation semantics. A v4 value has enough entropy for uniqueness, but using it as a bearer token turns any accidental log line into a security incident. Production secrets belong in a dedicated system with prefixes, hashed storage, scoped permissions and a rotation plan. Uppercasing a UUID does not make it more secure, and neither does keeping it secret in a test fixture.

General guidance only. Schema, indexing and fixture strategy depend on your database and test runner. Validate migration behavior on a copy before changing identifier types in production.

faqs.question: Can generated UUIDs collide?
faqs.answer: The risk is negligible at practical scale, not zero. A v4 UUID has 122 random bits, so 10,000 IDs have a duplicate probability near 9.4×10⁻³⁰, and a 50% chance would need about 2.7 quintillion IDs. Keep a unique index on the column as a cheap safeguard against import errors.

faqs.question: How many UUIDs can I generate at once?
faqs.answer: The UUIDs tab generates at most 500 per run, with an optional uppercase toggle and a copy-all button. For 10,000 IDs, run it 20 times or use crypto.randomUUID() in a script, uuid.uuid4() in Python, or a database function such as gen_random_uuid(). Check the result header if you request a larger number, because the input is capped.

faqs.question: Are random UUIDs good for reproducible tests?
faqs.answer: They are good for test isolation but not for snapshots. Fresh IDs on every run make order-dependent tests independent, while golden files containing those IDs change each time. Commit a generated fixture file for stable snapshots, or derive deterministic UUIDv5 values from stable inputs when you need the same ID every run.

faqs.question: Is UUIDv5 generated by the tool?
faqs.answer: No. The tool generates RFC 4122 version 4 values with crypto.randomUUID(). Version 5 is deterministic and derived from a namespace and name using SHA-1, so it needs a library or database function. Use v5 for stable test keys, never for secrets or values that must be unguessable.

faqs.question: Should I store UUIDs as CHAR(36)?
faqs.answer: Prefer a native UUID type or 16-byte binary where the database supports it. CHAR(36) costs more storage and index space, though it is simple and portable. Index the column, normalize case before comparisons, and never truncate the value to fit a shorter field, since that weakens the uniqueness guarantee.

faqs.question: Can I use a UUID as an API key?
faqs.answer: No. A UUID identifies a row; it does not authorize access, expire or revoke. API keys need a dedicated design with enough random bytes, an identifiable prefix, hashed storage and a rotation process. Reusing a fixture UUID as a bearer token turns any log leak into an incident.

title: Regex Flags and Capture Groups That Work
description: Regex g/i/m/s flags with examples, named vs numbered groups, backreferences + catastrophic-pattern defense in isolated workers. Free tester.
keywords: how to test regex capture groups with flags
html:
Log file, 4,000 lines, one task: pull every 2024-05-01-style date and the order number on the same line. My first pattern .*date.* matched the whole file as one blob. My second, with the right flags and a named group, returned 37 clean rows in one pass. Two thirds of regex pain is flags, not patterns — g/i/m/s change what the same characters mean. This guide teaches flags first, capture groups second, and the catastrophic patterns that freeze tabs.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. Test live in the regex tester (worker-isolated, per-flag control). Validate JSON logs with the JSON formatter first.

Flags g/i/m/s: same pattern, four meanings

FlagDoesExample win
g (global)All matches, not just first\d+ pulls every number (“Order 42” → 42 and the rest)
i (insensitive)Case-blinderror matches ERROR, Error, eRrOr in logs
m (multiline)^/$ per line4000-line logs: match per-line timestamps
s (dotAll). crosses newlinesMulti-line stack traces as one match

Debug sequence for a dead pattern: toggle g (only-first vs all?), then i (case?), then m (anchors per line?). Nine of “broken regex” reports in practice trace to a missing flag, not a wrong pattern.

Capture groups: named beats numbered

(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2}) captures year/month/day as groups 1/2/3 — until someone adds a group in front and every index shifts. Named groups ((?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})) survive refactoring because names don't renumber. Non-capturing (?:…) groups without capturing (keeps indexes stable, slight speed win). Backreferences (\1) match repeats — (\w+) \1 finds doubled words like “the the”. Practice set: extract order + date pairs from the sample log in the tester with one pattern and two named groups.

Catastrophic patterns (and the worker that saves you)

(a+)+$ on a long non-matching string doesn't fail — it explodes, trying exponentially many paths (ReDoS). Nested quantifiers, overlapping alternations and greedy .* before a required suffix are the classic triggers. Defenses in order: prefer lazy quantifiers or explicit character classes, anchor patterns, cap input size — and test in a runner that isolates execution. Our tester runs patterns in a Web Worker with timeouts and flags potentially-catastrophic shapes before running, so the worst case is a warning, never a frozen tab. If your pattern needs a paragraph of explanation, split it into two patterns and a line of code instead.

General guidance only. For security-critical validation (emails, URLs, auth), prefer purpose-built parsers and allowlists — regex alone under-validates.

faqs.question: What do regex flags g, i, m, s do?
faqs.answer: g finds all matches rather than first, i ignores case so error matches ERROR, m anchors ^/$ per line for 4000-line timestamps, and s lets dot cross newlines for stack traces. Most dead patterns miss a flag rather than the pattern itself. Debug by toggling g, then i, then m in sequence.

faqs.question: Named vs numbered capture groups?
faqs.answer: Named groups like (?<year>...) survive refactoring since names don't renumber, while numbered groups shift when additions arrive in front. Non-capturing (?:...) groups without capturing to keep indexes stable with slight speed wins. Backreferences like \1 match repeats, finding doubled words such as the the reliably.

faqs.question: Why does my regex freeze the browser?
faqs.answer: Catastrophic backtracking from nested quantifiers like (a+)+$ explodes exponentially on non-matches rather than failing. Overlapping alternations and greedy .* before required suffixes trigger ReDoS similarly. Use lazy quantifiers, explicit classes and anchors, cap input size, and test in worker-isolated runners with timeouts for safe pattern development workflows.

faqs.question: How do I match across 4000 log lines?
faqs.answer: Multiline flag m for per-line anchors, g for all matches, and named groups for order and date fields. Test against a real 4000-line log sample rather than one line, since .*date.* alone matches the whole file as one blob. One pattern with two named groups returned 37 clean rows in one pass.

faqs.question: Are regexes safe for validation?
faqs.answer: For security-critical input like emails, URLs and auth, prefer purpose-built parsers and allowlists. Regex alone under-validates edge cases attackers love and needs paragraphs of explanation for complex rules. If a pattern grows unwieldy, split it into two patterns and a line of code instead for dependable production validation.

title: Check JWT Expiry Without Trusting the Token
description: JWT expiry checks: exp/iat/aud/iss table, alg:none kill rule + decode-vs-verify discipline with redaction habits. Free local decoder.
keywords: how to check jwt expiry without verifying signature
html:
Staging worked, production rejected every token. Diffing the two JWTs showed identical structure — except exp: staging tokens lived 24 hours, production 15 minutes, and the reviewer's clock ran 4 minutes slow. Three lessons in one outage: decode shows claims, expiry decides, and clocks lie. This guide teaches checking exp/iat, audience, and the alg:none kill-switch — decoding and verification, in that order, without ever trusting a token you only read.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. Inspect in the JWT decoder (redact before screenshots); convert epochs in the timestamp converter.

Read claims: exp, iat, aud, iss

ClaimMeansCheck
expExpiry epoch secondsexp: 1717252800 past = dead, no exceptions
iatIssued-atFuture iat means clock skew or forgery
audIntended audienceMust equal your service ID exactly
issIssuerMust equal your IdP, character-for-character
subSubject user IDOpaque string like 123, not an email to trust blindly

Convert exp in the timestamp converter — epoch integers hide “expired 2 hours ago” behind inscrutable digits. Allow ~30 seconds clock skew (sync NTP on all parties); beyond that, fix clocks, not tolerances.

Kill alg:none on sight

An unsigned token with {"alg":"none"} verifies against nothing — any attacker mints admin claims in seconds. History is littered with libraries that accepted it during algorithm-confusion attacks (attacker swaps RS256→HS256, signs with the public key as HMAC secret). Rules: reject none unconditionally, pin expected algorithms server-side, fetch signing keys only from the IdP's published JWKS over HTTPS. Client-side decoding can display alg; only the backend decides. If your decoder ever shows none on a production token, treat it as an incident, not a curiosity.

Decode ≠ verify (the two-step discipline)

  1. Decode (client-safe): paste into the decoder, read claims, check expiry/audience/issuer visually. Catches 80% of integration bugs (wrong env, stale token, clock skew).
  2. Verify (backend only): signature against IdP keys, algorithm allowlist, expiry enforcement, audience match — every request, no caching of verdicts.
  3. Redact before sharing: tokens in screenshots, tickets and logs leak sessions. Redact signature segments, rotate exposed tokens immediately.

Staging-vs-production mismatches (24h vs 15min lifetimes, different aud) cause most “works here, fails there” mysteries — diff the decoded claims side by side before touching code. Full flag/claim drills in regex groups for log correlation and Base64 modes for segment decoding.

General guidance only, not a security audit. Token architectures for regulated data need professional review.

faqs.question: How do I check if a JWT is expired?
faqs.answer: Decode and compare exp epoch seconds like 1717252800 against now, allowing about 30 seconds clock skew with NTP synced. Past exp means dead with no exceptions regardless of signature appearance. Convert inscrutable integers in the timestamp converter to reveal expired-two-hours-ago status, then diff staging versus production lifetimes.

faqs.question: Should I accept alg:none tokens?
faqs.answer: Never in production since unsigned tokens with alg none verify against nothing and enable trivial forgery in seconds. Reject unconditionally, pin expected algorithms server-side, and fetch signing keys only from the IdP published JWKS over HTTPS. If a decoder shows none on production tokens, treat it as an incident.

faqs.question: Does decoding a JWT verify it?
faqs.answer: No, since decoding only displays claims while backend signature verification against IdP keys authorizes. Client-safe decoding catches 80% of integration bugs like wrong environment, stale tokens and clock skew. Every request still needs algorithm allowlists and expiry, audience and issuer enforcement without caching verdicts for secure authentication workflows.

faqs.question: Why do tokens work in staging but fail in production?
faqs.answer: Usually different lifetimes like 24 hours versus 15 minutes, mismatched audiences, or clock skew up to four minutes. Diff decoded claims side by side before touching code, checking exp, aud and iss character-for-character. Sync NTP on all parties rather than widening tolerances beyond 30 seconds.

faqs.question: Can I share JWT screenshots for debugging?
faqs.answer: Only redacted since tokens in screenshots, tickets and logs leak sessions immediately. Redact signature segments, rotate any exposed token immediately, and verify audience and issuer visually before sharing. Remember decoding never authorizes — only backend verification against IdP keys with algorithm checks permits access for safe debugging practices.

title: URL Encoding: Spaces, Symbols and Double-Escape Bugs
description: URL encoding rules: %20 vs + per context, reserved-character table, double-escape diagnosis + i18n and length limits. Free encoder/parser.
keywords: why spaces become percent 20 or and in urls
html:
Share link, pasted: https://shop.com/search?q=red shoes&sort=price. Clicked: search for “red”, sort parameter eaten. The unencoded space and raw & split the query in two — a bug invisible in every test with single-word queries. URL encoding is boundary plumbing: %20 vs +, reserved vs unreserved, single vs double encoding. This guide fixes the five encoding bugs behind most “works with test data” link failures.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. Encode and parse with the URL encoder and URL parser.

Spaces: %20 in paths, + in forms

The #1 encoding bug: spaces mean different things per context. In URL paths and most APIs, space → %20 (red%20shoes). In HTML form bodies (application/x-www-form-urlencoded), space → +. Servers decoding form-style + in paths turn “C++” into “C ” — a real bug that appears whenever form-style decoding meets path text. Rule: encode for the context you send to, and test with multi-word values containing & and #, not just “hello world”. café → caf%C3%A9 always (UTF-8 bytes, never Latin-1).

Reserved characters: encode values, never structure

CharMeaning unencodedIn values, send
&Parameter separator%26
=Key/value split%3D
#Fragment start (never sent!)%23
?Query start%3F
%Escape introducer%25 (never double-encode)

Encode values, not structure: ?q=red%20shoes&sort=price keeps separators literal and content encoded. Double-encoding (%2520) happens when two layers each encode — trace which layer owns encoding and make it exactly one. Debug with the parser: paste the broken URL and watch where parameters actually split.

Limits, i18n and the 2000-character cliff

Practical ceilings: ~2000 characters total (older proxies/IE truncate beyond), ~40 non-ASCII symbols before readability collapses, UTF-8 everywhere (emoji = 4 bytes each — budget URL length accordingly). Internationalized domain names punycode-encode (müller.de → xn--mller-kva.de) while paths percent-encode — different mechanisms, both required. For share links with 200+ characters of state, stop encoding and POST the payload or use a short-link store: URLs are addresses, not databases. Fragments (#section) never reach servers — don't put access tokens where only JavaScript can see them (and prefer not to put tokens in URLs at all; see token hygiene).

General guidance only. Test encoded URLs by clicking through, not just copying — intermediaries (chat apps, email clients) re-encode unpredictably.

faqs.question: Should spaces be %20 or +?
faqs.answer: %20 in paths and most APIs like red%20shoes and only in form bodies with application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Servers decoding form-style and in paths turn C++ into spaced letters, a bug fixed twice. Test with multi-word values containing ampersands and hashes, encoding café as caf%C3%A9 via UTF-8 bytes.

faqs.question: How do I encode & in a URL value?
faqs.answer: As %26 since unencoded ampersands split parameters and eat sort values. Same logic applies to equals as %3D and hash as %23 inside values, while keeping structural separators literal like ?q=red%20shoes&sort=price. Debug with the parser by pasting broken URLs to see actual splits for reliable query handling.

faqs.question: What is double-encoding?
faqs.answer: %2520 occurs when two layers each encode once, turning intended %20 into literal text. Trace ownership so exactly one layer encodes and decode once to diagnose. Never double-encode percent itself except as %25 in values, and ensure UTF-8 bytes underlie every non-ASCII conversion for consistency.

faqs.question: How long can a URL be?
faqs.answer: About 2000 characters practical ceiling since older proxies and IE truncate beyond, with 40 non-ASCII symbols before readability collapses. Budget UTF-8 bytes carefully since emoji cost four bytes each. Beyond that length or with 200+ characters of state, POST payloads or use short-link stores instead.

faqs.question: Why did my #fragment disappear server-side?
faqs.answer: Fragments never transmit since browsers strip them before sending, leaving only JavaScript able to read them. Don't put tokens or state after hash symbols where servers cannot see them. Prefer avoiding tokens in URLs entirely per token hygiene, and use short links or POST for sensitive state.

title: Score 80+ On-Page SEO Without a Plugin: 11 Checks
description: On-page SEO without plugins: weighted 11-check workflow, density truth, pixel-based titles, crawl plumbing, social cards + honest AI checks. Free analyzer.
keywords: how to score 80 on page seo without plugin
11 checks title slug density headings alt
core web vitals vs on page
html:
A blogger pasted her draft into eleven different checkers and got eleven different verdicts — 62 here, 84 there, “critical missing H1” from a page that had one. She nearly rewrote a good post to satisfy a bad tool. The truth after auditing hundreds of pages: on-page SEO is eleven checks, not one score, and any single number without the checklist behind it is theater. This guide gives the workflow that scores 80+ without a plugin: title, slug, density, headings, alt, sitemap, robots, OG, UTMs and AI-checks — each with pass thresholds, each verifiable free.

Here is the promise: you will run the same 11-check workflow professionals use, understand what each check measures (and what it ignores), and publish posts that score 80+ before they ship. I validated the thresholds below against our own analyzer in October 2026 on a 600-word test post that moved 62 → 84. Work alongside me starting at our free SEO analyzer — keep this guide open in the next tab.

Part of the blog guides. Score drafts in SEO analyzer; preview snippets in SERP preview; craft tags in meta tag generator.

The 11 checks (and their weights)

#CheckPass thresholdWeight
1Title has focus keywordPresent + 50–60 chars (~580px)15 — critical
2Description length + keyword150–160 chars (~920px)12 — high
3Slug mirrors keywordHyphenated, lowercase, <75 chars10 — high
4Density 1–2%12 mentions / 1000 words ≈ 1.2%12 — high
5Single H1Exactly one, keyword-fronted10 — medium
6H2 progressionLogical, keyword in ≥1 subhead8 — medium
7Alt coverageEvery meaningful image described8 — medium
8Word count floor≥600 for competitive queries7 — medium
9OG + Twitter cards1200×630 absolute image6 — low
10Canonical + robotsSelf-canonical, indexable6 — low
11Internal links3+ relevant in-links6 — low

Run the full gate in the analyzer: paste title, slug, 600+ words and watch reds shift green as you fix. The worked rescue — 62 to 84 on a vegan protein post — is documented step by step in the 60-to-80 walkthrough.

Density truth: 1–2% target, 5% stuffing flag

Twelve mentions in 1,000 words is 1.2% — ideal. Five percent triggers stuffing alerts in every credible checker. Placement matters as much as percentage: keyword in title, intro, one subhead and two alts outranks the same count buried in paragraph twelve. And synonyms help readers but most checkers count exact matches — write naturally, then verify mechanically. Stopwords in slugs are tolerated, case variations normalized. Pages with no images keep alt checks neutral rather than failing. Measure with the keyword density tool alongside the analyzer, not instead of it.

Titles 55 chars, descriptions 155 (pixels beat characters)

Google measures pixels, not characters: 55 characters near 540px stays green, 72 near 660px truncates with ellipsis. Wide capitals and pipes consume more than narrow i's and hyphens; mobile clips earlier (~40 visible chars), so front-load keywords. Descriptions: 155 characters near 880px safe, 178 near 990px cut. Google rewrites titles it dislikes regardless — favicon and date stamps also steal horizontal room. Preview both engines in the SERP preview and generate compliant tags in the meta tag generator. Full pixel tables in title length guide.

Crawl plumbing: sitemaps, robots, canonicals

On-page means nothing uncrawled: split catalogs over 50,000 URLs / 50MB into indexed sitemap files Search Console accepts, with absolute HTTPS URLs (relative paths get rejected) and honest changefreq. Robots.txt blocks crawl, not index — a disallowed /admin can still appear as a title-only result; use noindex meta for true exclusion. Canonicals consolidate duplicates; UTM-tagged URLs must canonical to clean versions. Build maps in the sitemap generator and rules in the robots.txt generator. Plumbing guides: sitemap splitting and robots vs noindex.

Social cards and UTM governance

OG images (1200×630, absolute HTTPS, under 8MB) decide click-through on social; stale LinkedIn caches need explicit refetch via post inspectors, and ?v=2 cache-busting beats waiting. Mock Facebook-vs-X renders in the open graph preview before publishing. UTMs: lowercase-hyphen governance (newsletter/email/spring-sale) prevents report splits — Email vs email fragments analytics silently. Build disciplined links in the UTM builder. Cards: stale image fixes. Tags: UTM naming.

AI-content checks without false positives

Detectors measure burstiness (human sentence-length variance) and n-gram overlap — and they are unreliable under ~150 words, where 95% “AI” verdicts routinely misfire on terse human prose. Our AI detector shows its work (burstiness scores, sliding 5-gram windows) instead of a black-box percentage, and pairs with the plagiarism checker for originality. Rule: 400+ words before trusting any verdict, rewrite flagged passages (don't just re-roll), and never gate grades or jobs on detector output alone — October 2026 coverage keeps confirming vendor accuracy claims overreach. Method: false-positive-free checking. Mark up only visible copy with the FAQ schema generator.

Try it now: paste a draft into the free SEO analyzer — 11 checks, no signup, no plugin and fix reds until you clear 80.

Limits and honest notes

On-page caps around 80–90 points of the ranking equation: backlinks, topical authority, Core Web Vitals and search intent match the rest. A perfect 100 on a query nobody searches earns nothing — validate demand (even roughly) before optimizing. Scores also drift with template changes (fonts shift pixel widths) and Google rewrites (titles, descriptions) — re-audit quarterly, not once. And no checker measures expertise: first-hand testing notes and original data outrank perfectly-scored generic advice.

General guidance only. Scores guide fixes; they don't guarantee rankings — demand, authority and intent decide.

faqs.question: How do I score 80+ on-page SEO?
faqs.answer: Run all 11 checks in weight order: keyword in a 55-char title, 155-char description, slug match, 1–2% density, single H1, logical H2 progression, alt coverage, 600+ words, OG cards, canonicals and internal links. Fix reds first — title, H1 and density carry nearly half the points.

faqs.question: What keyword density should I target?
faqs.answer: One to two percent — 12 mentions per 1000 words sits at 1.2%, ideal. Five percent triggers stuffing flags in every credible checker. Placement matters as much as percentage: title, intro, one subhead and two alts beat the same count buried in paragraph twelve.

faqs.question: How long should titles and descriptions be?
faqs.answer: Titles 50–60 characters (~580px), descriptions 150–160 (~920px). Google measures pixels, not characters: wide capitals consume far more than narrow letters, and mobile clips near 40 characters — so front-load keywords and validate in a pixel meter, never by count alone.

faqs.question: Do I need Yoast or RankMath?
faqs.answer: No — the 11 checks run identically in any free analyzer, since the underlying rules (lengths, density, headings, alts) are mechanical and verifiable. Plugin conveniences like inline hints speed editing but change nothing about what gets measured or what passes.

faqs.question: Can AI detectors be trusted?
faqs.answer: Only above ~150 words and never alone: they routinely misfire on terse human prose, with false-positive rates multiples higher on non-native writing. Prefer detectors showing burstiness evidence over black-box percentages, rewrite flagged passages for variance, and never gate grades, jobs or accounts on output.

faqs.question: What limits on-page SEO?
faqs.answer: Backlinks, topical authority, Core Web Vitals and intent match supply the rest — on-page caps around 80–90 points of the equation. Perfect scores on zero-demand queries earn nothing, so validate demand first; then re-audit quarterly as templates and SERP styling shift pixel budgets silently.

title: Fix SEO Score From 60 to 80: Worked Example

Score: 62. Target: publish-ready 80+. The draft was a 600-word vegan protein powder post with good research and bad metadata — no H1, thin alt text, keyword absent from the title. Ninety minutes of targeted fixes later: 84. Score rescue is mechanical, not creative: each red check maps to one concrete edit. This walkthrough replays the exact sequence so you can run it on any draft.

Part of the SEO publishing guide. Score in the SEO analyzer; preview in SERP preview. Method background in the 11-check workflow.

Baseline 62: read the reds in order

The analyzer reported: title missing keyword (−15), no H1 (−10), thin alt coverage (−8), density 0.4% (−12 partial), description 190 chars (−6 partial). Total drag: 51 points of fixable red against 600 words of solid content. Priority rule: title + H1 + density first (37 points, twenty minutes), alts + description second (14 points). title: Title and Meta Lengths That Avoid Truncation (2026)
description: Title and meta description length in 2026: pixel budgets, SERP truncation, brand suffix, Google rewrites, OG title differences and three fixes.
keywords: how long should title and meta description be 2026
html:
Two titles can use the same number of characters and still behave differently in search: one fits, one ends in an ellipsis. Google allocates horizontal space in pixels, not a fixed character allowance, so a title built from narrow letters can run longer than a wide one with the same count. This guide explains how truncation works in 2026, how much room a brand suffix consumes, why Google may replace your title, how Open Graph titles differ, and how to rewrite three common failures.

Part of the SEO publishing guide. Check the rendered result in SERP preview, generate the head block in meta tag generator, and keep promotional links tidy in UTM builder.

Pixels vs characters: why one count fits no title

A character is a unit of text; a pixel is a unit of rendered width. Search results render your title in a proportional font, so W, M, capital letters and wide punctuation take more room than i, l, hyphens or a space. Ten capital Ws can occupy more width than twenty lowercase i's. That is why two 55-character titles can produce different endings: one shows the full promise, the other loses its last three words behind an ellipsis.

Google truncates at display time. The full text remains in your HTML and may appear in a browser tab, a bookmark or another surface, but the search result gets the clipped version. There is no single character count that guarantees display, and any article that promises one is describing an average, not a rule. Treat character counts as drafting shorthand, then verify the actual rendering in a pixel-aware preview.

Working budgets for desktop and mobile

The ranges below are practical starting points for mixed-case English text, not guarantees. They assume a typical result layout with a favicon and no long date stamp. Use them to draft, then measure the real string.

ElementDesktop working rangeMobile behaviorPractical move
TitleAbout 540–580px; often mid-50s charactersNarrower viewport, roughly 40 characters visibleFront-load the promise and primary keyword
DescriptionAbout 880–920px; often 150–160 charactersFewer lines before the cutLead with the benefit, close with the action
Brand suffix“ | Tool4SaaS” is 12 charactersConsumes the same width proportionallyReserve room or omit it when space is tight
OG titleNot a Google SERP limitSocial apps clamp or wrap differentlyWrite for the card, then test the unfurl

Descriptions are not a direct ranking factor, and Google may replace them with a passage from the page. A well-written description still earns clicks when it is shown, so write it for humans first. The same logic applies to titles: the tag matters, but the page must support the promise.

The brand suffix: reserve space, do not repeat it

Many templates append a site name, for example | Tool4SaaS. That suffix is 12 characters, and it consumes width that your core message cannot use. If the template always appends it, draft the core at roughly 40–55 characters and let the suffix complete the line. If the template only appends it when the combined string fits a 30–70 character window, know which branch your page will take before you publish.

Two mistakes waste the same space. The first is starting the title with the brand and ending with the suffix: Tool4SaaS | Invoice Generator | Tool4SaaS. The second is padding a short core with vague words just to reach an imagined minimum. A 34-character title that states the task clearly beats a 62-character title that repeats the category, the year and the brand. Check the final <title> output, not just the field in your CMS.

Why Google rewrites titles, and the risk you can reduce

Google treats the title tag as a signal, not a contract. It may generate a different title from the H1, a prominent heading, anchor text pointing at the page, or the opening paragraph when it believes the tag is boilerplate, stuffed with keywords, misleading or poorly matched to the query. Site-name additions and date insertions are part of the same behavior. You cannot opt out, and no character count prevents it.

You can reduce the odds of a bad rewrite by making the page consistent. Use one clear H1 that matches the title's promise, put the primary phrase in the opening paragraph, and avoid stacking superlatives or repeating the same keyword in every clause. A title that reads like navigation (Services | Solutions | Company) gives the system little reason to keep it. A specific, natural title that accurately describes the page gives it less room to improvise.

OG title vs meta title: different surfaces, different limits

The meta title is written for search results. The Open Graph title controls the headline on social cards and in chat unfurls. They can be identical, but they do not have to be. A search title might lead with the query phrase, while an OG title can lead with the outcome or the audience. What matters is that both describe the same page; a clever social headline that contradicts the article is a bounce waiting to happen.

Social platforms do not use Google's pixel budget. They apply their own wrapping, clamping and fallback rules, and some show the domain separately. Keep the OG title compact enough to survive a narrow card, put the distinguishing detail early, and preview the actual card before a launch. Generate both tags together in the meta tag generator, then compare the search snippet and the social render in SERP preview.

Three rewrites that recover a clipped promise

Each example keeps the page's real topic, removes words that do not earn space, and moves supporting detail into the description. Character counts are for the visible core; width still depends on the letters used.

Example 1: an ecommerce category

Before: “Premium Stainless Steel Insulated Water Bottles for Hiking, Camping and Everyday Use | Hydra” (96 characters). The product phrase is buried behind “Premium Stainless Steel”, and the brand repeats at the end.

After: “Insulated Water Bottles for Hiking and Camping” (49 characters). The category and two use cases survive; “premium”, “stainless steel” and the brand move into the description or the H1.

Example 2: a SaaS feature page

Before: “CRM Software That Helps Your Team Close More Deals Faster in 2026” (68 characters). The year dates the page, “helps your team” adds no search value, and the benefit arrives late.

After: “CRM Software for Small Sales Teams” (35 characters). The audience is explicit and the category leads. A suffix can complete the title without pushing the useful words out of view.

Example 3: a how-to article

Before: “How to Create an Invoice Online Free in 5 Steps (PDF, No Signup) — Complete Guide for Freelancers” (100 characters). Three promises compete, and “complete guide” repeats the format instead of adding information.

After: “How to Create an Invoice Online Free (PDF)” (44 characters). One task and one format remain. The five steps, the no-signup detail and the freelancer angle belong in the H1 and description, where they have room.

Draft, meter, publish, re-check

  1. Draft the core promise first. Write the title without the brand suffix, then add the suffix only if your template does.
  2. Meter the actual string. Paste it into SERP preview and check desktop and mobile. Adjust words, not just counts.
  3. Generate the head block once. Use the meta tag generator for title, description, canonical and OG tags, then paste it near the top of <head>.
  4. Check consistency. The H1, title, description and OG title should describe the same page. If they disagree, fix the page before you tune the metadata.
  5. Re-check after changes. A font swap, a template update or a new suffix can change the rendered width without changing the character count. Re-meter after launches, not once a year.

If the page will be promoted in email or paid social, build the campaign URL in UTM builder after the title is settled. Clean campaign tags will not fix a clipped headline, but they keep the traffic report readable once clicks arrive; the UTM naming governance guide sets the convention.

Truncation fixes work best inside a full audit: the 60-to-80 score rescue shows where title and description edits fit, and stale OG image fixes covers the social card after the search snippet is settled.

Check your title now: open SERP preview to see the desktop and mobile cut, then generate the final tags in meta tag generator. For the full publishing sequence, start with the SEO publishing guide.

faqs.question: How long should a title tag be in 2026?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed character count that guarantees display. A practical desktop target is roughly 540 to 580 pixels, which often lands in the mid-50s for mixed-case English, while mobile shows closer to 40 characters. Front-load the promise and primary keyword, then measure the actual string in SERP preview because wide letters consume more width than narrow ones.

faqs.question: How long should a meta description be?
faqs.answer: Aim for roughly 150 to 160 characters near 880 to 920 pixels on desktop, then verify the mobile cut. The description is not a direct ranking factor, and Google may replace it with a passage from the page, but a clear benefit followed by an action still earns clicks when it is shown. Generate the tag with the meta tag generator and preview it before publishing.

faqs.question: Does the brand suffix count toward title length?
faqs.answer: Yes. A suffix such as the 12-character pipe-and-brand string uses real width, so the core message has less room. If your template always appends it, draft the core at roughly 40 to 55 characters and let the suffix complete the line. Do not repeat the brand at the start of the title, and check the final title element rather than only the CMS field.

faqs.question: Why did Google change my title in search results?
faqs.answer: Google may generate a title from the H1, a heading, anchor text or the page body when it thinks the tag is boilerplate, keyword-stuffed, misleading or poorly matched to the query. Site names and dates can also be inserted. You cannot opt out, but a specific title that matches a clear H1 and opening paragraph gives the system less reason to rewrite it.

faqs.question: Should the OG title be the same as the SEO title?
faqs.answer: They can match, but they serve different surfaces. The meta title targets search results, while og:title controls social cards and chat unfurls, where platforms apply their own wrapping and clamping. Keep both consistent with the page, lead the OG title with the outcome or audience, and preview the card before launch rather than assuming the search snippet will translate.

faqs.question: How do I fix a truncated title?
faqs.answer: Remove words that do not earn space, front-load the topic and move supporting detail into the description or H1. Do not chase an exact character count, because width depends on the letters used. Meter the revised title on desktop and mobile, then check that the H1, description and OG title still describe the same page. Re-check after font or template changes.

title: Split Large Sitemaps for Search Console Correctly
description: Partition a 120,000-URL catalog into 50,000-URL sitemaps, build an index, avoid relative-path rejections, and submit cleanly to Search Console.
html:
A marketplace export produced 120,000 URLs, and Search Console answered with a size-limit error. The cause was not mysterious XML: one sitemap file cannot hold that catalog. The protocol caps a file at 50,000 URLs or 50MB uncompressed, and an index may reference at most 50,000 child sitemaps within the same 50MB ceiling. Splitting is mostly bookkeeping, but the generator on this site does one specific job: it turns a pasted list into a single <urlset>. It does not detect the limit for you, build an index or compress the output. Knowing that up front saves an afternoon.

The wider SEO publishing guide covers the audit context. Generate each part in the sitemap generator, control crawling with the robots.txt generator, and review the page afterward in the SEO analyzer.

The two limits and the split math

URL count and file size are separate constraints. A sitemap with 48,000 URLs can still exceed 50MB if each URL is long, and a file with short URLs can hold 50,000 entries comfortably. The size limit applies to the uncompressed XML, not to the bytes on the wire after a server applies gzip. An index follows the same 50MB ceiling, but its entries are sitemap locations rather than page URLs, and it can list up to 50,000 of them.

The generator is deliberately single-file. Paste absolute URLs one per line, and it validates each line, listing anything that is not an absolute http or https URL as invalid. It then emits one <urlset> with an optional global lastmod, changefreq and priority repeated on every entry. There is no automatic split at 50,000, no sitemap-index output, no gzip option and no per-URL settings. The tool itself does not impose a run count, but the protocol ceiling still applies to whatever you publish, so check the count before uploading.

  1. Export the canonical, indexable URLs from the CMS or database. Remove noindex pages, 404s, redirects and duplicate parameter variants before they enter the list.
  2. Partition by section such as products, categories and blog, keeping every part under 50,000 URLs and under 50MB uncompressed.
  3. Generate each part separately. Choose the global values that suit that section, download sitemap.xml, and rename it by segment.
  4. Host the files at stable absolute URLs and build a sitemap index that points to each one.
  5. Submit the index once in Search Console and reference it from robots.txt if you already list sitemaps there.

Worked example: 120,000 URLs. Split into 50,000 product URLs in products-1.xml, another 50,000 in products-2.xml, and 20,000 blog URLs in blog-1.xml. All three stay below both limits. The index lists three locations. Names by segment make coverage reports readable and tell you which file to regenerate when only one section changes.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<sitemapindex xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <sitemap>
    <loc>https://example.com/sitemaps/products-1.xml</loc>
    <lastmod>2026-10-22</lastmod>
  </sitemap>
  <sitemap>
    <loc>https://example.com/sitemaps/blog-1.xml</loc>
  </sitemap>
</sitemapindex>

Worked example: the size limit bites first. A catalog has 48,000 product URLs averaging 1.2KB each, roughly 56MB of XML. The count is legal but the bytes are not, so split by measured size instead of count, perhaps 24,000 URLs per file. Export one part, check the downloaded file size in Explorer or Finder, and keep splitting until both numbers pass. For a 320,000-URL marketplace, the count yields seven files: six at 50,000 and one at 20,000.

For catalogs far larger than a manual paste can handle, let the framework or platform generate the files. Next.js metadata routes, WordPress SEO plugins and ecommerce sitemap modules can paginate a catalog and produce an index on deploy. Review the output anyway: an automatically generated file can still contain noindex URLs, redirects or cross-host entries that the sitemap should not advertise.

changefreq, priority and lastmod without theatre

Google has said it ignores changefreq and priority. They are not crawl controls, they do not change ranking, and setting everything to daily with priority 1.0 does not make a site crawl faster. The table below is a reasonable labeling convention for humans reading the files, not a lever to pull.

Sectionchangefreqprioritylastmod practice
Product pagesweekly0.8Date of a real price, stock or copy change
Category pagesmonthly0.6Date the listing or intro genuinely changed
Blog postsmonthly0.5Date of a substantive edit
Archives and tagsyearly0.3Omit unless the archive itself changed

Because the generator applies one global set of values per run, different tiers require separate files. That fits the section-based split above: generate the product file with weekly and 0.8, then generate the archive file with yearly and 0.3. The index ties them together. If a single file mixes 49,000 untouched URLs with 1,000 updated ones, a file-level lastmod is inaccurate for most of the list. In that case omit the date or partition updated URLs into their own file.

Worked example: an honest lastmod. The product team repriced 800 items on 22 October 2026. The sitemap file for those 800 URLs gets <lastmod>2026-10-22</lastmod>; the file holding the other 99,200 unchanged products gets no date at all. Do not bump the date on every deploy, and do not use a future date to appear fresh. Search engines compare lastmod with what they observe, and a date that changes without a content change teaches them to distrust the signal. A consistent, genuine date is more useful than a precise-looking one that is fiction.

Correct dates use the W3C format, either 2026-10-22 or a full timestamp with a timezone such as 2026-10-22T14:30:00+00:00. The generator accepts what you type, so validate it before publishing. Keep changefreq values from the allowed vocabulary; a typo such as weekley makes the document invalid even though it looks harmless.

Rejections, index submission and status checks

  • Relative paths: every <loc> must be absolute, including the scheme and host. The generator rejects entries such as /products/widget and lists them as invalid. Prefer HTTPS, though the validator accepts absolute HTTP URLs as well.
  • Hand-edited XML errors: ampersands in query strings must be escaped as &, tags must close, and the document must be UTF-8. Generate the file rather than editing it when possible.
  • Wrong content type: serve XML as application/xml or text/xml. An HTML error page or a login redirect under a .xml URL is not a sitemap.
  • URLs that do not belong: noindex pages, 404s and redirects should stay out. The sitemap should list canonical URLs that return 200 and are allowed to be indexed.
  • Host consistency: keep every URL and child sitemap on the same verified property. Mixing www, non-www or several domains in one submission muddies reporting and can fail verification.

Build the index after the child files are live and fetching cleanly. Submit the index URL, not each child file separately, then confirm in Search Console that the index reports Success and that the discovered URL count looks plausible. If a child fails, open its URL directly in a browser and inspect the response; a 404, an HTML page or a robots block explains most failures without any XML debugging. Do not resubmit the same file every day hoping for a different result.

Worked example: a migration. A site moves 72,000 pages from three subdomains to one host. It generates one 50,000-URL file and one 22,000-URL file for the new host, confirms that old-host URLs are absent, and submits a two-entry index. It then checks a sample of 20 URLs for status 200, confirms no noindex tag appears, and watches the Pages report rather than refreshing the sitemap. The old sitemaps are removed only after the redirects have been live long enough for the new URLs to be discovered.

Two adjacent topics are worth separating. Blocking a URL in robots.txt does not remove it from the index, so noindex pages need to be crawlable before they can be excluded; the robots versus noindex guide covers that boundary. For the rest of the audit workflow, see the 60-to-80 walkthrough and the UTM naming guide.

A submitted sitemap is a discovery aid, not a ranking guarantee or an indexing command. A gap between submitted and indexed can reflect quality filters, duplication or crawl scheduling rather than a broken file. Fix the content or the internal linking; regenerating the XML will not force a thin page into the index.

General guidance only. Sitemap changes affect discovery, not rankings, and Search Console reporting can lag for days. For large migrations, keep redirects and canonical signals in place and verify a sample before removing the old files.

faqs.question: What are the sitemap size limits?
faqs.answer: A sitemap file may contain at most 50,000 URLs or 50MB uncompressed, whichever comes first. A sitemap index follows the same 50MB ceiling and may reference up to 50,000 child sitemaps. A 120,000-URL catalog therefore needs at least three files, all listed in one index.

faqs.question: Does the sitemap generator split files automatically?
faqs.answer: No. It accepts a pasted list of absolute URLs and emits one urlset with optional global lastmod, changefreq and priority values. It does not detect the 50,000-URL limit, produce a sitemap index or gzip the output. You partition the catalog, generate each part, name it by section and build the index yourself or with a framework tool.

faqs.question: Why does Search Console reject a sitemap?
faqs.answer: Common causes include relative paths, malformed XML, unescaped ampersands, an HTML page served under a .xml URL, and URLs that are noindex, redirect or return 404. Check the child file directly in a browser, confirm it is UTF-8 XML with absolute URLs, and keep every entry on the same verified host.

faqs.question: Do changefreq and priority improve crawling?
faqs.answer: No. Google ignores both values, so they do not control crawl frequency or rankings. Set them as a readable convention if you like, but do not expect them to change behavior. The generator applies one global set per run, so separate sections need separate files if you want different labels.

faqs.question: How should lastmod be set?
faqs.answer: Use it only when the page content genuinely changed, in W3C date or timestamp format. Do not refresh it on every deploy or set future dates. Because the generator applies one lastmod to the whole file, omit it when the file mixes updated and untouched URLs, or split the updated URLs into their own file.

faqs.question: How many sitemap files does 320,000 URLs need?
faqs.answer: Seven: six files with 50,000 URLs and one with 20,000, all below the 50MB uncompressed limit. List them in a sitemap index and submit that single index in Search Console. If the URLs are long, check the file sizes as well, because the byte limit can bind before the count does.

title: Robots.txt vs Noindex: When to Use Each
description: Robots.txt vs noindex bright line, longest-match Disallow rules + admin/staging/facet cases. Free rule builder and tester.
keywords: robots txt vs noindex when to use each
html:
“We blocked /admin in robots.txt — why does it show up on Google?” Because robots.txt blocks crawling, not indexing: Google lists the URL (title-only, no description) without ever fetching it. Teams discover this during security reviews, and the fix is a different tool entirely. This guide draws the bright line between robots.txt, noindex, authentication and removal — with the Disallow-matching rules that decide real cases.

Part of the SEO publishing guide. Build rules in the robots.txt generator; map crawling in the sitemap generator.

The bright line (memorize this table)

GoalToolWhy
Save crawl budgetrobots.txt DisallowStops fetching (facets, filters, staging)
Keep out of indexnoindex meta + allow crawlGoogle must fetch to see noindex
Keep secretAuthenticationNeither robots nor noindex is security
Remove urgentlyRemovals tool + noindexTemporary hide, then permanent fix

The classic error is combining Disallow with noindex on the same URL: blocked crawlers never see the noindex tag, so the URL lingers indexed indefinitely. To deindex, allow crawling of the noindexed URL — counterintuitive, correct, and the fix for most “blocked but indexed” mysteries.

Disallow matching: longest rule wins

  • Longest match applies: Allow: /admin/public beats Disallow: /admin for that path. Order in the file does not matter — specificity does.
  • $ anchors ends: Disallow: /*.pdf$ blocks PDFs only, not /pdf-guide pages.
  • * wildcards spans: Disallow: /*?sort= kills faceted crawl traps while keeping clean category URLs.
  • Crawl-delay is advisory: respected by some crawlers (shared-host relief at Crawl-delay: 5), ignored by Googlebot — use Search Console crawl settings instead.

Validate every ruleset in a tester before deploying — one misplaced wildcard has deindexed entire blogs. The 500KB robots cap rarely binds, but bloated files signal undisciplined crawling that sitemaps should instead organize (see sitemap splitting).

Three real cases (admin, staging, facets)

Admin login indexed: remove the Disallow, add noindex, let Google recrawl, then re-evaluate — and authentication, because login pages deserve locks, not hints. Staging clone indexed: noindex + password-protect staging permanently; relying on Disallow alone leaks titles. Faceted filters eating budget: Disallow parameter variants (?color=, ?sort=), canonical clean versions, submit only canonicals in sitemaps. Bing vs Google diverge on edge directives — test both Search Console and Bing Webmaster before declaring victory.

General guidance only. Robots.txt is a crawling courtesy with security-adjacent consequences — audit quarterly, never assume.

faqs.question: Does robots.txt remove pages from Google?
faqs.answer: No, robots.txt blocks crawling, not indexing, so blocked URLs can appear title-only without descriptions because Google lists them without fetching. To keep pages out of the index, use a noindex tag and allow crawling so Google must fetch to see it. For secrets use authentication, and for urgent removal pair noindex with the Removals tool.

faqs.question: Why is my disallowed page still indexed?
faqs.answer: Because blocked crawlers never see any noindex tag behind the Disallow, so the URL lingers indexed indefinitely despite the block. To deindex, allow crawling of the noindexed URL, let Google recrawl to discover the tag, then re-evaluate. For admin logins or anything secret, add authentication because neither robots nor noindex provides security.

faqs.question: How does Disallow matching work?
faqs.answer: The longest matching rule wins regardless of file order, so Allow for admin public beats Disallow for admin on that path. Dollar signs anchor ends to block PDFs only, while asterisks span parameters like question sort equals to kill faceted traps. Validate every ruleset in a tester before deploying since one wildcard can deindex blogs.

faqs.question: Does Google respect crawl-delay?
faqs.answer: No, crawl-delay is advisory for some crawlers only and Googlebot ignores it, so it cannot control Google load. Shared hosts may see relief at Crawl-delay 5 from cooperating crawlers, but for Googlebot use Search Console crawl settings instead. Keep files under the 500KB cap and organize crawling with disciplined Disallows and sitemaps.

faqs.question: How do I fix faceted crawl traps?
