The ₹12–13L band is the knife-edge — marginal relief softens the cliff, but a small raise can still cost disproportionately. Run your exact CTC in the calculator with both regimes side by side; the crossover is personal, not universal.

Declaration discipline + in-hand reality

Employers need your regime choice early in the cycle — declare late and TDS defaults may over-withhold for months (recoverable at filing, painful meanwhile). Track HRA receipts, 80C proofs and home-loan certificates through the year; April scrambles lose deductions. Then convert CTC to monthly reality in the in-hand salary tool (PF, gratuity accounting, professional tax) — annual tax means little until it becomes monthly cash. Salaried with ESOPs, rent-free housing or foreign income: your edge cases need a CA, not a blog post.

Informational purposes only — not tax advice. Slabs, rebates and thresholds change yearly; verify current law and consult a qualified professional. See /terms.

faqs.question: Which regime is better for salaried in 2026?
faqs.answer: New regime suits low-deduction profiles with near-zero tax up to 12.75 lakh through 87A rebate and standard deduction. Old regime usually wins with heavy 80C, HRA and home-loan stacks, as shown by 15 lakh and 25 lakh crossover examples. Model your CTC side by side in the tax calculator because crossover is personal, not universal.

faqs.question: How does 87A rebate work?
faqs.answer: Section 87A zeroes computed tax up to the threshold income for eligible taxpayers, creating near-zero liability near 12.75 lakh for salaried under new regime. Just above the line, marginal relief softens the cliff so small raises do not cost disproportionately. Verify current limits yearly against the Finance Act because slabs and rebate thresholds move.

faqs.question: What is 115BAC?
faqs.answer: 115BAC is the new-regime slab structure offering graduated rates with minimal or no deductions and standard deduction for salaried. It contrasts with old-regime slabs that allow full 80C, HRA and home-loan claims at higher marginal rates. Compare both regimes on your exact salary because slab creep as pay rises changes the winner.

faqs.question: When must I declare my regime?
faqs.answer: Declare your regime choice early in the financial cycle to your employer so TDS reflects the correct slabs and rebate. Late declarations mean defaults may over-withhold for months, which is recoverable only at filing and painful meanwhile. Track HRA receipts, 80C proofs and home-loan certificates through the year to avoid April scrambles.

faqs.question: Does this replace a CA?
faqs.answer: No, this comparison covers standard salaried cases with salary, 80C, HRA and home loans, not complex edge situations. Salaried taxpayers with ESOPs, rent-free housing, foreign income or capital gains need a qualified professional. Slabs, rebates and thresholds change yearly, so verify current law and consult a CA for personalized advice.

title: Real vs Nominal Returns: Inflation-Adjusted Math
description: Real returns explained: deflation formula, Rule of 72 table, personal-vs-CPI inflation + SIP verdicts in real terms. Free calculator.
keywords: how inflation shrinks sip returns real vs nominal
html:
“12% returns!” — with 6% inflation quietly eating half. The statement showed growth; the grocery bill showed truth. Nominal returns impress, real returns feed: 12% minus 6% inflation is ~5.7% real, and ₹10,000 today buys ~₹5,540 in a decade at 6%. Every projection in this blog's calculators has this shadow twin. This guide teaches deflating any return, the Rule of 72 shortcut, personal-vs-CPI inflation, and why the SIP-vs-FD debate changes entirely in real terms.

Part of the India wealth & tax guide. Deflate projections in the inflation calculator; grow them in the SIP calculator first.

Deflate any return (the division, not subtraction)

Precisely: real = (1+nominal)/(1+inflation) − 1. At 12% and 6%: 1.12/1.06 − 1 ≈ 5.66% — close to naive 6%, and the gap widens at higher rates (never subtract when precision matters). Worked: ₹10,000 at 6% inflation for 10 years → 10000/1.06^10 ≈ ₹5,540 of today's purchasing power. A “₹1 crore corpus” at 6% inflation over 20 years spends like ₹31L today — still life-changing, but plan in real terms or retire surprised. Run both directions in the calculator: future value of money and required nominal for a real target.

Rule of 72 (and when it lies)

RateDoubling time ≈Use
6% inflation12 years to halve moneyPurchasing-power gut checks
12% returns6 years to doubleEquity horizon sanity
3% inflation24 years to halveConservative planning

72 ÷ rate ≈ doubling (or halving) years. Accurate within months for 4–12%; drifts at extremes (use exact math past 15%). The memorable corollary: money halves every 24 years even at “mild” 3% inflation — cash is a melting ice cube, and every idle-year decision should feel that cold.

Your inflation ≠ CPI (rent weighs 34%+ for you, maybe 10% for CPI)

CPI baskets average the nation; your basket is rent, education, healthcare and food in your city. Urban renters facing 8–10% annual hikes live 3+ points above headline CPI; homeowners with fixed EMIs live below it. Build a personal index: weight your top 5 expenses, track yearly, compare against the 6% default in projections. Then revisit the SIP-vs-FD verdict in SIP math — at 8% personal inflation, even 12% nominal leaves ~3.7% real, and horizons must extend or contributions rise (see ₹1 crore planning).

Informational purposes only — not financial advice. Inflation regimes shift; recheck assumptions yearly. See /terms.

faqs.question: What is the difference between real and nominal returns?
faqs.answer: Nominal is headline growth while real subtracts inflation through one and nominal divided by one and inflation minus one. Twelve percent nominal at 6 percent inflation equals about 5.7 percent real, not 6 percent by subtraction. Use division when precision matters because the gap widens at higher rates, then deflate projections in the inflation calculator.

faqs.question: How does the Rule of 72 work?
faqs.answer: Divide 72 by the rate for doubling or halving years, so 12 percent doubles in 6 years and 6 percent halves money in 12 years. The shortcut stays accurate for 4 to 12 percent but drifts at extremes. Use exact math past 15 percent and remember 3 percent halves money in 24 years.

faqs.question: Is CPI my inflation rate?
faqs.answer: Rarely, because CPI averages baskets while your spending weights rent, education, healthcare and food in your city. Urban renters facing 8 to 10 percent hikes often live 3 points above headline CPI, while homeowners with EMIs live below it. Build a personal index from your top five expenses and compare against the 6 percent default.

faqs.question: How much will ₹10,000 be worth in 10 years?
faqs.answer: About 5,540 of today's purchasing power at 6 percent inflation, calculated as 10,000 divided by 1.06 to the power 10. A 1 crore corpus over 20 years at 6 percent spends like 31 lakh, which is life-changing but different. Plan goals in real terms and run directions in the calculator for future value and nominal.

faqs.question: Does inflation change SIP vs FD choice?
faqs.answer: Yes, inflation compresses both options but fixed returns suffer more in real terms, changing SIP-versus-FD verdicts entirely. At 8 percent personal inflation, even 12 percent nominal leaves about 3.7 percent real. Extend horizons or raise contributions when personal inflation exceeds CPI, and revisit projections from SIP math with real targets.

title: SIP Needed for ₹1 Crore by Age 60
description: Required flat SIP for ₹1 crore at 12% by age 60, from 25 to 40, with 6% inflation-adjusted targets and realistic planning caveats.
html:
₹1 crore by 60 sounds like one goal. The monthly SIP needed to get there depends heavily on when you start. At a flat 12% annual return with monthly compounding, a 25-year-old needs about ₹1,540 a month. A 30-year-old needs about ₹2,833. A 35-year-old needs about ₹5,270, and a 40-year-old needs about ₹10,009. The target is identical; the monthly cost is not.

Those are nominal figures. If you want the corpus to have ₹1 crore of purchasing power in today's terms at 60, the target itself must grow with inflation. At 6%, the required SIP rises to about ₹11,833 at 25 and ₹32,099 at 40. The SIP calculator projects a flat contribution; it does not solve for a goal. This guide shows the reverse math, the inflation adjustment, and how to check your own number. It is part of the India wealth and tax guide.

Working backwards from ₹1 crore: SIP by start age

The flat SIP formula can be rearranged to solve for the contribution. If FV is the target, i is the monthly rate, and n is the number of months, then M = FV × i ÷ [((1 + i)^n − 1) × (1 + i)]. The (1 + i) factor again reflects a contribution at the start of each month.

Worked example one: a 25-year-old has 35 years, or 420 months, to age 60. With i = 0.01, the denominator works out to about 64.95, so ₹1 crore requires about ₹1,539.58 a month. Worked example two: a 40-year-old has 20 years, or 240 months. The same formula gives about ₹10,008.53 a month. The target did not change; the time to compound did.

Here is the full set. The nominal column keeps the target at ₹1 crore. The inflation-adjusted column raises the target by 6% a year to age 60, then solves for the SIP that would produce that larger nominal sum. Both columns use the same 12% return and start-of-month contributions.

Start ageYears to 60Nominal ₹1Cr SIPInflation-adjusted SIP
2535₹1,540₹11,833
3030₹2,833₹16,271
3525₹5,270₹22,617
4020₹10,009₹32,099

The jump is steep. A 10-year delay from 25 to 35 raises the nominal SIP from ₹1,540 to ₹5,270, about 3.4 times. Stretch the delay to 15 years, starting at 40, and the required amount becomes ₹10,009, about 6.5 times the age-25 figure. The later you start, the more each month has to carry because fewer months are available to compound.

The return assumption matters too. At 10%, the 30-year-old's nominal target needs about ₹4,387 a month; at 14%, about ₹1,800. A two-point change in the assumed return moves the answer by thousands. Twelve percent is a planning input, not a promise. Test 10% and 12% in the calculator before committing to a contribution you cannot sustain.

The SIP calculator has no goal mode. To find your number, enter a monthly amount and adjust it until the future value is close to the target, or solve the formula in a spreadsheet. The retirement calculator accepts an optional goal and shows a shortfall, which is useful for checking a plan, but it also does not calculate the required monthly contribution for you.

The reverse math also assumes the SIP starts from zero. If you already hold ₹5 lakh, that money compounds too: at 12% for 25 years it grows to about ₹85.0 lakh, leaving roughly ₹15 lakh to fund, so the required monthly contribution falls to about ₹790. The SIP calculator does not accept an existing balance. Subtract the future value of your current savings from the target before solving, or use the retirement calculator's corpus and shortfall view to see the combined effect.

Costs change the answer. A 1% annual expense ratio turns a 12% gross assumption into roughly 11% net; the age-30 requirement rises from ₹2,833 to about ₹3,533. Taxes on gains and any exit load add another drag. The calculator does not know your fund's expense ratio, so the 12% input should be treated as a gross assumption, not a net return you can spend.

Nominal versus real: why ₹1 crore may not be enough

₹1 crore received in 35 years is not ₹1 crore of today's spending. At 6% inflation, its purchasing power is about ₹13 lakh in today's money. A 25-year-old who wants ₹1 crore of today's purchasing power at 60 therefore needs a nominal target of about ₹7.69 crore. A 40-year-old needs about ₹3.21 crore because the money has only 20 years to lose value before it is spent. That is why the inflation-adjusted SIP column is so much larger.

Worked example: a 35-year-old investing ₹3,000 a month at 12% for 25 years accumulates about ₹56.9 lakh by 60. The nominal shortfall against ₹1 crore is about ₹43.1 lakh. Raising the SIP to the required ₹5,270 closes it on paper, but that still targets nominal ₹1 crore. If the goal is ₹1 crore in today's purchasing power, the target is about ₹4.29 crore and the required SIP is about ₹22,617. A ₹5,270 contribution would leave a much larger gap.

The common 4% withdrawal shortcut is another check. Four percent of ₹1 crore is ₹4 lakh a year, or about ₹33,000 a month in the first year. That is a starting point, not a guarantee. Taxes, fees, inflation, and the order in which returns arrive can all reduce what the corpus supports. A plan that assumes a smooth 12% return every year is ignoring sequence risk: a poor market early in retirement can hurt more than the same poor return later.

Keep nominal and real separate. The inflation-adjusted SIP column does not raise the return; it raises the target. The return stays 12% nominal, and 6% inflation means the real return is only about 5.7%. If inflation averages 5% or 7%, the required SIP moves in the opposite direction, so test both. The point of the real column is to stop a future ₹1 crore from feeling larger than it will be.

Other caveats belong in the same sentence as the projection: returns are not fixed, inflation may average more or less than 6%, equity gains are taxed, fund fees reduce the compounding rate, income may not grow as planned, and an emergency fund should sit outside the retirement corpus. The calculator cannot model a salary pause, a market crash, or a change in tax law. Use it to compare scenarios, not to certify an outcome.

Why ₹500 still matters, and how to close a shortfall

Small contributions are not enough for ₹1 crore on their own, but they change the starting point. At 12% for 30 years, ₹500 a month grows to about ₹17.65 lakh and ₹800 a month grows to about ₹28.24 lakh. The ₹300 difference becomes about ₹10.59 lakh, which is the cost of waiting to increase the amount. The point is not that ₹500 is sufficient; it is that a small, sustainable start is easier to raise later than a large contribution you abandon.

Starting early also beats starting bigger. ₹500 a month from age 25 for 35 years grows to about ₹32.48 lakh at 12%. ₹800 a month from age 35 for 25 years grows to about ₹15.18 lakh. The earlier start wins despite the smaller monthly amount, because the first contributions compound for a decade longer. This is the same lesson as the table, applied at a smaller scale.

If the projected corpus falls short, the levers are straightforward: contribute more, extend the horizon, lower the target, or add a lump sum when a bonus or inheritance arrives. Increasing a SIP by 5% or 10% a year is also powerful, but the calculator does not model step-up contributions. Work that schedule out separately, and keep the increase realistic. A plan that assumes a raise every year can fail in a year without one.

The most useful next step is to run your own age, contribution, and rate in the SIP calculator, then check the real value in the inflation calculator. The notes on real returns, ₹5,000 SIP growth, and tax regimes fill in the parts a single projection leaves out. Treat the result as a range, not a finish line.

Educational information only, not financial advice. The 12% return and 6% inflation inputs are illustrations, not forecasts. Returns, taxes, fees and inflation can all differ. See /terms.

faqs.question: How much SIP is needed for ₹1 crore by age 60?
faqs.answer: At a flat 12% return with monthly compounding, about ₹1,540 a month from age 25, ₹2,833 from 30, ₹5,270 from 35, or ₹10,009 from 40. The target is nominal ₹1 crore. Starting later leaves fewer months to compound, so the required contribution rises sharply.

faqs.question: Why does starting at 25 cost so much less than starting at 40?
faqs.answer: The age-25 investor has 35 years, or 420 monthly contributions, while the age-40 investor has 20 years, or 240. Earlier contributions compound for longer. The required SIP rises from about ₹1,540 to ₹10,009, roughly 6.5 times, even though the target stays at ₹1 crore.

faqs.question: How do I adjust ₹1 crore for inflation?
faqs.answer: Grow the target by your inflation assumption to age 60, then solve for the SIP. At 6%, a 25-year-old needs a nominal target of about ₹7.69 crore and a SIP near ₹11,833. A 40-year-old needs about ₹3.21 crore and ₹32,099. These are illustrations, not guaranteed outcomes.

faqs.question: Does the SIP calculator have a goal mode?
faqs.answer: No. It accepts a monthly investment, an annual rate, and a number of years, then returns the future value. To work backwards, change the monthly amount until the result is close to your target, or use a spreadsheet. The retirement calculator can compare a projected corpus with a goal and show a shortfall, but it does not solve for the required SIP.

faqs.question: What if I start late or my corpus is short?
faqs.answer: A 35-year-old investing ₹3,000 a month at 12% for 25 years reaches about ₹56.9 lakh, leaving a nominal shortfall of about ₹43.1 lakh against ₹1 crore. Raising the contribution, extending the horizon, adding a lump sum, or lowering the target can close the gap. Test the combination in the calculator rather than relying on one lever.

faqs.question: Is a 12% return realistic for a long SIP?
faqs.answer: Twelve percent is an illustrative assumption for comparing start ages, not a promise. At 10%, the 30-year-old's required SIP is about ₹4,387; at 14%, about ₹1,800. Markets deliver variable returns, and taxes, fees, inflation and the sequence of returns can reduce the realised result. Plan with a range.

title: Equity LTCG vs FD Tax: Post-Tax Keep Rates
description: Equity LTCG 12.5% vs FD slab tax: holding-period table, ₹1.25L exemption harvesting, cess + horizon-based keep rates. Free tax tool.
keywords: how equity ltcg tax compares to fd tax india
html:
₹2L equity gains, ₹2L FD interest. Tax bills: ~₹9,500 vs ~₹62,400. Same profit, 6.5× different tax — India taxes how you earn more than how much you earn. Equity LTCG at 12.5% above a ₹1.25L annual exemption vs FD interest at full slab rates rewrites every “which is better” comparison that ignores tax. This guide runs the FIFO holding rules, exemption math, cess layering and post-tax keep-rates so comparisons use net numbers.

Part of the India wealth & tax guide. Compute liabilities in capital gains tax; model FD legs in FD calculator.

Holding rules: 12 months vs 24 months, FIFO always

AssetLong-term afterLTCG rateShort-term rate
Listed equity12 months12.5% above ₹1.25L/yr20%
Property, gold24 months12.5% (no indexation)Slab rate
FD interestN/A (always income)—Slab rate

FIFO ordering decides which units sell first — and therefore which rate applies. Partial profit-booking across financial years splits gains under the ₹1.25L annual exemption repeatedly (see exemption play below). Debt fund taxation follows its own post-2026 treatment; verify current classification before assuming equity-like rates.

The ₹1.25L exemption play (plus 4% cess)

Equity LTCG exempts ₹1.25L per year — harvest gains annually up to the line and reset cost basis, legally compounding tax-free slices. Example: ₹2L gain → taxable ₹75,000 → 12.5% = ₹9,375 + 4% cess ≈ ₹9,750 total. Same ₹2L as FD interest at 30% slab: ₹60,000 + cess ≈ ₹62,400. Then layer cess mentally last: 4% on computed tax, small but never zero, and the line most hand-math forgets. Use the capital gains tool with exemption-used tracking across the year.

Post-tax keep-rate: the only comparison that counts

  • Equity 3-year hold, 30% slab investor: ~13% gross → ~12%+ net after exemption-efficient harvesting. Winner for horizons past 3 years.
  • FD 3-year hold, same investor: 7% gross → ~4.8% net. Certainty costs ~7 points vs equity — acceptable for goals, fatal for retirement.
  • 1-year horizon: equity STCG 20% vs FD slab — FD often wins net; match instrument to horizon, not headlines.
  • Gold/property: 24-month clock + 12.5% LTCG; illiquidity and transaction costs dominate the tax story — model all-in, not rates alone.

Revisit every budget: exemption limits, holding periods and surcharge slabs move. Pair with regime planning — salary slab determines which keep-rate table row you live in.

Informational purposes only — not tax advice. Rates, exemptions and classifications change; verify current law and consult a qualified professional. See /terms.

faqs.question: How is equity LTCG taxed in India?
faqs.answer: Listed equity held over 12 months pays 12.5 percent above a 1.25 lakh annual exemption and 4 percent cess on computed tax. Holdings under 12 months pay 20 percent as short-term gains. Harvest gains annually up to the exemption line to reset cost basis, track exemption used across the year, and verify debt classifications separately.

faqs.question: Is FD interest taxed more than equity gains?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for upper slabs because 2 lakh FD interest at 30 percent costs about 62,400 including cess, while equivalent equity LTCG costs about 9,750 after exemption. Equity exempts 1.25 lakh yearly, leaving 75,000 taxable at 12.5 percent and cess. That 6.5-times gap shows India taxes how you earn more than how much you earn.

faqs.question: What is FIFO in capital gains?
faqs.answer: First-in-first-out ordering decides which units sell first and therefore which holding period and rate apply on partial sales. Book profits partially across financial years to split gains under the 1.25 lakh annual exemption repeatedly. That harvesting resets basis legally and compounds tax-free slices instead of bunching gains in one year.

faqs.question: Should short horizons still use equity?
faqs.answer: Rarely, because 1-year equity short-term gains at 20 percent often net below FD certainty after tax and volatility. FD interest taxed at slab still wins net for brief horizons where compounding has little time. Match instrument to horizon rather than headlines, reserving equity for horizons past 3 years where keep-rates dominate.

faqs.question: Do gold and property follow equity rules?
faqs.answer: No, gold and property turn long-term after 24 months with 12.5 percent LTCG and no indexation, while short-term gains follow slab rates. Illiquidity and transaction costs often dominate the tax story beyond headline rates. Model all-in costs, revisit budgets yearly for exemption and holding changes, and pair with regime planning for your slab.

title: Budget 2026 Verdict: What Changed for Salaried Savers
description: Budget 2026 left FY 2026-27 slabs unchanged. What the new tax Act, capital gains rules and TCS changes mean for salaried savers.
html:
Budget 2026, presented on 1 February 2026, did not change the income-tax slabs for FY 2026-27. For salaried taxpayers, that is the headline: no rate cut, no new slab, no windfall. The new-regime structure remains nil to ₹4 lakh, 5% to ₹8 lakh, 10% to ₹12 lakh, 15% to ₹16 lakh, 20% to ₹20 lakh, 25% to ₹24 lakh, and 30% above ₹24 lakh. The ₹75,000 standard deduction and the 87A rebate remain part of the calculation.

The larger change is legislative. The Income-tax Act, 2025 takes effect on 1 April 2026, replacing the 1961 Act. The substance largely continues; the numbering, rules, and forms are new. That distinction matters when you read a tax article, fill a return, or compare this year's payroll deduction with last year's. This is part of the India wealth and tax guide.

The verdict table: what Budget 2026 kept for FY 2026-27

ElementStatus for FY 2026-27What it means
New-regime slabsUnchanged: nil to ₹4L, 5% to ₹8L, 10% to ₹12L, 15% to ₹16L, 20% to ₹20L, 25% to ₹24L, 30% above ₹24LNo rate cut; plan on known numbers
Standard deduction₹75,000 for salaried new-regime incomeSupports zero tax up to about ₹12.75L gross
87A rebateUp to ₹60,000 for taxable income up to ₹12LZero tax at ₹12L taxable; marginal relief just above
Old regimeExisting slabs, ₹12,500 rebate and ₹50,000 standard deduction retainedStill available on opting; real deductions decide
Listed-equity LTCG12.5% above the ₹1.25L annual exemption under s.112AHarvesting discipline still matters
Listed-equity STCG20% under s.111AShort holding periods cost more
Income-tax Act, 2025Effective 1 April 2026New numbering and forms; broad structure continues

The 87A rebate is a rebate, not a slab change. It can reduce tax to zero, but it does not alter the marginal rate that applies once taxable income crosses ₹12 lakh. The familiar “zero tax up to ₹12.75 lakh” figure assumes salary income, the ₹75,000 standard deduction, and no other income or deductions. Add rental income, capital gains, or a second salary and the calculation changes.

Worked example one: a salaried taxpayer with gross salary of ₹12.75 lakh and only the standard deduction has taxable income of ₹12 lakh. Slab tax is ₹60,000—nothing on the first ₹4 lakh, 5% on the next ₹4 lakh, and 10% on the last ₹4 lakh. The 87A rebate of up to ₹60,000 wipes that out, leaving no income tax. Worked example two: at ₹16 lakh gross, taxable income is ₹15.25 lakh. There is no rebate at that level, and the tax works out to about ₹1.13 lakh including the 4% cess, assuming no other deductions.

Capital gains were not changed either. Listed-equity long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption under section 112A, while listed-equity short-term gains are taxed at 20% under section 111A. Other-asset long-term gains are generally taxed at 12.5% without indexation, with grandfathering available for eligible land or buildings acquired before 23 July 2024. Those are broad statements; the asset type, holding period, and acquisition date decide the actual treatment. Use the capital gains tax calculator for a simplified estimate.

Other Budget 2026 announcements worth noting: STT on futures rises from 0.02% to 0.05%; options premium STT from 0.1% to 0.15%, and exercise STT from 0.125% to 0.15%; buyback proceeds are taxed as capital gains for shareholders, with an additional levy on promoters; TCS on LRS remittances above the applicable threshold is 2% for education and medical purposes and 20% for other purposes; overseas tour packages face 2% TCS; TDS on manpower services is set at 1% or 2%; the revised-return window extends to 31 March with a fee; and MAT is 14% as a final tax for companies. These are Budget proposals and announcements, not all of which affect salaried employees. Verify the Finance Act text and notified rules before acting.

What the unchanged slabs mean by income band

Under ₹12.75 lakh gross. A salaried taxpayer with only the standard deduction is effectively outside income tax under the new regime. That does not mean every deduction disappears: professional tax, employee PF, and other payroll items still reduce take-home pay. The practical move is to direct the cash flow toward an emergency fund and long-term investments rather than buying a tax-saving product you do not need. The ₹1 crore SIP math is a better use of the planning energy than a last-minute 80C purchase.

₹12.75 lakh to ₹20 lakh. This is where the slab climb becomes visible. At ₹16 lakh gross, the new-regime tax is about ₹1.13 lakh including cess, as the example above shows. The old regime can compete only if actual HRA, 80C, 80D, and home-loan interest claims are large enough to overcome its higher slab rates. A deduction you would not otherwise use is not a reason to buy a product. Model both regimes with your real numbers in the in-hand salary calculator, which estimates CTC-to-take-home under the new regime. It is not a full filing calculator.

Above ₹20 lakh. The 25% and 30% slabs do most of the work. Old-regime deductions can still matter, especially for someone with a large home loan, substantial HRA, or a family health premium. The answer depends on the size and legitimacy of those claims, not on a generic “old is better” or “new is better” rule. Compare the final tax, not just the taxable income.

Capital income. Holding-period discipline remains valuable. A ₹2 lakh listed-equity LTCG with no prior exemption used leaves ₹75,000 taxable at 12.5%, or about ₹9,750 including cess. The same ₹2 lakh treated as STCG is taxed at 20%, or about ₹41,600 including cess. These simplified figures exclude surcharge and special cases, but they show why the holding period matters. The sibling note on equity LTCG versus FD tax compares the post-tax outcomes.

The practical verdict and the actions that follow

The verdict for salaried savers is unglamorous: no windfall from the slabs, and no reason to overhaul a sensible plan. The useful actions are about using the rules you already have, not chasing a headline.

  1. Do not budget for a tax cut. Recalculate your payroll TDS with the current slabs rather than last year's rumour. If your salary and declarations are unchanged, your tax should be broadly unchanged.
  2. Use the new regime as the default when deductions are low. Compare the old regime only with real HRA, 80C, 80D, and home-loan claims. A hypothetical deduction is not a saving. The old versus new regime guide covers the crossover logic.
  3. Treat the payroll regime choice as a withholding decision. It affects TDS during the year, but salaried taxpayers without business income can generally change the regime when filing the return. The final return reconciles the difference. Confirm the current rule before relying on it.
  4. Do not buy a tax product just to save tax. ELSS, insurance-cum-investment plans, and PPF should fit the goal first. In the new regime, 80C usually does not apply, so a product bought only for the deduction can leave you with a poor fit and a locked-in commitment. Check the PPF extension choices before locking money for another block.
  5. Keep capital-gains harvesting disciplined. Use the ₹1.25 lakh annual equity LTCG exemption where it fits your plan, track holding periods, and avoid bunching sales into March. Harvesting above the exemption triggers tax, so it is not a free exercise.

The Income-tax Act, 2025 adds a transition cost: new section numbers, new forms, and rules that may be notified after the Act takes effect. Do not assume an old section number still applies. When a payroll portal or a tax article cites a section, check it against the current Act and the latest departmental guidance. The broad structure is familiar, but the labels are not.

Official sources: Income Tax Department and Press Information Bureau. Budget announcements take effect through the Finance Act and notified rules; verify the final text before filing. The in-hand salary calculator linked above is an estimate, not a filing tool, and the capital gains calculator is simplified.

Educational information only, not tax or financial advice. Slabs, rebates and capital-gains rules can change; confirm your position with the current law and a qualified professional. See /terms.

faqs.question: Did Budget 2026 change income-tax slabs?
faqs.answer: No. The old and new regime slabs for FY 2026-27 remain unchanged. New-regime rates stay at nil to ₹4 lakh, 5% to ₹8 lakh, 10% to ₹12 lakh, 15% to ₹16 lakh, 20% to ₹20 lakh, 25% to ₹24 lakh, and 30% above ₹24 lakh. The ₹75,000 standard deduction and the 87A rebate also remain, so a salaried taxpayer with only that deduction can still reach zero tax at about ₹12.75 lakh gross.

faqs.question: What is the Income-tax Act, 2025?
faqs.answer: It is the law that replaces the Income-tax Act, 1961 and takes effect on 1 April 2026. The broad tax structure continues, but section numbers, rules, and forms change. Treat it as a numbering and process transition rather than a rate cut. Check current departmental guidance before citing a section or filling a new form.

faqs.question: Did capital-gains tax rates change?
faqs.answer: The main listed-equity rates were unchanged. LTCG is 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption under section 112A, and STCG is 20% under section 111A. Other-asset LTCG is generally 12.5% without indexation, with grandfathering for eligible land or buildings acquired before 23 July 2024. Asset type and holding period still decide the actual treatment.

faqs.question: Should a salaried taxpayer choose the old regime?
faqs.answer: Only if the real deductions make it cheaper. Compare the final tax under both regimes using actual HRA, 80C, 80D, and home-loan interest claims. A deduction you would not otherwise use is not a reason to buy a product. With low deductions, the new regime is usually the simpler default, but the answer depends on your numbers.

faqs.question: Can I change the regime after telling payroll?
faqs.answer: Salaried taxpayers without business income can generally change the regime when filing the return, even if a different option was declared to the employer for TDS. The payroll choice affects withholding during the year; the return reconciles the final liability. Confirm the current rule and any exceptions before relying on this.

faqs.question: What should salaried savers do after Budget 2026?
faqs.answer: Do not budget for a tax cut. Recalculate TDS, use the new regime as the default when deductions are low, compare the old regime only with real claims, and avoid buying tax products for the deduction alone. Keep equity LTCG harvesting within the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption and track holding periods. Verify the Finance Act and notified rules.

title: Percentage Calculator Guide: Formulas, Discounts & Real-Life Uses
description: Percentage formulas for everyday math: percent of a number, increase, discounts, tax, margin and percentage points, with worked examples.
html:
A percentage is a comparison squeezed into a small number. It can describe a pay raise, a clearance tag, a tax line or the gap between two supplier quotes, but the arithmetic changes with the question. This guide gives you the formulas, the worked examples and the traps, then points you to the right view in the percentage calculator.

Read it in order or jump straight to the section you need. The numbers stay simple on purpose so you can check each result on paper.

What a percentage actually means

Percent means “per hundred.” One percent is one part in one hundred, written as 1/100 or 0.01. So 37% is 37 parts per hundred, 0.37 as a decimal, and 37/100 as a fraction. The same quantity can wear all three outfits: 3/8 equals 0.375, which equals 37.5%.

That definition explains why percentages are so useful. They put different-sized things on one scale. A ₹200 increase sounds bigger than a ₹150 increase until you learn the first was on a ₹10,000 salary and the second on a ₹3,000 fee. As percentages, those are 2% and 5%.

The catch is the base. “20% off” means 20% of the marked price, not 20% of the price you eventually pay. “A 10% raise followed by a 10% cut” does not return you to the starting salary. Almost every percentage mistake comes from multiplying by the wrong base or adding percentages that were calculated from different bases.

Keep two phrases in mind. “Of” usually means multiply: 18% of 250 is 0.18 × 250. “What percent” usually means divide, then multiply by 100: 45 out of 180 is 45 ÷ 180 × 100. Simple, but only if you identify the whole.

Percentages also hide the size of the thing they describe. A 5% fee on ₹200 is ₹10; the same 5% on ₹2,00,000 is ₹10,000. The rate is identical, the consequence is not. Before comparing two percentages, ask what base each one sits on and whether the two bases are measured the same way.

The four formulas behind almost every question

Most percentage requests fit one of four patterns. Learn the pattern first, then reach for a calculator. This table is the compact version; the sections below unpack each row.

QuestionFormulaExampleAnswer
What is X% of Y?(X ÷ 100) × Y18% of 25045
A is what percent of B?(A ÷ B) × 10045 out of 18025%
Old value to new value((New − Old) ÷ Old) × 100240 to 300+25%
Reverse a percentage changeFinal ÷ (1 ± rate)68 after 15% off80 original

Two more formulas cover comparisons that are easy to confuse with change. Percentage difference divides the gap by the average of the two values: 60 and 80 differ by 20, and 20 ÷ 70 × 100 = 28.57%. Percentage error divides the gap by the true or accepted value instead. Those distinctions matter in reports, so they get their own sections later.

Read the table from the question backward. If the sentence gives a rate and asks for an amount, you are multiplying. If it gives two amounts and asks for a rate, you are dividing one by the other. If it gives a starting point and an ending point, the starting point is the denominator for change. If it gives only the ending point, you are reversing a change that has already happened.

Percent of a number, and the two reverse questions

Start with the easiest case. To find 20% of 150, convert the rate to a decimal and multiply: 0.20 × 150 = 30. To find 7.5% of 240, use 0.075 × 240 = 18. If the rate is friendly, the fraction route is faster: 25% is one quarter, so 25% of 84 is 21.

The reverse question — “45 is what percent of 180?” — flips the division. Put the part over the whole: 45 ÷ 180 = 0.25, then multiply by 100 for 25%. The part always goes on top. Reversing those positions gives 400%, which is technically an answer but almost never the one you want.

A third version asks for the whole: “12 is 30% of what number?” Divide the part by the rate as a decimal. 12 ÷ 0.30 = 40. This is the same move you use to recover a pre-discount price or a pre-tax subtotal. The percent of a number tutorial walks through all three arrangements with more examples, and the reverse percentage guide focuses on the cases where the final number is already on the receipt.

Increase and decrease: direction changes the denominator

Percentage change compares a new value with an old one. Subtract old from new, divide by the old value, then multiply by 100. From 240 to 300 the gap is 60, and 60 ÷ 240 × 100 = 25%. The move from 300 back to 240 is a different calculation: −60 ÷ 300 × 100 = −20%.

That asymmetry is not a rounding quirk. The same absolute gap is being measured against a different base. A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease leaves 96, not 100: 100 becomes 120, then 120 × 0.80 = 96. To undo a 20% rise you need a 16.67% fall, because 20 ÷ 120 = 0.1667.

Decreases work the same way. A price that drops from 480 to 420 has fallen by 60; 60 ÷ 480 × 100 = 12.5%. If a value falls by 15% to 68, the original was 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80. Notice that reversing a decrease means dividing by 0.85, not multiplying by 1.15. Adding 15% to 68 gives 78.20, which is why “add back the discount” so often produces a number that does not match the tag.

Use change when there is a clear before and after: monthly revenue, website traffic, body weight, electricity use. Use percentage difference when neither value is a baseline and you want a neutral comparison. The increase and decrease guide covers business cases, and the percentage difference tutorial explains the symmetric version.

Discounts, sale prices and tax

A discount is a percentage of the original price. If a ₹120 item is 25% off, the saving is 0.25 × 120 = ₹30 and the sale price is 120 − 30 = ₹90. The quick route is to multiply by the complement: 120 × 0.75 = ₹90. Both methods agree because the discount and the amount you pay add up to 100% of the original.

Stacked discounts are where shoppers get surprised. “20% off, then an extra 10% off” does not mean 30% off. Apply the first cut to ₹100 and you have ₹80. Apply the second cut to ₹80 and you save ₹8 more, leaving ₹72. The total saving is ₹28, or 28% — not 30%. Sequential percentages multiply, so the combined factor is 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72.

Tax usually applies after the discount. Take the ₹90 sale price and add 8% sales tax: 90 × 0.08 = ₹7.20, for a total of ₹97.20. Charging tax on the original ₹120 would overstate the bill by 8% of ₹30, or ₹2.40. The order matters, even when both rates look small.

Coupons, cashback and loyalty points are not interchangeable. A ₹100 coupon on a ₹500 bill cuts the price by 20%. A 20% cashback offer returns ₹100 later, but you still pay ₹500 at checkout and may spend the reward on something else. If the cashback is capped at ₹50, the effective saving is 10%. Compare offers by the money that actually leaves your account, not by the headline rate.

GST works the same way but frequently travels in the opposite direction. A ₹4,800 service invoice at 18% GST carries 4,800 × 0.18 = ₹864 tax, for ₹5,664 total. If all you have is the inclusive total, extract the base with 5,664 × 100 ÷ 118 = ₹4,800, leaving ₹864 tax. Multiplying 5,664 by 0.18 would give ₹1,019.52, which is wrong because the total already contains the tax.

The discount calculator handles markdowns and optional tax in one pass. The GST calculator switches between adding tax to a net figure and extracting it from a gross figure. For the shopping logic in more detail, read the discount and sale price guide.

Margin and markup: same profit, different denominator

Business pricing runs on two percentages that sound interchangeable and are not. Margin divides profit by revenue. Markup divides profit by cost. A product that costs ₹60 and sells for ₹100 earns ₹40 profit. Margin is 40 ÷ 100 = 40%. Markup is 40 ÷ 60 = 66.67%.

Because the denominators differ, the markup number is always larger for a profitable sale. The gap widens as margin rises. At a 50% margin, markup is 100%; at a 20% margin, markup is 25%. If a supplier says “I use a 50% markup,” the resulting margin is 33.33%, not 50%. That is a costly misunderstanding when you are setting a price list.

To price from a target margin, divide cost by one minus the margin. A ₹60 item at a 40% target margin needs 60 ÷ (1 − 0.40) = ₹100. At a 50% target it needs 60 ÷ 0.50 = ₹120. To price from a target markup, multiply cost by 1.5 for a 50% markup: ₹60 × 1.50 = ₹90, which carries only a 33.33% margin.

Margin also shrinks faster than price when you discount. Cutting a ₹100 price by 10% removes ₹10 of revenue and, with cost unchanged at ₹60, removes ₹10 of profit. Profit falls from ₹40 to ₹30 and margin from 40% to 33.33%. In relative terms, a 10% discount cost 16.67% of the margin. That is why a promotion that looks modest on the tag can wipe out the reason you stocked the item.

These are gross figures. Payment fees, shipping, returns, rent and advertising all come out of that margin before anything reaches your bank account. Treat the calculation as a pricing checkpoint, not a profit guarantee. The profit margin calculator shows profit, margin and markup together, and the markup vs margin guide works through target pricing and discount damage. This is general information, not financial advice.

Percentage points vs percent change

When a rate itself moves, there are two honest ways to describe the move. A savings rate that goes from 4% to 5% has risen by 1 percentage point. Relative to where it started, it has risen by 25%, because 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25. Both statements are true; they answer different questions.

Newsletters and product pages often choose whichever number sounds more dramatic. If a conversion rate moves from 2% to 3%, that is 1 point but a 50% relative increase. If a fee moves from 12% to 9%, that is a 3-point drop but a 25% relative decrease. State the unit and you avoid the argument. The percentage points guide has a longer set of examples.

Measurement error is a separate calculation. If a scale reads 48 kg for an object with a true mass of 50 kg, the error is (48 − 50) ÷ 50 × 100 = −4%. The absolute error is 4%, and the sign tells you the reading was low. The percentage error guide covers accepted values, absolute error and the cases where a negative sign is meaningful.

Which percentage calculator view to use

Most mistakes happen before any arithmetic, when someone picks the wrong relationship. Match the wording of the question to the view below, then enter the numbers.

  • “What is 15% of 80?” Use the percent view. Rate and base go in; the part comes out. 0.15 × 80 = 12.
  • “18 is what percent of 72?” Use the what-percent view. Part divided by whole: 18 ÷ 72 × 100 = 25%.
  • “Sales went from 1,200 to 1,500.” Use the change view. 300 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 25% growth.
  • “The price is 68 after 15% off.” Use the reverse view. 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80.
  • “Compare 60 with 80.” Use the difference view for a neutral 28.57% gap, not a directional change.

Write the question in words before touching the keypad. “Percent of” and “percent change” look similar in a search box and behave nothing alike on the page. A five-second translation saves a wrong quote, a mispriced invoice or a confusing chart.

Common mistakes and a 10-second sanity check

Percentage errors rarely come from bad multiplication. They come from choosing the wrong base, skipping a step, or reporting a relative change as if it were an absolute one.

  1. Adding percentages from different bases. A 10% rise then a 10% fall is not zero. It is −1% overall, because 100 → 110 → 99.
  2. Discounting the tax-inclusive total. A 20% coupon on a ₹1,180 GST-inclusive bill does not necessarily reduce the tax by 20%; the discount usually applies to the taxable value, then tax is recalculated.
  3. Using markup as margin. A 50% markup on ₹60 gives ₹90 and a 33.33% margin. Calling it a 50% margin overstates profitability.
  4. Reversing with the wrong operator. To undo a 20% increase, divide by 1.20. Do not subtract 20% from the new value.
  5. Reporting points as percent. A move from 4% to 5% is 1 point and a 25% relative increase. Pick one and label it.
  6. Rounding too early. Keep full precision through the steps, then round the final money amount to two decimals. Rounding a rate to a whole number midway can shift a total by several rupees.

A quick check catches most of these. Ten percent of a number is one decimal shift left: 10% of 250 is 25. One percent is two shifts: 2.50. If your answer for 18% of 250 lands far from 45, the decimal point probably moved. For money, ask whether the final total is plausible against the original. A ₹90 item with 8% tax should land near ₹97, not ₹107 or ₹81.

Finally, distinguish gross margin from net margin. Gross margin subtracts the direct cost of the item; net margin also subtracts overhead, fees and tax. A 40% gross margin can become a 12% net margin after marketplace commission, shipping and returns. Both numbers are useful, but they answer different questions, and quoting one while meaning the other is how a healthy product line starts to look unprofitable.

Run your own numbers: open the free percentage calculator for percent-of, what-percent, change and difference in one place. For shopping math use the discount calculator; for pricing use the profit margin calculator; for tax use the GST calculator. This guide is general information, not financial or tax advice.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a percentage of a number?
faqs.answer: Turn the rate into a decimal and multiply it by the base. For 18% of 250, compute 0.18 × 250 = 45. For 7.5% of 240, compute 0.075 × 240 = 18. If the rate is a familiar fraction, 25% of 84 is simply one quarter, or 21. The percentage calculator shows the same formula beside the result.

faqs.question: What is the difference between percentage points and percent?
faqs.answer: A move from 4% to 5% is 1 percentage point, because the two rates differ by one unit. It is also a 25% relative increase, because the change of 1 is divided by the starting rate of 4. Use points when describing the rate itself and percent when describing growth relative to the starting value.

faqs.question: Why does a 20% increase not cancel a 20% decrease?
faqs.answer: The two changes use different bases. Start at 100, add 20% to reach 120, then take 20% of 120, which is 24, leaving 96. To return from 120 to 100 you need a fall of 20 ÷ 120 = 16.67%. The same absolute gap is being compared with a larger base on the way down.

faqs.question: How do I find the original price after a discount?
faqs.answer: Divide the sale price by one minus the discount rate. A price of 68 after 15% off means 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80. Do not add 15% to 68, which gives 78.20. For a price after a 20% increase, divide by 1.20 instead. The reverse percentage tutorial covers both directions.

faqs.question: Is markup the same as margin?
faqs.answer: No. A product costing 60 and selling for 100 earns 40 profit. Margin is 40 ÷ 100 = 40%, while markup is 40 ÷ 60 = 66.67%. Margin uses revenue as the denominator and markup uses cost. A 50% markup therefore produces a 33.33% margin, which matters when you set prices from a target.

faqs.question: How do I remove GST from an inclusive total?
faqs.answer: Divide the gross amount by 1.18 at 18%. A total of 5,664 becomes 5,664 ÷ 1.18 = 4,800, so the tax is 864. Multiplying 5,664 by 0.18 is incorrect because the gross figure already includes tax. Use the GST calculator in extract mode to avoid that inversion.

faqs.question: Which calculator view should I choose?
faqs.answer: Use percent-of when you have a rate and a base, what-percent when you have a part and a whole, change when you have an old and new value, and difference when neither value is a baseline. For a total that already includes tax or a discount, use reverse. Writing the question in words before entering numbers prevents most errors.

title: How to Calculate Percent of a Number (With Examples)
description: Find percent of a number with three formula layouts, worked examples, mental-math shortcuts and fixes for base errors. Free calculator included.
keywords: how to calculate percentage of a number
find the whole from a percentage

toc.text: What percent of a number means

html:
A percentage question looks harmless until the numbers are on the page. “What is 18% of 250?” is straightforward. “45 is what percent of 180?” requires a different division. “12 is 30% of what number?” reverses the whole thing. All three appear in tips, invoices, grades and sales reports, and all three are easy to get wrong when you grab the wrong number as the base.

This tutorial sticks to percent of a number and its two close cousins. It shows the arithmetic line by line, then gives you mental shortcuts and a calculator workflow. Keep the percentage calculator open if you want to check each step.

What “percent of a number” actually means

Percent means “per hundred,” so 15% is 15 per 100, or 15/100, or 0.15. Finding 15% of 80 means taking 15 hundredths of 80. The arithmetic is 0.15 × 80 = 12. Nothing more complicated than that.

Because multiplication is commutative, 15% of 80 and 80% of 15 give the same answer: 0.15 × 80 = 12 and 0.80 × 15 = 12. That trick can make a question easier. If someone asks for 4% of 75, flip it to 75% of 4, which is 3. If they ask for 60% of 45, try 45% of 60: 0.45 × 60 = 27. The numbers are the same; one arrangement just fits your head better.

The word “of” is the signal to multiply. The number after “of” is the base, also called the whole. In “18% of 250,” the base is 250. In “18% of the invoice total,” the base is whatever that total happens to be. Identify the base before you touch a keypad, because every variation below depends on knowing which number represents 100%.

One more distinction: a percentage is a ratio, not a unit. You can have 150% of a target, which is 1.5 times the target, and you can have 150% of a daily apple budget. The base decides what the percentage is allowed to describe.

The formula, rearranged three ways

Every percent-of question contains three quantities: the rate, the part and the whole. If you know two, you can find the third. The rearrangements below cover the entire family.

  • Find the part: Part = (Rate ÷ 100) × Whole. Example: 18% of 250 = 0.18 × 250 = 45.
  • Find the rate: Rate = (Part ÷ Whole) × 100. Example: 45 ÷ 180 × 100 = 25%.
  • Find the whole: Whole = Part ÷ (Rate ÷ 100). Example: 12 ÷ 0.30 = 40.

The common thread is the decimal rate. Convert the percentage to a decimal before multiplying or dividing, then convert back to a percentage at the end if the question asks for one. Mixing the two forms mid-calculation is the source of many “off by a factor of 100” answers.

Label the quantities in the actual sentence. “45 is what percent of 180?” gives you the part (45) and the whole (180), so the rate is the unknown. “12 is 30% of what number?” gives you the part (12) and the rate (30%), so the whole is unknown. “What is 18% of 250?” gives you the rate and the whole, so the part is unknown. This sounds pedantic until you catch yourself dividing 180 by 45 and getting 400%.

Worked examples with the arithmetic shown

Example 1: Find 18% of 250. Convert the rate to a decimal: 18 ÷ 100 = 0.18. Multiply by the base: 0.18 × 250 = 45. To check with mental math, split 18% into 10% and 8%: 10% of 250 is 25, 8% of 250 is 20, and 25 + 20 = 45. The two methods agree.

Example 2: Find 7.5% of 240. Convert to 0.075, then multiply: 0.075 × 240 = 18. A second check: 5% of 240 is 12, 2.5% is half of 5%, or 6, and 12 + 6 = 18. If you had mistakenly used 0.75, you would have landed at 180 — a good reminder to count the decimal places.

Example 3: 45 is what percent of 180? Divide the part by the whole: 45 ÷ 180 = 0.25. Multiply by 100: 0.25 × 100 = 25%. Check forward: 25% of 180 = 0.25 × 180 = 45. The part goes on top because the question is asking how large 45 is relative to 180.

Example 4: 12 is 30% of what number? Convert 30% to 0.30, then divide the part by the rate: 12 ÷ 0.30 = 40. Check forward: 30% of 40 = 0.30 × 40 = 12. Dividing by 30 instead of 0.30 would give 0.4, which is not a plausible whole when the part is 12.

QuestionKnown valuesArithmeticAnswer
18% of 250Rate 18%, whole 2500.18 × 25045
7.5% of 240Rate 7.5%, whole 2400.075 × 24018
45 of 180Part 45, whole 18045 ÷ 180 × 10025%
12 is 30%Part 12, rate 30%12 ÷ 0.3040

Mental math shortcuts that hold up

You do not need a calculator for most everyday percentages if you can move a decimal point and take halves.

  • 10%: shift the decimal one place left. 10% of 84 is 8.4.
  • 1%: shift two places left. 1% of 84 is 0.84.
  • 5%: take half of 10%. 5% of 84 is 4.2.
  • 15%: add 10% and 5%. 15% of 84 is 8.4 + 4.2 = 12.6.
  • 20%: double 10%. 20% of 84 is 16.8.
  • 25%: divide by four. 25% of 84 is 21.
  • 75%: take three quarters. 75% of 84 is 63.

For a rate like 35%, combine 30% and 5%. Thirty percent of 80 is 24, 5% is 4, so 35% is 28. For 12.5%, take half of 25%: 25% of 96 is 24, so 12.5% is 12. For 6%, take half of 12%, or add 5% and 1%.

Estimation prevents embarrassing answers. If you need 19% of 400, start with 20% (80) and subtract 1% (4) to get 76. If a restaurant bill is 84.50 and you want an 18% tip, use 20% (16.90) and subtract 2% (1.69): 15.21. That is faster than opening a calculator and gives you a number you can defend.

Common mistakes that flip the answer

  1. Using the wrong base. “20% more than 50” is 60, but “50% more than 20” is 30. The rate and the base both changed. Read the sentence twice before calculating.
  2. Dividing by the percentage instead of its decimal. To find the whole from a part, divide by 0.30, not 30. The decimal conversion is not optional.
  3. Assuming a part cannot exceed the whole. A 150% increase takes 80 to 200. Percentages above 100% are valid when the comparison allows growth beyond the original.
  4. Adding percentages from different bases. A 10% rise on 100 gives 110; another 10% on 110 gives 11, not 10. The second increase is larger in absolute terms.
  5. Rounding the rate too early. Keep the full decimal through the multiplication, then round the final amount. Rounding 7.5% to 8% before multiplying changes 18 into 19.20 on a 240 base.
  6. Forgetting the percent sign at the end. “45 of 180” is 0.25, while “45 of 180” as a percentage is 25%. Decide which form the answer needs.

A ten-second sanity check catches most of these. One percent of the base is your smallest building block; ten percent is ten of those. If the answer is wildly outside that scale, check the decimal point. If the question asks for a rate, the answer should usually sit between 0% and 100% unless growth or a comparison beyond the whole is involved.

Using the percentage calculator without second-guessing

The free percentage calculator groups the three arrangements into clear views. Pick “percent of” when you know the rate and base, “what percent” when you know the part and whole, and the reverse field when you know the part and rate. The tool displays the formula beside the answer, so you can see which number was treated as 100%.

  1. Write the question in plain words: “What is 18% of 250?”
  2. Identify the known pair: rate 18%, whole 250.
  3. Enter both values in the percent-of view and read 45.
  4. Check with a rough estimate: 10% is 25, so 18% should be under 50. It is.

When the question involves a change rather than a fixed part, switch to the percentage increase and decrease guide. When you know the final value after a change and need the starting point, the reverse percentage tutorial shows why dividing by 1 plus the rate works. The full percentage guide connects both to discounts, tax and margin.

Check your number: open the percentage calculator, enter your rate and base, and compare the displayed formula with the arithmetic above. No signup, and the calculation runs on your device.

faqs.question: What is the fastest way to find 15% of a number?
faqs.answer: Take 10% by shifting the decimal one place left, then add half of that for the 5% portion. For 15% of 84, 10% is 8.4 and 5% is 4.2, so the answer is 12.6. The same split works for 35% (30% and 5%) or 18% (10% and 8%).

faqs.question: How do I find what percent one number is of another?
faqs.answer: Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100. For 45 out of 180, 45 ÷ 180 = 0.25, which becomes 25%. The part goes on top because you are measuring 45 against the full 180. If the result looks like 400%, you probably inverted the two numbers.

faqs.question: How do I find the whole when I know the part and the percentage?
faqs.answer: Convert the percentage to a decimal and divide the part by it. If 12 is 30% of a number, then 12 ÷ 0.30 = 40. Check the result by multiplying back: 0.30 × 40 = 12. Dividing by 30 instead of 0.30 is the usual error and produces an answer that is far too small.

faqs.question: Can a percentage be greater than 100?
faqs.answer: Yes. A value can be 150% of its original, meaning 1.5 times as large. If a target was 80 and actual output reached 200, that is 250% of target. Rates above 100% are common in growth, completion and comparison contexts. They only become impossible when the base itself is a fixed maximum.

faqs.question: Why does 15% of 80 equal 80% of 15?
faqs.answer: Both expressions multiply the same two numbers after converting the rate to a decimal: 0.15 × 80 and 0.80 × 15 both equal 12. Multiplication does not care which factor comes first. This lets you flip awkward percentages into easier ones, such as turning 4% of 75 into 75% of 4.

faqs.question: What is the difference between percent of a number and percentage change?
faqs.answer: Percent of a number finds a slice of a fixed base, like 18% of 250. Percentage change compares an old value with a new one, like 240 growing to 300, which is 25% growth. The change formula divides by the starting value, so the direction and the base both matter.

title: Percentage Increase and Decrease: Formula & Examples
description: Percentage increase and decrease with the formula, worked examples, reverse checks and the mistakes that flip the base. Includes a free calculator.
html:
Revenue moved from 1,200 to 1,500. A supplier raised a price from 480 to 540. Your electricity bill fell from 2,400 to 1,800. Each sentence describes a change, and each one needs the same three-step calculation. The only difference is whether the answer carries a positive or negative sign.

Percentage increase and decrease is where otherwise careful people mix up the starting point. The formula is short, but the base matters more than the subtraction. This guide, part of the percentage calculator guide, works through the arithmetic, shows why a rise and a fall of the same rate do not cancel, and gives you a clean way to check the result with the percentage calculator.

The percentage change formula

Percentage change compares a new value with an old value:

Percentage change = ((New − Old) ÷ Old) × 100

Subtract the old value from the new one, divide by the old value, then multiply by 100. If the result is positive, the value increased. If it is negative, the value decreased. The old value is always the denominator because it represents the starting point — the 100% baseline.

From 240 to 300, the gap is 300 − 240 = 60. Divide by the old value: 60 ÷ 240 = 0.25. Multiply by 100: 25%. The value grew by a quarter of where it started.

From 300 to 240, the gap is 240 − 300 = −60. Divide by the old value: −60 ÷ 300 = −0.20. Multiply by 100: −20%. Same absolute gap, different base, different percentage. That is not a mathematical inconsistency; it is the whole point of measuring change relative to a starting point.

When the old value is zero, the formula breaks because division by zero is undefined. Going from 0 to 50 cannot be expressed as a percentage increase of the starting point. Describe it as “started from zero” and report the absolute change instead.

Worked examples, including one decrease

Example 1: Sales rose from 1,200 to 1,500. New minus old is 1,500 − 1,200 = 300. Divide by old: 300 ÷ 1,200 = 0.25. Multiply by 100: 25% increase. Check by applying the rate forward: 1,200 × 1.25 = 1,500.

Example 2: A price fell from 480 to 420. The gap is 420 − 480 = −60. Divide by the old price: −60 ÷ 480 = −0.125. Multiply by 100: 12.5% decrease. Check by applying the rate: 480 × (1 − 0.125) = 480 × 0.875 = 420.

Example 3: A salary went from 48,000 to 55,200. The increase is 7,200. Divide by 48,000: 7,200 ÷ 48,000 = 0.15. Multiply by 100: 15% raise. Check: 48,000 × 1.15 = 55,200.

Example 4: Output dropped from 80 to 68. The change is −12. Divide by 80: −12 ÷ 80 = −0.15. Multiply by 100: 15% decrease. The new value is 85% of the old one, which is another way to see the same result.

ChangeOld valueNew valueArithmeticResult
Sales growth1,2001,500300 ÷ 1,200 × 100+25%
Price drop480420−60 ÷ 480 × 100−12.5%
Salary raise48,00055,2007,200 ÷ 48,000 × 100+15%
Output fall8068−12 ÷ 80 × 100−15%
Round trip300240−60 ÷ 300 × 100−20%

Why reversing a change is not symmetric

Start with 100. A 20% increase gives 120. Now apply a 20% decrease to 120: 120 × 0.80 = 96. You are four short of where you began, even though the rate looks identical in both directions.

The reason is that the second calculation uses 120 as its base, not 100. Twenty percent of 120 is 24, while twenty percent of 100 is 20. The fall removes a larger slice than the rise added. To get from 120 back to 100, you need a decrease of 20 ÷ 120 = 16.67%, not 20%.

The same logic applies to any pair of opposite changes. A 15% increase followed by a 15% decrease leaves 100 × 1.15 × 0.85 = 97.75, a net loss of 2.25%. A 50% increase followed by a 50% decrease leaves 75, a net loss of 25%. The gap grows as the rate grows, and it never disappears unless one of the rates is zero.

This is why “we raised prices 10%, then offered a 10% discount” does not restore the original price. The discount applies to the higher price. If the original was 200, the raise takes it to 220, and a 10% discount takes 22 off, leaving 198. The customer pays 1% less than before, and the business earns 1% less per unit before costs.

To reverse a known percentage change, divide by the factor rather than subtracting the rate. If a value rose 20% to 120, the original is 120 ÷ 1.20 = 100. If it fell 20% to 80, the original is 80 ÷ 0.80 = 100. The reverse percentage guide covers the division in more detail.

Where percentage change helps in business

Percentage change is useful because it normalizes movement across different-sized numbers. A 300-unit increase means something different for a shop selling 1,000 units a month than for one selling 10,000. As percentages, those are 30% and 3%.

  • Revenue and volume: compare this month with the same month last year, not with an arbitrary earlier period. Seasonal businesses can post a huge “increase” in December that disappears in January.
  • Cost control: a supplier quote moving from 480 to 420 is a 12.5% reduction. Put that next to the volume you buy to see the absolute saving.
  • Pricing: a 10% price rise does not produce a 10% profit rise if unit costs stay fixed. Profit changes by a larger percentage because the base is smaller. Model the profit line separately.
  • Conversion rates: moving from 2% to 3% is a 1-point gain and a 50% relative increase. Both descriptions are accurate, but they answer different questions.

Keep the old and new values in the same units and the same scope. Comparing a partial month with a full month, or revenue including tax with revenue excluding tax, produces a percentage that looks precise and means nothing. Write the definition down before the number travels into a slide.

For price cuts specifically, the discount and sale price guide shows how the same percentage affects the customer’s total and the seller’s margin. A 20% discount is a 20% revenue cut on that unit, but it can be a much larger percentage cut to profit.

Mistakes that flip the sign or the size

  1. Dividing by the new value. Change is measured against the old value. Using the new value makes an increase look smaller and a decrease look larger. From 80 to 100, the correct change is 20 ÷ 80 = 25%, not 20%.
  2. Dropping the negative sign. A fall from 480 to 420 is −12.5%, not +12.5%. The sign carries the direction. If the context already says “decrease,” you can report the magnitude, but do not mix the two conventions in one table.
  3. Adding and subtracting rates. A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall is not 0%. Multiply the factors: 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, a 1% net decrease.
  4. Confusing percentage points with percent. A rate moving from 4% to 5% is 1 point and a 25% relative increase. Decide which one your audience needs.
  5. Averaging percentages without weighting. A 10% rise in one product and a 50% rise in another do not average to 30% unless both products have the same base. Weight by the underlying values.
  6. Using a zero base. Change from zero is undefined. Report the absolute movement and say so.

A quick check: apply your answer back to the old value. If the old value was 480 and you calculated a 12.5% decrease, then 480 × 0.875 should equal 420. If it does not, the base or the sign is wrong. This one step catches more errors than rereading the formula.

Using the percentage calculator for change

The percentage calculator has a change view that takes the old value and the new value in that order. Enter 1,200 as old and 1,500 as new, and it returns +25% with the formula shown. Swap the entries and you get −16.67%, which is the correct change from 1,500 down to 1,200 — not a bug.

  1. Label the starting value as old. This is the number that represents 100%.
  2. Label the ending value as new. Order matters; reversing the two changes the denominator.
  3. Read the percentage and the sign. Positive means growth, negative means decline.
  4. Check by multiplying the old value by 1 plus the rate. The result should match the new value.

If you need a neutral comparison where neither value is a baseline, use the difference view instead. Comparing 60 with 80 gives a 28.57% difference either way, while change gives +33.33% from 60 to 80 and −25% from 80 to 60. The percentage difference guide explains when that symmetry is the right choice.

Test a change: open the percentage calculator, enter your old and new values, and confirm the sign before you put the number in a report. The calculation stays on your device.

faqs.question: What is the formula for percentage increase?
faqs.answer: Subtract the old value from the new value, divide the difference by the old value, then multiply by 100. Going from 1,200 to 1,500 gives 300 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 25%. The old value stays in the denominator because it is the starting baseline.

faqs.question: Why is a 20% rise followed by a 20% fall not zero?
faqs.answer: The fall is calculated on the larger value. Start at 100, rise to 120, then take 20% of 120, which is 24, leaving 96. The net change is −4%. To return to 100 from 120, the required fall is 20 ÷ 120 = 16.67%, not 20%.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a percentage decrease?
faqs.answer: Use the same formula with the new value below the old one. A price falling from 480 to 420 has a change of −60, and −60 ÷ 480 × 100 = −12.5%. The negative sign means decrease. You can report the magnitude as 12.5% if the direction is already stated.

faqs.question: Can I reverse a percentage increase by subtracting the same rate?
faqs.answer: No. If a value rose 20% to 120, subtracting 20% of 120 removes 24 and leaves 96. Divide by 1.20 instead: 120 ÷ 1.20 = 100. For a decrease, divide by one minus the rate, so a value that fell 20% to 80 came from 80 ÷ 0.80 = 100.

faqs.question: What does a 100% increase mean?
faqs.answer: A 100% increase doubles the value. Going from 45 to 90 is a 100% rise. A 200% increase triples it, taking 45 to 135. Percentages above 100 are valid for growth, but they often get confused with “100% of,” which means the original amount, not double.

faqs.question: Why is change from zero undefined?
faqs.answer: The formula divides by the old value, and division by zero has no finite result. Moving from 0 to 50 cannot be expressed as a percentage increase of the starting point. Report the absolute change of 50 and note that the baseline was zero instead of inventing a percentage.

title: Discount Calculator: Sale Price and Savings Explained
description: Use a discount calculator to find sale price, savings and tax after markdown, including stacked coupons and reverse checks. Worked examples inside.
html:
A clearance tag says 30% off. A coupon adds another 10%. Tax waits at checkout. By the time the receipt prints, the number on screen and the number in your head have drifted apart. A discount calculator exists to close that gap: it turns a list price and a rate into the amount you save, the amount you pay, and the tax that follows.

This guide, part of the percentage calculator guide, covers the arithmetic behind sale prices, including stacked offers, tax order and the reverse question every shopper eventually asks. Use the discount calculator to check your own cart as you read.

The discount formula in one line

A discount is a percentage of the original price. The saving is list price × rate ÷ 100. The sale price is list price − saving. The shortcut is to multiply by the complement: paying 75% of the price is the same as taking 25% off.

For a 120 item at 25% off, the saving is 120 × 0.25 = 30. The sale price is 120 − 30 = 90. The complement method gives 120 × 0.75 = 90 directly. Both routes are correct because the discount and the amount you pay add up to 100% of the original.

The formula assumes the discount applies to the full list price. If a product is already reduced, or if the coupon excludes certain items, the base changes. Read the terms before multiplying. A “25% off” sign attached to a price that was quietly raised last week is a discount relative to the new tag, not the old one.

Two worked examples with the arithmetic shown

Example 1: 120 at 25% off. Convert the rate to 0.25. Saving = 120 × 0.25 = 30. Sale price = 120 − 30 = 90. Check with the complement: 120 × 0.75 = 90. If the local sales tax is 8%, tax is calculated on the sale price: 90 × 0.08 = 7.20, so the total is 97.20. Charging tax on 120 instead would add 9.60 and produce 99.60, a 2.40 overcharge.

Example 2: 249 at 30% off. Saving = 249 × 0.30 = 74.70. Sale price = 249 − 74.70 = 174.30. Check: 249 × 0.70 = 174.30. With 8% tax, the tax is 174.30 × 0.08 = 13.944, which rounds to 13.94, and the total is 188.24. If the register shows 188.25, it rounded the tax differently; a one-cent difference is normal and not a reason to abandon the calculation.

List priceDiscountYou saveSale priceWith 8% tax
12025%30.0090.0097.20
24930%74.70174.30188.24
8015%12.0068.0073.44
10020% then 10%28.0072.0077.76

Stacked discounts multiply, they do not add

“20% off, then an extra 10% off” is the most misunderstood phrase in retail. It does not mean 30% off. The first discount applies to 100, taking it to 80. The second applies to 80, taking another 8 off and leaving 72. The total saving is 28, which is 28% of the original.

Multiplying the factors shows why: 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72. You pay 72% of the list price, so the effective discount is 28%. If the order is reversed — 10% first, then 20% — the result is the same: 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.72. Multiplication is commutative, so the sequence does not change the final price when both rates apply to the running balance.

Three discounts behave the same way. 20%, then 10%, then 5% gives 0.80 × 0.90 × 0.95 = 0.684, an effective 31.6% off. The headline rates add to 35%, but the actual saving is smaller because each cut is calculated on a smaller base.

Fixed-amount coupons work differently. A 20 coupon on a 100 order is a 20% discount only at that exact price. On a 50 order, the same coupon is 40% off, and many stores set a minimum spend to prevent that. When a coupon and a percentage discount combine, apply the rules in the order the store specifies; the result is not always the same as applying them in the order that looks convenient.

Tax usually comes after the discount

In most retail systems, sales tax or GST is calculated on the discounted price, not the original tag. The 90 sale price from the first example attracts 8% tax of 7.20, for 97.20 total. That order is standard because the customer never pays the undiscounted amount.

India’s GST follows the same principle for a straightforward markdown: discount first, tax on the net amount. A 4,800 service with 18% GST becomes 5,664. If a 10% discount is applied first, the taxable value falls to 4,320, the GST becomes 777.60, and the total is 5,097.60. Applying the discount after tax would give a different, usually incorrect, result.

Some situations complicate the order. Manufacturer rebates may arrive after the sale and do not reduce the taxable price at checkout. Shipping charges may be taxed separately. A “free gift” with a purchase can have its own tax treatment. When the receipt matters for a business expense, keep the tax invoice and check the taxable value rather than reconstructing it from the total.

For quick checks, a GST calculator can add tax to a net figure or extract it from a gross figure. The discount tool handles the markdown; the tax tool handles the rate. Keeping the two steps separate makes it easier to see which number changed. This is general information, not tax advice.

Comparing two offers without getting fooled

A percentage is only one part of the cost. Shipping, tax, membership requirements and return fees can reverse the ranking of two deals that look obvious at first glance.

  • Normalize to the final amount. Compare what leaves your account, including tax and shipping, not the headline discount.
  • Check the minimum spend. A 20% coupon that requires a 150 purchase can cost more than it saves if you only needed a 60 item.
  • Separate cashback from discount. A 20% cashback offer returns money later; a 20% discount reduces the amount you pay now. If the cashback is capped or expires, the effective saving is lower.
  • Watch the base. A 30% discount on a marked-up price can be worse than a 15% discount on a lower price. Compare final totals, not rates.
  • Account for returns. If you might return the item, check whether the refund is based on the discounted price and whether the original shipping is returned.

Suppose Store A sells a 120 item at 25% off with 8% tax and free shipping: total 97.20. Store B sells the same item for 110 with 15% off and 8% tax but charges 6 shipping: sale 93.50, tax 7.48, total 106.98. Store A wins even though Store B’s sticker is lower. The only fair comparison is the final line.

For a business, the same logic applies to promotional pricing. A discount reduces revenue per unit, and the margin falls faster than the price. The markup vs margin guide shows how a 10% markdown can remove a much larger share of profit. The percentage increase and decrease guide covers the reverse calculation when you know the sale price and need the original.

Using the discount calculator step by step

The discount calculator takes a list price and a discount rate, then returns the saving, the sale price and an optional tax-inclusive total. It also handles a second discount for stacked offers.

  1. Enter the price on the tag, not the price you remember from last month.
  2. Enter the first discount rate. If the offer says “extra 10% at checkout,” add that as a second stage rather than combining the rates.
  3. Add the tax rate only if you want the out-the-door total. Leave it at zero for a pre-tax comparison.
  4. Read the saving and the sale price, then check the arithmetic with the complement method: sale = list × (1 − rate).

To reverse a sale price, divide by the complement. A 68 price after 15% off means the original was 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80. Adding 15% to 68 gives 78.20, which is not the original and will make a return or price-match conversation confusing. The reverse percentage method is the same one used for tax extraction: divide by the factor that produced the final number.

Price your cart: open the discount calculator, enter the list price, the markdown and any tax, and compare the final total with the tag. No signup, and the numbers stay on your device.

faqs.question: How do I calculate 25% off a price?
faqs.answer: Multiply the list price by 0.25 to get the saving, then subtract it. For 120, the saving is 30 and the sale price is 90. The faster route is to multiply by 0.75, the complement of the discount. Both methods give the same answer before tax.

faqs.question: Why is 20% off then 10% off not 30% off?
faqs.answer: Each discount applies to the remaining balance, not the original price. On 100, the first cut leaves 80 and the second takes 8 more, leaving 72. The total saving is 28, or 28% of the list price. Multiplying 0.80 by 0.90 gives the same 0.72 factor.

faqs.question: Is tax calculated before or after a discount?
faqs.answer: In most retail and GST systems, tax is calculated on the discounted price. A 90 sale price with 8% tax adds 7.20 for a 97.20 total. Taxing the original 120 would overstate the bill because the customer never pays that amount. Confirm unusual cases with the seller or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I find the original price from a sale price?
faqs.answer: Divide the sale price by one minus the discount rate. If 68 is the price after 15% off, the original is 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80. Do not add 15% to 68, which gives 78.20. The division reverses the multiplication that produced the sale price.

faqs.question: Is cashback the same as a discount?
faqs.answer: No. A discount reduces what you pay at checkout. Cashback returns money later, often with conditions, caps or expiry dates. A 20% cashback offer on 100 returns 20 eventually, while a 20% discount takes 20 off immediately. If the cashback is capped at 10, the effective saving is only 10%.

faqs.question: How do I compare a percentage discount with a fixed coupon?
