faqs.answer: Convert both offers to the final amount you pay for the same basket. A 25% discount on 120 saves 30; a fixed 35 coupon saves 35 on that basket, so the coupon is better there. On a 250 basket, the percentage saves 62.50 and wins. Compare totals, not headline rates.

title: Markup vs Margin: Formula, Examples & Pricing
description: Markup vs margin explained with formulas, a comparison table and worked pricing examples, the discount trap and a free margin calculator.
html:
Two sellers buy the same item for 60. One prices it at 100 and says, “That is a 66.7% markup.” The other looks at the same numbers and says, “That is a 40% margin.” Both statements are correct. They are describing different ratios, and confusing them is one of the fastest ways to misprice a product.

This guide separates markup from margin, shows the conversion formulas, and works through target pricing and discount damage. Keep the profit margin calculator nearby if you want to test your own cost and price.

What markup and margin each measure

Profit is the same number in both calculations: selling price minus cost. What changes is the denominator. Margin divides profit by revenue, while markup divides profit by cost.

Margin answers a simple question: of every rupee or dollar that comes in, how much is left after the direct cost of the item? A 40% margin means 40% of the selling price is gross profit and 60% covers the cost. It is the ratio retailers usually quote when they talk about the health of a product line.

Markup answers a different question: how much was added on top of the cost? A 66.7% markup means the price is 1.667 times the cost. It is the ratio a contractor or wholesaler often uses when building a quote from a cost sheet.

Neither ratio is more honest. They are two views of the same transaction. The trouble starts when someone sets a price using markup and then reports the result as margin, or when a target margin gets translated into the wrong multiplier. A 50% markup does not produce a 50% margin; it produces a 33.3% margin.

The formulas, side by side

Let profit equal price minus cost. Then:

  • Margin % = (Profit ÷ Price) × 100
  • Markup % = (Profit ÷ Cost) × 100
  • Price from margin = Cost ÷ (1 − Margin)
  • Price from markup = Cost × (1 + Markup)

To convert one ratio into the other, use the relationship between price and cost. Since price = cost + profit, markup is profit divided by cost, and margin is profit divided by (cost + profit). A 66.67% markup becomes 66.67 ÷ 166.67 = 40% margin. A 40% margin becomes 40 ÷ 60 = 66.67% markup.

The general conversions are Margin = Markup ÷ (1 + Markup) and Markup = Margin ÷ (1 − Margin), with both rates written as decimals. These are worth memorizing if you move between a cost sheet and a price list. They save you from guessing which multiplier the other person used.

CostPriceProfitMarginMarkup
601004040%66.67%
60903033.33%50%
45753040%66.67%
801204033.33%50%
801608050%100%

Worked examples with the arithmetic shown

Example 1: Cost 60, price 100. Profit = 100 − 60 = 40. Margin = 40 ÷ 100 × 100 = 40%. Markup = 40 ÷ 60 × 100 = 66.67%. The price is 1.667 times the cost, and 40% of the price is profit.

Example 2: Cost 45, price 75. Profit = 75 − 45 = 30. Margin = 30 ÷ 75 × 100 = 40%. Markup = 30 ÷ 45 × 100 = 66.67%. Different cost and price, same ratios, because both numbers moved by the same proportion. This is a useful check: if cost and price both double, margin and markup stay the same even though the absolute profit doubles.

Example 3: A 30% discount on the 60-cost, 100-price item. The new price is 70. Profit falls to 70 − 60 = 10. Margin is 10 ÷ 70 × 100 = 14.29%. Markup is 10 ÷ 60 × 100 = 16.67%. A discount that looks like 30% of the price removed 75% of the profit and 64.3% of the original margin in relative terms. This is why discounting a low-margin item is dangerous: the price can still look healthy while the profit nearly disappears.

Example 4: Cost 80, target margin 50%. Price = 80 ÷ (1 − 0.50) = 160. Profit = 80, markup = 80 ÷ 80 = 100%. If you had used a 50% markup instead, the price would be 80 × 1.50 = 120, with a profit of 40 and a margin of 33.33%. The same “50%” label produces two very different prices.

Pricing from a target margin

Most pricing decisions start with a margin target, not a markup target. A business wants to keep a certain share of revenue after direct costs, then work backward to a price. The formula is price = cost ÷ (1 − margin). The subtraction is important: a 40% margin means cost is 60% of price, so dividing cost by 0.60 gives the price.

If the cost is 60 and the target margin is 40%, the price is 60 ÷ 0.60 = 100. If the target is 50%, the price is 60 ÷ 0.50 = 120. If the target is 25%, the price is 60 ÷ 0.75 = 80. Notice how quickly the required price rises as the target margin approaches 100%. A 90% margin target would require 60 ÷ 0.10 = 600, which may be impossible in a competitive market.

To go the other way, from a target markup, multiply cost by 1.5 for a 50% markup: 60 × 1.50 = 90. The resulting margin is 30 ÷ 90 = 33.33%. A 100% markup gives 120 and a 50% margin. The markup number will always be larger than the margin number for a profitable sale, and the gap widens as the rates rise.

Use the same basis for every product in a comparison. If one spreadsheet column is margin and another is markup, the totals will not reconcile. Label the column, state the formula in the header, and convert before ranking products. The GST calculator can help separate tax from revenue if your prices include GST, since margin should be calculated on the tax-exclusive selling price. This is general information, not financial advice.

Why discounts hit margin harder than they look

Discounts reduce revenue, but cost stays the same. That leverage makes margin fall faster than price. Take the 60-cost item at 100 with a 40% margin. A 10% discount lowers the price to 90, profit to 30, and margin to 33.33%. The price fell 10%, but profit fell 25% and margin fell 6.67 percentage points.

At a 20% discount, the price is 80, profit is 20, and margin is 25%. Profit has halved. At 30% off, the price is 70, profit is 10, and margin is 14.29%. At 40% off, the price equals the cost and profit is zero. Every additional point of discount removes a larger share of the remaining profit.

Volume has to compensate. After the 10% discount, the seller earns 30 per unit instead of 40. To keep the same total gross profit, they need 40 ÷ 30 = 1.333, or 33.3% more units. After the 20% discount, they need 40 ÷ 20 = 2, or twice the volume. Whether that volume is achievable depends on demand, capacity and the cost of acquiring more customers, which is why a discount should be modeled before it is launched.

This is the same arithmetic covered in the discount and sale price guide, viewed from the seller’s side. The customer sees the sale price; the seller needs to see the profit line. A promotion that raises revenue can still lower gross profit if the margin falls faster than volume rises.

Using the profit margin calculator

The profit margin calculator takes a unit cost and a selling price, then returns profit, margin and markup together. Seeing all three numbers side by side is the quickest way to catch a label error.

  1. Enter the fully loaded direct cost per unit: materials, labor and packaging. Leave overhead for a separate net-margin calculation.
  2. Enter the tax-exclusive selling price. If your price includes GST or sales tax, remove the tax first so the margin is not flattered by money you collect on behalf of the government.
  3. Read the profit, margin and markup. Check that the margin is profit ÷ price and the markup is profit ÷ cost.
  4. Change the price by a few units and watch the margin move. A small price change can produce a much larger percentage change in profit.

For a target-margin price, divide cost by one minus the target. For a target-markup price, add the markup rate to 1 and multiply by cost. Compare the two results before choosing a list price, and remember that discounts, payment fees, shipping and returns all come out of the gross margin afterward. The percentage calculator guide connects these pricing ratios to the broader formulas for change, tax and percentage points.

Check your pricing: open the profit margin calculator, enter cost and price, and compare margin with markup before you publish the number. The calculation runs locally with no signup.

faqs.question: What is the difference between markup and margin?
faqs.answer: Margin divides profit by selling price; markup divides the same profit by cost. A 60 cost sold at 100 yields 40 profit, which is a 40% margin and a 66.67% markup. Margin shows the share of revenue retained, while markup shows the uplift applied to cost.

faqs.question: How do I convert markup to margin?
faqs.answer: Add 1 to the markup as a decimal, then divide. A 66.67% markup is 0.6667 ÷ 1.6667 = 0.40, or 40% margin. For a 50% markup, 0.50 ÷ 1.50 = 0.3333, or 33.33% margin. The markup number is always larger when there is a profit.

faqs.question: How do I price for a 40% margin?
faqs.answer: Divide the cost by one minus the target margin. If the cost is 60, the price is 60 ÷ 0.60 = 100. A 50% target would require 60 ÷ 0.50 = 120. Do not multiply cost by 1.40, which produces 84 and only a 28.57% margin.

faqs.question: Why does a 50% markup give only a 33% margin?
faqs.answer: A 50% markup on 60 adds 30, producing a 90 price. Profit of 30 divided by the 90 price is 33.33%. The markup is measured against the smaller cost base, while margin is measured against the larger price base. The two rates cannot be equal unless profit is zero.

faqs.question: How much does a 10% discount reduce margin?
faqs.answer: On a 60-cost, 100-price item, a 10% discount lowers the price to 90 and profit to 30. Margin falls from 40% to 33.33%, a drop of 6.67 percentage points. Profit falls 25% in dollar terms, so volume would need to rise 33.3% to recover the same gross profit.

faqs.question: Should I use margin or markup for pricing?
faqs.answer: Use margin when you need to know how much of each sales dollar survives after direct cost, especially if you offer discounts or pay sales commissions. Use markup when building a price from a cost sheet or quote. Whichever you choose, label it clearly and convert before comparing products.

title: Percentage Difference vs Change: When to Use Each
description: Percentage difference vs change: formulas, a comparison table and worked examples for 60 vs 80 and revenue growth. Use the right measure.
html:
Two numbers move from 60 to 80. One report calls that a 33.33% increase; another calls it a 28.57% difference. Both are right because they answer different questions. Percentage change measures movement from a known starting point. Percentage difference measures the gap between two peers when neither value is the baseline. Swap the order and change flips from +33.33% to −25%, while difference stays 28.57%. This guide gives both formulas, runs them on identical numbers, and shows which one belongs in a KPI report, a lab comparison, or a price check.

Part of the Percentage Calculator Guide. Run both views in the free percentage calculator, and read percentage increase and decrease when direction is the story.

The two formulas side by side

Percentage change answers a before-and-after question. You need an old value and a new value, and the old value is the denominator: change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. From 60 to 80, the gap is 20, the baseline is 60, so the result is 20 ÷ 60 = 0.3333, or +33.33%. Reverse the direction and the baseline becomes 80: (60 − 80) ÷ 80 = −25%. The sign matters because the movement has a direction.

Percentage difference answers a peer-to-peer question. There is no old or new, only A and B, and the denominator is their average: difference = |A − B| ÷ ((A + B) ÷ 2) × 100. For 60 and 80, the gap is 20, the mean is 70, so the result is 20 ÷ 70 = 0.2857, or 28.57%. Enter 80 and 60 instead and the numerator stays 20 while the denominator stays 70. The answer does not move.

That average denominator is the whole trick. Dividing by one of the values would reintroduce a baseline and destroy symmetry. Dividing by the midpoint treats the two values as equal citizens, which is exactly what you want when comparing two suppliers' quotes, two labs' readings, or two regions' rates. The cost is interpretive: a symmetric number cannot tell you whether something grew or shrank, so it should never replace change in a trend report.

Memory hook: change asks “how far did we travel from where we started?” Difference asks “how far apart are these two values?” One has a starting line; the other does not.

Same numbers, different answers

Example 1 — 60 and 80

Forward change: (80 − 60) ÷ 60 × 100 = 20 ÷ 60 × 100 = 33.33%. Backward change: (60 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = −20 ÷ 80 × 100 = −25%. Percentage difference: |60 − 80| ÷ ((60 + 80) ÷ 2) × 100 = 20 ÷ 70 × 100 = 28.57%. Notice that 28.57% is not the average of +33.33% and −25%; that average would be 4.17%, which answers nothing useful. Difference has its own denominator, so it deserves its own line in your spreadsheet.

Example 2 — revenue from $150,000 to $180,000

Change: (180,000 − 150,000) ÷ 150,000 × 100 = 30,000 ÷ 150,000 × 100 = 20%. Difference: |180,000 − 150,000| ÷ ((180,000 + 150,000) ÷ 2) × 100 = 30,000 ÷ 165,000 × 100 = 18.18%. The difference is smaller than the change because the average, $165,000, is larger than the old value, $150,000. If you report “18.18% difference” in a growth review, a reader may assume growth stalled; if you report “20% growth,” you have correctly named the baseline.

Example 3 — 120 planned hours vs 150 actual hours

Change against the plan: (150 − 120) ÷ 120 × 100 = 30 ÷ 120 × 100 = 25% over budget. Difference: |150 − 120| ÷ ((150 + 120) ÷ 2) × 100 = 30 ÷ 135 × 100 = 22.22%. If the plan is authoritative, 25% is the honest number. If you are comparing two teams' estimates and neither is the official baseline, 22.22% is the fairer gap. The arithmetic is similar; the story is not.

When to use each

The choice follows from the question, not from which formula looks more familiar. Use change when one value is genuinely the starting point and the other is the result. Use difference when the two values are peers and either order should produce the same answer.

Question you are answeringMeasureFormulaResult for 60 and 80
How much did it grow or fall from the old value?Percentage change(new − old) ÷ old × 100+33.33% forward, −25% backward
How far apart are two peers with no baseline?Percentage difference|A − B| ÷ mean × 10028.57% either order
What part of the whole is this?Percentage sharepart ÷ whole × 10060 is 75% of 80
How many points did a percentage rate move?Percentage pointsend rate − start rateNot applicable to counts
  • Use change for: monthly revenue, traffic this quarter vs last, a price before and after a known increase, weight lost from a starting weight, or any KPI where the earlier period is the reference.
  • Use difference for: two suppliers' quotes, two labs measuring the same sample, two cities' rates, two ad variants with no control, or any comparison where neither side is the official baseline.
  • Use neither for: “what percent of the total is this?” and “how many percentage points did the rate move?” Those are separate calculations, and forcing them into a change-or-difference frame is how reports end up with the wrong label.

Traps: order, zero and signed values

Order changes the answer for change, never for difference. If someone presents a change without saying which value is old, the number is incomplete. From 80 to 60 is a 25% fall; from 60 to 80 is a 33.33% rise. The same pair carries two different change values, which is why press releases often choose the flattering direction.

Zero breaks change. If old = 0, the formula divides by zero and the result is undefined. Going from 0 to 50 is not “infinity percent growth” in a management report; write “from zero” and show the absolute increase. Percentage difference handles 0 vs 50: |0 − 50| ÷ 25 × 100 = 200%. If both values are zero, the denominator is also zero, so report 0 rather than an error.

Negative values need care. When one value is negative, the mean denominator can shrink toward zero and create a huge, misleading percentage. A profit of −$10,000 turning into +$10,000 is a $20,000 swing, but a percentage built on a mean near zero is not meaningful. For signed quantities such as profit and loss, compare absolute changes or declare a fixed baseline instead of forcing the formula.

Percent is not a percentage point. A rate moving from 4% to 5% rose 1 percentage point, which is a 25% relative increase. The formulas above operate on the underlying numbers; the percentage-point distinction applies when the numbers themselves are rates. Keep the two vocabularies separate and half the confusing headlines disappear.

Label every number in the report. “Sales rose 20%” and “the two regions differ by 18.18%” are different claims. A reader who cannot see the denominator cannot reproduce either figure, so pair each percentage with the two inputs that produced it.

Use the calculator without mixing modes

The percentage calculator separates the two questions into different views, which is the main defense against accidental mode-mixing. Work through this sequence once and the labels become obvious:

  1. Open the tool and choose the Difference view. Enter 60 and 80 in either field.
  2. Read 28.57% with the formula shown. Swap the two inputs; the result should stay 28.57%.
  3. Switch to the Change view for a timeline. Enter old 150,000 and new 180,000 to get +20%.
  4. Reverse the pair to get −16.67%. If that feels wrong, the baseline changed, not the arithmetic.
Try it: open the percentage calculator, run 60 vs 80 in Difference, then run 150 to 180 in Change. For the full set of percent formulas and use cases, start with the Percentage Calculator Guide.

faqs.question: What is the formula for percentage difference?
faqs.answer: Percentage difference equals the absolute gap between two values divided by their average, then multiplied by 100. For 60 and 80: |60 − 80| ÷ ((60 + 80) ÷ 2) × 100 = 20 ÷ 70 × 100 = 28.57%. The absolute value makes the result symmetric, so entering the values in either order gives the same 28.57%.

faqs.question: Why is percentage difference symmetric?
faqs.answer: It uses the mean of the two values as the denominator instead of picking one value as the baseline. The gap between 60 and 80 is 20 either way, and their mean is 70 either way, so the result is 28.57% whichever value you type first. That neutrality suits peer comparisons such as two quotes, two lab readings or two regions.

faqs.question: When should I use percentage change instead?
faqs.answer: Use percentage change whenever one value is genuinely the starting point and the other is the result. Revenue moving from $150,000 to $180,000 is (180,000 − 150,000) ÷ 150,000 × 100 = 20% growth. The same pair read backward is a 16.67% decline, which is why a change figure must always name its baseline.

faqs.question: Can percentage difference be larger than percentage change?
faqs.answer: Yes. If the average of the two values is smaller than the baseline used for change, the difference will be larger. Comparing 100 with 50 gives a 50% change downward but a 66.67% difference, because the gap of 50 is divided by the mean of 75 rather than by 100. The denominators, not the gap, create the gap between the answers.

faqs.question: What happens if one of the values is zero?
faqs.answer: Percentage change is undefined when the old value is zero because the formula divides by zero. Percentage difference still works for 0 and 50: the gap is 50 and the mean is 25, so the difference is 200%. If both values are zero, the difference is 0 rather than an error; report that no gap exists.

faqs.question: Should I use percentage difference to compare prices?
faqs.answer: Only when neither price is the reference. Comparing two stores' prices for the same item is a peer comparison, so difference is defensible. Measuring a price before and after a known discount is a change question, so use change and keep the original price as the baseline. Label the measure in the report so readers know which question was asked.

title: Reverse Percentage: Find the Original Price or Number
description: Reverse percentage calculator method: find the original price before a discount, remove GST from a total and undo a raise with worked examples.

toc.text: Reverse GST and reverse a raise

html:
A jacket marked 20% off costs $72. What was the original price? The tempting move is to add 20% to $72 and call it $86.40. That is wrong, and the receipt makes the error easy to see: 20% of $90 is $18, and $90 − $18 = $72. The original was $90. Reverse percentage undoes a percentage change by dividing, not by adding the rate back. This guide covers the formula for discounts, GST-inclusive totals and raises, with checks you can do in your head.

Part of the Percentage Calculator Guide. Run the division in the percentage calculator, see forward sale math in discount and sale price, and split inclusive tax with the GST calculator.

The reverse percentage formula

Start with the forward equation. A price after a discount is final = original × (1 − r), where r is the discount rate as a decimal. A value after an increase is final = original × (1 + r). To go backward, divide both sides by that factor:

Original after a decrease = final ÷ (1 − r). Original after an increase = final ÷ (1 + r). The rate must be a decimal in the division: 20% becomes 0.20, not 20.

For the jacket: 72 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 72 ÷ 0.80 = 90. For a salary of $56,000 after a 12% raise: 56,000 ÷ 1.12 = 50,000. The same logic works when you know a part and its share of the whole: whole = part ÷ (rate ÷ 100). If 30 is 20% of a number, the number is 30 ÷ 0.20 = 150.

The common mistake is subtracting the rate from the final value. A 20% discount is 20% of the original, not 20% of the sale price, so the final value cannot serve as the base. The error grows with the size of the rate. At 50% off, a $50 sale price implies a $100 original; subtracting 50% from $50 gives $25, which is not even close. At 10% off, the shortcut lands at $79.20 instead of $80, a small miss that still compounds across a cart.

Check forward, not backward: after finding the original, multiply it by the same factor. If 90 × 0.80 returns 72, the reverse step is correct. This one-line check catches most mistakes.

Worked example: original price before a discount

Take the $72 jacket at 20% off. The forward factor is 1 − 0.20 = 0.80. Divide: 72 ÷ 0.80 = 90. Verify: 90 × 0.20 = 18 discount, and 90 − 18 = 72. The original price was $90 and the shopper saved $18.

A second case: a desk sells for $84 after 25% off. The factor is 0.75. Divide: 84 ÷ 0.75 = 112. Verify: 112 × 0.25 = 28, and 112 − 28 = 84. The original was $112, the saving $28. Notice that $84 is 75% of $112, not 75% of some smaller number; the sale price always represents the remaining share of the original.

Stacked discounts need one extra step. Suppose a $72 final price followed a 20% clearance and then an extra 10% at the register. Each cut applies to the balance left by the previous one, so the combined factor is 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72. Divide: 72 ÷ 0.72 = 100. Verify forward: 100 → 80 after 20% off → 72 after 10% off. Dividing by 0.70 would give 102.86, which is wrong because the two rates do not add.

Final amountWhat already happenedReverse factorOriginalForward check
$7220% discount÷ 0.80$9090 × 0.80 = 72
$8425% discount÷ 0.75$112112 × 0.75 = 84
₹1,18018% GST added÷ 1.18₹1,0001,000 × 1.18 = 1,180
$56,00012% raise applied÷ 1.12$50,00050,000 × 1.12 = 56,000

One pattern to remember: a discount factor is below 1, so dividing by it makes the number larger; an increase factor is above 1, so dividing by it makes the number smaller. If your answer moves in the wrong direction, you used the wrong sign.

Reverse GST and reverse a raise

A total of ₹1,180 includes 18% GST. The base is not 1,180 − 18% of 1,180, because the tax was calculated on the pre-tax amount. Divide by 1.18: 1,180 ÷ 1.18 = ₹1,000. The tax portion is ₹180, confirmed by 1,000 × 0.18 = 180 and 1,000 + 180 = 1,180. If you subtract 18% from the inclusive total you get ₹967.60 and a tax figure of ₹212.40, both wrong.

Order matters when a discount and a tax meet. A $100 item with 20% off and then 10% sales tax ends at 100 × 0.80 × 1.10 = $88. To reverse a final $88 in one step, divide by 0.88, the product of the two factors. Dividing by 1.10 and then by 0.80 returns the same $100. What you cannot do is subtract 20% and then 10% from the final amount; percentages applied in sequence multiply, so reverse them by dividing by each factor in turn.

The same reversal handles pay raises. A salary of $56,000 after a 12% increase means the old salary was 56,000 ÷ 1.12 = $50,000. The raise was $6,000, which is 12% of $50,000. Subtracting 12% from the new salary gives $49,280 and understates the old salary by $720, because 12% of $56,000 is not the raise that was applied.

This is also where margin and markup get confused. A $100 price with a 20% margin leaves $80 of cost, so you multiply by 0.80. A $100 price built from a 20% markup on cost implies a cost of 100 ÷ 1.20 = $83.33. The words describe different bases, and reversing the wrong one puts your cost off by several dollars per unit.

Five mistakes that produce the wrong original

  • Adding the discount back to the sale price. 20% of $72 is $14.40, but the actual discount was 20% of $90, or $18. The final value is the wrong base.
  • Subtracting an included tax from the gross total. 18% of ₹1,180 is ₹212.40, while the GST inside the total is ₹180. Always divide by 1 + rate to find the base first.
  • Adding stacked rates. 20% then 10% is not 30%. The combined factor is 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, so a $72 final price points to a $100 original.
  • Rounding before the final step. A $72.99 item after 15% off gives 72.99 ÷ 0.85 = 85.8706, or $85.87. Rounding the sale price to $73 first gives $85.88, a one-cent miss; rounding the factor 0.85 to 0.9 gives $81.10, a four-dollar miss.
  • Mixing percent with percentage points. If a rate falls from 5% to 4%, that is 1 percentage point, not a 1% cut. The relative decline is 1 ÷ 5 = 20%. Reversing a points change and reversing a percent change are different operations.

A four-step workflow you can repeat

  1. Write the forward relationship: final = original × factor. Name whether the change was a discount, tax or raise.
  2. Turn the rate into a factor: 1 − r for a decrease, 1 + r for an increase. For stacked cuts, multiply the factors first.
  3. Divide the final amount by the factor. Keep at least four decimals until the last step.
  4. Multiply the answer forward by the same factor. If it does not match the final amount, recheck the rate or the direction.

For a quick second opinion, enter the original and rate in the percentage calculator and confirm the forward result. For GST-inclusive invoices, the GST calculator extracts the base and tax in one pass, which removes the temptation to subtract the rate from the gross total.

Try it: open the percentage calculator and reverse the $72 jacket at 20% off, then check ₹1,180 at 18% GST in the GST calculator. The pillar guide covers the forward formulas and the rest of the percentage family.

faqs.question: How do I reverse a percentage discount?
faqs.answer: Divide the sale price by 1 minus the discount rate. A $72 price after 20% off means 72 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 72 ÷ 0.80 = $90. Check forward: 90 × 0.20 = $18 discount, and 90 − 18 = 72. Adding 20% to $72 gives $86.40, which uses the wrong base.

faqs.question: How do I find the original amount before a percentage increase?
faqs.answer: Divide the final amount by 1 plus the rate. A $56,000 salary after a 12% raise implies 56,000 ÷ 1.12 = $50,000. The raise was 12% of $50,000, or $6,000. Subtracting 12% from the new salary would give $49,280 and understate the original by $720.

faqs.question: How do I remove GST from an inclusive total?
faqs.answer: Divide the gross total by 1 plus the GST rate. For ₹1,180 at 18%, the base is 1,180 ÷ 1.18 = ₹1,000 and the tax is ₹180. Subtracting 18% of ₹1,180 would wrongly produce ₹967.60, because the tax was charged on ₹1,000 rather than on the inclusive amount.

faqs.question: Why can't I just subtract the percentage from the final value?
faqs.answer: Because the percentage was calculated on the original value, not the final one. Twenty percent of $72 is $14.40, while the actual discount was 20% of $90, or $18. The bigger the rate, the bigger the error: at 50% off, a $50 sale price implies a $100 original, not $75.

faqs.question: How do I reverse two discounts in a row?
faqs.answer: Multiply the two remaining fractions, then divide once. A 20% discount followed by 10% leaves 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72 of the original, so $72 ÷ 0.72 = $100. Verify forward: 100 → 80 → 72. Adding the rates and dividing by 0.70 would give $102.86, which is wrong.

faqs.question: What is the reverse percentage formula in one line?
faqs.answer: Original = final ÷ (1 + r) for an increase, and original = final ÷ (1 − r) for a decrease, where r is the rate as a decimal. For a part-and-whole question, whole = part ÷ (rate ÷ 100). Multiply the answer forward by the same factor to verify it.

title: Percentage Error Formula: Measure Accuracy Correctly
description: Percentage error formula explained: absolute error, signed error and worked examples for 98 g vs 100 g. Measure accuracy without mixing terms.
html:
A kitchen scale reads 98 g for a 100 g reference weight. The percentage error is 2%. That number says the scale is low by 2% of the true mass, not by 2 g. The distinction matters because percentage error normalizes the miss against the accepted value, letting you compare a 2 g error on a 100 g sample with a 2 g error on a 10 g sample. Percentage error = |measured − true| ÷ |true| × 100. This guide shows the arithmetic, explains signed versus absolute error, and flags the cases where the formula stops being useful.

Part of the Percentage Calculator Guide. Check the division in the percentage calculator, and read percentage difference vs change before comparing two measurements without a reference.

The percentage error formula

The numerator is the absolute gap between what you measured and the accepted value. The denominator is that accepted value, also in absolute bars so a negative reference does not flip the sign. Multiply by 100 to turn the decimal relative error into a percentage:

Percentage error = |measured − true| ÷ |true| × 100. The measured value is the reading from your instrument, experiment or model. The true value is the accepted reference, the theoretical result, or the calibrated standard you are checking against. Keep the two labels fixed; swapping them changes the answer because the denominator changes.

For the scale: |98 − 100| ÷ 100 × 100 = 2 ÷ 100 × 100 = 2%. The relative error is the same fraction before the final multiplication, 0.02. If a report asks for relative error, give 0.02; if it asks for percentage error, give 2%. Mixing those two formats is a common source of a result that looks 100 times too small.

Many labs also track signed error: (measured − true) ÷ true × 100. A positive result means the measurement came in above the reference; a negative result means it came in below. The absolute version above answers “how far off,” while the signed version answers “which way and how far.” Report the absolute percentage error and state the direction in words, for example “2 g low,” to avoid ambiguity.

Worked examples with the arithmetic shown

Example 1 — 98 g against a 100 g standard

Gap: 98 − 100 = −2 g, so the absolute gap is 2 g. Divide by the true value: 2 ÷ 100 = 0.02. Multiply by 100: 0.02 × 100 = 2%. Signed error: (−2 ÷ 100) × 100 = −2%, an underestimate. The scale is accurate to within 2% at this load.

Example 2 — 52.5 cm against a 50 cm reference

Gap: 52.5 − 50 = 2.5 cm. Divide: 2.5 ÷ 50 = 0.05. Multiply: 0.05 × 100 = 5%. Signed error is +5%, an overestimate. A 2.5 cm miss is 5% of 50 cm but only 2.5% of 100 cm, which is why the denominator belongs in the sentence, not just the spreadsheet cell.

Example 3 — 9.60 m/s² against the accepted 9.81 m/s²

Gap: 9.60 − 9.81 = −0.21. Divide by the reference: 0.21 ÷ 9.81 = 0.0214067. Multiply by 100: 2.14%. The signed value is −2.14%, so the experimental result sits below the accepted gravitational acceleration. Rounding to 2.1% is reasonable; keeping 2.14067% implies precision the inputs do not support.

True valueMeasuredSigned errorAbsolute gapPercentage errorReading
100 g98 g−2.00%2 g2.00%2 g low
100 g103 g+3.00%3 g3.00%3 g high
50 cm52.5 cm+5.00%2.5 cm5.00%2.5 cm long
9.81 m/s²9.60 m/s²−2.14%0.21 m/s²2.14%0.21 low

The same absolute miss can produce very different percentages. A 2 g error is 2% of 100 g, 20% of 10 g and 0.2% of 1,000 g. Before comparing two percentage errors, confirm that the reference values are in the same range; otherwise you may be ranking the denominators rather than the instruments.

Forecasting uses the same arithmetic. If the forecast was 4,800 units and actual demand was 5,100, the percentage error is |4,800 − 5,100| ÷ 5,100 × 100 = 300 ÷ 5,100 × 100 = 5.88%. Treat actual demand as the true value, keep the sign to show whether you over- or under-forecast, and use the absolute number on the accuracy dashboard.

Percentage error measures accuracy, not precision

Accuracy is closeness to the true value. Precision is closeness of repeated measurements to each other. A scale that reads 103.0, 103.1 and 102.9 is highly precise but consistently about 3% high; a scale that reads 99.8, 100.1 and 100.0 is less consistent but more accurate on average. Percentage error catches the first problem and misses the second. Report both the error against the reference and the spread across repeats if the decision depends on measurement quality.

A single reading can also be lucky. If the true value is 100 and four readings are 98, 102, 99 and 101, the average is exactly 100, yet the individual errors are 2%, 2%, 1% and 1%. The average signed error is zero while every trial is off. When accuracy matters, calculate the absolute percentage error per trial and summarize the worst case, not just the mean.

Percentage error is not percentage difference

Percentage error requires a true value. Percentage difference does not. Take 80 and 100. If 100 is the accepted reference, the percentage error is |80 − 100| ÷ 100 × 100 = 20%. If neither number is authoritative, the percentage difference is |80 − 100| ÷ ((80 + 100) ÷ 2) × 100 = 20 ÷ 90 × 100 = 22.22%. A change from 100 to 80 is −20%. Three labels, three meanings, all from the same pair.

Use percentage error for calibration checks, lab results against a standard, model validation against ground truth, and forecast accuracy when actual demand is known. Use percentage difference for two peers with no baseline. Use percentage change for a before-and-after series. The difference vs change guide walks through the denominator choice in more detail.

When percentage error misleads

  • A true value of zero. Division is undefined, no matter how small the absolute miss. Report the absolute error instead.
  • A true value near zero. A tiny denominator inflates the percentage. An absolute miss of 0.01 on a true value of 0.02 is 50%, which can sound alarming until you see the raw units.
  • Negative reference values. The absolute denominator keeps the arithmetic valid, but the direction becomes confusing. State the convention explicitly if you publish the number.
  • Arbitrary-zero scales such as Celsius. A rise from 10°C to 20°C is not a 100% increase in heat. Convert to Kelvin before making ratio statements about temperature.
  • Peer comparisons without a reference. If neither measurement is authoritative, percentage difference is the honest measure; calling one of them “true” manufactures false confidence.

Always publish the absolute error next to the percentage. A 2% error is 20 units on a 1,000-unit batch and 0.2 units on a 10-unit batch. The percentage tells you how large the miss is relative to the reference; the absolute figure tells you how much material, money or time is actually involved.

Calculate it in four steps

  1. Subtract the true value from the measured value and drop the sign: |98 − 100| = 2.
  2. Divide by the true value: 2 ÷ 100 = 0.02.
  3. Multiply by 100: 0.02 × 100 = 2%.
  4. Record the direction separately: the reading is 2 g below the reference.

To check the division, open the percentage calculator, use the Percent view with part 2 and whole 100, and confirm it returns 2%. For a full set of percent formulas, from discounts to percentage points, start with the Percentage Calculator Guide.

Try it: open the percentage calculator and check 2 ÷ 100, then rerun it with 52.5 and 50 to confirm the 5% result. If you are comparing two measurements with no accepted reference, switch to the Difference view instead.

faqs.question: What is the percentage error formula?
faqs.answer: Percentage error = |measured − true| ÷ |true| × 100. For a reading of 98 g against a 100 g standard: |98 − 100| ÷ 100 × 100 = 2 ÷ 100 × 100 = 2%. The denominator is the accepted or reference value, not the measured value, which is why the order of the two numbers matters.

faqs.question: Should percentage error be positive or negative?
faqs.answer: The standard percentage error is positive because the numerator uses an absolute gap. If you also want direction, report signed error = (measured − true) ÷ true × 100. A reading of 98 against 100 has a signed error of −2%, meaning 2% low; 103 against 100 has +3%, meaning 3% high. State which convention you are using.

faqs.question: What counts as a good percentage error?
faqs.answer: There is no universal threshold. A 2% error may be excellent for a kitchen scale and unacceptable for a calibrated analytical balance. Judge the number against the tolerance for that instrument, test or decision, and publish the absolute error alongside it so readers can see the units involved.

faqs.question: What is the difference between percentage error and percentage difference?
faqs.answer: Percentage error divides the gap by a known true value; percentage difference divides it by the average of two peers. For 80 and 100, treating 100 as true gives a 20% error, while treating them as peers gives a 22.22% difference. Use error for accuracy checks and difference when neither measurement is the reference.

faqs.question: Can I use percentage error with a negative true value?
faqs.answer: The formula with an absolute denominator still produces a number, but the interpretation gets awkward. For a true value of −20 and a measured value of −18, the gap is 2 and the absolute percentage error is 10%. State the convention clearly, or use absolute error when the sign itself carries meaning.

faqs.question: Why is percentage error undefined when the true value is zero?
faqs.answer: Because the formula divides by the true value, and division by zero has no defined result. An absolute miss of 0.5 on a true value of zero cannot be expressed relative to zero. Report the absolute error, 0.5, and avoid presenting a percentage that suggests a ratio exists.

title: Percentage Points vs Percent: Avoid the Classic Mistake
description: Percentage points vs percent: why 4% to 5% is 1 point but a 25% rise, with a conversion table and clear worked rate examples.
html:
A savings account raises its rate from 4% to 5%. The difference is 1 percentage point. The relative increase is 25%. A headline that says the rate “rose 1%” describes something else entirely: 4% × 1.01 = 4.04%, not 5%. A percentage point is the arithmetic difference between two percentages; a percent change is the relative change from the starting percentage. The same one-point move can be a doubling at the bottom of the scale or a rounding error at the top, so the two units answer different questions.

Part of the Percentage Calculator Guide. Run the relative change in the percentage calculator, and read percentage increase and decrease for the forward formula.

The difference in one sentence

Percentage points measure the gap between two percentages. Percent measures the size of that gap relative to where you started. From 4% to 5%, the point change is 5 − 4 = 1 percentage point. The relative change is (5 − 4) ÷ 4 × 100 = 1 ÷ 4 × 100 = 25%. Both statements are correct, but they are not interchangeable.

The confusion starts because “percent” is both a unit and an operation. As a unit, 1% means one part in 100. As an operation, a “1% increase” means multiply by 1.01. A rate moving from 4% to 5% did not multiply by 1.01; it added one point. That is why the phrase “up 1%” is ambiguous and “up 1 percentage point” is not.

The gap widens as the starting rate gets smaller. From 1% to 2% is a 1-point move but a 100% relative increase, because the gap equals the entire starting value. From 50% to 51% is also a 1-point move but only a 2% relative increase. Same points, wildly different relative changes. Neither number is wrong; each becomes misleading when the other is omitted.

Worked examples with both numbers

Savings rate: 4% to 5%

Point change: 5 − 4 = 1 percentage point. Relative change: (5 − 4) ÷ 4 × 100 = 1 ÷ 4 × 100 = 25%. On a $10,000 balance, interest rises from 10,000 × 0.04 = $400 to 10,000 × 0.05 = $500. The extra $100 is 1 point of the principal and 25% more interest. Because the principal is unchanged, the relative change in interest matches the relative change in the rate.

GST rate: 18% to 20%

Point change: 20 − 18 = 2 percentage points. Relative change: 2 ÷ 18 × 100 = 11.11%. On a ₹1,000 pre-tax invoice, GST rises from ₹180 to ₹200, a ₹20 increase. Saying “GST went up 2%” would imply ₹180 × 1.02 = ₹183.60, which is not the new figure. “GST went up 2 percentage points, or 11.11%” is precise and fits in one line.

Exam pass rate: 72% to 78%

Point change: 78 − 72 = 6 percentage points. Relative change: 6 ÷ 72 × 100 = 8.33%. If 1,000 students took the exam, the number passing rose from 720 to 780, a gain of 60 students. The school improved by 6 points, while the count of passing students rose 8.33%. Both are useful; the first compares rates, the second compares the size of the change against the old rate.

Start rateEnd ratePoint changeRelative changeClear wording
4% savings5%+1 pp+25%Up 1 point, or 25% more
6% loan8%+2 pp+33.33%Up 2 points, one-third more
18% GST20%+2 pp+11.11%Up 2 points, 11.11% higher
72% pass rate78%+6 pp+8.33%Up 6 points, 8.33% better
1% fee2%+1 pp+100%Doubled, up 1 point

Why headlines get it wrong

“Unemployment rose 2%” could mean the rate moved from 5.0% to 5.1%, a relative rise of 2%, or from 5% to 7%, a rise of 2 percentage points. The first is a modest change; the second is a large one. In economics and policy writing, the convention is to use “percentage points” for the difference and “percent” for the relative change, but the rule is not universal, so the reader often has to guess.

You can remove the guesswork with a simple rule: name the unit and, where space allows, show both. “The rate rose 2 percentage points, from 5% to 7%, a 40% increase” leaves nothing to interpret. “The rate rose 2%” does not. The same discipline applies to dashboards and reports: a column labeled “change” without “pp” or “%” is an invitation to misread the number.

Avoid “2% percentage points” and “percent of a percentage point.” A point is already the unit for the difference; adding percent in front doubles the ambiguity. In tables, “pp” is a fine abbreviation if the header defines it. In prose, spell out “percentage points” the first time and use “points” after that.

When the relative number misleads

Relative change is sensitive to the starting value. A 1-point move from 1% to 2% is a 100% increase, while the same point move from 10% to 11% is a 10% increase. If you report only the percentage, the first sounds enormous and the second sounds routine, even though both add the same one point to the rate. If you report only the point change, the first looks small despite doubling the rate.

Money impact follows the point change, not the relative change. A 1-point fee increase on a $100,000 balance costs $1,000 whether the fee went from 1% to 2% or from 10% to 11%. The relative increase is 100% in the first case and 10% in the second, but the cash difference is identical. For a borrower or investor, the dollar or rupee amount is often the decision-relevant number; the percentage framing explains how dramatic the change is relative to the old rate.

Report both: “2 points, or 11.11%” is only seven words and removes the ambiguity. If you can report only one, use points when comparing rates and percent when comparing amounts or counts.

Converting between points and percent

To convert a point change into a relative percentage, divide the point change by the starting rate and multiply by 100. Three points starting from 6% is 3 ÷ 6 × 100 = 50%. The same three points starting from 30% is 3 ÷ 30 × 100 = 10%. The point change alone cannot tell you the relative change; you always need the starting rate.

To go the other way, multiply the starting rate by 1 plus the relative change. A 10% relative increase from a 20% rate gives 20 × 1.10 = 22%, a 2-point move. A 10% relative increase from a 5% rate gives 5 × 1.10 = 5.5%, a 0.5-point move. This is the same forward percentage formula used for prices and salaries; the only difference is that the base is itself a percentage.

Watch the direction. A fall from 5% to 4% is −1 point and −20% relative, because 1 ÷ 5 = 0.20. A rise back from 4% to 5% is +1 point but +25% relative, because 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25. The point change is symmetric; the relative change is not.

Check both numbers in the calculator

  1. Subtract the starting rate from the ending rate to get the point change: 5 − 4 = 1 point.
  2. Divide the point change by the starting rate and multiply by 100: 1 ÷ 4 × 100 = 25%.
  3. Label both results. A single “1” in a report is meaningless without its unit.
  4. Use the Change view in the tool to verify the relative figure with the start and end values.

Open the percentage calculator and enter old 4, new 5 to confirm the 25% relative change. Then run old 1, new 2 to see the 100% result that a one-point move can produce. For the underlying formulas across discounts, margins and taxes, the pillar guide collects the whole family in one place.

Try it: open the percentage calculator, confirm 4 → 5 is +25%, then check 72 → 78 for +8.33%. Report the point change and the relative change together, and the classic points-versus-percent mistake disappears from your next report.

faqs.question: What is the difference between percentage points and percent?
faqs.answer: A percentage point is the arithmetic difference between two percentages, while percent describes a relative change from a starting value. A rate from 4% to 5% rises 1 percentage point, but that is a 25% relative increase because 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25. The point change is the gap; the percent change scales the gap to the starting rate.

faqs.question: Is 2% the same as 2 percentage points?
faqs.answer: No. Two percentage points is a fixed gap between rates, such as 5% to 7%. A 2% change is relative and depends on the starting rate: 2% of 5% is 0.1 point, while 2% of 50% is 1 point. Saying “up 2%” when you mean 2 points understates the move in most cases.

faqs.question: How do I convert percentage points to percent?
faqs.answer: Divide the point change by the starting rate and multiply by 100. A 2-point rise from 6% is 2 ÷ 6 × 100 = 33.33%. The same 2-point rise from 20% is 2 ÷ 20 × 100 = 10%. Because the starting rate is in the denominator, points alone are never enough to produce the relative percentage.

faqs.question: Why is a move from 1% to 2% a 100% increase?
faqs.answer: The gap is 1 point, and the starting value is 1%, so the relative change is 1 ÷ 1 × 100 = 100%. The rate doubled. A move from 10% to 11% is also 1 point but only a 10% increase, because the same gap is measured against a much larger base. This is why point changes and relative changes must be reported together.

faqs.question: Should reports say percentage points or percent?
faqs.answer: Use percentage points when comparing two rates, and percent when comparing amounts, counts or a change relative to a starting value. “The rate rose 2 percentage points, from 5% to 7%, a 40% increase” is unambiguous. “The rate rose 2%” is not, because readers cannot tell which unit was intended.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a percentage point change?
faqs.answer: Subtract the starting rate from the ending rate. From 18% to 20%, the change is 20 − 18 = 2 percentage points. On a ₹1,000 base, the tax rises from ₹180 to ₹200, a ₹20 increase. The relative change is 2 ÷ 18 × 100 = 11.11%, which is a different and equally valid number.

title: BMI Calculator Guide: Healthy Weight, Calories & Water Needs
description: BMI explained end to end: formula, adult bands, weight ranges, sex differences, athletes, children, calories and water needs, with clear limits.

toc.text: Turning bands into a weight range

html:
BMI is one of the most widely used numbers in health and one of the least self-explanatory. It arrives as a single value — 22.9, 27.4, 31.1 — attached to a label such as “healthy” or “overweight.” The label sounds final. The arithmetic behind it is simple, and the interpretation is not.

This guide covers the whole chain: how the ratio is calculated, what the adult bands mean, how to turn them into a weight range, where the number misleads for women, men, athletes and children, and how calorie and water needs fit around it. It does not prescribe a diet or a goal weight. It gives you the reference points and the caveats so a conversation with a clinician starts from something accurate.

What BMI measures, and what it does not

Body mass index is weight divided by height squared. In metric units, kilograms divided by metres squared; in imperial units, 703 times pounds divided by inches squared. The output is a ratio, not a percentage and not a diagnosis.

The index dates to the 19th century, when Adolphe Quetelet used a weight-to-height ratio to describe population averages. The modern name and cutoffs arrived much later. That origin explains both its strength and its weakness: it was built to compare groups, not to diagnose an individual. A population curve can be a useful map; it is not a medical record.

A BMI of 22.9 at 1.75 m corresponds to 70 kg. The same height at 90 kg gives 29.4. The difference of 20 kg moves the number by 6.5 points, which is why BMI responds quickly to weight change and slowly to almost everything else.

What it does not measure is body composition. It cannot tell lean mass from fat mass, and it cannot see whether fat is stored around the organs or on the hips. At a population level, higher BMI values are associated with higher average body fat and higher risk of certain conditions. At the level of one person, the association is weaker. A muscular athlete and a sedentary adult can share the same score.

That is not a reason to discard the number. It is a reason to use it as a first question rather than a final answer. BMI is cheap, quick and consistent, which makes it useful for screening and for tracking trends. It becomes more useful when paired with a waist measurement, an activity history and routine clinical checks.

How BMI is calculated

The metric calculation takes three steps. Convert height to metres, square it, then divide weight by the square. For 70 kg at 175 cm: 175 ÷ 100 = 1.75 m; 1.75² = 3.0625; 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.857, which rounds to 22.9.

The imperial calculation is BMI = 703 × pounds ÷ inches². For 180 lb at 70 in: 70² = 4,900; 703 × 180 = 126,540; 126,540 ÷ 4,900 = 25.8. Converted to metric, 180 lb is 81.65 kg and 70 in is 1.778 m, and 81.65 ÷ 3.161 = 25.8. The two systems agree when the conversions are done correctly.

The 703 is a unit conversion, not a health threshold. One pound is 0.453592 kg and one inch is 0.0254 m, so the factor is 0.453592 ÷ (0.0254 × 0.0254) = 703.07. Rounding to 703 changes a result by less than 0.1%. Using 700 instead would bias the answer low by about 0.4%, which matters only near a category edge.

Most mismatches between calculators come from inputs rather than formulas. A height measured with shoes on can be 2 cm taller, which lowers BMI by about 0.5 points at 70 kg. A weight taken after a meal can be 1 to 2 kg higher than a morning reading. Rounding also matters at boundaries: 76.4 kg at 1.75 m is 24.947, which displays as 24.9 but sits a hair below 25.0. The full formula guide walks through metric and imperial examples step by step.

Reading the adult BMI bands

The standard reference categories for non-pregnant adults are under 18.5 for underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 for the healthy range, 25.0 to 29.9 for overweight and 30.0 or above for obesity. At 1.75 m, those cutoffs correspond to the weights in the table below, using weight = BMI × 3.0625.

BMICategoryWeight at 1.75 mWhat it is useful for
Below 18.5UnderweightBelow 56.7 kgFlagging possible undernutrition or unexplained loss
18.5 to 24.9Healthy range56.7 to 76.3 kgA population reference band, not a personal target
25.0 to 29.9Overweight76.6 to 91.6 kgPrompting a waist and risk-factor review
30.0 and aboveObesity91.9 kg and abovePrompting clinical assessment, not a label

The small gaps between 76.3 and 76.6, or 91.6 and 91.9, are rounding artifacts. The underlying scale is continuous. At this height, 0.1 BMI point is 0.31 kg, so a large glass of water can move the displayed number by a tenth without changing anything meaningful.

Obesity is sometimes split into class 1 (30.0–34.9), class 2 (35.0–39.9) and class 3 (40.0 and above). Those subdivisions are used in clinical and public-health settings; they are not a measure of personal worth and they do not describe fitness, diet quality or mental health. A BMI of 31 and a BMI of 39 both sit in the obesity range, but the clinical conversation around them may differ substantially.

Treat every band as a screening prompt. A result inside the healthy range is not proof of metabolic health. A result outside it is not proof of disease. Blood pressure, fasting glucose, lipids and family history can be abnormal at any BMI, and they can be normal at a BMI of 30.

Turning the bands into a healthy weight range

A range is more honest than a single target. Multiply 18.5 and 24.9 by your height squared to get the interval. At 1.63 m, 1.63² = 2.6569, so the range is 18.5 × 2.6569 = 49.2 kg to 24.9 × 2.6569 = 66.2 kg. At 1.80 m, it is 59.9 to 80.7 kg.

The interval is wide on purpose. At 1.75 m it spans 19.6 kg, and at 1.90 m it spans 23.1 kg. Two people at the same height can sit at opposite ends and both be inside the reference band. There is no health bonus for the midpoint, and no failure at 24.5 rather than 21.5.

Use the range as a corridor, not a bullseye. If you are above it, the useful questions are about trend, waist and habits rather than the exact distance to the upper bound. If you are below it, unexplained weight loss or low muscle mass deserves a clinical conversation. The healthy weight range chart lists the interval for common heights in kilograms and pounds.

BMI for women and men

The formula and the adult cutoffs are the same for both sexes. Average body composition is not. Women tend to carry a higher percentage of body fat at the same BMI, and fat distribution differs on average. Men are more likely to store fat abdominally, which is why waist circumference often adds more information for men at the same score.

Take two examples. A woman at 1.65 m and 65 kg has a BMI of 23.9. If her waist is 94 cm, her waist-to-height ratio is 94 ÷ 165 = 0.57. A man at 1.80 m and 95 kg has a BMI of 29.3. If his waist is 86 cm, his ratio is 86 ÷ 180 = 0.48. The first BMI looks better; the first waist ratio looks worse. Neither number alone tells the whole story.

Pregnancy is a separate case. BMI is not valid during pregnancy because the formula was designed for non-pregnant adults and cannot distinguish pregnancy-related weight from fat. Postpartum readings are also noisy while fluid shifts and healing continue. Use pre-pregnancy BMI only as one input in a clinical conversation, never as a reason to restrict food during pregnancy.

The BMI for women guide covers menopause, pregnancy and waist thresholds in more detail. The BMI for men guide focuses on muscle, abdominal fat and age-related composition changes.

Athletes and children need different readings

A lean, muscular athlete can score in the overweight or obesity range without excess fat. At 1.80 m, 95 kg gives 29.3 whether that weight is muscle or fat. A strength athlete with an 86 cm waist may have a waist-to-height ratio of 0.48 and excellent metabolic markers. A sedentary adult with the same BMI and a 104 cm waist may have a very different risk profile.

This does not mean a high BMI in an athlete is always harmless. Muscle mass can coexist with visceral fat, and retired athletes can lose muscle while keeping weight. The ratio is ambiguous in both directions. Waist circumference, body-fat trend and performance measures are more informative for this group. The BMI for athletes guide works through the muscle confound.

Children and teenagers are a different measurement problem entirely. Adult bands do not apply because body composition changes rapidly with growth. A 10-year-old at 1.40 m and 38 kg has a BMI of 19.4, but that value has to be placed on an age-and-sex percentile chart. Under the CDC reference, below the 5th percentile is underweight, the 5th to below the 85th is healthy, the 85th to below the 95th is overweight, and the 95th or above is obesity. The BMI for children and teens guide explains why the adult number cannot be reused.

BMI does not set your calorie needs

Two people can share a BMI and have very different energy requirements. Calorie needs depend on age, sex, weight, height, activity, muscle mass, health conditions and medication. BMI captures only weight and height, so it cannot produce a personal calorie target.

A common estimate starts with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation for basal metabolic rate. For a 30-year-old man at 70 kg and 175 cm: 10 × 70 = 700; 6.25 × 175 = 1,093.75; 5 × 30 = 150; so 700 + 1,093.75 − 150 + 5 = 1,648.75, or about 1,649 kcal at rest. Multiply by 1.55 for moderate activity and the total daily estimate is about 2,556 kcal.

For a 30-year-old woman at 65 kg and 165 cm: 10 × 65 = 650; 6.25 × 165 = 1,031.25; 5 × 30 = 150; so 650 + 1,031.25 − 150 − 161 = 1,370.25, or about 1,370 kcal at rest. With the same 1.55 activity factor, the total is about 2,124 kcal.

These are estimates, not prescriptions. Individual variation of 10–15% is common, and thyroid function, medication, sleep and label accuracy all add noise. A 500 kcal daily deficit is sometimes used as an illustration: 500 × 7 = 3,500 kcal per week, and at roughly 7,700 kcal per kilogram of fat, that implies about 0.45 kg per week. Real loss is not linear, includes water and lean tissue, and slows as body mass falls. The calorie deficit guide explains the arithmetic and the limits, and the calorie calculator shows BMR, total daily expenditure and macro splits.

Water needs scale with weight, activity and climate

Hydration estimates often start with 35 mL per kilogram of body weight. At 70 kg: 70 × 35 = 2,450 mL, or 2.45 L. Add 500 mL for regular activity or a hot climate and the estimate becomes 2,950 mL, about 12 glasses at 250 mL each. At 55 kg, the base is 55 × 35 = 1,925 mL, or about 8 glasses.

Those numbers are starting points, not rules. Food contributes water, especially fruit, vegetables, soup and yogurt. Coffee and tea count toward fluid intake for most people. Sweat rate varies with fitness, clothing and humidity. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney disease, heart failure and diuretic medication all change the picture, sometimes in opposite directions.

Thirst and urine colour are practical guides for everyday hydration; pale yellow is a reasonable target, while persistent dark urine or little output deserves attention. Drinking far beyond thirst is not a virtue and can be dangerous during endurance events, where excessive water without sodium can dilute blood sodium. The daily water intake guide covers climate, exercise and electrolyte exceptions, and the water intake calculator turns your weight and activity into litres and glasses.

Limitations, better metrics and next steps

BMI has known blind spots: age, sex, ethnicity, pregnancy, muscle mass, bone density, fluid status and fat distribution. Some guidelines use lower action points for people of South Asian or East Asian descent because metabolic risk can appear at a lower BMI. Amputations and edema change the relationship between weight and body size. None of these are edge cases in a real clinic; they are ordinary reasons to interpret the number carefully.

The table below compares BMI with measurements that add information. None of them is a diagnosis on its own.

MeasureWhat it addsExampleMain limitation
BMIWeight-for-height screening70 kg at 1.75 m = 22.9Cannot separate muscle from fat
Waist circumferenceAbdominal fat94 cmCutoffs vary by sex and population
Waist-to-height ratioAbdominal fat relative to frame94 ÷ 175 = 0.54Screening heuristic, not a diagnosis
Body-fat estimateProportion of mass that is fatMethod-dependentCalipers, impedance and DEXA have different error
BMI-for-ageGrowth screening under 1838 kg at 1.40 m = 19.4Needs age-and-sex percentile charts

A sensible next step is to use the BMI calculator for the ratio, add a waist measurement, and look at the trend over several weeks rather than a single day. If the numbers disagree, or if you have symptoms, a family history of metabolic disease, are pregnant, are under 18 or are managing a condition that affects weight or fluid balance, take the conversation to a qualified clinician.

Start with your own numbers: open the free BMI calculator for the index and category, then use the calorie calculator for an energy estimate and the water intake calculator for a fluid starting point. Each tool shows its formula and keeps the arithmetic visible.

This article is general information, not medical advice. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis, and no BMI range guarantees health. Do not use this guide to prescribe calories, restrict food or replace care from a qualified clinician, especially during pregnancy, adolescence or while managing a medical condition.

faqs.question: What is BMI and what does it measure?
faqs.answer: BMI is weight divided by height squared, using kilograms and metres or 703 times pounds divided by inches squared. It estimates weight-for-height at a population level and sorts adults into underweight, healthy, overweight and obesity bands. It does not measure body fat, muscle mass or fat distribution, so it is a screening input rather than a diagnosis.

faqs.question: What is a healthy BMI for an adult?
faqs.answer: The common reference band is 18.5 to 24.9 for non-pregnant adults, with under 18.5 underweight, 25.0 to 29.9 overweight and 30.0 or above obesity. At 1.75 m, that band is roughly 56.7 to 76.3 kg. These are population ranges, not personal targets, and they do not guarantee or rule out health.

faqs.question: Why can a muscular person have a high BMI?
faqs.answer: Muscle is denser than fat, so a lean athlete can weigh as much as a less lean person of the same height. At 1.80 m, 95 kg gives a BMI of 29.3 regardless of body composition. A waist measurement helps: 86 cm gives a waist-to-height ratio of 0.48, while 104 cm gives 0.58. The BMI is arithmetically correct but incomplete.

faqs.question: Does BMI differ for men and women?
faqs.answer: The formula and adult cutoffs are identical. Average body composition and fat distribution differ, so the same score can carry different context. Women tend to carry more body fat at the same BMI, and men are more likely to store fat abdominally. Waist circumference and clinical markers help interpret the number for either sex.

faqs.question: Can I use BMI for children and teenagers?
faqs.answer: Not with adult bands. Children and teenagers are assessed with BMI-for-age and sex percentile charts because body composition changes during growth. Under the CDC reference, below the 5th percentile is underweight, the 5th to below the 85th is healthy, the 85th to below the 95th is overweight, and the 95th or above is obesity. Use a paediatric clinician.

faqs.question: How many calories should I eat based on my BMI?
faqs.answer: BMI cannot set a calorie target. Needs depend on age, sex, weight, height, activity, muscle mass, health conditions and medication. A 30-year-old man at 70 kg and 175 cm has an estimated resting need near 1,649 kcal and a moderate-activity total near 2,556 kcal, but that is an estimate for illustration, not a prescription. Discuss personal targets with a clinician or dietitian.

faqs.question: How much water should I drink each day?
faqs.answer: A common starting estimate is 35 mL per kilogram, so 70 kg gives about 2.45 L, or 2.95 L with an activity or heat adjustment. Food, coffee and tea also contribute. Needs rise with sweat losses and fall with some medical conditions. Thirst and pale-yellow urine are practical everyday guides; persistent dark urine or reduced output deserves medical advice.

title: How BMI Is Calculated: Formula, Metric & Imperial
description: How BMI is calculated in metric and imperial units, with worked examples, unit conversions and the rounding quirks that change the category.

toc.text: The metric formula step by step
What the number cannot tell you

html:
BMI is a ratio, so the calculation itself is short: weight divided by height squared. The parts people get wrong are the unit conversions and the order of operations. A height entered in centimetres instead of metres turns 22.9 into 0.00229 unless you scale it back. A weight in pounds dropped into the metric formula produces a number that looks plausible and is wrong by a factor of 2.2.

This walkthrough does the arithmetic twice, once in kilograms and metres and once in pounds and inches, then shows why the two answers converge. Keep the BMI calculator open if you want to check your own numbers; it runs the same formulas and places the result in a category band.

What the BMI formula actually measures

Body mass index compares weight with height. The metric version divides kilograms by metres squared. The result carries units of kg/m², although the number is usually quoted bare: a BMI of 22.9, not 22.9 kg/m².

That ratio is a screening shortcut, not a body-composition test. It cannot tell a kilogram of muscle from a kilogram of fat, and it says nothing about where fat sits. Two adults can both score 22.9 while carrying very different amounts of muscle, bone and abdominal fat. The number is useful because it is cheap, quick and comparable across large groups; it is limited because an individual is not a group.

The formula is identical for adult men and women. The four category bands are also the same for non-pregnant adults. What changes is how much weight to give the result when muscle mass, age, ethnicity or pregnancy make the ratio less representative. That context gets its own sections later.

The core idea is simple: for a fixed height, BMI rises in a straight line with weight. At 1.75 m, every extra kilogram adds 1 ÷ 3.0625 = 0.33 BMI points. At 1.60 m, every kilogram adds 1 ÷ 2.56 = 0.39 points, because the same weight is being spread over a smaller frame. That is why a 2 kg change matters more at 1.55 m than at 1.90 m.

The metric formula, step by step

Use kilograms and metres. If your height is in centimetres, divide by 100 first; if it is already in metres, skip that step. Then square the height and divide the weight by the result.

  1. Convert 175 cm to metres: 175 ÷ 100 = 1.75 m.
  2. Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625 m².
  3. Divide weight by the square: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.857.
  4. Round to one decimal place: 22.9.

Check the arithmetic in reverse: 22.9 × 3.0625 = 70.1 kg, close to the starting weight. That backward multiplication is a useful sanity check because it catches a height that was squared incorrectly.

Second example: 85 kg at 180 cm. First, 180 ÷ 100 = 1.80 m. Then 1.80² = 3.24. Finally, 85 ÷ 3.24 = 26.234, which rounds to 26.2. That sits in the overweight band (25.0 to 29.9).

Third example: 50 kg at 175 cm. The height square is still 3.0625, so 50 ÷ 3.0625 = 16.326, or 16.3. This time the result falls below 18.5, the underweight band.

If you enter centimetres by mistake, the raw result is 70 ÷ 30,625 = 0.00229. Multiply by 10,000 and you recover 22.9, because one square metre contains 10,000 square centimetres. Some calculators do that scaling internally; others expect metres. Knowing the factor makes the difference obvious rather than mysterious.

The imperial formula and the 703 factor

The imperial version is BMI = 703 × pounds ÷ inches². The 703 is not arbitrary decoration. It folds the pound-to-kilogram and inch-to-metre conversions into one constant so the output lands on the same scale as the metric formula.

Example: 180 lb at 70 in (5 ft 10 in).

  1. Square the height in inches: 70 × 70 = 4,900.
  2. Multiply weight by 703: 703 × 180 = 126,540.
  3. Divide by the height square: 126,540 ÷ 4,900 = 25.824.
  4. Round: 25.8.

Convert the same measurements to metric and the answer should match. 180 lb ÷ 2.20462 = 81.65 kg. 70 in × 2.54 = 177.8 cm = 1.778 m. Squaring gives 3.161 m², and 81.65 ÷ 3.161 = 25.83. The small difference comes from rounding the converted inputs, not from a different formula.

Second example: 140 lb at 65 in (5 ft 5 in). 65² = 4,225. 703 × 140 = 98,420. 98,420 ÷ 4,225 = 23.295, or 23.3. In metric terms that is 63.50 kg at 1.651 m, and 63.50 ÷ 2.726 = 23.3.

Height in feet and inches has to be converted to a single inch count before squaring. Five feet ten inches is 5 × 12 + 10 = 70 in, not 5.10 ft and not 5.9 ft. Typing 5.9 as a decimal is a common slip: it represents 5 ft 10.8 in, almost two inches taller than intended.

Converting between the two systems

The conversions are worth memorising because they explain most mismatches between apps.

  • Centimetres to metres: divide by 100. 163 cm = 1.63 m.
  • Inches to centimetres: multiply by 2.54. 69 in = 175.26 cm.
  • Pounds to kilograms: divide by 2.20462. 165 lb = 74.84 kg.
  • Feet and inches to inches: feet × 12, then add the remaining inches. 5 ft 9 in = 69 in.

Take 165 lb at 5 ft 9 in. The height is 69 in, or 1.7526 m; the weight is 74.84 kg. The metric calculation is 74.84 ÷ (1.7526 × 1.7526) = 74.84 ÷ 3.0716 = 24.36, which rounds to 24.4. The imperial calculation is 703 × 165 = 115,995, and 115,995 ÷ 4,761 = 24.36. Same answer.

One subtlety: 5 ft 9 in is 175.26 cm, not exactly 175 cm. Across a 1 cm height difference at this weight, BMI moves by roughly 0.3 points. That is small, but it can matter at a category boundary. Use the most precise height you have rather than a rounded guess.

Worked examples in both systems

The table below repeats the calculations with the intermediate values visible. Every row uses the same formulas; only the units change.

ProfileCalculationBMIBand
70 kg, 175 cm70 ÷ 3.062522.9Healthy
85 kg, 180 cm85 ÷ 3.2426.2Overweight
50 kg, 175 cm50 ÷ 3.062516.3Underweight
180 lb, 70 in703 × 180 ÷ 4,90025.8Overweight
140 lb, 65 in703 × 140 ÷ 4,22523.3Healthy

The bands in the final column are reference ranges for non-pregnant adults: under 18.5 is underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 is healthy, 25.0 to 29.9 is overweight and 30.0 or above is obesity. They are not individual diagnoses, and a result within a band does not guarantee anything about blood pressure, insulin sensitivity or fitness.

Why your result may not match another calculator

Most disagreements come from inputs, not formulas. A height measured in shoes can be 2 cm taller than one measured barefoot. At 70 kg, entering 1.77 m instead of 1.75 m changes the result from 22.9 to 22.3, a difference of about 0.5 points. Weighing after a meal or later in the day can add 1 to 2 kg, which moves BMI by 0.3 to 0.7 points at this height.

Rounding produces smaller discrepancies. The exact result of the first example is 22.857. A calculator that truncates shows 22.8; one that rounds shows 22.9. Both are defensible, but the truncation is not a different measurement. At a boundary the effect can look dramatic: 76.4 kg at 1.75 m gives 24.947, which rounds to 24.9 and stays in the healthy band, while a tool that rounds up to 25.0 would label it overweight. The underlying weight is the same.

Age and pregnancy change the interpretation, not the arithmetic. Children and teenagers need BMI-for-age percentiles rather than adult bands. Pregnancy adds weight that the standard ratio was never designed to interpret. A muscular athlete can carry a high BMI with a low body-fat percentage. None of those cases makes the division wrong; they make the label less useful.

What the number cannot tell you

BMI does not measure visceral fat, cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle mass, bone density, blood pressure or blood glucose. It also uses one population-level cutoff set for everyone, while risk varies with age, sex, ethnicity and family history. Some guidelines use lower action points for people of South Asian or East Asian descent, and clinicians may weigh waist circumference more heavily when BMI sits near a boundary.

A BMI inside the healthy band is not proof of metabolic health, and a BMI inside the overweight band is not proof of disease. The ratio is a first pass that becomes more useful when paired with a waist measurement, an activity history and routine clinical checks. If you are pregnant, under 18, very muscular, over 65, or managing a condition that affects weight or fluid balance, treat the number as a conversation starter rather than a conclusion.

Check your own arithmetic: open the BMI calculator in metric or imperial mode and compare the displayed formula with the steps above. For the range of weights that maps to 18.5–24.9 at your height, read the healthy weight range chart. If you are using the result to think about energy intake, the calorie calculator shows why BMI cannot set a calorie target by itself. The full BMI guide connects the bands, weight ranges, calories and hydration.

This article is general information, not medical advice. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Talk with a qualified clinician about your own health, especially during pregnancy, adolescence or while managing a medical condition.

faqs.question: What is the formula for BMI in metric units?
faqs.answer: Divide weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. For 70 kg at 175 cm, convert the height to 1.75 m, square it to 3.0625, then divide: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.857, or 22.9. If you only have centimetres, multiply the result of kg ÷ cm² by 10,000 to get the same number.

faqs.question: What is the formula for BMI in imperial units?
faqs.answer: Multiply weight in pounds by 703, then divide by height in inches squared. For 180 lb at 70 in, 703 × 180 = 126,540 and 70² = 4,900, so 126,540 ÷ 4,900 = 25.8. The 703 constant folds the pound and inch conversions into the formula so the result matches the metric scale.

faqs.question: Why does my BMI differ by a few tenths between calculators?
faqs.answer: The formula is the same; the inputs and rounding differ. A height taken with shoes on can be 2 cm taller, and 2 cm at 70 kg changes BMI by about 0.5 points. Some tools truncate 22.857 to 22.8 while others round to 22.9. Weigh at the same time of day and enter height barefoot for a fair comparison.

faqs.question: Is BMI calculated differently for men and women?
faqs.answer: No. The adult formula and the 18.5, 25 and 30 cutoffs are the same for both sexes. Body composition and fat distribution differ on average, so the same number can carry different context. Clinical tools sometimes add waist circumference or sex-specific risk factors, but those are additions to BMI, not changes to its arithmetic.

faqs.question: Can I use the adult BMI formula for children?
faqs.answer: No. Children and teenagers are assessed with BMI-for-age and sex percentile charts because normal body composition changes substantially during growth. A value that would be healthy for an adult can sit above the 85th percentile for a 10-year-old. Use a paediatric growth chart and a clinician for anyone under 18.

faqs.question: What BMI is considered healthy for an adult?
faqs.answer: The common reference band is 18.5 to 24.9 for non-pregnant adults, with under 18.5 underweight, 25.0 to 29.9 overweight and 30.0 or above obesity. These are population screening ranges, not personal targets. A healthy result does not guarantee metabolic health, and a result outside the band does not by itself diagnose a problem.

title: BMI for Women: Ranges, Limitations & Better Metrics
description: BMI ranges for women explained with worked examples, and why pregnancy, menopause, muscle and fat distribution change the number.

toc.text: The adult bands apply to women
Better metrics to use alongside BMI

html:
Search “BMI for women” and you will find plenty of charts that imply women need a different formula. They usually do not. The adult calculation is the same for both sexes: weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, with the same 18.5, 25 and 30 reference points. What differs is the context around the number — body composition, where fat tends to sit, pregnancy, menopause and the fact that a single ratio cannot see any of it.

This guide keeps the arithmetic visible, then spends most of its time on interpretation. If you just want the number, the BMI calculator will produce it in either metric or imperial units. If you want to know what to do with it, read on.

The adult bands apply to women too

For non-pregnant adults, the standard reference bands are:

  • Under 18.5: underweight.
  • 18.5 to 24.9: healthy weight range.
  • 25.0 to 29.9: overweight.
  • 30.0 and above: obesity.

At a height of 1.65 m, those bands translate into the weights in the table below. The arithmetic is weight = BMI × height², so each boundary is 18.5, 25 or 30 multiplied by 1.65 × 1.65 = 2.7225 m².

BMICategoryWeight at 1.65 m
Below 18.5UnderweightBelow 50.4 kg
18.5 to 24.9Healthy range50.4 to 67.8 kg
25.0 to 29.9Overweight68.1 to 81.4 kg
30.0 and aboveObesity81.7 kg and above

The gaps between 67.8 and 68.1, or between 81.4 and 81.7, are rounding artifacts at the category edges; the underlying BMI values are continuous. A woman who weighs 67.9 kg at this height has a BMI of 24.94, which rounds to 24.9 and stays inside the healthy band. At 68.2 kg the BMI is 25.05, which rounds to 25.1 and crosses into overweight. A 300 g difference does not represent a meaningful change in health, but it can change the label.

Worked examples at 1.65 m: 65 kg ÷ 2.7225 = 23.9, inside the healthy band. 72 kg ÷ 2.7225 = 26.4, inside the overweight band. 55 kg ÷ 2.7225 = 20.2, also inside the healthy band. The middle example is only 7 kg above the first, yet it moves from the healthy band into overweight because the distance from 23.9 to 26.4 is 2.5 BMI points, and one point at this height is 2.72 kg.
