Six months later the same wall-clock time produces a different result. On December 15, 2026, New York is on EST at UTC−5. 15:00 becomes 20:00 UTC, and Tokyo receives 05:00 on December 16. The local meeting time did not change; the offset did. This is why a recurring “3 p.m. New York” series drifts by an hour for the Tokyo participant after a switch.

Two daylight saving edge cases break naive converters. On March 8, 2026, clocks in New York jump from 02:00 to 03:00, so 02:30 does not exist. On November 1, 2026, clocks fall back from 02:00 to 01:00, so 01:30 occurs twice. A converter must choose an offset or reject the input for the first case, and must label which occurrence it used for the second. Schedules built on local wall-clock strings cannot resolve that ambiguity without an explicit offset or a UTC anchor.

The safe pattern for distributed teams is to store the instant in UTC, display it in each participant’s zone, and include the zone name and offset in the invitation. “15:00 America/New_York (UTC−4)” is unambiguous. “3 p.m. EST” is not, because the abbreviation is sometimes used loosely in summer, and “IST” can mean India, Ireland or Israel.

Unix timestamps: one integer, one instant

Unix time counts seconds from 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. The value 1,700,000,000 corresponds to 2023-11-14 22:13:20 UTC. In New York, which was on EST at UTC−5 on that date, the same instant is 17:13:20. In Kolkata, at UTC+5:30, it is 03:43:20 on November 15. In Tokyo, at UTC+9, it is 07:13:20 on November 15. One integer, three local readings, three different dates or times.

The unit is the most common source of bugs. JavaScript’s Date.now() returns milliseconds, so the same instant appears as 1,700,000,000,000, a 13-digit number. A ten-digit value is almost always seconds; a thirteen-digit value is almost always milliseconds. Multiplying or dividing by 1,000 at the wrong point shifts the date by decades, not by a small rounding error.

Useful anchors: 0 is 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. −86,400 is 1969-12-31 00:00:00 UTC. 1,735,689,600 is 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. 1,792,627,200 is 2026-10-22 00:00:00 UTC. If a log entry shows a number near 1.79 billion, it is a 2026 date in seconds; if it shows 1.79 trillion, it is the same date in milliseconds.

Unix time ignores leap seconds. The system pretends every day has exactly 86,400 seconds, so a leap second inserted at the end of a day is not represented as a distinct value. For scheduling, logging and most application logic this simplification is fine. For astronomical timing or leap-second-aware protocols, a Unix timestamp is not a complete record of elapsed SI seconds.

Leap years and February 29

The Gregorian rule is short: a year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except that century years are not leap years unless they are divisible by 400. So 2024 and 2028 are leap years, 2026 is not, 2000 is a leap year, and 2100 is not. The rule keeps the calendar aligned with the seasons over centuries.

A February 29 birthday has two separate questions. The elapsed-day count is unambiguous: from February 29, 2000 to October 22, 2026 is 9,732 days. The year-month-day label depends on the convention for the missing date. If the birthday is observed on February 28, the label is 26 years, 7 months and 24 days. If it is observed on March 1, the label is 26 years, 7 months and 21 days. Both describe the same number of midnights crossed.

Legal and administrative conventions vary by country and by purpose. Some documents treat March 1 as the anniversary in common years; others use February 28. The practical rule is to pick the convention your jurisdiction or form expects, write it down, and apply it consistently. The leap year birthday guide covers the legal and scheduling variations in more detail.

Leap days also affect date arithmetic that has nothing to do with birthdays. One-year terms show the leap day: March 1, 2023 to March 1, 2024 spans 366 days because February 29, 2024 falls inside, while March 1, 2024 to March 1, 2025 spans 365. An annual interest calculation that divides by 365 will differ by one day’s worth of interest between the two periods. The convention should be stated in the contract, not assumed by the spreadsheet.

Which guide and tool to use

The eight cluster guides follow the questions people actually ask. Start with the one that matches your wording, then use the linked tool to check the result:

  • How to calculate exact age — the borrow method with three checked birth dates.
  • Age difference between two dates — comparing siblings, colleagues or records.
  • Date difference calculation — elapsed days, weeks, months and working days.
  • Time zone conversion — DST-aware meeting scheduling.
  • Unix timestamp conversion — seconds, milliseconds and ISO strings.
  • Leap year birthdays — February 29 conventions and century rules.
  • Add and subtract dates — offsets, month-end clamping and deadlines.
  • Age in days, hours and minutes — total-unit conversions and milestones.

Use the age calculator when the input is a birth date and the output is an age. Use the date calculator when the input is two dates or a date and an offset. Use the time zone converter when the input is a meeting time in a named zone. Use the timestamp converter when the input is an integer from a log, an API or a database. Choosing the right input model removes most of the ambiguity before any arithmetic begins.

Mistakes that survive a second look

  1. Treating a month as 30 days. One month after January 31 is February 28 or 29, not March 2. Calendar months clamp to the target month’s last day.
  2. Mixing inclusive and exclusive counts. A 45-day interval covers 46 dates if both endpoints count. State the convention before comparing two systems.
  3. Assuming today’s offset applies all year. New York, London, Sydney and most of Europe change offsets. Always resolve the offset at the specific instant.
  4. Adding offsets in the wrong direction. To convert 15:00 EDT to UTC, add 4 hours; to convert UTC back to EDT, subtract 4. The sign follows the offset, not the direction of travel.
  5. Confusing seconds with milliseconds. Ten digits versus thirteen. A timestamp near 1.79 billion is seconds; near 1.79 trillion is milliseconds.
  6. Ignoring the time of birth. A person born at 23:30 on June 15 is not yet 36 years and 4 months old at 09:00 on October 22. Date-only calculators drop the time, which suits forms but not precise legal deadlines.
  7. Using ambiguous abbreviations. CST can mean US Central, China Standard or Cuba Standard. Use IANA names such as America/Chicago, Asia/Shanghai or America/Havana.

A final sanity check works for every row in the table: convert the result back. Add the age components to the birth date and see whether you land on the comparison date. Add the day count to the start date and see whether you reach the end date. Convert the local time back to UTC and compare. If the reverse operation does not return the original, the definition changed somewhere in the middle.

Check your own dates: open the age calculator for a birth date, the date calculator for an offset or interval, the time zone converter for a meeting, and the timestamp converter for a log value. Each tool shows the result on your device, and the eight cluster guides explain the arithmetic behind it.

faqs.question: How is exact age calculated in years, months and days?
faqs.answer: Subtract the birth date components from the comparison date, borrowing days from the previous month and months from the year when a component is negative. For June 15, 1990 to October 22, 2026, the result is 36 years, 4 months and 7 days. Adding the parts back returns October 22, 2026, which checks the borrow logic.

faqs.question: Why can the same date produce different ages in two time zones?
faqs.answer: A date label is not an instant. If one system evaluates the comparison at 00:30 in Tokyo and another at 00:30 in New York, the two instants fall on different UTC dates. A birth time near midnight can therefore shift the age by a day. Convert both moments to UTC, or fix a single time-zone convention for the comparison.

faqs.question: When does a February 29 birthday turn a year older?
faqs.answer: There is no universal answer. Some jurisdictions observe the birthday on February 28 in common years, others on March 1, and some documents simply use the last day of February. Elapsed days are unaffected. Choose the rule required by the form or contract, record it, and apply it consistently rather than letting each system guess.

faqs.question: How many days old is someone born on June 15, 1990?
faqs.answer: On October 22, 2026 that person has lived 13,278 days. The calculation is 36 years × 365 = 13,140 days, then add 9 leap days from 1992 through 2024 and 129 days from June 15 to October 22, 2026. The same total equals 1,896 weeks and 6 days, or 318,672 hours.

faqs.question: Does the date calculator count the start date?
faqs.answer: The difference view counts elapsed midnights, so January 1 to February 15, 2026 is 45 days. That interval touches 46 calendar dates if both endpoints are included. The add-subtract view treats the start date as day zero and lands 40 days later on February 10, 2026. State which convention a contract or payroll system expects.

faqs.question: How do I avoid daylight saving errors in a meeting invitation?
faqs.answer: Name the IANA zone and include the UTC offset at the meeting instant, for example 15:00 America/New_York (UTC−4). Convert through UTC rather than adding a remembered city-to-city gap. For recurring meetings, recheck both zones after every transition date, because the United States, Europe and Australia switch on different weekends.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a Unix timestamp and a date?
faqs.answer: A Unix timestamp is a count of seconds from 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, so it identifies one instant without a time zone. A calendar date is a label whose meaning depends on a zone. The same timestamp can be November 14 in New York and November 15 in Tokyo. Keep storage in UTC and convert only for display.

title: How to Calculate Exact Age in Years, Months & Days
description: Learn how to calculate age by hand in years, months and days, with leap-year rules, borrow examples and a 13,278-day walkthrough.
keywords: calculate age from date of birth

toc.text: The borrow method, step by step

html:
“How old are you?” sounds like one question, but a form, a paediatrician and a pension calculator may each want a different answer. One wants completed years. Another wants years, months and days. A third wants the age on a future eligibility date. The arithmetic is the same calendar subtraction, but the stopping rule changes the output.

This tutorial is part of the age calculator guide. It works through the borrow method, checks three birth dates against October 22, 2026, and shows how to convert the result into total months, weeks, days and hours. Keep the age calculator open if you want to verify each step.

Three kinds of age, three different answers

Before subtracting anything, decide which age the question wants.

  • Exact age on a date: the calendar distance from birth to a chosen comparison date, expressed as years, months and days. Born June 15, 1990, on October 22, 2026 you are 36 years, 4 months and 7 days.
  • Completed years: the year component of that result, with the months and days dropped. The same person is 36 for a form that asks for age in whole years, even though the next birthday is almost eight months away.
  • Age on another date: the same subtraction with a different endpoint. On June 15, 2027 the person turns 37; on June 14, 2027 the exact age is still 36 years, 11 months and 30 days.

Age differences between two people use the same machinery with two birth dates instead of a birth date and today. That case has its own guide, but the borrow rules are identical. The most common mistake is answering a completed-years question with a decimal such as 36.35, which is neither a calendar age nor a useful eligibility value.

The borrow method, step by step

Write the comparison date above the birth date, aligned by year, month and day. Subtract the day column first, then the month column, then the year column. If a column would go negative, borrow from the column to its left.

Start with June 15, 1990 and October 22, 2026:

  • Days: 22 − 15 = 7.
  • Months: 10 − 6 = 4.
  • Years: 2026 − 1990 = 36.

The result is 36 years, 4 months and 7 days. Reverse it to check: add 36 years to 1990-06-15 to reach 2026-06-15, add 4 months to reach 2026-10-15, and add 7 days to reach 2026-10-22. The endpoint matches, so no borrowing was needed.

Now take a case that does need borrowing. Compare July 19, 2015 with February 3, 2019. The day column is 3 − 19 = −16. Borrow the number of days in the month before the comparison month, which is January 2019 with 31 days: 3 + 31 − 19 = 15. The month column is now 1 − 7 = −6, so borrow 12 months from the year column: 1 + 12 − 7 = 6, and the year count becomes 2019 − 2015 − 1 = 3. The age gap is 3 years, 6 months and 15 days.

Check it forward: add 3 years to 2015-07-19 to reach 2018-07-19, add 6 months to reach 2019-01-19, and add 15 days to reach 2019-02-03. The elapsed total is 1,295 days. Both the calendar label and the day count describe the same interval.

The borrow source matters. When the comparison month is March, borrowing from February uses 28 or 29 days, not 30. That single choice is why 2024 and 2023 can produce different day remainders for dates that look similar.

Three birth dates, three checked results

Example 1: November 2, 1988 to October 22, 2026. Days: 22 − 2 = 20. Months: 10 − 11 = −1, so borrow 12: 10 + 12 − 11 = 11, and the year count drops to 2026 − 1988 − 1 = 37. The age is 37 years, 11 months and 20 days. Total days: 37 × 365 = 13,505. The 9 leap days from 1992 through 2024 add 9, giving 13,514 to November 2, 2025. Another 354 days reaches October 22, 2026, for 13,868 days.

Example 2: April 10, 2008 to October 22, 2026. Days: 22 − 10 = 12. Months: 10 − 4 = 6. Years: 2026 − 2008 = 18. The age is 18 years, 6 months and 12 days. Total days: 18 × 365 = 6,570. The leap days in 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024 add 4, giving 6,574 to April 10, 2026. Another 195 days reaches October 22, for 6,769 days. The result matters for an 18-plus check: the person crossed the threshold on April 10, 2026, not on January 1.

Example 3: February 29, 2000 to October 22, 2026. The day and month columns have no February 29 to subtract from in 2026. Elapsed days avoid the ambiguity: 9,732 days. The year-month-day label depends on whether the birthday is observed on February 28 or March 1. The next section explains why both labels can be correct.

Birth dateComparison dateExact ageTotal daysTotal hours
1990-06-152026-10-2236y 4m 7d13,278318,672
1988-11-022026-10-2237y 11m 20d13,868332,832
2008-04-102026-10-2218y 6m 12d6,769162,456
2000-02-292026-10-2226y 7m 24d or 26y 7m 21d9,732233,568

The February 29 row carries two labels because the birthday convention changes the month-and-day remainder. Both labels share the same 9,732-day total, which is the number to use when a form asks for days lived rather than a calendar age.

Converting the result to months, weeks, days and hours

The year-month-day answer is not the only useful format. Each total below comes from a different multiplication, and each answers a different question.

  • Months: 36 × 12 + 4 = 436 months and 7 days. This is a calendar-month count, not days divided by 30.
  • Weeks: 13,278 ÷ 7 = 1,896 weeks with 6 days left over.
  • Hours: 13,278 × 24 = 318,672 hours.
  • Minutes: 318,672 × 60 = 19,120,320 minutes.

Do not mix the formats. Dividing 13,278 days by 30.44 gives about 436.2 average months, which is close to the calendar answer but not identical. Dividing by 365 gives about 36.38 years, which is a duration in average years, not the calendar age of 36 years and 4 months. If a form asks for completed years, take the year component. If it asks for total days, use the day total. If it asks for months, decide whether it means calendar months or an average-month conversion before calculating.

The age in days, hours and minutes guide covers milestone conversions, including the difference between a 10,000-day celebration and a 10,000-day legal threshold.

Leap years and month ends

The Gregorian leap rule has three parts. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year. A century year is not a leap year unless it is divisible by 400. So 2024 is a leap year, 2026 is not, 2000 is a leap year, and 2100 is not. The extra day is February 29, which adds one to the year and raises the day-of-year number of every later date by one.

That shift changes age calculations in two places. First, an interval that crosses February 29 contains one more day than the same calendar interval in a common year. From February 28, 2024 to March 1, 2024 is 2 days; from February 28, 2023 to March 1, 2023 is 1 day. Second, a birth date of February 29 has no exact anniversary in three out of four years, so the comparison date must adopt a convention.

Two conventions dominate: observe the birthday on February 28, or observe it on March 1. On October 22, 2026, the elapsed total for someone born February 29, 2000 is 9,732 days under every convention. The year-month-day label is 26 years, 7 months and 24 days with the February 28 clamp, or 26 years, 7 months and 21 days with the March 1 observance. The leap year birthday guide covers legal and scheduling differences; the arithmetic point is that the elapsed days stay fixed while the label moves.

Month-end clamping causes a similar split. One month after January 31, 2026 is February 28, 2026, because the target month has no 31st. One month after January 31, 2024 is February 29. If a form expects March 1 instead, it is using a roll-forward rule, not the standard clamp. Neither rule is wrong, but a payroll or eligibility system must state which one it applies.

Checking the result in the age calculator

Enter the birth date and the comparison date, then read three values: the years-months-days label, the total days, and the next birthday countdown. The label is the one to use for most forms. The total days is the one to use for milestone maths. The countdown is separate from age and should not be confused with it.

  1. Enter 1990-06-15 as the birth date and 2026-10-22 as the comparison date.
  2. Confirm the label reads 36 years, 4 months and 7 days.
  3. Confirm the total reads 13,278 days, or 318,672 hours if the tool shows hours.
  4. Add the components back to the birth date and check that you land on October 22, 2026.

If the tool returns a different day count, check whether it used a time zone or a time of birth. A birth time near midnight can move the instant across a date boundary, especially when the birth and comparison locations are in different zones. Date-only calculators avoid that by treating both dates as labels, which is the right choice for forms and the wrong choice for exact legal deadlines.

Run your own date: open the age calculator, enter the birth date and comparison date, and check the years, months, days and total-day figures against the arithmetic above. No signup, and the calculation stays on your device.

faqs.question: What is the formula for exact age?
faqs.answer: Subtract the birth year, month and day from the comparison date in that order, borrowing 12 months or the previous month’s day count when a column goes negative. June 15, 1990 to October 22, 2026 gives 36 years, 4 months and 7 days. The check is to add the three parts back and confirm the comparison date.

faqs.question: How do you borrow when the day number is smaller?
faqs.answer: Take the number of days in the month before the comparison month, add it to the comparison day, and subtract the birth day. For February 3, 2019 minus July 19, 2015, borrow 31 days from January 2019: 3 + 31 − 19 = 15 days. The month column then borrows 12 from the year column, producing 3 years, 6 months and 15 days.

faqs.question: Why is total days different from years multiplied by 365?
faqs.answer: Years multiplied by 365 ignores leap days. The interval from June 15, 1990 to October 22, 2026 includes nine February 29 dates, adding nine days to the 13,140-day base and giving 13,278 days after the final 129-day segment. Use the day count when a form asks for days lived, and the calendar label when it asks for age.

faqs.question: How do I calculate age on a future date?
faqs.answer: Use that future date as the comparison date instead of today. For a person born June 15, 1990, the age on October 22, 2026 is 36 years, 4 months and 7 days; on June 15, 2027 it is exactly 37 years. Completed years change only when the birthday is reached, not when the calendar year changes.

faqs.question: Should the birth day itself count as day one?
faqs.answer: For an age calculation, the birth date is the start instant and the comparison date is the end instant, so the elapsed count runs from the beginning of the start date to the beginning of the end date. That is why January 1 to February 15 is 45 elapsed days but touches 46 dates. Forms that ask for age in years do not care about this distinction, but day-count and notice-period questions do.

faqs.question: How is age calculated for someone born on February 29?
faqs.answer: The elapsed-day total is unambiguous. The years-months-days label needs a convention: clamp the anniversary to February 28 in common years, or observe it on March 1. Born February 29, 2000, the person has lived 9,732 days by October 22, 2026, which is 26 years, 7 months and 24 days with the February 28 clamp or 26 years, 7 months and 21 days with March 1.

title: Age Difference Between Two Dates (With Examples)
description: Compare two birth dates with an age difference calculator: exact gaps in years, months and days, borrow cases, leap days and same-day checks.

toc.text: The borrow method with two dates

html:
Two people born four years apart are not always four years apart on paper. Around birthdays, a completed-years comparison can say three while the exact gap is three years and eleven months. The difference depends on whether you subtract birth dates or subtract current ages, and on which date you evaluate the result.

Part of the age calculator guide, this tutorial compares birth dates directly, shows the borrow arithmetic, and works through three pairs and a month-end case that defeats naive subtraction. The same method answers “who is older”, “what is the age gap” and “how many days apart were they born”.

Two ways to compare ages

The first method subtracts one birth date from the other. Born November 2, 1988 and March 14, 1992, the younger person is 3 years, 4 months and 12 days younger, a gap of 1,228 days. This is a fixed interval: it does not change as the two people age, because both endpoints are fixed.

The second method computes each person’s age on a chosen date and compares the two ages. On October 22, 2026, the first person is 37 years, 11 months and 20 days old and the second is 34 years, 7 months and 8 days old. Subtracting those ages gives the same 3 years, 4 months and 12 days. Done consistently, the two methods agree because both measure the same two birth dates against the same endpoint.

The disagreement appears when one method drops smaller units. Completed years on that date are 37 and 34, a difference of 3, while the exact gap is 3 years and 4 months. A form that asks “how many years apart are you?” usually wants completed years. A genealogy record or a paediatric milestone chart may want the full years-months-days gap. Write down which one you need before subtracting.

The same borrow method, with two birth dates

Put the later birth date on top and subtract year, month and day. Start with November 2, 1988 and March 14, 1992:

  • Days: 14 − 2 = 12.
  • Months: 3 − 11 = −8. Borrow 12 months: 3 + 12 − 11 = 4.
  • Years: 1992 − 1988 − 1 = 3.

The gap is 3 years, 4 months and 12 days. Add it back: add 3 years to November 2, 1988 to reach November 2, 1991, add 4 months to reach March 2, 1992, and add 12 days to reach March 14, 1992. The endpoint matches.

Total days follow the same pattern as age. Three common years contribute 3 × 365 = 1,095 days to November 2, 1991. The remaining segment to March 14, 1992 is 133 days, and it contains February 29, 1992. The total is 1,228 days. Notice that the leap day is not in the three-year base; it is inside the final four-month segment.

If the day column is negative, borrow from the month before the later date. Compare July 19, 2015 with February 3, 2019. Days: 3 − 19 = −16. January 2019 has 31 days, so 3 + 31 − 19 = 15. Months: 1 − 7 = −6, borrow 12 to get 6, and the year count becomes 3. The gap is 3 years, 6 months and 15 days, or 1,295 days. Adding it back from July 19, 2015 lands on February 3, 2019.

The exact age tutorial covers the same borrow logic with a single birth date and a comparison date. Read it first if the column-borrowing step is unfamiliar.

Three pairs, checked against the calendar

Siblings: November 2, 1988 and March 14, 1992. The older sibling was 3 years, 4 months and 12 days old when the younger was born. The gap is 1,228 days. It stays 1,228 days forever; only the labels “older” and “younger” remain fixed while both ages grow.

Cousins: July 19, 2015 and February 3, 2019. The gap is 3 years, 6 months and 15 days, or 1,295 days. The subtraction needed a day borrow from January 2019 and a month borrow from the year column. Add the result back to July 19, 2015 to confirm the later date.

Colleagues: December 30, 1985 and August 21, 1994. Days: 21 − 30 = −9. Borrow from July 1994, which has 31 days: 21 + 31 − 30 = 22. Months: 8 − 12 = −4, borrow 12 to get 8, and the year count becomes 1994 − 1985 − 1 = 8. The gap is 8 years, 7 months and 22 days, or 3,156 days. In a workplace age-gap question, the full gap is more informative than the difference between completed ages, which can read as 8 or 9 depending on the month.

PairEarlier dateLater dateCalendar gapTotal days
Siblings1988-11-021992-03-143y 4m 12d1,228
Cousins2015-07-192019-02-033y 6m 15d1,295
Colleagues1985-12-301994-08-218y 7m 22d3,156
Same birthday2002-05-122010-05-128y 0m 0d2,922

The last row is a sanity check. Two people born on the same month and day are exactly 8 years apart, and the interval contains the leap days of 2004 and 2008: 8 × 365 = 2,920. The two leap days add 2, for 2,922 days. No borrowing is needed when the day and month match.

The month-end case that breaks naive borrowing

Compare January 31, 2001 with March 1, 2005. The day column is 1 − 31 = −30. Borrowing from February 2005 gives 28 days, so 1 + 28 − 31 = −2, still negative. A single borrow is not enough because the earlier date sits on the longest possible day of a 31-day month and the later date sits on the first day of a month whose predecessor is short.

The reliable method is addition, not subtraction. Start at January 31, 2001, add 4 years to reach January 31, 2005, add 1 month to reach February 28, 2005 under the standard clamp, and add 1 day to reach March 1, 2005. The gap is 4 years, 1 month and 1 day. The elapsed total is 1,490 days. A calculator that blindly borrows 28 days will report a negative remainder or silently land on a different March date.

The same issue appears when a birth date is the 29th, 30th or 31st and the comparison month is shorter. The clamp rule says the anniversary of January 31 falls on February 28 in a common year, not March 3. Apply that rule before subtracting, and the negative-remainder case disappears.

Leap days and same-birthday comparisons

When both people share a birthday, the gap is a whole number of years. Born May 12, 2002 and May 12, 2010, they are exactly 8 years apart, and the interval is 2,922 days because 2004 and 2008 are leap years. Because the birthdays coincide, the completed-year difference also stays at 8; no month of the year produces a temporary 7 or 9.

February 29 introduces the only genuine convention choice. Compare a child born February 29, 2020 with one born March 1, 2021. The fixed gap between the two birth dates is 1 year and 1 day, or 366 days. The older child’s age on March 1, 2021 depends on the convention: 1 year and 1 day if the birthday is clamped to February 28, or exactly 1 year if it is observed on March 1. For the gap between the two people, use the birth dates and ignore the convention.

If you need total days rather than a calendar label, the leap-day debate disappears. The age in days and hours guide shows how to convert the day total into weeks and hours and where the 24-hour multiplication stops being meaningful across daylight saving changes.

Checking an age gap in the calculator

The age difference calculator takes the earlier birth date first and the later birth date second. Read the years-months-days gap and the total-day count. Then add the gap to the earlier date; if the result is not the later date, one of the borrow rules was applied differently.

  1. Enter 1988-11-02 and 1992-03-14. Confirm 3 years, 4 months and 12 days, and 1,228 total days.
  2. Enter 2015-07-19 and 2019-02-03. Confirm 3 years, 6 months and 15 days, and 1,295 total days.
  3. Enter 2001-01-31 and 2005-03-01. Confirm 4 years, 1 month and 1 day, not a negative day count.
  4. Swap the dates. The direction reverses, but the absolute gap and the day total should not change.

If you are comparing two people rather than two historical records, decide whether the question is “what is the fixed gap between their births” or “what is the difference in their ages today”. Both are legitimate, but only the second changes with the calendar. Most forms want the first.

Compare two dates: open the age calculator, enter both birth dates, and check the calendar gap against the total-day count. If the addition check fails, the month-end clamp is the first rule to inspect.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the age difference between two birth dates?
faqs.answer: Subtract the earlier date from the later one, column by column. Borrow the previous month’s day count when the day is negative, then borrow 12 months when the month is negative. November 2, 1988 to March 14, 1992 is 3 years, 4 months and 12 days. Add the result back to the earlier date to verify it.

faqs.question: Why does the age gap change around birthdays?
faqs.answer: The fixed gap between two birth dates never changes. The difference between completed ages can. If one person was born in March 1990 and the other in July 1991, the completed-age gap is 1 for most of the year but 2 between March and July, when the older has had a birthday and the younger has not. The birth-date gap stays 1 year and 4 months.

faqs.question: What if one birth date is January 31?
faqs.answer: Use the month-end clamp. Add the years and months first, clamp to the last day of the target month, then add the remaining days. January 31, 2001 to March 1, 2005 is 4 years, 1 month and 1 day: the first anniversary lands on February 28, 2005. Naive borrowing can produce a negative day remainder, which is why the addition check matters.

faqs.question: How do leap years affect an age gap?
faqs.answer: A leap day inside the interval adds one day to the total but does not change the calendar label by itself. The gap from November 2, 1988 to March 14, 1992 is 3 years, 4 months and 12 days and 1,228 days, including February 29, 1992. For people born on February 29, choose February 28 or March 1 as the anniversary convention and state it.

faqs.question: Should I subtract current ages or birth dates?
faqs.answer: Birth dates give a fixed interval that does not move as time passes. Current ages give a snapshot that changes around birthdays and depends on the evaluation date. Use birth dates for records, eligibility and genealogy; use current ages when the question is about how old each person is today. Do not mix the two by subtracting completed years and then adding months from the birth dates.

faqs.question: How many days apart are two people born eight years apart?
faqs.answer: Eight calendar years contain 2,920 days and one extra day for each February 29 in the interval. From May 12, 2002 to May 12, 2010 the leap days are in 2004 and 2008, so the total is 2,922 days. Count the leap days explicitly; multiplying by 365 alone understates every multi-year gap.

title: Date Difference Calculator: Days, Weeks & Months
description: Count days between two dates correctly, including inclusive counts, leap days, weeks, months and working days, with checked examples.
html:
A date difference is a count of midnights, not a count of days on a calendar page. From January 1 to February 15, 2026, 45 midnights pass, yet the interval touches 46 printed dates. Hotels, payroll systems and contract clauses choose one convention or the other, and the gap between 45 and 46 is exactly the kind of detail that turns a correct calculation into a disputed invoice.

This guide is part of the age calculator guide. It covers elapsed versus inclusive counts, leap days, week and month breakdowns, working-day totals, and adding or subtracting an offset. Every example is checked against the calendar so you can reproduce it.

Elapsed days versus dates touched

Subtract the start date from the end date and you get elapsed days. January 1 to February 15, 2026 is 45 days: January contributes 31 days to February 1, and February 1 to February 15 contributes 14. The start date is day zero, and the end date is day 45. Most software, contract intervals and age calculations work this way.

Count every printed date in the range and you get 46: January 1 through January 31 is 31 dates, and February 1 through February 15 is 15 more. This is the inclusive count. A hotel stay from January 1 to February 15 charges for 45 nights but covers 46 days of occupancy language. A project plan that says “46 calendar days including both endpoints” is using the inclusive convention.

Neither number is wrong. The error is using one label for the other. A leave policy that grants 45 days but counts 46 dates will overspend by one day per request. A rental contract that charges 46 nights for a 45-night stay will overbill. Write the convention into the request before calculating: “45 elapsed days” or “46 dates inclusive”.

Time of day is a separate axis. Date-only arithmetic treats both endpoints as midnight labels, so the result is a whole number. If the inputs include clock times, the difference can include a fraction of a day. A task that starts at 09:00 and ends at 17:00 on the same date is zero elapsed dates but eight hours of work. Decide whether the question is about dates or durations before subtracting.

Three intervals, checked by hand

January 1 to February 15, 2026. January has 31 days, so the first month contributes 31. February 1 to February 15 contributes 14. The total is 45 elapsed days, or 46 dates inclusive. In weeks, 45 ÷ 7 = 6 weeks and 3 days. The interval starts on Thursday, January 1 and ends on Sunday, February 15.

March 1 to April 1, 2026. March has 31 days, so the total is 31 days, or 32 dates inclusive. That is 4 weeks and 3 days. March 1, 2026 is a Sunday and April 1 is a Wednesday. The month length, not a fixed 30-day assumption, determines the result.

October 22 to December 31, 2026. October 22 to November 1 contributes 10 days, November contributes 30, and December 1 to December 31 contributes 30. The total is 70 days, or 71 dates inclusive, which is exactly 10 weeks. The interval starts and ends on a Thursday, so the weekday pattern repeats every seven days.

IntervalElapsed daysDates inclusiveWeeksWeekdays
2026-01-01 to 2026-02-1545466w 3d32
2026-03-01 to 2026-04-0131324w 3d22
2026-10-22 to 2026-12-31707110w 0d50
2024-02-28 to 2024-03-01230w 2d2
2023-02-28 to 2023-03-01120w 1d1

The weekday column counts Monday through Friday before public holidays. The January–February interval contains 32 weekdays; the March interval contains 22 because March 2026 has five Sundays and four Saturdays. If a weekday public holiday falls inside the range, subtract one per holiday. The count is a calendar count, not a promise about which days a business is open.

Leap days inside the interval

The leap-year rule is divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400. So 2024 is a leap year, 2026 is not, 2000 is, and 2100 is not. The extra day is February 29, and it appears in the count only when the interval crosses it.

The shortest illustration is February 28 to March 1. In 2024 the interval is 2 days because February 29 sits between the endpoints. In 2023 the same dates give 1 day. A date calculator that assumes February always has 28 days loses a day from every 2024 interval that includes the 29th.

At the year scale, 2024 contains 366 days and 2026 contains 365. A one-year contract from March 1, 2023 to March 1, 2024 covers 366 days because February 29, 2024 falls inside. The same contract from March 1, 2024 to March 1, 2025 covers 365 days. If interest, rent or service fees are calculated per day, the leap year changes the total by one day’s worth even though the calendar anniversary is unchanged.

Leap days also shift weekdays. Because 366 = 52 × 7 + 2, a date after February 29 in a leap year moves forward by two weekdays relative to the previous year, not one. That is why a fixed-date holiday can fall on a different weekday after a leap year even though the month and day are identical.

Weeks, months and working days

Weeks are the cleanest subdivision because every week is exactly seven days. Divide the elapsed total by 7 and keep the remainder: 45 days is 6 weeks and 3 days; 31 days is 4 weeks and 3 days; 70 days is exactly 10 weeks. A remainder of zero means the interval is a whole number of weeks, which is useful for sprint planning and recurring schedules.

Months are not clean. January 1 to February 15, 2026 is 1 month and 14 days in calendar terms, but February 15 to March 15 is 28 days in 2026 and 29 days in 2024. A month can be 28, 29, 30 or 31 days, so “one month” is not a fixed duration. A 30-day clause and a one-month clause can produce different dates when the target month is shorter than the starting day, most visibly in February and at year-end.

Working days need the weekday count and a holiday list. The January 1 to February 15, 2026 interval contains 32 Monday-to-Friday dates. Remove one for each weekday public holiday observed inside the range. Weekend work adds back only if the schedule explicitly includes it. Do not estimate working days as elapsed days × 5 ÷ 7: 45 × 5 ÷ 7 = 32.14, which happens to round near the correct 32 here, but the shortcut fails on short intervals and around holiday clusters.

If the interval crosses a daylight saving transition, date-only totals are unaffected. A calendar day is still a calendar day even when it contains 23 or 25 clock hours. Durations measured in hours are a different calculation; they need a time zone and an explicit start instant. The age difference guide covers calendar subtraction between two fixed dates, and the add-subtract guide covers offsets.

Adding and subtracting an offset

The same calendar rules run in reverse. Add 40 days to January 1, 2026: 30 days after January 1 is January 31, and 10 more days is February 10, 2026. Adding days never depends on month length assumptions because each step advances one printed date at a time.

Adding months does depend on month length. One month after January 31, 2026 is February 28, 2026, because February has 28 days and the result clamps to the last valid date. One month after January 31, 2024 is February 29. One month after March 31 is April 30. A billing system that rolls forward to March 1 instead is using a different convention, not making an arithmetic error.

Subtraction crosses year boundaries in the same way. Ten days before January 5, 2026 is December 26, 2025: five days reach December 31, and five more enter December. If you subtract a 240-hour duration instead of 10 calendar days, a daylight saving change inside the interval can move the wall-clock time by an hour. Choose the unit that matches the question.

For deadline work, decide whether the offset is measured in calendar days or business days. “Net 30” usually means 30 calendar days from the invoice date, which can include four or five weekends. “30 business days” is roughly six calendar weeks and needs a holiday calendar. The two phrases are not interchangeable, and a contract that uses one while the software uses the other will disagree at the boundary.

Using the date calculator without second-guessing

Enter the two dates in the difference view. Read the elapsed-day total first, then the week breakdown. If the question is inclusive, add one to the elapsed total and label it “dates inclusive”; do not change the underlying start and end dates.

  1. Enter 2026-01-01 and 2026-02-15. Confirm 45 elapsed days and 6 weeks 3 days.
  2. Enter 2024-02-28 and 2024-03-01. Confirm 2 days, then repeat with 2023 and confirm 1 day.
  3. Enter 2026-10-22 and 2026-12-31. Confirm 70 days, or exactly 10 weeks.
  4. For an offset, switch to add-subtract and enter 2026-01-01 with an offset of 40 days. Confirm 2026-02-10.

The add and subtract dates guide goes deeper on month-end clamping, negative offsets and recurring schedules. The pillar guide connects date differences to age, time zones and timestamps.

Count your interval: open the date calculator, enter both dates, and compare the elapsed total with the inclusive count before you put either number in a contract or invoice. No signup, and the calculation runs on your device.

faqs.question: Does the date difference include the start date?
faqs.answer: The difference view counts elapsed midnights, so the start date is day zero and the end date is the total. January 1 to February 15, 2026 is 45 days. The range touches 46 calendar dates if you count both endpoints. Add one for an inclusive count and label it clearly, because payroll and rental systems may expect either convention.

faqs.question: How do I count days between two dates by hand?
faqs.answer: Split the range at month boundaries. Count the days remaining in the first month, add the full days of each month in between, then add the day number of the end date. January 1 to February 15 is 31 days to February 1 and 14 more to February 15, for 45 days. Add one more if the contract counts both endpoints.

faqs.question: Is one month always 30 days?
faqs.answer: No. Calendar months contain 28, 29, 30 or 31 days. One month after January 31 clamps to February 28 in a common year and February 29 in a leap year. A 30-day clause and a one-month clause can produce different dates when the target month is shorter than the starting day, most visibly in February and at year-end, so the contract should name the unit.

faqs.question: How do leap years change a date difference?
faqs.answer: A leap day inside the interval adds one to the total. February 28 to March 1, 2024 is 2 days because February 29 is included; the same dates in 2023 are 1 day. A full leap year contains 366 days, so a one-year interval that includes it is one day longer than the same interval in a common year.

faqs.question: How do I count working days between two dates?
faqs.answer: Count Monday through Friday dates in the range, then subtract one for each weekday public holiday observed inside it. January 1 to February 15, 2026 contains 32 weekdays before holidays. Do not use elapsed days × 5 ÷ 7 as a substitute; it fails on short ranges and around holiday clusters. Weekend shifts need an explicit rule.

faqs.question: Can I add days and months in the same calculator?
faqs.answer: Yes, but use the add-subtract view rather than the difference view. Adding 40 days to January 1, 2026 gives February 10. Adding one month to January 31 gives February 28 in 2026 or February 29 in 2024 because the result clamps to the target month’s last day. Days and months follow different rules and should be entered as separate steps.

title: Time Zone Converter: Schedule Across Zones Without Errors
description: Convert meeting times across IANA time zones with DST-aware examples, UTC anchors, date rollovers and a repeatable scheduling checklist.

toc.text: An offset is a rule, not a constant

html:
“Can you do 3 p.m. my time?” is a complete sentence and an incomplete instruction. It omits the date, the zone and the offset, and any one of those can move the meeting by an hour or a day. A time zone converter works only when the input identifies a place and an instant, not just a clock reading.

This guide is part of the age calculator guide. It explains why offsets change, converts several 2026 meetings through UTC, and lists the daylight saving cases that break otherwise careful schedules. The examples use IANA zone names so the rules stay attached to the place.

An offset is a rule, not a constant

UTC−5 is not “the New York offset”. It is the offset New York uses while standard time is in effect. From March 8 to November 1, 2026, New York uses UTC−4 under daylight saving time. London uses UTC+0 in winter and UTC+1 from March 29 to October 25. Sydney moves in the opposite direction on the calendar because it is in the southern hemisphere: daylight time began there on October 4, 2026 and ends on April 4, 2027.

Because the switch dates differ by country, the gap between two cities is not stable. New York and London are normally five hours apart. Between March 8 and March 29, 2026, New York has already sprung forward while London has not, so the gap is four hours. The same four-hour gap returns between October 25 and November 1, when London has fallen back and New York has not. A converter that stores “New York is five hours behind London” will be wrong during both windows.

Abbreviations make the problem worse. EST and EDT are reasonably specific, but CST can mean US Central, China Standard or Cuba Standard. IST can mean India Standard, Irish Standard or Israel Standard. Use IANA identifiers such as America/New_York, Europe/London, Asia/Kolkata and Australia/Sydney. The identifier carries the full rule set, including historical changes and future scheduled transitions.

India is a useful reminder that “no daylight saving” is not the same as “never changes”. India currently observes UTC+5:30 without a seasonal shift, but the converter should still resolve the zone rule for the date rather than hard-code a permanent offset. Historical dates and future legislation can differ from the current rule.

Converting through UTC, with the arithmetic shown

Convert the source local time to UTC, then convert UTC to the target. The two steps keep the signs straight and make the date rollover visible.

March 10, 2026, 15:00 in New York to Tokyo. New York is on EDT at UTC−4, so 15:00 + 4 hours = 19:00 UTC. Tokyo is on JST at UTC+9, so 19:00 + 9 hours = 28:00, which is 04:00 on March 11. The target date is one day later than the source date.

December 15, 2026, 15:00 in New York to Tokyo. New York is on EST at UTC−5, so 15:00 + 5 = 20:00 UTC. Add 9 hours for Tokyo: 29:00, or 05:00 on December 16. The local clock time is the same as in March, but the conversion is one hour later because New York’s offset changed.

March 10, 2026, 15:00 in London to New York. London is still on GMT at UTC+0, so the UTC time is 15:00. New York is on EDT at UTC−4, so subtract 4 hours: 11:00 in New York. The four-hour gap is temporary. On April 10, London is on BST at UTC+1, so 15:00 London is 14:00 UTC and 10:00 in New York, a five-hour gap.

Source local timeUTCTarget zoneTarget local timeDate shift
2026-03-10 15:00 America/New_York (UTC−4)19:00Asia/Tokyo (UTC+9)2026-03-11 04:00+1 day
2026-12-15 15:00 America/New_York (UTC−5)20:00Asia/Tokyo (UTC+9)2026-12-16 05:00+1 day
2026-03-10 15:00 Europe/London (UTC+0)15:00America/New_York (UTC−4)2026-03-10 11:00same day
2026-04-10 15:00 Europe/London (UTC+1)14:00America/New_York (UTC−4)2026-04-10 10:00same day
2026-10-22 09:00 America/New_York (UTC−4)13:00Asia/Kolkata (UTC+5:30)2026-10-22 18:30same day
2026-10-22 09:00 America/New_York (UTC−4)13:00Australia/Sydney (UTC+11)2026-10-23 00:00+1 day

The last row is the one people miss. Sydney is 15 hours ahead of New York on that date, so a 09:00 call in New York is midnight at the start of the next day in Sydney. The date changes even though the conversion is only a few hours of arithmetic.

DST gaps, repeated hours and mismatched switch dates

Spring forward creates times that do not exist. On March 8, 2026, New York clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00, so 02:30 is not a valid local time. A scheduler that accepts it must either reject the input or shift it forward to 03:30. On March 29, 2026, London does the same at 01:00, so 01:30 is missing there.

Fall back creates times that exist twice. On November 1, 2026, New York clocks move from 02:00 back to 01:00, so 01:30 occurs once in EDT and again in EST. The two occurrences are an hour apart in UTC. An invitation that says “01:30” without an offset is ambiguous; one of the two will be wrong for at least one participant.

Mismatched transition dates create a quieter problem. A weekly 15:00 New York–London call is five hours apart for most of the year, four hours apart from March 8 to March 29, and four hours apart again from October 25 to November 1. If the series is stored as “15:00 New York” and “20:00 London”, the London time is wrong during those windows. If it is stored as a UTC instant, the local times shift automatically but the wall-clock hour changes for both sides.

Decide which promise the meeting makes. “Same local time every week” preserves the clock reading and lets the UTC instant move. “Same absolute instant every week” preserves the UTC time and lets the local clock move. Both are valid; a series that silently mixes them is not.

Date rollover and the international date line

Date rollover is not limited to the date line. Any conversion that pushes the local time past midnight changes the date. New York to Tokyo at 15:00 produces 04:00 the next day. New York to Sydney at 09:00 produces midnight the next day. A meeting at 23:00 in Los Angeles to London lands at 07:00 the next morning when the usual eight-hour gap applies.

The international date line adds a full-day difference between some pairs. Auckland, at UTC+13 during southern summer, is 17 hours ahead of New York at UTC−4. A 09:00 New York call on October 22 is 02:00 on October 23 in Auckland. Tokelau and Samoa sit at UTC+13; American Samoa sits at UTC−11, so the two Samoas are 24 hours apart despite being close neighbours.

When the output date differs from the input date, say so explicitly in the invitation. “March 10, 15:00 New York / March 11, 04:00 Tokyo” is clearer than “15:00 New York” with a separate note that Tokyo is ahead. The date is part of the conversion, not an afterthought.

A scheduling checklist that survives transitions

  1. Name the zones, not the abbreviations. Use America/New_York and Asia/Tokyo. Add the offset at the meeting instant as a human-readable check.
  2. Convert through UTC. Write the UTC time down. It is the one value that does not change when a government adjusts a rule.
  3. Check both ends of the meeting. A call that starts before a transition and ends after it can span two clock hours while only one hour of real time passes, or the reverse.
  4. Check the date on both sides. If the target date differs, include it in every message and calendar entry.
  5. Test transition weekends. March 8, March 29, October 25 and November 1, 2026 are the dates to inspect for US, UK and EU participants. Australia’s dates are separate.
  6. State the recurrence rule. “Every Tuesday at 15:00 New York” and “every Tuesday at 19:00 UTC” behave differently after a transition. Pick one and write it down.
  7. Ask a second person to read the invitation. A local participant will catch a wrong offset faster than any amount of arithmetic.

For logs and APIs, store the UTC instant and the IANA zone separately. The instant answers “when did it happen”; the zone answers “what time was it for the user”. Storing only a local string loses the offset, and storing only an offset loses the zone rule. The Unix timestamp guide covers the integer side of that pair, and the date difference guide covers the calendar side.

Using the time zone converter

Pick the date and time, then choose the source and target zones by name. Read three things: the converted local time, the date on each side, and the offset in effect. If the tool shows a UTC row, compare it with the arithmetic above; that row is the anchor that makes the rest checkable.

  1. Enter 2026-03-10 at 15:00 with America/New_York as the source and Asia/Tokyo as the target. Confirm 04:00 on March 11.
  2. Change the date to 2026-12-15 and confirm 05:00 on December 16, one hour later than the March result.
  3. Convert 2026-03-10 15:00 Europe/London to America/New_York and confirm 11:00, not 10:00.
  4. Convert 2026-10-22 09:00 America/New_York to Australia/Sydney and confirm 00:00 on October 23.

If a result looks an hour off, check the transition weekend first. If it looks a day off, check the date line and the target date. If it looks several hours off, check whether the source zone was entered with the right city, not just the right country.

Convert your meeting: open the time zone converter, enter the date, time and IANA zones, and compare the local results with the UTC anchor. Then send the invitation with the date, zone and offset spelled out.

faqs.question: How do I convert a meeting time from one time zone to another?
faqs.answer: Convert the source local time to UTC using the offset in effect on that date, then apply the target zone’s offset. For March 10, 2026 at 15:00 in New York, EDT is UTC−4, so the instant is 19:00 UTC. Tokyo at UTC+9 is 04:00 on March 11. Convert through UTC to keep the signs and the date rollover visible.

faqs.question: Why is New York sometimes four hours behind London instead of five?
faqs.answer: The two cities switch daylight saving on different dates. In 2026 New York starts on March 8 and London on March 29. Between those dates New York is on EDT at UTC−4 while London is still on GMT at UTC+0, so the gap is four hours. The same four-hour gap returns from October 25 to November 1, when London has fallen back but New York has not.

faqs.question: What happens to a meeting at 2:30 a.m. on a spring-forward date?
faqs.answer: That local time does not exist. On March 8, 2026 New York clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00, so 02:30 is skipped. A converter should reject the input or shift it forward. On March 29, 2026 the same gap occurs in London at 01:00. Schedule the meeting at 03:30 or later, or anchor it to a UTC time instead.

faqs.question: Does a time zone converter handle daylight saving automatically?
faqs.answer: A converter that uses IANA zone identifiers resolves the rule for the specific date, so it should apply the correct standard or daylight offset. It cannot guess which of two repeated fall-back times you meant. On November 1, 2026, 01:30 in New York occurs twice, once in EDT and once in EST, so include an offset or a UTC anchor when the time falls in that ambiguous hour.

faqs.question: Why does the date change when I convert New York to Tokyo or Sydney?
faqs.answer: The target clock can pass midnight even when the source is in the afternoon. New York at 15:00 on March 10 is 04:00 on March 11 in Tokyo. New York at 09:00 on October 22 is 00:00 on October 23 in Sydney because Sydney is 15 hours ahead on that date. The date is part of the conversion and belongs in the invitation.

faqs.question: Is UTC the same as GMT?
faqs.answer: They currently read the same on civil clocks, but they are not the same concept. UTC is the time standard used to coordinate clocks worldwide; GMT is a time zone name based on Greenwich mean time. Neither observes daylight saving. For scheduling and storage, write UTC because it is the unambiguous reference, and use Europe/London when you specifically mean the civil zone.

title: Unix Timestamp Converter: Seconds, Milliseconds & Dates
description: Convert Unix timestamps in seconds and milliseconds to UTC and local dates. Worked arithmetic, timezone offsets, DST and the 2038 limit explained.
html:
A Unix timestamp looks like a random number until you need to read it. A log line shows 1700000000; a JavaScript payload shows 1700000000000; a database column shows 2023-11-14 22:13:20+00. All three can describe the same instant. The conversion is simple once you know the unit and the reference point, and most mistakes come from mixing seconds with milliseconds or reading a UTC value as local time.

This guide is part of the age calculator guide. Open the Unix timestamp converter to check each example as you read.

Two questions decide every conversion: which unit the number is in, and which zone should display it. The epoch and the arithmetic are fixed; the display is a choice. Keep those separate and a timestamp stops being mysterious.

What Unix time actually counts

Unix time counts seconds from 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, the epoch, in UTC. 0 is that instant. 86400 is 1970-01-02T00:00:00Z because one day has 86,400 seconds. The number is not a clock face and carries no timezone; it names one instant on the global timeline.

Why 1970? It was a convenient origin for early Unix systems, close enough to their own era to keep values small and far enough back to cover useful history. The choice is a convention, not an astronomical event. Other systems use different origins, which is why a timestamp from a Windows file property or a GPS receiver should not be pasted into a Unix converter without checking its epoch.

The count ignores leap seconds. Unix time treats every day as 86,400 seconds, so the UTC label around an inserted leap second can differ from a strict count of SI seconds. For ordinary logging, scheduling and date arithmetic that difference is irrelevant. For precision timing systems, it is not.

Timestamps can be negative: -86400 is 1969-12-31T00:00:00Z. They also have a range limit on older systems. A signed 32-bit seconds value stops at 2147483647, which is 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z. That is the much-discussed 2038 problem. Modern 64-bit systems handle dates far beyond it, but embedded devices and old database columns may not.

Seconds vs milliseconds: how to tell them apart

Unix seconds and Unix milliseconds share the same epoch and differ by a factor of 1,000. 1700000000 seconds and 1700000000000 milliseconds are the same instant. Digit length is the quickest check: a present-day seconds value has 10 digits, and the same instant in milliseconds has 13. A 16-digit value is usually microseconds, which require dividing by 1,000,000.

APIs disagree about units. Many HTTP APIs and database functions return seconds; JavaScript's Date.now() returns milliseconds. If a converted date lands in 1970 or in the year 56,000, the unit is wrong by a factor of 1,000. Divide or multiply once and recheck the year before doing anything else.

UnitDigits in this exampleValueUTC rendering
Seconds1017000000002023-11-14T22:13:20Z
Milliseconds1317000000000002023-11-14T22:13:20Z
Microseconds1617000000000000002023-11-14T22:13:20Z
ISO 8601 string20 characters2023-11-14T22:13:20Z2023-11-14T22:13:20Z

The ISO row is not a different time; it is a different notation. The trailing Z means UTC, so an ISO string with a Z and a Unix timestamp can be compared directly. An ISO string with +05:30 or -04:00 describes the same kind of instant with an explicit offset attached.

Which unit should you store?

Store the unit your consumers expect, and write it into the field name or schema. A column called created_at with no unit is a future bug; created_at_ms or an ISO 8601 text field removes the guess. Milliseconds are convenient for JavaScript and for ordering events that occur within the same second. Seconds are smaller and match many APIs. Microseconds and nanoseconds appear in instrumentation and high-resolution logs, where 16 or 19 digits are normal.

When a value arrives without documentation, test it against a known event. A 10-digit value near 1.7 billion is late 2023 in seconds; the same digits with three more zeros are milliseconds. A 9-digit number is 2001 or earlier in seconds, while a 12-digit number is likely milliseconds between 1973 and 2001, or a non-Unix epoch. The year is the tell, not the digit count alone.

Converting in both directions, with the arithmetic shown

To convert seconds to UTC, divide by 86,400 to get whole days after the epoch, then turn the remainder into hours, minutes and seconds. Example 1: 1,700,000,000 seconds. The division gives 19,675 days with a remainder of 80,000 seconds. 80,000 seconds is 22 hours (79,200), 13 minutes (780) and 20 seconds. Day 19,675 after 1970-01-01 is 2023-11-14, so the instant is 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z.

To go the other way, count the days from the epoch and multiply. Example 2: 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z is 19,723 days after the epoch. 19,723 × 86,400 = 1,704,067,200, so the timestamp is 1704067200. Example 3: 2024-03-01T00:00:00Z is 60 days later, because January has 31 days and February 2024 has 29. 60 × 86,400 = 5,184,000, and 1,704,067,200 + 5,184,000 = 1,709,251,200. That matches 2024-03-01T00:00:00Z.

For milliseconds, multiply the seconds result by 1,000. The 2024-01-01 example becomes 1,704,067,200,000 milliseconds. Going back, divide by 1,000 before doing the day arithmetic. For microseconds, divide by 1,000,000. Doing the day division on a millisecond value is the single most common conversion error, and it produces a date tens of thousands of years away.

Fractional seconds are not part of the integer count. 1700000000.5 is half a second after the whole-second instant, and ISO would show 2023-11-14T22:13:20.500Z. If a system truncates the fraction, two events can appear in the wrong order. Keep the fractional part when ordering high-frequency logs, and round only when displaying a human-readable time.

Where timezones and daylight saving enter

A timestamp does not change when you change timezones; the local rendering does. 1,700,000,000 is 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z everywhere. On that date New York was on EST, UTC−5, so the local clock read 17:13:20. Berlin was on CET, UTC+1, so it read 23:13:20. Tokyo was at UTC+9, so it read 07:13:20 on 15 November. The instant is identical; the labels differ.

Offsets are rules, not constants. New York uses EST in winter and EDT in summer, and the switch dates are set by local law. A timestamp near a boundary can therefore render with one offset in January and another in July. For example, 2026-03-08 05:00 UTC is 00:00 EST in New York. At 07:00 UTC that same morning, the city has sprung forward and the local time is 03:00 EDT. The two-hour UTC gap contains a one-hour local jump, not a missing timestamp.

That is why logs should store UTC and render in a named IANA zone such as America/New_York, not a fixed UTC-5. A fixed offset is correct only until the next clock change. Use the timezone conversion guide for meeting-time examples, and keep the zone name with any timestamp you archive.

When you render a timestamp for a user, show the zone abbreviation or the offset alongside it. "22:13" is ambiguous; "22:13 UTC" or "17:13 EST" is not. The converter's local pane uses the device zone, which may not be the zone the user expects if they are travelling or if the browser is set to a different region.

Common mistakes that produce the wrong date

  1. Treating milliseconds as seconds. The year jumps to roughly 56,000. Divide by 1,000 before converting.
  2. Treating seconds as milliseconds. The date collapses to January 1970. Multiply by 1,000 and look again.
  3. Reading a UTC timestamp as local. A log stamped 22:13Z is not 22:13 in New York; it is 17:13 EST that day.
  4. Using a fixed offset for a DST zone. A value that is correct in January is off by an hour in July. Use the IANA zone and a date-aware conversion.
  5. Dropping the Z. An ISO string without a zone can be interpreted as local time by the receiving system, which shifts the instant.
  6. Assuming 2038 is only a hardware problem. Any database column or API field still storing signed 32-bit seconds has the same ceiling.
  7. Confusing a duration with a timestamp. The number of seconds between two events is not a date. Adding 3,600 to a timestamp is fine; adding 3,600 to a duration is just arithmetic.

A quick sanity check catches most of these. A 2023 or 2024 timestamp in seconds sits near 1.7 billion; the same instant in milliseconds is near 1.7 trillion. If the digit count and the year do not agree, stop and check the unit before debugging the timezone.

A clean converter workflow

The timestamp converter accepts seconds or milliseconds and displays UTC and local versions together. Paste the value, confirm the digit count, compare the two panes, then copy the ISO string into your code or log. If you need to add days to a date rather than translate an instant, the date calculator handles calendar arithmetic without timestamp conversions.

  1. Paste the number and note whether it has 10, 13 or 16 digits.
  2. Check the UTC result against a known event or a second source.
  3. Switch the local zone and confirm the offset for that specific date.
  4. Copy the ISO 8601 string with its Z or offset attached.
Try it: paste 1700000000 into the Unix timestamp converter, confirm 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z, then switch the local zone and watch the clock change while the instant stays fixed.

faqs.question: What is a Unix timestamp?
faqs.answer: It is the number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, ignoring leap seconds. 1700000000 means 2023-11-14T22:13:20Z. The number identifies an instant and has no timezone; local clocks display that instant according to their offset and DST rules.

faqs.question: How do I know if a timestamp is seconds or milliseconds?
faqs.answer: Count the digits. A present-day seconds value has 10 digits, the same instant in milliseconds has 13, and microseconds have 16. 1700000000 and 1700000000000 are the same moment. If the converted year is 1970 or around 56,000, the unit is off by a factor of 1,000.

faqs.question: Does a Unix timestamp change with timezone?
faqs.answer: No. The timestamp is tied to UTC, so 1700000000 is the same instant in New York, Berlin and Tokyo. Only the displayed local time changes: 17:13:20 EST in New York, 23:13:20 CET in Berlin and 07:13:20 the next day in Tokyo.

faqs.question: Why does my converted date land one day off?
faqs.answer: A one-day shift usually comes from applying the wrong offset or reading a UTC date as local. A timestamp near midnight UTC can be the previous or next date in another zone. Convert to the zone that governs the record and keep the date and offset together.

faqs.question: What is the 2038 problem?
faqs.answer: A signed 32-bit seconds counter reaches its maximum at 2147483647, which is 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z. Systems that still store time that way will overflow unless they move to 64-bit values. Modern databases and languages generally use wider types.

faqs.question: Can a Unix timestamp be negative?
faqs.answer: Yes. Negative values represent instants before 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z; for example, -86400 is 1969-12-31T00:00:00Z. Some APIs reject negative values, so check the receiving system before sending historical dates.

title: Leap Year Birthdays: How Age and Dates Work
description: Leap year birthdays explained: the Gregorian rule, how 29 February ages work, day-count arithmetic and the 28 February vs 1 March conventions.
keywords: how old is a leap year baby

toc.text: Age arithmetic for a leap-day birthday

html:
A leap year birthday on 29 February is a calendar edge case with a simple core: the date exists only in leap years. In 2026 it does not exist, and the next one is 2028. That affects birthday plans, age labels and any form that expects a date, but it does not make the underlying day count ambiguous.

This guide is part of the age calculator guide. It covers the Gregorian rule, the common ways to assign a birthday in a common year, and the arithmetic that keeps age in years, months and days consistent. Use the age calculator to test a date while you read.

The Gregorian leap-year rule

The Gregorian calendar adds a leap day when the year is divisible by 4, except for century years. A century year is a leap year only when it is divisible by 400. So 2024 and 2028 are leap years; 2026 is not; 2100 is not; 2000 is. The exception matters because it keeps the average year close to the solar year: 97 leap years in every 400-year cycle.

February in a leap year has 29 days; in a common year it has 28. The extra day is inserted after 28 February, which is why 29 February is the only date that can disappear from the calendar for three years at a time. The gap can be longer around a skipped century leap year: 2096 is followed by 2104, with no 29 February in 2100.

If dates were spread evenly, a 29 February birthday would fall on about 97 out of every 146,097 calendar days, roughly 1 in 1,506. Real birth dates are not evenly spread, so treat that as a calendar fact rather than a prediction about any hospital ward or generation.

The rule applies to the proleptic Gregorian calendar, which extends the modern leap-year pattern backward before 1582. Historical dates from countries that adopted the Gregorian calendar later can be off by the local Julian calendar, so a genealogy calculation may need a manual adjustment. For dates from the twentieth century onward, the rule above is the one to use.

How often 29 February arrives

For most people the pattern is every four years. The sequence around now is 2024, 2028, 2032 and 2036. In 2026 and 2027 there is no 29 February, so a leapling's birthday falls on a date that has to be chosen by convention. The table shows how the century rule changes the answer.

YearDivisible by 4?Century ruleLeap year?Days in February
2024YesNot a century yearYes29
2026NoNot applicableNo28
2028YesNot a century yearYes29
2100YesDivisible by 100, not by 400No28
2000YesDivisible by 400Yes29

Do not use "every four years" as a calculation rule without the century check. A simple four-year loop would mark 2100 as a leap year and put every date after it one day off. A date library that follows the proleptic Gregorian calendar handles this correctly; a hand-written rule needs the 100 and 400 tests.

Three ways to mark a 29 February birthday

There are three practical conventions for a common year:

  • 28 February: treat the last day of February as the anniversary, so the age increments on 28 February.
  • 1 March: treat the first day of March as the anniversary, so the age increments on 1 March.
  • Wait for 29 February: hold the celebration until the date returns. That can mean a four-year gap and, around 2100, an eight-year gap.

None of these changes the number of days the person has lived. They change the label attached to a particular day. Legal and administrative rules are jurisdiction-specific. Some systems specify 28 February, others specify 1 March, and some laws define age by the anniversary of birth without addressing the missing date. Check the rule that applies to the form, licence or statute instead of assuming one convention is universal.

For everyday purposes, pick a convention inside the family and use it consistently. For official purposes, follow the document. Mixing the two is how a person ends up celebrating on 28 February and filing paperwork as if the birthday were 1 March.

For a child, the convention can affect school cutoff dates by a day, which matters in districts with a strict 1 March or 28 February boundary. For an adult, the practical effect is usually the celebration date, not the legal age. The day count is the stable measure; the annual label is the local rule.

Age arithmetic for a leap-day birthday

Example 1: born 29 February 2000, observed on 28 February 2026. Under the 28 February convention, the person has completed 26 years. The day count is 26 × 365 = 9,490, and the leap days from 2004 through 2024 add 6 more, for 9,496 days. That is 26 years, 0 months and 0 days under that convention. Under the 1 March convention, the same 28 February date is 25 years, 11 months and 27 days, because the 2026 anniversary has not arrived yet.

Example 2: born 29 February 2000, observed on 1 March 2026. Under the 1 March convention, the person is exactly 26 years old on that date. The day count is 9,497 days: 9,496 days to 28 February 2026, and one more day to 1 March. The one-day difference between the two conventions is the entire dispute in most birthday arguments.

Example 3: an ordinary leap-year effect. From 2024-01-01 to 2025-01-01 there are 366 days because 2024 contains 29 February. From 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01 there are 365. Someone born on 1 January gains an extra day in the first interval, which is why multiplying age in years by 365 always undercounts.

Notice what stays fixed. The day count between two dates is a fact; the year and month breakdown depends on where you place the anniversary. If a form asks for age in years, use its convention. If you are measuring time lived, use the dates and count days.

If you need the age in months as well, count complete months first, then the leftover days. From 29 February 2000 to 28 February 2026 under the 28 February convention, the complete months are 312 (26 × 12), with 0 leftover days. Under the 1 March convention, the complete months are 311, with 27 leftover days. The month count and the day count move together; they are not independent estimates.

What this means for documents and milestones

Age in years is a legal and social label; age in days is a count. A 29 February birthday creates ambiguity only in the first. For school cutoffs, driving eligibility, retirement or visa forms, use the date of birth the document expects and apply the local rule. For a day count, use both dates and count the boundaries between them.

Time zones add a second edge. A baby born at 23:30 on 29 February in one zone may already be 1 March in UTC. If a record stores only the local date, keep that local date; if it stores an instant, convert to the zone that governs the record before deciding which calendar date applies. Do not combine a UTC timestamp with a local birthday convention.

Leap-day birthdays also affect recurring reminders. A calendar app that simply repeats "29 February every year" will skip three years at a time. A reminder set for 28 February or 1 March will fire annually, but it will not match the legal date if the governing rule uses the other convention. Decide which behavior you want before you create the event.

Checking a leap-day date in the age calculator

The age calculator takes a birth date and a comparison date and returns years, months and days, total days, and the next birthday. Enter 2000-02-29 and 2026-02-28 to see the 28 February convention in action, then change the comparison date to 2026-03-01 and compare.

  1. Enter the birth date exactly as recorded, including 29 February if that is the legal date.
  2. Choose the date you are measuring to; today is the default.
  3. Read the year-month-day result and the total days separately.
  4. Check the next-birthday line, which points to 2028 when the current year is common.

For a pure day count that ignores birthday conventions, use the age in days guide. For the difference between two arbitrary dates, the date difference tutorial covers inclusive and exclusive counting.

Test a leapling date: open the age calculator, enter 2000-02-29, and compare 2026-02-28 with 2026-03-01. The day total moves by one; the year label depends on the convention.

faqs.question: Is 2026 a leap year?
faqs.answer: No. 2026 is not divisible by 4, so February 2026 has 28 days and there is no 29 February. The next leap year is 2028, followed by 2032 and 2036. The century exception is separate: 2100 will not be a leap year because it is divisible by 100 but not by 400.

faqs.question: How old is someone born on 29 February 2000 in 2026?
faqs.answer: On 28 February 2026 they are 26 under the 28 February convention, with 9,496 days lived. Under the 1 March convention they are 25 years, 11 months and 27 days on 28 February, then 26 on 1 March, with 9,497 days. The day count differs by one because the anniversary placement differs.

faqs.question: Why is 2100 not a leap year when 2000 was?
faqs.answer: A century year is a leap year only if it is divisible by 400. 2000 is divisible by 400, so it had 29 February. 2100 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it has 28 February. This keeps the calendar aligned with the solar year over long periods.

faqs.question: Do leap-year babies age more slowly?
faqs.answer: No. Their day count is the same as anyone else's born on the same date. Only the annual label is awkward in common years. A person born on 29 February 2000 has lived 9,496 days by 28 February 2026, regardless of whether the family celebrates in February or March.

faqs.question: What date should legal forms use for a 29 February birthday?
faqs.answer: Use the date recorded on the birth certificate and follow the rule of the jurisdiction or agency receiving the form. Some systems specify 28 February in common years, others 1 March, and some define age by the anniversary without addressing the missing date. Do not assume a universal rule.

faqs.question: How many days are there from 29 February 2000 to 28 February 2026?
faqs.answer: There are 9,496 days. Start with 26 × 365 = 9,490, then add the six leap days in 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024. One more day reaches 1 March 2026 and a total of 9,497 days.

title: Add or Subtract Days From a Date (Including Weekends)
description: Add or subtract days from any date with calendar math, month-end clamping, business-day counting and clear inclusive vs exclusive rules.
html:
Adding 30 days to 31 January does not land on the same date as adding one month. That is not a bug in the calculator; it is the difference between a fixed day count and calendar arithmetic. Once you separate the two, most date planning becomes predictable.

This guide is part of the age calculator guide. It covers adding and subtracting calendar days, the month-end clamping rule, business-day counts and the inclusive-versus-exclusive distinction that can move a deadline by one day. Follow along in the date calculator.

Calendar days are not 24-hour blocks

A calendar day is a date on the wall, not a fixed duration. Adding one calendar day to 8 March 2026 in New York takes you to 9 March 2026, even though the clocks spring forward in between and only 23 hours elapse. If you instead add 24 hours to the instant 2026-03-08 00:00 EST, you land at 2026-03-09 01:00 EDT, not at midnight. Both operations are correct; they answer different questions.

For deadlines, anniversaries and billing dates, calendar-day arithmetic is usually what people mean. For elapsed time, shifts, logs and countdowns, use exact durations. A date calculator should work on dates, not on 24-hour blocks, because otherwise a spring-forward day silently shifts every result after it.

Most date calculators accept only a date, with no time or zone. That is a feature: it removes the DST ambiguity and makes the result reproducible. If your input includes a time, strip it only after deciding which zone's date you mean. A timestamp at 23:30 UTC is already the next date in Tokyo, so the "start date" can differ by zone before any arithmetic begins.

Adding days with the arithmetic shown
