Example 1: 2026-01-01 plus 40 days. January has 31 days. From 1 January, 30 days takes you to 31 January, and 10 more days takes you to 2026-02-10. Check by day of year: 1 January is day 1, so day 41 is 10 February because January supplies 31 days and February supplies the remaining 10.

Example 2: 2026-03-01 minus 45 days. Going back from 1 March, February 2026 has 28 days, so 1 March minus 28 days is 1 February. That leaves 17 more days to subtract; 1 February minus 17 days is 2026-01-15. A forward check: 15 January and 16 days reach 31 January, then 28 days of February and 1 day to 1 March gives 16 + 28 + 1 = 45.

Example 3: 2026-01-01 minus 10 days. Subtract 1 day to 31 December 2025, then 9 more to 2025-12-22. The year boundary is just another month boundary; no special case is needed. The same method works for positive and negative offsets, which is why a single add-or-subtract field is enough.

Weeks, months and the month-end clamp

Weeks are unambiguous: add 2 weeks means add 14 days. Months are not. Adding one month to 31 January 2026 gives 28 February 2026, because February has no 31st and the result is clamped to the last valid day. In 2024, the same operation gives 29 February. Adding 30 days to 31 January 2026 gives 2 March 2026, a different result.

This clamping rule is why subscription renewals, lease terms and payroll dates need a written convention. "One month" can mean the same day number next month, the last day of the next month, or a fixed 30-day period. Pick one and state it. If the contract says "the same date next month," a 31 January start usually renews on the last day of February, not on 3 March.

Leap years change the clamp only in February. A 29 February start advanced by one year lands on 28 February in a common year and 29 February in the next leap year. A 31 March start advanced by one month is 30 April in every year, because April always has 30 days. The rule is about the target month's length, not about the starting month.

Years follow the same clamp. Adding one year to 29 February 2024 gives 28 February 2025, and adding four years gives 29 February 2028. A 31 December start advanced by one year is 31 December, because December always has 31 days. The operation is calendar-aware, not a fixed 365-day add, which is why a leap year never shifts a December anniversary.

Weekends and business-day counts

Calendar days include weekends and holidays. Business-day arithmetic skips them, but the definition of a business day is local: Monday to Friday in many offices, Sunday to Thursday in others, and holiday calendars differ by country and year.

Example 4: add 10 business days to Monday 2026-03-02. If the start day counts as day 1, the sequence is 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 March for five days, then 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 March for ten, so the result is Friday 2026-03-13. If counting begins on the next business day, the result is Monday 2026-03-16. The one-day gap is a convention, not an arithmetic error.

Holidays can move the result further. A 10-business-day promise that crosses a public holiday is 11 weekdays unless the holiday is excluded. The date calculator counts calendar days and can show weekday breakdowns; it does not know your local holiday list, so subtract those separately.

OperationStart dateResultWhy
Add 40 calendar days2026-01-012026-02-1031 days in January, then 10 in February
Subtract 10 calendar days2026-01-012025-12-22Crosses the year boundary
Add 1 month2026-01-312026-02-28Clamped to the last day of February
Add 30 days2026-01-312026-03-02Fixed count ignores month lengths
Add 10 business days, start counts2026-03-022026-03-13Weekends skipped

Inclusive vs exclusive counting

Date differences are either inclusive or exclusive of an endpoint. From 1 January to 10 January, the exclusive count is 9 days: 2 January is day 1, and 10 January is day 9. The inclusive count is 10 dates because both 1 January and 10 January are included. Neither is wrong; the contract or question decides.

The same split appears in "add 7 days." Starting 1 January, 7 days later is 8 January, which is 7 elapsed days but 8 dates touched if you count both ends. Hotel stays use nights, so a check-in on 1 January and check-out on 8 January is 7 nights. A project that runs "from 1 January for 7 days" may include 1 January and end on 7 January, or start counting on 2 January and end on 8 January. Write the end date, not just the duration.

Age calculations use the same convention. A baby born on 1 January is 0 days old on 1 January, 1 day old on 2 January, and 365 or 366 days old on the next 1 January. An inclusive count would call the birth date day 1 and add one to every total. If two systems disagree by exactly one day, check this first.

Mistakes that move the date

  1. Using 30 days for every month. Months have 28, 29, 30 or 31 days, and February changes with the leap-year rule.
  2. Adding months by day number without clamping. One month after 31 January is not 3 March; it is the last valid day of February.
  3. Mixing calendar days with 24-hour durations across DST. A calendar-day add and a 24-hour add can differ by an hour at the transition.
  4. Forgetting weekends and holidays. A 10-day promise in calendar days can be 8 business days or fewer once a holiday lands inside it.
  5. Counting both endpoints when the contract counts one. The difference is one day, which is enough to miss a filing window.
  6. Assuming "between" means inclusive. Many calculators return the exclusive gap, so confirm before you rely on the number.

Using the date calculator

The date calculator has an add-or-subtract mode and a difference mode. Use add-or-subtract mode when you need to add days to a date or count backward from one; enter the start date and a positive or negative number of days, weeks or months. In difference mode, enter two dates and read the day total and weekday breakdown. Both modes use calendar arithmetic and handle leap years.

  1. Choose add/subtract or difference.
  2. Enter the start date, or both dates for a difference.
  3. Pick days, weeks or months; use a negative number to subtract.
  4. Read the result and check the weekday if the deadline is business-sensitive.

For age-specific date math, the age in days guide converts a birth date to total days and hours. The date difference tutorial goes deeper on inclusive counting.

Run your date: open the date calculator, add 40 days to 2026-01-01, then switch to difference mode and check the same pair. The result should read 2026-02-10 and 40 days.

faqs.question: How do I add 30 days to a date?
faqs.answer: Count forward through the calendar rather than assuming every month has 30 days. From 2026-01-31, 30 days lands on 2026-03-02: February contributes 28 days and the remaining 2 fall in March. A date calculator handles the month boundary automatically and reports the weekday.

faqs.question: What is 40 days after 1 January 2026?
faqs.answer: It is 10 February 2026. January has 31 days, so 30 days after 1 January is 31 January, and 10 more days reaches 10 February. The same result comes from day-of-year counting: 1 January is day 1, so day 41 is 10 February.

faqs.question: Why does one month after 31 January land on 28 February?
faqs.answer: February has no 31st, so calendar arithmetic clamps the result to the last valid day of the target month. In 2026 that is 28 February; in 2024 it is 29 February. Adding a fixed 30 days instead gives 2 March 2026, which is a different operation.

faqs.question: Are weekends included when adding days?
faqs.answer: Calendar-day addition includes weekends and holidays. Business-day addition skips them, but the definition of a business day depends on the country and office. Adding 10 business days to Monday 2026-03-02 gives Friday 13 March if the start day counts, or Monday 16 March if counting starts the next day.

faqs.question: How many days are there from 1 January to 10 January?
faqs.answer: The exclusive count is 9 days, because the span stops before 10 January. The inclusive count is 10 dates because both endpoints are included. A hotel stay from 1 January to 8 January is 7 nights, using the exclusive convention, while a project that includes both start and end dates would add one.

faqs.question: Does daylight saving change date addition?
faqs.answer: It changes elapsed time, not calendar dates. Adding one calendar day to 2026-03-08 in New York gives 9 March even though only 23 hours pass. Adding 24 hours to the instant lands at 01:00 on 9 March. Choose the method based on whether you need a date or a duration.

title: Age in Days, Hours and Minutes: Exact Conversion
description: Calculate exact age in days, hours and minutes with leap-day arithmetic, worked examples and the DST caveat for elapsed time.

toc.text: Why age in days is not years times 365
Converting days to hours and minutes

html:
"Age in days" sounds like a multiplication problem: take the years, multiply by 365, then add something for leap years. That shortcut gets close, but it misses the exact count by days, and it cannot answer hours or minutes at all. The reliable method is to count calendar days between the birth date and the target date, then convert the total.

This guide is part of the age calculator guide. It works through three examples, including the leap-day correction, and explains where timezones and daylight saving break the simple 24-hour conversion. Use the age calculator to check your own dates.

Why age in days is not years times 365

A year is not 365 days on average. The Gregorian calendar averages 365.2425 days, and any span of years contains a whole number of leap days. Someone born on 15 June 1990 and measured on 16 September 2026 has lived through the leap days of 1992, 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024: nine extra days. Multiplying 36 years by 365 gives 13,140 days; adding the nine leap days gives 13,149; the remaining 3 months and 1 day add 93. The exact total is 13,242 days.

That is the whole correction. The month and day remainder is not a fraction to estimate; it is a calendar count from 15 June to 16 September: 15 days left in June, 31 in July, 31 in August and 16 in September, for 93. The year-month-day label and the total-day count describe the same span in different units.

The shortcut is still useful for a rough estimate. Thirty years times 365.2425 is about 10,957 days, which matches the exact count in the next section. The average works over long spans, but it can be off by a day or two for a specific birth date, and it cannot tell you which day is the 10,000th. Use it for a sanity check, not for the final number.

Counting exact days between two dates

For a date-only age, day 0 is the birth date. The next day is day 1. This is the exclusive convention used by most age calculators: the birth date is not counted as a full day lived. If you need an inclusive count, add one. The distinction matters for milestone celebrations and for any form that asks for days rather than years.

Example 1: 30th birthday. Born 10 May 1996; target 10 May 2026. The span is 30 years. Leap days after the birth date and up to the target are 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024: seven. 30 × 365 = 10,950; 10,950 + 7 = 10,957 days. In hours: 10,957 × 24 = 262,968 hours. In minutes: 262,968 × 60 = 15,778,080 minutes.

Example 2: 1,000 days old. Starting 1 January 2023: 2023 contributes 365 days, 2024 contributes 366, and 365 + 366 = 731. The remaining 269 days run through 2025: January 30 days after the 1st, February 28, March 31, April 30, May 31, June 30, July 31, August 31 and September 27. The 1,000th day is 27 September 2025. Check: 365 + 366 + 269 = 1,000.

Example 3: the long span. From 15 June 1990 to 16 September 2026, the 36 years contribute 13,140 days, the nine leap days contribute 9, and the 15 June to 16 September remainder contributes 93. The sum is 13,140 + 9 + 93 = 13,242 days. That is the figure to use for a day-count milestone, not 36 × 365 = 13,140.

A 10,000-day milestone from the same birth date falls on 31 October 2017. The remaining 3,242 days reach 16 September 2026, which is why the two totals differ by exactly that amount. Milestone dates are easier to find by adding the day count than by converting years.

Counting across a leap day

A span that includes 29 February has one more day than the same span in a common year. From 1 January 2024 to 1 January 2025 is 366 days; from 1 January 2025 to 1 January 2026 is 365. If you are counting backward, the leap day is inside the interval whenever it falls between the two dates, regardless of whether the start or end year is the leap year. That is why subtracting two dates is safer than adding 365 repeatedly.

Converting days to hours and minutes

Once you have the day total, the rest is multiplication: 1 day = 24 hours, 1 hour = 60 minutes, 1 minute = 60 seconds. For 13,242 days: 13,242 × 24 = 317,808 hours; 317,808 × 60 = 19,068,480 minutes; 19,068,480 × 60 = 1,144,108,800 seconds.

Those figures assume every day has 24 hours. That is true for civil-date arithmetic and false for elapsed time in a zone with daylight saving. The next section explains the gap. For most age milestones, the date-based figure is the one people expect; for a precise elapsed duration between two timestamps, use the UTC difference instead.

DaysHoursMinutesSeconds
1,00024,0001,440,00086,400,000
10,957262,96815,778,080946,684,800
13,242317,80819,068,4801,144,108,800

Daylight saving: when a day is not 24 hours

In a zone that springs forward, one local day has 23 hours; in autumn, one has 25. New York's 8 March 2026 is 23 hours long, and 1 November 2026 is 25 hours long. A date-only age calculator that counts 13,242 days and multiplies by 24 gets a clean number, but it is not the exact number of elapsed hours between two local timestamps.

For an exact elapsed duration, subtract the two instants in UTC, then convert. If both records are local times, convert each to UTC with the offset that applied on that date, not the offset that applies today. A birth at 23:30 on 29 February and a target at 00:30 on 1 March can be one hour apart in elapsed time and two calendar dates apart. Decide whether the question is "how many date boundaries" or "how much time."

Cross-zone records add the same issue. A birth certificate may record a local date in one country, while the person now lives in another. Age in days from the recorded civil dates is not the same as elapsed hours from the recorded instants. Keep the dates and the zone attached to them, and state which interpretation a result uses.

What counts as a day

Age in days is usually the number of completed days, so the birth date itself is day 0. Some cultures and forms count the birth date as day 1. Legal age is normally expressed in years, not days, and a day count does not override the legal rule. For a passport, school admission or retirement calculation, use the official date-of-birth rule; for a milestone or a data visualization, use the exact day count.

Inclusive counting also changes anniversaries. From 1 January to 1 January next year, the exclusive count is 365 or 366 days, and the inclusive count adds one. A 1,000-day celebration based on an exclusive count lands one day earlier than one based on an inclusive count. State the convention before comparing two numbers.

Time of birth is a separate input. A date-only calculation treats everyone born on the same date as having the same age in days, regardless of whether the birth was at 00:01 or 23:59. That is appropriate for calendar milestones and insufficient for elapsed-time records. If the exact hour matters, store the timestamp and the zone, not just the date.

If you need an age in days for a legal or medical record, confirm whether the receiving office wants completed days or a date range. A medical record may care about the exact time of birth; a school form may care only about the date. The arithmetic is the same, but the input precision is not.

Checking the total in the age calculator

The age calculator returns years, months and days, total days, and a next-birthday countdown. Enter a birth date and a target date, then read the totals separately:

  1. Enter the birth date, including the correct year.
  2. Set the comparison date; today is fine for a current age.
  3. Read the total days figure before converting to hours or minutes.
  4. Check the next-birthday line if you need the upcoming anniversary date.

For leap-day birthdays, the leap year birthday guide explains the 28 February and 1 March conventions. For a plain interval between two dates, the date difference tutorial covers inclusive counting and weekday breakdowns.

Get your total: open the age calculator, enter 15 June 1990 and 16 September 2026, and confirm 13,242 days. Then multiply by 24 to check the 317,808-hour figure.

faqs.question: How do I calculate my age in days?
faqs.answer: Count the calendar days from your birth date to the target date, then add the leap days in the span. For 15 June 1990 to 16 September 2026, 36 × 365 = 13,140, the nine leap days add 9, and the 3-month, 1-day remainder adds 93, for 13,242 days. The age calculator does this in one step.

faqs.question: Is age in days just years multiplied by 365?
faqs.answer: No. That omits leap days and the partial year. For a 30th birthday from 10 May 1996 to 10 May 2026, 30 × 365 = 10,950, but the seven leap days raise the exact total to 10,957 days. The error grows with the length of the span.

faqs.question: How many hours are in 13,242 days?
faqs.answer: 13,242 × 24 = 317,808 hours. That is 19,068,480 minutes or 1,144,108,800 seconds. The result assumes 24-hour days, which is correct for calendar-date arithmetic but not for exact elapsed time across daylight-saving transitions.

faqs.question: Does daylight saving change age in days?
faqs.answer: It does not change a calendar-date day count. It does change elapsed hours: a spring-forward day in New York has 23 hours, and a fall-back day has 25. For exact duration, subtract the two UTC instants rather than multiplying the day count by 24.

faqs.question: Is the birth date day 0 or day 1?
faqs.answer: Most age calculators use day 0, so the birth date is not counted as a completed day. An inclusive count treats the birth date as day 1 and adds one to the total. Agree on the convention before comparing results from two systems.

faqs.question: Why is 1,000 days after 1 January 2023 on 27 September 2025?
faqs.answer: 2023 contributes 365 days and 2024 contributes 366, for 731. The remaining 269 days run from 1 January 2025 to 27 September 2025: 30 days in January after the 1st, 28 in February, and 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31 and 27 in the following months. The sum is 365 + 366 + 269 = 1,000.

title: Proforma Invoice vs Tax Invoice: Key Differences
description: Proforma invoice vs tax invoice explained: purpose, tax status, numbering and accounting, with two worked examples and a conversion checklist.
html:
A proforma invoice can move a project forward, but it cannot do the job of a tax invoice. Buyers use it to open a purchase order, arrange an advance or clear an import; sellers use it to confirm price and scope before supply. Confusing the two creates expensive paperwork: money collected against a document that was never a tax invoice, or tax charged on a proforma that never became a bill. This guide separates the documents, shows the conversion arithmetic and lists the fields that prevent rework.

Part of the free invoice generator guide. The examples use rupees and dollars; the rules here are general information, not tax or legal advice.

What a proforma invoice is (and is not)

A proforma invoice is a preliminary commercial document. It states what you intend to supply, at what price, on what terms and by when. It usually arrives after a quote is accepted but before goods ship or services are delivered. It can look almost identical to a tax invoice — same logo, line items, discount and shipping estimate — yet its legal job is different. It is not a demand for tax, it is not a statutory tax document, and it normally does not create a bookable sale.

Typical uses include requesting an advance, helping a buyer raise a purchase order, supporting an import licence or customs declaration, freezing a price for a stated period, and confirming a milestone before work starts. The label matters. Print PROFORMA INVOICE at the top, give it a separate sequence such as PI-2026-018, and add “not a tax invoice” where local rules or the buyer require it. A customer who needs to reclaim VAT or GST needs the tax invoice that follows, not the proforma.

Proforma invoice vs tax invoice: the differences that matter

Both documents can carry the same line items. The difference is what each one is allowed to do when money and tax are recorded.

FeatureProforma invoiceTax invoice
PurposeConfirms terms, supports a PO or requests an advanceDemands payment for a taxable supply
Legal statusCommercial document, not a statutory tax invoiceStatutory document that supports tax recovery and books
TaxEstimates tax or omits it; no tax is charged by the document itselfCharges tax at the applicable rate with a clear breakdown
NumberingSeparate PI series, e.g. PI-2026-018Invoice series, e.g. INV-2026-042
AccountingNo sales revenue or receivable in the usual senseRecorded as a sale and a receivable
TimingBefore supplyOn or after supply, within the time limit that applies
What followsConverted to a tax invoice, often with a referenceStands as the billing document; later changes use a credit or debit note

The dividing line is timing and tax. A proforma says “this is what we agreed”; a tax invoice says “this is what you now owe, and this is the tax.” Once the supply happens, the proforma has done its job. Reusing it as the final bill is the mistake that causes most disputes.

When to use a proforma (and when not to)

  • Before an advance: send a proforma with the deposit amount, tax estimate and balance formula. The customer's finance team can pay against it while your tax invoice waits for the tax point.
  • When the buyer needs a PO: enterprise procurement often cannot raise a purchase order from a quote alone. A proforma with a validity date and payment terms clears that step.
  • For imports and customs: authorities may ask for a proforma showing value, origin, freight and terms. Keep it consistent with the commercial invoice that follows.
  • To lock pricing: state “valid 30 days” and the currency. Without both, a slow signature can reopen a price you thought was closed.
  • For milestone approval: a proforma can confirm the next payment slice without pretending the work is complete.

Do not use a proforma after delivery has happened and the customer needs to recover tax. Do not print “tax invoice” on it to satisfy a buyer's portal. And do not assume an advance is tax-free: in India, tax on advances for goods can arise when the advance is received, and service timelines differ; EU and UK rules have their own tax points. Confirm the treatment with your accountant before you collect.

Two worked examples: advance and price validity

Example 1 — ₹80,000 project with a 50% advance

PI-2026-018 shows a design sprint at ₹80,000, a 50% advance of ₹40,000 and IGST at 18% on the advance, ₹7,200. The proforma total is ₹47,200. The customer pays that amount and work begins.

After delivery, INV-2026-042 bills the full taxable value of ₹80,000 with IGST of ₹14,400, for a total of ₹94,400. It then deducts the advance already received, ₹47,200, leaving ₹47,200 due. If the supply is intra-state, replace IGST with CGST of ₹3,600 and SGST of ₹3,600; the total stays the same. If you issued a tax invoice for the advance, reference that invoice number on the final bill so the customer's accounts team can match both entries without paying twice.

Example 2 — a proforma that expires before signature

PI-2026-019 quotes 120 hours at $45, a 5% early-commitment discount and 10% local tax for illustration. The arithmetic: 120 × $45 = $5,400; 5% of $5,400 = $270; net $5,130; tax $513; total $5,643. The proforma says “valid 30 days.”

The client signs on day 41. The supplier reissues at $48 per hour: 120 × $48 = $5,760; the same 5% discount is $288; net $5,472; tax at 10% is $547.20; total $6,019.20. The difference from the original is $376.20. The validity date did not prevent the increase, but it made the conversation honest: the old price expired, the new one was documented, and the buyer could compare both numbers. If you intend to honour the old price, say so in writing before the proforma lapses.

Six mistakes that turn a proforma into a problem

  1. Using it as the tax invoice. The customer cannot recover tax, your books miss the sale, and the correction needs a proper invoice or credit note.
  2. Charging tax without a tax invoice. A line labelled “GST 18%” on a proforma is an estimate, not a tax charge. Issue the statutory document when the tax point arrives.
  3. Mixing numbering series. Keep PI and INV sequences separate. Reusing invoice numbers on proformas creates duplicates that are painful to unwind; see the invoice numbering guide.
  4. Letting details drift. If the final invoice changes quantity, price or tax rate, the buyer's PO match fails. Note the reason for every change and reference the proforma.
  5. Omitting validity, currency or delivery terms. Cross-border proformas need an ISO currency code and the agreed Incoterm or service scope. “$5,000” is not a currency.
  6. Forgetting the advance. A final invoice that does not deduct the deposit gets short-paid or rejected. Show the advance as a negative line and attach the earlier document number.

Tax treatment of advances, exports and reverse-charge supplies varies by country and changes over time. This page is general information, not tax or legal advice; confirm the tax point and invoice wording with a qualified adviser. For field-level GST rules, read the GST invoice format guide.

Proforma invoice checklist before you send

  • Label reads “Proforma Invoice”, not “Tax Invoice”, and the number starts with PI.
  • Both parties' legal names, addresses and tax IDs are correct; the buyer's PO or contact is named.
  • Line items show quantity, unit, rate and a specific description, not “services”.
  • Currency is an ISO code; tax is labelled as an estimate or omitted with a note.
  • Validity date, payment terms, advance amount and balance formula are visible.
  • The document states what happens next: “A tax invoice will be issued on delivery.”
Build both documents: open the free invoice generator to draft the proforma, then convert it to a numbered tax invoice with the advance deducted. Keep the PI and INV files together so the customer's accounts team can match them.

faqs.question: Is a proforma invoice a demand for payment?
faqs.answer: No. A proforma invoice is a preliminary commercial document that confirms price, scope and terms before supply. It can support an advance request or a purchase order, but it is not a statutory tax invoice and not a demand for tax. The tax invoice issued at the tax point is the document that supports payment and tax recovery.

faqs.question: When does a proforma become a tax invoice?
faqs.answer: It does not convert by renaming the file. You issue a new tax invoice with its own INV number when the supply or tax point occurs, then reference the proforma and deduct any advance already paid. In the example, a ₹80,000 project with a ₹40,000 advance becomes a ₹94,400 invoice with ₹47,200 still due after the deposit.

faqs.question: Can I charge GST on a proforma invoice?
faqs.answer: A proforma can show an estimated tax amount so the buyer can budget, but the document itself does not charge tax. The actual charge belongs on the tax invoice with the correct rate and CGST/SGST or IGST split. Advances can create a tax point in some jurisdictions, so confirm timing with your accountant before collecting.

faqs.question: Should proforma and tax invoices use the same number series?
faqs.answer: Keep them separate. Use PI-2026-018 for proformas and INV-2026-042 for tax invoices, then cross-reference them in the notes. Separate series prevent duplicates, make the audit trail readable and stop a buyer's accounts software from treating a preliminary document as a second bill.

faqs.question: What should a proforma invoice include for an overseas buyer?
faqs.answer: Add an ISO currency code such as USD or EUR, the agreed Incoterm and named place for goods, the service scope and place of supply for services, a validity date and the payment route. State clearly that it is a proforma and that a tax invoice will follow. Without those fields, the buyer cannot raise a PO or arrange the transfer.

faqs.question: How do I handle an advance on the final invoice?
faqs.answer: Show the full taxable value and tax first, then a negative line for the advance received, with the earlier invoice or receipt number. In the ₹80,000 example, the final total is ₹94,400 and the ₹47,200 deposit leaves ₹47,200 due. That layout lets the customer's accounts team match the payment without treating it as a duplicate.

title: Credit Note vs Debit Note: When to Use Each
description: Credit note vs debit note: what each adjusts, when to issue one, GST wording, numbering and two worked examples with the original invoice math.
html:
A credit note and a debit note both adjust an invoice that already exists. One reduces what the buyer owes; the other increases it. Problems start when they arrive as informal emails, when the original invoice is never referenced, or when tax is adjusted without a paper trail. This guide explains the direction, the wording and the arithmetic, with a return example and an extra-scope example.

Part of the free invoice generator guide. The figures are illustrative and this page is general information, not tax or legal advice.

What a credit note is

A credit note is a document a seller issues to reduce the amount a buyer owes on a previous invoice. It fits a return, an overcharge, a cancelled order, a post-invoice discount, damaged goods, or a correction to quantity, price or tax. It must point back to the original invoice, state the reason, show the taxable value being reduced and split the tax adjustment the same way the original invoice split it. Number it in a separate series such as CN-2026-007.

Two boundaries matter. A credit note is not a refund receipt: it reduces the debt, while the refund is the movement of money, recorded separately. And it is not a new sale with a negative price; it is an adjustment to an existing supply. If the invoice was never sent, correct or void it before sending rather than issuing a note for a document the buyer never saw. Keep the note short and factual: the original invoice carries the full description, and the note only needs to explain what changed.

What a debit note is

A debit note increases the amount owed on a prior invoice. It fits underbilling, work added after the invoice, a price revision agreed later, omitted freight or tax charged at the wrong rate. Like a credit note, it references the original invoice number and date, explains the reason and shows the added taxable value with its tax. Number it separately, for example DN-2026-004. Some businesses call this a supplementary invoice, but the label should match the local tax rules and your numbering policy rather than change from client to client.

The phrase has a second life in bookkeeping: a buyer may raise a debit note against a supplier for a purchase return. That is an internal accounts document, not the supplier's tax adjustment. Keep the direction clear in the description so the two meanings do not collide. The rest of this guide uses the supplier's meaning: a debit note that increases the customer's balance.

Credit note vs debit note: the key differences

The simplest test is direction. Ask whether the amount on the original invoice should go down or up. Down means a credit note; up means a debit note.

FeatureCredit noteDebit note
EffectReduces the amount owedIncreases the amount owed
Typical triggerReturn, overbilling, cancellation, later discountExtra work, underbilling, price revision, short-charged tax
Tax adjustmentReverses the proportionate taxAdds the proportionate tax
NumberingSeparate CN series, e.g. CN-2026-007Separate DN series, e.g. DN-2026-004
Link to originalOriginal invoice number and date are mandatoryOriginal invoice number and date are mandatory
BooksReduces revenue and the receivableAdds revenue and the receivable
Common confusionTreated as a cash refundUsed for a brand-new order

Both notes preserve history. Editing the original invoice after the buyer has received it hides the change and breaks the customer's PO match. A note keeps the original visible and adds a second, traceable entry that explains the movement.

Two worked examples: a return and extra scope

Example 1 — credit note for two returned units

INV-2026-031 bills 10 units at ₹6,000 with IGST at 18%. The taxable value is ₹60,000, IGST is ₹10,800 and the total is ₹70,800. The buyer returns two units.

CN-2026-007 covers 2 × ₹6,000 = ₹12,000 taxable, IGST of ₹2,160 and a credit total of ₹14,160. The outstanding balance becomes ₹70,800 − ₹14,160 = ₹56,640. That also matches the eight units kept: 8 × ₹6,000 = ₹48,000 taxable, ₹8,640 tax and ₹56,640 total. Show the note as a negative line on the customer statement. If the customer already paid, decide whether the credit becomes a refund or an offset against the next invoice, and record which one you agreed.

Example 2 — debit note for approved extra hours

INV-2026-036 bills a three-month retainer at ₹15,000 per month: ₹45,000 taxable, IGST of ₹8,100 and a total of ₹53,100. After delivery, the client approves 10 extra hours at ₹1,600, which is ₹16,000, with IGST of ₹2,880. DN-2026-004 totals ₹18,880.

The revised taxable value is ₹45,000 + ₹16,000 = ₹61,000, tax is ₹8,100 + ₹2,880 = ₹10,980, and the revised total is ₹71,980. That matches ₹53,100 + ₹18,880. Reference both documents in the covering email and state the new balance. Do not edit the original invoice to hide the added work; the note is the record that the scope changed after billing.

Tax and recordkeeping rules that keep the notes credible

  • Mirror the original tax split. If the invoice used IGST, the note uses IGST. If it split CGST and SGST, the note repeats that split. A different tax type on the adjustment invites a query.
  • Show the reason in words. “Return of 2 units, INV-2026-031” is auditable. A bare negative amount is not.
  • Keep separate sequences. Never reuse an invoice number for a note. A clean CN or DN series makes reconciliation and audits much easier; the invoice numbering guide covers the format rules.
  • Respect timing rules. Credit notes usually reduce output tax in the period they are issued, subject to local conditions and time limits; debit notes add tax. Those rules differ by jurisdiction and change, so confirm the treatment before filing.
  • Reconcile monthly. Opening balance, invoices, credit notes, debit notes, payments and closing balance should tell one story. A note that exists in email but not in the ledger is a future dispute.

Under GST, a credit note generally needs the original invoice reference, the reason and the tax adjustment, and the recipient's input tax credit may need a corresponding reversal. The exact conditions and deadlines are jurisdiction-specific. Use the GST invoice format guide for field placement, and ask your accountant about disclosure and timing. This page is general information, not tax or legal advice.

Five mistakes that make adjustments worse

  1. Issuing a note with no original reference. The buyer cannot match it to a PO, and the ledger shows an unexplained credit or charge.
  2. Calling a refund a credit note. The note reduces the debt; the refund moves cash. Record both, with dates and the payment method.
  3. Using a debit note for a new order. New work needs a new invoice. A debit note is for a change to an existing supply, not a substitute invoice series.
  4. Leaving out the tax breakdown. A single “adjustment” line hides whether tax was reversed or added, which is exactly what accounts and auditors need to see.
  5. Deleting or overwriting the original. Keep the original invoice unchanged and let the note carry the correction. If the invoice was never sent, void it instead of inventing a paper trail.
Keep the trail clean: open the free invoice generator to create the original invoice, then issue the credit or debit note with the same tax split and a clear reference. Store both PDFs under the customer name and invoice number.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a credit note and a debit note?
faqs.answer: A credit note reduces the balance on an earlier invoice, usually after a return, overcharge or cancellation. A debit note increases that balance for extra work, underbilling or a later price change. Both reference the original invoice and adjust its tax proportionately. The direction of the adjustment is the whole distinction.

faqs.question: When should I issue a credit note instead of a refund?
faqs.answer: Issue the credit note when the debt itself needs to go down, for example two returned units on a ₹70,800 invoice. The note reduces the receivable to ₹56,640. A refund is the separate movement of cash if the customer already paid. Record the note and the refund as two events so the ledger shows both the reduced sale and the payment.

faqs.question: Can a debit note be used for a new order?
faqs.answer: No. A new order needs a new invoice with its own number and a fresh description of the supply. A debit note adjusts an existing invoice, such as ₹16,000 of extra hours added to a ₹45,000 retainer. Using a debit note as a substitute invoice confuses the series and can break the customer's PO match.

faqs.question: Does a credit note need to reference the original invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes. Include the original invoice number, its date, the reason for the adjustment, the taxable value being reduced and the tax split. Without that link, the buyer's accounts team cannot match the note to the purchase, and the tax adjustment looks unexplained. The note should stand on its own as an audit trail.

faqs.question: How is tax handled on credit and debit notes?
faqs.answer: Mirror the original invoice. If it charged IGST at 18%, the note adjusts IGST at 18% on the returned or added value. If it split CGST and SGST, repeat that split. Credit notes usually reduce output tax and debit notes add it, subject to local timing conditions. Confirm the filing treatment with your accountant.

faqs.question: What numbering should credit and debit notes use?
faqs.answer: Use separate sequences such as CN-2026-007 and DN-2026-004, never the invoice series. Keep the numbers sequential and log each note against the original invoice. Separate series make reconciliation readable and prevent a note from being mistaken for a duplicate bill. Never reuse or backfill numbers.

title: Invoice International Clients: Currency, Tax & Terms
description: Invoice international clients with confidence: currency and FX clauses, VAT/GST reverse charge, Incoterms, bank details and two worked examples.
html:
An international invoice has to satisfy three systems at once: the client's accounts payable team, your bank, and the tax authority on one or both sides of the border. A domestic invoice missing a currency code can still get paid. A cross-border invoice usually cannot. This guide covers the fields that change, the wording that prevents short payments, and two worked examples.

Part of the free invoice generator guide. Tax rules vary by country and by the nature of the supply; treat this as general information, not tax or legal advice.

Currency and exchange: say exactly what you expect

State the invoice currency as an ISO code: USD, EUR, GBP, AED or INR. Write USD 4,800, not $4,800, because several currencies use a dollar sign and the buyer's accounts software may guess wrong. Use one currency for every line, the subtotal, the tax and the total. If you quote in one currency and expect settlement in another, put that in the contract and repeat it on the invoice.

A currency clause prevents a silent discount. The invoice can be paid in full and still leave a gap if the client's bank deducts a fee or converts at a weaker rate. Decide in advance who absorbs that difference. A simple clause: “Payment must be made in USD. All bank charges and correspondent fees are for the client's account. Any shortfall remains due.” Whether such a clause is enforceable depends on your contract and local law, so keep it consistent with what the client signed.

  • Invoice currency: the currency of the prices and tax on the document.
  • Settlement currency: the currency that actually arrives in your account. If it differs, name the conversion rate or the source of the rate.
  • Validity: exchange rates move. A 7-day or 30-day validity on the quote protects the price without hiding the risk.
  • Rounding: show two decimals on unit prices and totals. Round only the final figure, and state the rounding convention if the client asks.

The invoice generator lets you set the currency on the document, but the commercial terms around conversion still belong in your contract or invoice notes.

Tax treatment: name the basis, not just “0%”

Cross-border tax starts with two questions: what is supplied, and where is it taxed? For services, the place of supply often follows the customer's location in business-to-business deals, which can push VAT or GST to the buyer through the reverse charge. For goods, export rules, Incoterms and import VAT all matter. Never print “0% tax” without a reason; state the legal basis in one short sentence.

SituationTypical treatmentWording to consider
B2B services to an EU VAT-registered clientPlace of supply is the customer's country; reverse charge applies“VAT to be accounted for by the recipient. Customer VAT no. …”
Indian export of services under LUTZero-rated, with no IGST charged when the conditions are met“Export of services under LUT. IGST not charged.”
US client, no sales-tax nexusNo US sales tax collected“No US sales tax collected.”
UK B2B services where the customer belongs abroadOutside the scope of UK VAT; reverse charge may apply“Outside the scope of UK VAT. Reverse charge applies.”
Goods sold DDP to an overseas buyerSeller arranges carriage and import clearance; import VAT or duty may be included“DDP [named place]. Import VAT and duty included where stated.”

Indian exporters should keep the LUT reference and shipping or service evidence with the invoice. EU suppliers should validate the customer's VAT number before using reverse-charge wording. US sellers need to know whether they have nexus in the buyer's state, because a foreign client does not automatically mean “no US tax”. Withholding tax is a separate layer: some countries require the buyer to deduct tax at source, so agree whether your fee is gross or net and whether a gross-up clause applies.

Incoterms and place of supply: different tools for goods and services

Incoterms describe goods, not services. Name the term and the place: DAP Rotterdam, FOB Nhava Sheva or DDP Berlin. The term decides who pays freight, insurance and import duty, and where risk passes. DAP leaves import clearance and duty to the buyer; DDP puts them on the seller. That difference can be larger than your margin, so never leave the term implied.

Service invoices do not use Incoterms. Use place of supply and a reverse-charge statement instead. Putting FOB on a consulting invoice signals that the document was copied from a goods template, and the buyer's tax team will query it. For a mixed contract, split the goods and services into separate lines with the right treatment for each, or issue separate invoices.

Check the named place against the buyer's address. “DAP France” is not precise enough for a carrier or a customs broker; “DAP 75008 Paris” is. If the buyer arranges collection, say so and use the correct term rather than inventing a hybrid.

Payment details and terms that survive the journey

  • Legal name and address exactly as held on the bank account. A trading name that differs from the account name can trigger a compliance hold.
  • Account number or IBAN, SWIFT/BIC and currency. Add the intermediary bank when your bank requires one.
  • Payment reference: the invoice number, so the remittance advice matches the bill.
  • Fee clause: state whether the client pays correspondent charges. “SHA” usually splits them; “OUR” puts them on the sender. Spell out the commercial intent rather than relying on the code alone.
  • Verification: confirm any change of bank details by phone using a number you already know. Email interception and fake supplier invoices are common.
  • Terms: Net 15 or Net 30 with a calendar due date, and a late-payment clause that fits the contract.

Put the bank block in text on the PDF, not only in the email body. If the client forwards the PDF internally, the payment details travel with it. Keep the invoice and the remittance advice together; they are the evidence you will need if a transfer is traced or reversed. The payment terms and follow-up guide covers reminder timing and wording.

Two worked examples: a short payment and a VAT mistake

Example 1 — a $35 fee becomes a real shortfall

INV-2026-058 bills 20 days at $240, for a total of USD 4,800, with no tax under the applicable export treatment. The client's bank deducts a $35 correspondent fee and remits USD 4,765. Your bank converts at 83.10, producing ₹395,971.50. Had the full USD 4,800 arrived at the same rate, the credit would have been ₹398,880.

The gap is ₹2,908.50, which is exactly $35 × 83.10. The invoice was “paid” but not settled. If the terms say bank charges are for the client's account, issue a small debit note or ask for the difference; if they do not, you have just absorbed the fee. Reconcile the received amount against the invoice total before marking it paid, not after month-end.

Example 2 — reverse charge versus an accidental VAT line

INV-2026-059 bills €9,500 of consulting to a VAT-registered EU business under the reverse charge. VAT is 0% with the note “VAT to be accounted for by the recipient”, so the total is €9,500. If the invoice wrongly adds 20% VAT, the VAT line is €1,900 and the total becomes €11,400.

The client's accounts payable team self-accounts the VAT and may pay only the net €9,500, leaving €1,900 open. Or it may reject the invoice outright because the VAT treatment contradicts the purchase order. The fix is a credit note for €1,900 referencing the original invoice, followed by a corrected invoice at €9,500. That is more work than getting the wording right the first time.

International invoice checklist before you send

A reusable international invoice template should carry every field below. Leaving one to a covering email is how short payments and tax queries start.

  • Currency appears as an ISO code on every amount and matches the contract.
  • Tax basis is stated: reverse charge, zero-rated export, outside scope or no nexus, with the customer's tax ID where relevant.
  • Goods invoices name the Incoterm and the precise place; service invoices state the place of supply.
  • Bank details include the account name, IBAN or account number, SWIFT/BIC, currency and payment reference.
  • Bank charges and any conversion shortfall are addressed in the terms.
  • Due date is a calendar date, and the late-payment clause matches the contract.
  • The PDF uses the same language as the contract, or includes a translated summary.
  • File name follows a predictable pattern such as invoice-acme-058.pdf, and the invoice number is on every page.
Draft the next one: open the free invoice generator, set the currency and tax notes, add the bank block and print a clean PDF. For layout choices and field placement, see the invoice template formats guide.

faqs.question: What should an international invoice include?
faqs.answer: Include both parties' legal names and addresses, an invoice number and date, ISO currency codes, a specific description of the goods or services, unit prices and totals, the tax basis and any customer tax ID, the Incoterm and named place for goods or the place of supply for services, bank details, payment terms and a due date.

faqs.question: Should I invoice in my currency or the client's?
faqs.answer: Invoice in the currency agreed in the contract, and state it as an ISO code such as USD or EUR. If the client pays in a different currency, name the conversion basis and decide who absorbs the difference. A clear currency clause prevents a full payment from leaving a shortfall after bank fees or a weaker exchange rate.

faqs.question: When do I use reverse-charge wording?
faqs.answer: Use it when the place of supply is the customer's country and local rules shift the VAT obligation to the buyer, typically for B2B services within the EU. Include the customer's VAT number and a line saying the recipient accounts for VAT. Confirm the rule for the specific country and service before relying on it.

faqs.question: Do Incoterms apply to service invoices?
faqs.answer: No. Incoterms apply to goods and describe freight, insurance, import clearance and risk. Service invoices use place-of-supply and reverse-charge wording instead. For a mixed contract, separate goods and services into different lines or invoices so each gets the correct treatment and the buyer's tax team can review it.

faqs.question: Who pays the bank fees on an international invoice?
faqs.answer: Decide before invoicing and say so on the document. Correspondent fees and conversion costs can turn a full payment into a short settlement. If the client bears them, state that all bank charges are for the client's account and reconcile the amount received against the invoice total. If you bear them, price the fee into your rate.

faqs.question: How do I handle withholding tax on a cross-border invoice?
faqs.answer: Find out whether the buyer's country requires tax to be deducted at source. If it does, agree whether your fee is gross or net and whether the contract includes a gross-up clause. Keep the withholding certificate with the invoice and remittance advice. This is general information, so confirm the treaty position with a tax adviser.

title: Google Review QR Code: Get More Reviews
description: Turn your Google Business Profile review link into a QR code customers can scan at the counter. Sizes, placement, policy tips and scan tests.

toc.text: Why the direct review link wins

html:
A customer who has just paid is the easiest person to ask for a review, and the hardest to send on a scavenger hunt. Telling them to open Google, search your business, scroll past the map and tap “Write a review” loses the moment. A google review qr code collapses that journey into one tap: the review form opens with the star rating on screen. The code takes a minute; the link inside it, the wording and the timing decide whether the scan becomes a published review.

This guide is part of the free QR code generator guide. It covers the only link worth encoding, placement, policy and the scan test that prevents a silent failure at the counter.

Why the direct review link wins

There are three links a business owner can put behind a QR code, and only one is useful. The ordinary Google Maps listing opens photos, hours, directions and a review section the customer still has to find. The Business Profile dashboard link asks for a login and shows internal controls, which is worse. The review form link Google generates for the location opens a page with the business name and five stars, ready to rate.

That direct link matters because friction is cumulative. The customer needs a Google account, a connection and patience to finish. Every extra tap before the form is a chance to abandon. The direct link removes the searching and the doubt about which listing is correct. It does not remove the sign-in requirement or write the review. It puts the form where the customer already is.

A QR code also beats a printed URL because nobody has to type a 30-character address. The pattern carries the full link, including the place identifier, so it cannot be mistyped.

Get your review link from Business Profile

Sign in at business.google.com with the account that manages the location, choose the location if you manage several, and find the reviews card. Google labels the action “Get more reviews” or “Ask for reviews” depending on the dashboard version. The link it offers opens the review form for that specific location, which is exactly what you want to encode.

Google also publishes a direct form at https://search.google.com/local/writereview?placeid=YOUR_PLACE_ID, with the place ID from the Maps Platform Place ID Finder. This URL is useful when the dashboard link is awkward to copy, but it is long and easy to break by hand. Copy it whole and test it signed out.

  • Never encode the Maps listing URL. It adds search steps and often opens the Maps app instead of the form.
  • Never encode the dashboard URL. It asks for a login and exposes controls customers should not see.
  • One location, one link. One per branch, each labelled.
  • Re-check after a listing change. Listing merges and name changes can break the link.

Where to place the code

Placement decides more than graphic design. The code should appear when the customer is most satisfied and least rushed: after payment, after a successful appointment, or while waiting for takeaway. A code by the door competes with traffic and rain. A code on the bill folder arrives while the customer is still seated and still thinking about the service.

PlacementViewing distanceMinimum sizeWhy it works
Bill folder or receipt sleeve30–40 cm3–4 cmArrives at payment, when the visit is fresh
Counter card50–80 cm5–8 cmVisible while waiting, easy for staff to point at
Table tent40–70 cm4–7 cmWorks during a long meal without staff prompting
Reception frame1–2 m10–20 cmSeen while queuing or checking in
Takeaway bag sticker40–60 cm4–6 cmExtends the ask beyond the shop

The sentence next to the code does more work than the code. “Loved your visit? 10 seconds” sounds friendly but quietly filters: a customer who had a mixed experience reads it as an invitation for happy people only. Google’s policies discourage selective solicitation, and the practice distorts the feedback you need. Use neutral wording such as “Tell us about your visit — two minutes.” Staff can add a spoken prompt at payment.

Size, contrast and scan testing

Use the same rule as any print code: minimum width in centimetres is roughly viewing distance divided by 10, with a 2 cm floor for short URLs. A Business Profile review link is usually short — often a g.page/r/... address — so the pattern is sparse. That does not make 2 cm sensible on a folder picked up and photographed at an angle. Give it 3 cm at 30 cm, 5–6 cm at 50–60 cm, and 10–20 cm for a poster read from two metres.

Export 512px for prints up to about 5 cm and 2048px above that; never upscale. Keep black modules on white, leave the four-module quiet zone untouched, and choose matte lamination. A glossy card reflecting a ceiling light is the most common reason a review code fails at a counter. The full distance table is in the QR code size and print guide.

Test before the print run. Print one copy at 100%, disable “fit to page”, then scan it signed out of Google with two phones. The form should appear without a login prompt or permission error. Scan at the real distance under the real lighting, and try an older Android as well as an iPhone. If the camera struggles, the print is the problem; the not-scanning fixes walk through size, contrast, glare and file faults.

Google policy: ask everyone, never gate

Google’s prohibited content policy bans incentives: no discount, free dessert, prize draw or staff bonus tied to a review. It also bans review gating, the trick of asking only customers who answer a satisfaction question positively. A code that opens the review form for every customer is fine. A code that opens a screening survey first is not. Reviews can be removed and ratings filtered.

Ask once, ask everyone, and never write the review for them. Do not stand over the customer or hold the phone. The code should make the honest path easy, not manufacture a rating. If a customer had a bad experience, the same code gives them a way to say so before they tell the neighbourhood. That is useful information arriving while you can still act on it.

Two worked setups

Example 1 — neighbourhood café, Kochi. A 28-seat café prints 4 cm codes on matte card stock for the bill folder. The destination is the Business Profile review link, generated at 2048px because the folder sits 30–40 cm from the customer’s phone and is handled constantly. The line above the code reads “Tell us about today’s visit — two minutes.” Staff slide the folder across with the card facing up and say one sentence. It is tested at 40 cm in daylight and pendant light on an iPhone and a budget Android. If the review link changes after a listing merge, only the folder card is reprinted; the table tents use a separate file.

Example 2 — dental clinic, Jaipur. A two-chair clinic places a 6 cm framed code at reception, with a 3 cm version on the appointment card. The frame is 60 cm from a seated patient, so 6 cm gives a comfortable margin over the distance rule. The card asks after the appointment is booked, not while the patient is in the chair. The frame is matte, fixed flat to the wall and wiped weekly. The receptionist can point to it if someone hesitates, but does not hand over a phone or dictate the wording. A small line reads “Reviews help other patients choose carefully.” That sentence is true whether the review is glowing or critical.

Measure reviews, not scans

A static QR code carries no analytics. You will not know how many people scanned it, and any service promising scan counts is routing your link through its own server. For a review code that trade is wrong: the link is short, the destination is Google, and a redirect that expires would break every printed card. Measure new reviews week by week and the proportion that mention a server, a dish, a treatment or a repair. Ask staff to note when a customer says they scanned the code; a paper tally at the till is enough.

Keep the link and the code in one document: the review URL, the date it was last tested, the print files and who approved the wording. When a manager changes, the next person can regenerate the code in a minute.

Your next step: copy the review link from your Business Profile, paste it into the free QR code generator, download a 2048px PNG and print one test card before ordering a batch. The code is static, so it keeps working for as long as the review link does.

faqs.question: Where do I find my Google review link?
faqs.answer: Sign in at business.google.com, select the location and open the reviews card labelled Get more reviews or Ask for reviews. Copy the link it offers and test it in a private window while signed out. Google also publishes a direct writereview URL using a place ID from the Maps Platform Place ID Finder, but the dashboard link is shorter and easier to verify.

faqs.question: Can I offer a discount for scanning the review code?
faqs.answer: No. Google prohibits incentives such as discounts, free items, prize draws or staff bonuses tied to reviews, and it prohibits review gating that shows the form only to happy customers. Ask every customer with neutral wording and keep the code optional. Incentives risk removed reviews and damage the accuracy of the feedback you are trying to collect.

faqs.question: What size should a review QR code be?
faqs.answer: Use 3–4 cm on a bill folder or receipt sleeve viewed at 30–40 cm, 5–8 cm for a counter card at 50–80 cm, and 10–20 cm for a reception poster read from one to two metres. The distance rule is width in centimetres roughly equal to viewing distance divided by 10. Export 512px up to 5 cm and 2048px above that.

faqs.question: Do QR codes for Google reviews expire?
faqs.answer: The QR code is static, so the pattern itself never expires. The destination can change if the Business Profile is merged, moved or closed, or if a third-party redirect in front of the link shuts down. Keep the review link on your own printed card, test it quarterly, and regenerate the code only if the underlying link changes.

faqs.question: Can I track how many people scan the review QR code?
faqs.answer: Not with a static code. There is no scan counter because the pattern carries the destination directly. Watch new reviews on the Business Profile and ask staff to tally customers who mention scanning. Avoid putting a dynamic redirect in front of a review link just for analytics, since an expired subscription would break every printed card.

faqs.question: Why does the review form ask customers to sign in?
faqs.answer: Posting a Google review requires a Google account, so the sign-in prompt is expected. What is not expected is a request for access to a file or a message that you need permission. That usually means the encoded link points to the Business Profile dashboard or a restricted document instead of the public review form. Re-copy the review link and test it signed out.

title: Restaurant Menu QR Code: Setup & Best Practices
description: Set up a restaurant menu QR code that opens a fast mobile page or PDF. Print sizes, table placement, update rules and scan tests for 2026.
html:
A restaurant menu QR code is not a design object. It is a bridge between a hungry customer and a page that must load before they lose interest. Most failed menus fail for a boring reason: the code points at a PDF that downloads instead of opens, or at a desktop page that needs pinch-zoom to read a price. The square scans fine; the destination is the problem. This guide covers the destination, the code, print sizes and the update routine that saves reprints.

Part of the free QR code generator guide.

Choose the destination before the code

Three options exist, and they are not equal. A mobile web page is the best default: text stays crisp, prices are easy to update, search engines can read it, and customers can jump to a section. A PDF is acceptable for a short, stable menu. A photo of a printed menu is the weakest: it cannot reflow, blurs when zoomed, and a screen reader cannot read it.

The test is simple. Open the link on a phone using mobile data, not office WiFi. Time how long it takes to show prices, and read the cheapest and most expensive item without zooming. If the page forces a download, opens a Drive preview toolbar, or shows a cookie wall before the food, fix the destination first.

  • Mobile page: one column, text-based, sections for starters, mains, drinks and allergens.
  • PDF: selectable text, one or two pages, under about 2 MB, stable URL on your own domain.
  • Drive or Dropbox: only if anyone with the link can view; preview chrome gets in the way.
  • Image-only menu: avoid it; it is a picture of a menu, not a menu.

Build a menu page that works on a phone

Keep the page brutally simple: restaurant name, a one-line description, then menu sections. Use real text for dish names and prices. Group items so a customer can find a vegetarian dish, a gluten-free option or a drink without scrolling through everything. State allergens where you can and tell customers to inform staff of serious allergies.

Set the page to load fast on a mid-range Android: compressed images, no autoplay video, no blocking web font, no email pop-up before the menu. A menu is not a lead magnet. Keep the font readable and test on a flaky connection.

If you must use a PDF

Export from the original design file. Use selectable text, embed the fonts, and name the file lunch-menu-october.pdf. Host it on your own domain and link directly. Test on an iPhone and an Android; some browsers open PDFs, others download them. Print a short URL under the code as a second route. A two-page PDF is fine; a 20-page drinks book is not a menu link.

Generate and size the code

Shorten the link before encoding it. A clean address such as https://example.com/menu produces a sparse pattern that scans at 3–4 cm. A booking URL with tracking parameters can run past 100 characters and produce a dense grid that needs a larger print. If you need a short link, use one on your own domain that you control. Avoid a free shortener you do not administer; if it disappears, every printed code dies with it.

Generate a 2048px PNG for table tents, counter cards and window signs, and 512px only for small cards viewed at arm’s length. Keep black on white with the four-module quiet zone intact. Do not place the code over a food photo, dark brand colour or patterned tablecloth. Matte lamination beats gloss because it does not throw a ceiling light into the camera. The sizing rules are in the QR code print size guide.

Placement: table, counter, window

Put the code where a seated customer can scan it without getting up, and a second where takeaway customers wait. Table tents should sit flat, not inside a curved holder that distorts the pattern. Counter cards need a stand that stops them sliding. Window decals need exterior-grade material out of direct sun, because fading kills contrast.

PlacementViewing distanceMinimum sizeMaterial and notes
Table tent40–60 cm4–6 cmMatte laminated card, flat base, one per table
Counter card50–80 cm5–8 cmRigid stand, wipeable, near the till or pickup point
Window or door1.5–3 m15–30 cmExterior-grade vinyl, shaded from direct sun, 2048px
Bill folder30–40 cm3–4 cmMatte card, paired with a payment prompt
Takeaway bag40–60 cm4–6 cmMatte sticker, placed on a flat panel, not a fold

Label the code with its job: “Menu” is enough. If you run separate lunch and dinner pages, label them clearly and keep the codes physically separate. Two unlabelled codes side by side force the customer to guess, and guessing at a table is how a menu QR code gets ignored. If both menus live on one page with tabs, one code is simpler and easier to maintain.

Update the menu without reprinting

A static QR code cannot be edited after printing, but the page behind it can. That suits most restaurants: encode a stable URL you control, then change prices, mark items as sold out and swap the lunch PDF at that URL. The printed code keeps working because the destination has not moved.

If you need to change the destination itself, you have two options. Reprint the code, which is cheap for a table tent and expensive for a window decal, or use a dynamic QR code that routes through a provider. Dynamic codes allow editing and scan counts, but they depend on a subscription; stop paying and the printed code stops working. For a single restaurant with a stable page, a static code paired with a page you control is simpler and has no recurring cost. The trade-offs are compared in static vs dynamic QR codes.

Test the scan before the lunch rush

Print one table tent and one counter card at 100% scale. Disable “fit to page” in the printer dialog, because it shrinks the pattern by a few percent and can eat the quiet zone. Scan both with two phones at the real distance, in daylight and pendant light. Open the menu over mobile data, not restaurant WiFi, and check the load time. Try an older phone with a weaker camera. If the code scans but the PDF downloads, the problem is the destination, not the print.

Do this before a busy service, not during one. A code that fails at 12:30 on a Saturday is a queue of customers holding phones while a server tries to explain. Keep one printed test card behind the till with the date on the back. When the menu changes, test again; a new PDF can break a link that worked last month. Most restaurant failures are destination problems: a moved file, a permission change or a page that no longer exists.

Two worked setups

Example 1 — 40-cover neighbourhood restaurant, Bengaluru. The restaurant builds a one-page menu at https://example.com/menu with sections for small plates, mains, breads, desserts and drinks. Prices are text, not images, and the page loads quickly over mobile data on a mid-range Android. The code is generated at 2048px and printed at 5 cm on matte laminated table tents, one per table, with a second 6 cm card at the pickup counter. The line above the code reads “Scan for the menu.” The manager updates the page when a dish sells out and changes prices there, never on the printed card. A test scan is repeated after every menu edit.

Example 2 — 12-seat bakery, Pune. The bakery has a single-page PDF at https://example.com/bakery-menu.pdf, exported from the original design file with selectable text and a file size under 2 MB. The code is printed at 6 cm on an A5 counter card and at 4 cm on takeaway bags. Because some Android browsers download PDFs instead of opening them, the card also prints the short URL in 14-point type underneath. The owner tests the link on an iPhone and a budget Android after each seasonal change, and keeps the previous PDF at the same URL until the new one works.

Five mistakes that ruin a menu code

  1. Encoding a login-only file. Set sharing so anyone with the link can view, then test signed out.
  2. Printing too small. A dense 120-character URL at 2.5 cm fails on older phones. Shorten it or print at 5 cm.
  3. Using curved or glossy stock. Reflections and distortion break the pattern. Use flat matte material.
  4. Letting the destination die. Replacing menu-final-v3.pdf breaks the old link. Keep stable URLs.
  5. Skipping the mobile test. A page that looks fine on a laptop can be unreadable on a phone.
Make the code: open the free QR code generator, paste your stable menu URL, export 2048px, and print one test tent before ordering a full set.

faqs.question: Should a restaurant menu QR code open a page or a PDF?
faqs.answer: A mobile web page is the better default because text reflows, prices are easy to update and the page is accessible. A short text-based PDF is acceptable for a stable one-page menu, but test that it opens in the browser instead of downloading. Never use a photo of a printed menu; it cannot reflow and blurs when zoomed.

faqs.question: What size should a table tent QR code be?
faqs.answer: Use 4–6 cm for a table tent viewed at 40–60 cm, and 5–8 cm for a counter card at 50–80 cm. Window codes read from 1.5–3 m need 15–30 cm. The working rule is width in centimetres roughly equal to the viewing distance in centimetres divided by 10, with a 2 cm floor for short links.

faqs.question: Can I change the menu after printing the QR code?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the code points to a page or file URL you control. Edit the page or replace the PDF at the same address and the printed code keeps working. A static code cannot change its destination, so if you move to a new URL you must reprint. Dynamic codes allow redirects but depend on a subscription.

faqs.question: Do menu QR codes expire?
faqs.answer: A static QR code never expires because the destination is embedded in the pattern. The menu can still break if the page is deleted, the PDF is moved, or a third-party shortener shuts down. Use a stable URL on your own domain, test it after every menu change, and keep the PDF at the same address until the replacement is confirmed.

faqs.question: Why does the menu PDF download instead of opening?
faqs.answer: Browsers handle PDFs differently, especially on Android, where some download the file rather than display it. Host the PDF on your own domain, link directly to the file, keep it under about 2 MB and test on both iPhone and Android. Print a short URL under the code as a fallback for customers whose browser downloads it.

faqs.question: How many menu QR codes does a restaurant need?
faqs.answer: One code per distinct menu or location is enough. If lunch and dinner use separate URLs, print two clearly labelled codes; if both live on one page with tabs, use one code. Groups with multiple branches need a separate code per branch so the destination matches the location. Avoid placing two unlabelled codes side by side.

title: QR Code for Google Forms: Share a Survey Fast
description: Create a QR code for Google Forms in minutes. Copy the responder link, fix sharing permissions, size it for print and test it signed out.

toc.text: Build the form and copy the link
Set sharing for anyone with the link
Turn the link into a QR code
What you can and cannot track

html:
A QR code for Google Forms is the fastest way to move a survey from a link someone will never click to a form already open on their phone. The mechanics take a minute: build the form, copy the responder link, generate the code. The part that fails is sharing. A form that looks public in the editor can still ask respondents to sign in, request permission, or refuse responses, and the printed code cannot explain any of that. This guide fixes the permissions before the ink dries.

Part of the free QR code generator guide.

Build the form, then copy the responder link

Create the form and add only the questions you will act on. A form with 15 fields gets abandoned; four questions and an optional comment get finished. Decide whether to collect email addresses, limit responses per person or allow edits after submitting; each choice affects who can open the form.

When the form is ready, click Send and choose the link tab. If the dialog offers Shorten URL, enable it; a forms.gle/... address produces a sparser pattern than the full docs.google.com/forms/d/e/.../viewform URL. The short version scans more easily when printed small. Do not copy the browser URL while editing: the editor link ends in /edit and opens the design view, not the respondent form.

  • Responder link: ends in /viewform or uses forms.gle. Encode this one.
  • Editor link: ends in /edit. It asks for a login and must never be printed.
  • Embed code: HTML for an iframe, not a URL.
  • Prefilled link: a long URL with answers filled. Useful, but dense.

Set sharing so anyone with the link can respond

Open the responder link in a private window while signed out of every Google account. This is the only test that matches what a customer will experience. The form should load and accept an answer without a login prompt. If it asks you to sign in or says you need permission, it is not open to everyone with the link, and a QR code will not fix that.

Forms links are normally open to anyone with the URL, but there are three common exceptions. A Workspace administrator can restrict sharing so only domain accounts respond. A file upload question requires sign-in because the file needs an owner. Limit to 1 response also requires sign-in so Google can identify each respondent. Turn those off if anonymous answers matter more.

Confirm the form is still accepting responses. A closed form shows a message saying it is no longer accepting responses, which looks like a broken code from the customer’s side. Reopen the existing form for a new round rather than creating a new one, so the printed code keeps working. In Workspace, ask the admin to confirm link sharing is allowed before printing cards.

Turn the link into a QR code

Paste the responder link into the generator, preview the pattern, and export at the size your placement needs. Google Forms URLs are long, especially the full viewform address, so the pattern is denser than a short menu link. That is the main reason to enable the short link and print larger. A 40-character forms.gle link at 5 cm is comfortable; a 150-character prefilled link at 3 cm is not.

Use black on white, keep the quiet zone clear and choose matte stock. Do not put the code on a glossy poster behind glass or tint it to match a brand palette. Print at the size the room demands: 15–20 cm for an exit poster read from two metres, 5–6 cm for a desk card. The distance tables are in the QR code size and print guide.

Placement and print sizes

Put the code where the respondent is already holding a phone and has a reason to answer. An exit poster catches people before they leave; a desk card catches a student before class; a counter card catches a patient at check-in. A code in a newsletter or slide competes with every other link, so print it on the handout too if the room is physical.

Use caseExample formPrint sizePlacement
Event feedbackFour questions and one comment15–20 cmExit poster at 1.5–2 m, with a handout
Classroom exit ticketThree quick questions5 cmDesk card or printed worksheet corner
Clinic intakeContact details and history8 cmReception counter at 80 cm
Maintenance requestLocation, issue, photo upload4–5 cmLaminated label on the equipment
Restaurant feedbackRating and one comment3–4 cmBill folder at 30–40 cm

Label the code with the action and time cost: “30-second feedback” or “Report a fault.” A bare square is easy to ignore. If the form asks for personal data, say so on the card and link to a privacy notice; the code is a shortcut, not a consent mechanism.

Prefilled links and long URLs

Google Forms can prefill answers through the three-dot menu and Get pre-filled link. Fill the fields, click Get link, and copy the result. This is useful for a session, location or cohort without asking the respondent to choose. The values are visible in the URL and can usually be changed, so do not treat them as secure data.

Prefilled URLs are much longer than the plain responder link. A 200-character URL creates a dense pattern that needs a larger print and a better camera. For a table tent, use the plain link and ask the question inside the form. For attribution, a short forms.gle link to a separate form per channel scans more easily. Fewer characters is the cheapest scanability upgrade.

Test like a respondent, not an editor

Scan the printed code with a phone signed out of Google, over mobile data. Confirm four things: the form loads, the questions are readable without zooming, submit works, and the confirmation appears. Then check the Responses tab for the test answer. Delete it if it would distort your data, or use a duplicate form for testing.

Repeat at the real distance and lighting. A poster code that works at arm’s length may fail at two metres; a laminated card may glare under a fluorescent tube. Test an older Android as well as an iPhone, because a long forms.gle URL is the kind of dense pattern budget cameras struggle with. If it will not scan, the not-scanning fixes start with size and contrast.

Re-test after every edit. Changing a question, closing the form or toggling a setting changes what the respondent sees while the printed code stays the same. Write the test date on the back of one card.

Two worked setups

Example 1 — conference session feedback, Hyderabad. The organiser builds a five-question form with a session code, two rating scales and a comment box, then leaves email collection off so respondents can answer anonymously. The responder link is shortened to forms.gle, encoded at 2048px and printed at 18 cm on a poster beside the exit, with a 6 cm version on the handout. The poster is tested from two metres in the venue’s afternoon light, and the first test submission is checked in the Responses tab. The form stays open for a week, so late scans still work.

Example 2 — dental clinic intake, Kochi. A two-chair clinic creates a form for name, contact number, reason for visit and preferred appointment time. Because it does not need file uploads or one-response limits, the link opens without a Google sign-in.
