Each guide below solves one part of the job. Start with the creation walkthrough, then follow the size and transparency guides as your documents demand.

  • How to create a signature online — the drawing, typing and export workflow.
  • Transparent signature PNG — checkerboard checks and the JPG trap.
  • Signature size for PDF — dimensions, DPI, scaling and portal limits.
  • Drawn versus typed signature — which method fits which document.
  • Sign a PDF without printing — placing an image in a PDF workflow.
  • Signature image for email — sizing and contrast for footers.
  • Electronic signature validity — image versus recognized signing process.
  • Signature for exam forms — strict form boxes and upload limits.
Make your signature: open the free signature maker, draw or type your name on the 1200 by 400 canvas, adjust the ink, and download a transparent PNG. Everything runs locally, one signature at a time, with no account required.

faqs.question: Can I draw a signature with a mouse, finger or pen?
faqs.answer: Yes. The canvas accepts mouse, touch and stylus input. A pen or stylus gives the smoothest curves, while a finger or mouse works for a simple name. Slow the stroke down, leave a margin around the letters, and preview the result at the size it will appear in the document. If a stroke goes wrong, start a fresh signature rather than trying to repair it.

faqs.question: Does the signature maker export SVG or only PNG?
faqs.answer: It exports a transparent PNG. There is no SVG export. The 1200 by 400 pixel canvas gives enough resolution for contracts, forms and email when the image is placed at two or three inches wide. Keep the PNG as your master and avoid repeated screenshots or format conversions, which can soften the edges.

faqs.question: Does the tool sign PDFs or verify my identity?
faqs.answer: No. It creates an image of a signature. It does not edit or sign PDFs, verify identity, issue a certificate or provide an audit trail. You insert the PNG into a document with a word processor or PDF editor. If a document requires a recognized electronic signature service or a handwritten original, follow the process it specifies.

faqs.question: Why is my signature background white instead of transparent?
faqs.answer: You are probably looking at a JPG or a screenshot. JPG has no alpha channel, so transparent areas are filled with a solid color, usually white. The maker's PNG keeps the background empty. Open the PNG in an editor and look for the checkerboard pattern, which indicates transparency, then place that PNG on the page.

faqs.question: What size should I place the signature at?
faqs.answer: Match the document's signature line. A contract block commonly sits around 2.0 to 2.5 inches wide, a form field around 1.5 to 2.0 inches, and an email footer around 150 to 225 pixels. At 150 DPI, a 2-inch placement uses about 300 pixels. Always scale by width and keep the original 3:1 ratio to avoid stretching.

faqs.question: Is my signature uploaded anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. Drawing, typing and PNG generation run locally in your browser. There is no account and no server copy. The tradeoff is that the canvas is temporary: refreshing or closing the tab clears the signature. Download the PNG before you leave and keep a master copy for future documents.

title: How to Create a Signature Online (Step-by-Step)
description: Draw or type a signature on a 1200x400 canvas, adjust stroke and color, then export a transparent PNG and place it in documents.
keywords: how to create a signature online

toc.text: Place the PNG in a document

html:
Making a signature image takes less time than finding a pen. The signature maker opens with a 1200 by 400 canvas, accepts a mouse, finger or stylus, and also renders a typed name in a cursive font. You adjust the ink, download a transparent PNG, and place it wherever the document needs it.

This walkthrough covers the complete sequence: preparing the name, drawing or typing it, choosing a stroke and color, exporting the PNG, and using the file without damaging its transparency. It also covers the problems that show up after export, which are usually placement mistakes rather than drawing mistakes.

Before you start: decide the name and the destination

Write the name exactly as you want it to appear. A formal contract may need a full first and last name, while an email footer may use a shorter form. Changing the name after you have drawn a signature means starting over, so settle that detail first.

Next, identify where the image will go and what color sits behind it. A white contract page needs dark ink, and a dark header needs light ink. One file cannot be visible on both backgrounds. Note the width of the signature line or form box as well, because that width guides the final placement.

No account or upload is needed. The tool runs locally, creates one signature at a time, and exports PNG only. It does not sign PDFs or verify identity.

Draw your signature with a mouse, finger or pen

Drawing is the more personal route. The canvas records your hand movement, so the result carries the small variations that make a signature look written. A stylus gives the most control, a touch screen is close, and a mouse works if you move slowly.

  1. Open the signature maker and choose the drawing option.
  2. Set a medium stroke and a dark ink color as a starting point.
  3. Draw the name across the middle of the canvas, leaving a margin at the top, bottom and sides.
  4. Pause and inspect the joins between letters. If a stroke is badly placed, start a fresh signature rather than adding repairs.
  5. Preview the result against a white and a dark background before exporting.

Example 1: a drawn signature for a lease. Maya uses a pen tablet to sign a printed lease that will be scanned and emailed. She draws “Maya Ortiz” with a medium black stroke, keeping the capital M about one third of the canvas height and leaving space below the tail of the y. She exports the PNG, places it at 2.4 inches wide on the signature line, and checks the printed page. Because the ink is dark and the paper is white, the transparent background is invisible and the signature sits naturally above the date line.

A mouse can produce a usable signature, but short, jerky strokes look like a polyline rather than handwriting. If your hand is unsteady, a typed signature may give a cleaner document mark.

Type your signature in a cursive font

Typing gives you a repeatable shape. The tool renders the name in the available cursive faces, and you choose the one that keeps every letter readable. A font that looks dramatic in a large preview can become a tangle in a 1.5-inch form field, so judge it at final size.

  1. Select the typing option and enter the name exactly as it should appear.
  2. Cycle through the cursive fonts and read the full name, not just the first letter.
  3. Check letters with descenders and ascenders so nothing collides with the canvas edge.
  4. Set the stroke weight and ink color for the intended background.
  5. Export the transparent PNG and place it at the document's signature width.

Example 2: a typed signature for a freelance invoice. Daniel sends monthly invoices and wants a consistent mark on each one. He types “Daniel Okafor” in a cursive face with a medium navy stroke, exports the PNG once, and saves it as daniel-okafor-signature.png. On each invoice he places the image at 2.0 inches wide above the payment terms. At 150 DPI that is about 300 pixels from the 1200-pixel master, so the edges stay clean. The transparent background lets the white space show through.

Typed signatures do not need to imitate a hand perfectly; their advantage is consistency. If a recipient expects a handwritten mark, draw instead. The drawn versus typed comparison explores the tradeoff.

Adjust stroke and color for the final size

Stroke width is the setting most likely to look wrong after scaling. A delicate line can fade in a form field, while a bold line can swallow the gaps inside letters. Preview at the actual placement size, not at full canvas size.

SettingStarting choiceBest forWatch out
StrokeMediumContracts, forms, invoicesThin strokes fade when reduced
Dark inkBlack or deep navyWhite paper and light formsCan disappear on dark themes
Light inkWhite or pale grayDark slides and dark email templatesInvisible on white paper
MarginsClear space on all sidesEvery placementClipped capitals look like errors

Color should contrast with the page, not with the preview panel. Deep navy reads as a formal signature and separates slightly from black body text. Pure black is stronger and reproduces well in print. If the document uses a colored header or a dark background, make a second export with light ink rather than recoloring the placed image.

Check the whole name after each change. A heavier stroke can close the loops in letters such as a, e and o, and a light color can make a thin stroke look weaker than expected.

Export the transparent PNG

When the preview looks right, download the file. The maker produces a PNG with an empty background, so the page color will show through wherever there is no ink. That is the feature that makes the image useful on contracts, letterheads and colored forms. It is also the feature that disappears if you later convert the file to JPG.

Give the download a descriptive name. Include the ink color if you keep both versions, for example signature-dark.png and signature-light.png. Save the master somewhere you can find it again. The tool does not keep a gallery, and the canvas is temporary; closing or refreshing the tab clears the work.

The export is a raster image, not an SVG. It has a fixed pixel grid of 1200 by 400. That is enough for ordinary document placement, especially at two or three inches wide. It is not a vector file that can be enlarged indefinitely without softening. If a designer asks for SVG, this tool is the wrong source; use a vector editor instead.

Place the PNG in a document, form or email

In a word processor, use the insert-image command, choose the PNG, and set the image to appear in front of or behind text as needed. Drag the corner handle to resize while holding the aspect lock, or type the width and let the height follow. The source ratio is 3:1, so a 2.4-inch-wide signature should be about 0.8 inches tall. If the box is shorter, reduce the width rather than squashing the height.

In a PDF editor, add the PNG as an image layer, position it over the signature line, and export a flattened copy if the recipient needs one file. The signature maker does not edit PDFs and cannot fill a signature field. It only creates the image. For a full placement workflow, see the sign a PDF without printing guide.

Web forms vary. Some accept a PNG upload, some demand JPG, and some enforce a pixel box or a file-size cap. If the portal refuses PNG, convert the file with the image format converter, which handles JPG, PNG and WebP one file at a time up to 10MB and does not resize. If the portal also limits dimensions or bytes, use the image compressor to resize or compress the converted file. The signature size guide covers the arithmetic.

For email, place the signature at a modest width so it does not dominate the message. A dark-ink file works in a white message body; a light-ink file is safer in a dark template. Test the message in the client you actually use, because some clients block images or render them at a different size.

Fix the problems that appear after export

  1. The background is white, not transparent. The file was saved or converted as JPG, or it is a screenshot. Re-export the PNG and place that file.
  2. The signature looks stretched. The width and height were changed independently. Reinsert the image and scale only by width, keeping the 3:1 ratio.
  3. The lines are too faint. The stroke was too thin for the final size. Create a new export with a heavier stroke and preview it at the document's width.
  4. A letter is clipped. The name touched the canvas edge. Redraw or retype it with a margin, then export again.
  5. The signature vanishes on a dark page. Dark ink on a transparent background cannot contrast with a dark surface. Make a light-ink version.
  6. The upload is rejected. Check the portal's format, dimensions and byte limit. Convert or resize a copy, and keep the original PNG as the master.

One final check catches most of these before anyone else sees the document. Open the PNG on its own and confirm the checkerboard background. Place it in the document and zoom to the final size. If both views look clean, the export and the placement are doing their jobs.

title: Transparent Signature PNG: Clean Edges, No White Box
description: Make a transparent signature PNG, check the checkerboard, avoid the JPG white-box trap, and keep clean edges on dark and light pages.

toc.text: Using it on white and dark

html:
A signature looks finished on the canvas and then ruins the page it lands on. The usual culprit is a white rectangle around the name: the signature was saved as JPG, or captured as a screenshot, and the empty canvas became solid white. On a white contract nobody notices. On a cream letterhead, a gray form or a dark slide, the rectangle is the first thing the eye finds.

A transparent PNG avoids that problem. The signature maker exports one directly: the ink is stored as pixels, the empty space is stored as transparency, and the document supplies the background color. This guide explains how to verify transparency, how the JPG trap works, and how to keep the edges clean when you resize or convert the file.

What a transparent signature actually means

A PNG can carry an alpha channel. Each pixel stores a color and an opacity value. Where the signature has ink, the pixel is opaque. Where the canvas is empty, the pixel is fully transparent. When the image is placed on a page, the page shows through the transparent pixels. The signature behaves like ink printed on the document rather than a picture pasted on top of it.

JPG cannot store that opacity. It has no alpha channel, so every pixel must have a color. When a transparent PNG is converted to JPG, the converter has to invent a color for the empty area, and the usual choice is white. The signature still looks correct on a white page, which is why the problem stays hidden until the file is used somewhere else.

Transparency is also different from a white background that happens to match the page. A white-background image placed on a white page looks fine, but it still carries a rectangle of white pixels. Move it to a colored header and the rectangle appears. A true transparent PNG carries no background color at all, so it adapts to whatever sits behind it.

FormatTransparencyBest use for a signatureResult on a colored page
PNGYes, alpha channelContracts, forms, slides, emailPage color shows through
JPGNoWhite pages where JPG is mandatoryVisible white or black rectangle
WebPYesWeb pages that accept WebPPage color shows through

The maker exports PNG only. It does not produce SVG, JPG or WebP. If a portal demands another format, conversion is a separate step, and that step is where transparency is most often lost.

The checkerboard check before you upload

Image editors display transparency as a gray and white checkerboard. The pattern is a display convention, not part of the file. Seeing it is a good sign: it means the editor recognizes transparent pixels. Seeing a flat white or black area instead means the image has a solid background.

Run this check before placing or uploading a signature:

  1. Open the downloaded PNG in an image viewer or editor that supports transparency.
  2. Look for the checkerboard behind the name. Zoom in until the pattern is obvious.
  3. Place the image on a dark surface or a colored document page and confirm that the page color appears around the strokes.
  4. Zoom to the final display size and check that no square edge or halo follows the signature.

The tool's own preview is useful too. It shows the signature against light and dark backgrounds, which exposes both a hidden white rectangle and dark ink that disappears on a dark surface. If the signature looks correct on both, the transparency is working.

The JPG white-background pitfall

The white-box problem has three common causes. The first is exporting or saving the file as JPG. The second is taking a screenshot of the canvas, which captures the page background along with the signature. The third is pasting the PNG into a document that automatically converts images to JPG on export.

Example 1: the colored form. A signed consent form uses a pale blue header block. The signature was saved as JPG, so the empty canvas became a white rectangle. On the white body of the form the signature looked fine. In the blue header the rectangle stood out immediately, and the recipient asked for a corrected copy. Re-exporting the PNG and placing it directly over the blue area removed the rectangle because the blue pixels showed through the transparent background.

If a portal insists on JPG, decide the background deliberately. Composite the signature onto white first, so the result is a clean white card rather than a surprise rectangle. Use that version only where a white block is acceptable. Do not convert a transparent PNG to JPG and then place it on a colored page expecting the background to disappear; it cannot.

The same caution applies to screenshots. A screenshot of a white canvas includes the white canvas, even if the signature looks clean in the tool. Always use the download button and keep the original PNG.

A clean digital export from the canvas

Start with a signature that has room to breathe. The 1200 by 400 canvas is wide enough for a full name, and the empty margins protect the edges when the image is placed. If the name touches the canvas boundary, a capital letter or flourish can be clipped, and clipping looks like a mistake even when the ink is otherwise perfect.

Use a stroke weight that holds up at the final size. A thin line can fade when reduced; a heavy line can close the gaps inside letters. Preview the signature at the width of the signature line, not at full canvas size. Then export the PNG and give it a name that identifies the ink version, such as signature-dark.png or signature-light.png.

Keep the master file untouched. Place copies in documents rather than editing the original. Every re-save, screenshot or format conversion is a chance to lose transparency or soften the edges. If you need a different size, resize a copy and keep the 1200 by 400 master for future use.

Edges, halos and dark backgrounds

Signature strokes are anti-aliased, meaning the edge pixels blend gradually between ink and transparency. That blending is what makes a diagonal line look smooth instead of jagged. On a white page the blend is invisible. On a dark background, a dark stroke can lose its outer edge because the anti-aliased pixels are close to the background color.

The fix is contrast, not more sharpening. Export a light-ink version for dark surfaces. White or pale gray ink keeps the signature visible and lets the anti-aliased edge blend into the dark page naturally. For a document that will appear on both light and dark backgrounds, keep two masters rather than trying to make one file work everywhere.

Compression can create halos of its own. Saving a transparent signature as a low-quality JPG produces faint blocks around the strokes, especially on colored pages. If you must convert, use a high quality setting and inspect the result at 100 percent zoom. Better still, keep the PNG for placement and convert only the copy that a specific portal requires.

Resize and convert without losing the background

Resizing and converting are different operations. The image format converter changes a file between JPG, PNG and WebP, one file at a time and up to 10MB. It does not resize, so it will not fix a signature that is too large in pixels. The image compressor can resize or compress an image and is the right tool when a portal enforces a pixel box or a byte limit.

Example 2: a dark website header. A freelancer wants the signature in a site header with a charcoal background. The original dark-ink PNG disappears into the header. She creates a second export with white ink, keeps the same 1200 by 400 canvas, and places it at 180 pixels wide. Because the background is transparent, the charcoal shows through and the white strokes remain crisp. The dark-ink master stays untouched for white invoices.

When converting for a portal, check the order of operations. If the portal requires JPG and a specific width, resize first with the compressor, then convert the resized copy, or convert and then resize if the compressor accepts the converted format. Keep the PNG master separate so a rejected upload never damages the original. For the wider format tradeoffs, see PNG vs JPG vs WebP in the image guide.

Using one signature on white and dark surfaces

Most documents are white, so a dark-ink PNG covers the majority of placements. Contracts, invoices, letters and printed forms all expect a dark mark on a light page. The transparent background is still useful there because it removes the faint rectangle that appears when a white-background image sits on slightly cream or gray paper.

Dark surfaces need their own export. Presentation slides, dark email templates and website headers are common examples. Light ink on a transparent background reads as a deliberate signature rather than a missing image. If the surface is mid-gray, test both versions; contrast matters more than the color name.

Email adds a practical constraint: many clients block images by default or display them at a reduced size. Keep the signature simple, place it at a modest width, and include the typed name in the message body as well. The image is a visual mark, not a guarantee that the recipient will see it.

Finally, acceptance is separate from file quality. A clean PNG does not by itself make a document valid or accepted. Organizations may require a handwritten original or a recognized electronic signature process. This guide is general information, not legal advice; follow the instructions attached to the document. The electronic signature validity guide covers that distinction.

faqs.answer: Yes, if the resizing tool preserves the alpha channel. Use a copy and keep the original master. The image format converter changes formats but does not resize; the image compressor can resize or compress. After either operation, place the result on a dark surface to confirm the background is still empty.

faqs.answer: The transparent background takes on the page color, so dark ink on a dark surface has almost no contrast. Export a second version with white or pale ink. Keep separate dark-ink and light-ink masters rather than trying to recolor the placed image or adding a white background block.

faqs.answer: A PNG is only an image. Whether a document accepts an image-based signature depends on the organization, the document type and the process it specifies. Some require a handwritten original or a recognized electronic signature service. This is general information, not legal advice, so check the document's instructions before relying on the image.

title: Signature Size for PDF: Dimensions, DPI and Scaling
description: Choose signature dimensions for PDFs, contracts and forms, scale a 1200x400 PNG without stretching, and follow portal size limits.
html:
A signature can be perfectly drawn and still look wrong because it is the wrong size. Too wide and it collides with the date line. Too narrow and the strokes turn into gray smudges. Stretched to fill a box and the letters lean like a funhouse mirror. The fix is not a new signature; it is a placement decision made before the PNG goes into the document.

The signature maker exports a 1200 by 400 pixel transparent PNG. That fixed source gives you plenty of pixels to work with. This guide explains how to choose dimensions for PDFs, contracts and forms, how 150 DPI guidance translates into placement width, how to scale without stretching, and what to check when a portal imposes its own limits.

Why signature size is a document decision

The image does not have a single “correct” size. The document decides. A signature that fills a 2.5-inch line on a contract may be far too large for a form field that is 1.5 inches wide, and far too detailed for an email footer that displays at 160 pixels. What stays constant is the shape: the maker's canvas is 3:1, so the placed image should remain 3:1 unless you deliberately crop it.

Size affects three things at once. Legibility is the first: thin strokes disappear when reduced too far. Balance is the second: a signature should look like it belongs on the line, not like a banner pasted over the page. File size is the third: a large placed image may still be a small PNG, but some portals limit bytes and dimensions independently, so a visually correct file can fail an upload check.

Start by measuring the destination, not by choosing a number that sounds professional. Note the width of the signature line, the height of the form box, the page size, and any pixel or byte limit printed in the portal instructions. Those measurements turn the rest of this guide into simple arithmetic.

Pixels, inches and what 150 DPI means

A digital image is measured in pixels. A printed page is measured in inches or millimeters. DPI, dots per inch, connects the two: at 150 DPI, one inch of paper holds 150 pixels. A two-inch-wide signature therefore uses about 300 pixels of image width. At 300 DPI, the same two inches would use 600 pixels.

The maker's 1200-pixel width supports a signature up to 8 inches wide at 150 DPI, or 4 inches wide at 300 DPI. That is far larger than a normal signature block, which is why the source file has room to spare. When you place the PNG at two inches wide, the effective resolution is 1200 divided by 2, or 600 DPI. The image is being downscaled, which generally keeps edges clean.

Placed widthPixels needed at 150 DPIEffective DPI from a 1200 px sourceTypical use
1.5 inches225 px800 DPINarrow form field
2.0 inches300 px600 DPIInvoice or letter
2.5 inches375 px480 DPIContract signature block
4.0 inches600 px300 DPILarge printed form
8.0 inches1200 px150 DPIPractical upper limit

Treat 150 DPI as a floor for printed work, not a target to hit exactly. A signature placed at 2 inches wide from the 1200-pixel master is comfortably above it. If a document will be printed at a large size, keep the placed width under four inches so the effective resolution stays at 300 DPI or better.

Starting dimensions for PDFs, contracts and forms

The table below gives practical starting widths. These are not universal standards; they are sensible ranges that keep a signature readable without dominating the page. Adjust them to the document's actual line and the space around it.

PlacementWidth rangeHeight at 3:1Notes
PDF contract block2.0 to 2.5 inches0.67 to 0.83 inchesLeave room for a printed name and date
Offer letter2.0 to 2.5 inches0.67 to 0.83 inchesAlign the baseline with the signature rule
Consent or exam form1.5 to 2.0 inches0.50 to 0.67 inchesMatch the printed box, not the page margin
Invoice1.8 to 2.2 inches0.60 to 0.73 inchesKeep clear of totals and payment terms
Email footer150 to 220 pixels50 to 73 pixelsScreen use; DPI does not apply

For a PDF, the page size matters mainly because it limits the space around the signature block. A US Letter page is 8.5 by 11 inches; A4 is 8.27 by 11.69 inches. A 2.5-inch signature fits comfortably in either when the block is laid out correctly. The risk is not the page size but a cramped block where the signature overlaps a date, a title or another signature line.

Scaling without stretching

Stretching happens when width and height are changed by different amounts. The letters become wider or taller than they should be, and the signature looks artificial even if the ink is clean. The cure is to scale by one dimension and let the other follow, or to type both values in the same 3:1 relationship.

For a 1200 by 400 source, the height is always one third of the width. A 2.4-inch-wide placement should be 0.8 inches high. A 300-pixel-wide placement should be 100 pixels high. If the destination box is 2.4 by 0.7 inches, do not force the height to 0.7; reduce the width to 2.1 inches so the signature fits at its natural ratio.

Some editors offer a “fit to frame” command that changes both dimensions independently. Avoid it for signatures. Use “fit width” or hold the aspect-lock key while dragging a corner. If the signature must fill a box with a different ratio, pad the transparent canvas around the image rather than distorting the strokes. That preserves the letter shapes and keeps the background invisible.

Cropping is the other legitimate way to change the ratio. Trimming empty transparent margins can make a wide canvas fit a narrower box without touching the ink. Do that on a copy, keep the full master, and check that no flourish or descender was cut off.

Portal-specific limits and how to meet them

Upload portals rarely share one standard. Before you resize anything, read the instructions for four numbers: maximum width, maximum height, maximum file size, and accepted format. Some portals state a pixel box, some state a physical size in inches or millimeters, and some state only a byte limit. Each constraint needs a different response.

  • Pixel box: resize a copy to fit inside the box while keeping the 3:1 ratio. A 300 by 100 box matches the canvas exactly. A 600 by 200 box is the same shape at twice the size.
  • Physical size: convert to pixels at the portal's DPI. A 2-inch width at 150 DPI is 300 pixels; at 300 DPI it is 600 pixels. One inch equals 25.4 millimeters.
  • Byte cap: compress a copy after resizing. The image compressor can resize and compress; lower the quality setting gradually and check the result at 100 percent zoom.
  • Format: the image format converter handles JPG, PNG and WebP, one file at a time up to 10MB, but it does not resize. Convert a resized copy, not the master.

A portal that demands an exact box with a different ratio is the awkward case. If the box is 400 by 150 pixels, the 3:1 signature would be 400 by 133 pixels, leaving a 17-pixel gap. Padding the transparent canvas to 400 by 150 keeps the ink undistorted. Stretching the signature to fill the box is faster but visibly wrong.

Upload limits can also reject a file that looks small on screen. Keep the original PNG, work on copies, and test the upload before an important deadline. If the portal shows a preview, inspect it: some portals resize or re-encode uploads, and the preview is the version that matters.

Compress only after the dimensions are right

Resizing and compressing solve different problems. Resizing changes the pixel dimensions; compressing changes how many bytes those pixels occupy. Do the dimensions first, because compressing a 1200-pixel image that will be displayed at 300 pixels wastes effort and can soften detail that was about to be discarded anyway.

The signature maker's PNG often stays small because most of the canvas is transparent and the ink covers a limited area. If a portal still imposes a byte cap, open a copy in the image compressor, resize to the required box if needed, and reduce the quality setting until the file fits. Check the strokes at 100 percent zoom after each pass; a signature that meets the byte limit but turns fuzzy has solved the wrong problem.

Keep the transparent PNG master. Compression can introduce faint artifacts around anti-aliased edges, especially on colored pages. A compressed copy for one portal should not replace the clean file you use everywhere else. If the portal accepts PNG, prefer it; if it demands JPG, remember that transparency will be lost and the background will become solid.

Two worked examples

Example 1: a contract with a 2.2-inch signature line. The line is 2.2 inches wide on a white page. At 150 DPI, the placement needs 330 pixels of width. The 1200-pixel master is more than enough, so the image is downscaled and the effective resolution is about 545 DPI. The height follows the 3:1 ratio: 2.2 divided by 3 is about 0.73 inches. That leaves room above the printed name and below the date. No stretching is needed because the signature line and the canvas share a wide shape.

Example 2: an exam form with a 300 by 100 pixel box. The portal states an exact pixel box, so the 1200 by 400 canvas maps to 300 by 100 by dividing both dimensions by four. The ratio is unchanged and the strokes stay proportional. If the form also caps the file at a modest byte size, the resized copy goes through the compressor, and the result is checked in the portal preview. If the box were 400 by 150 instead, the signature would be placed at 400 by 133 and the transparent canvas padded to 150 pixels high rather than stretching the letters.

faqs.answer: At 150 DPI, multiply the width in inches by 150. A two-inch signature needs about 300 pixels, and a 2.5-inch signature needs about 375 pixels. The maker's 1200-pixel canvas covers up to 8 inches at 150 DPI, though normal document placement is much smaller and therefore sharper.

faqs.answer: Yes. The image compressor can resize and compress an image, so it is the right tool when a portal enforces a pixel box or a byte limit. faqs.answer: Resize a copy to fit inside the box while keeping the 3:1 ratio. A 300 by 100 box matches the canvas exactly, and a 600 by 200 box is the same shape at twice the size. faqs.answer: For most printing and document placement, pixel dimensions and the placed size matter most. DPI is a relationship between pixels and inches. Some portals read a DPI tag, so follow their instructions if they mention one. The maker focuses on a 1200 by 400 pixel canvas, and you control the placed width in the document.

title: Drawn vs Typed Signature: Which Should You Use?
description: Compare drawn and typed signatures for consistency, legibility at small sizes, style, accessibility and daily use, with a clear workflow for each method.

toc.text: What the tool does not do

html:
A drawn signature and a typed signature can carry the same name and still behave very differently once they leave your screen. One records hand movement. The other is a font rendering of your name. Both can be exported as a transparent PNG from the same tool, and both remain images rather than cryptographic signatures, but the choice affects consistency, legibility at small sizes, accessibility and how natural the result looks on a contract.

This comparison sticks to practical differences and ends with a workflow for each method. The signature maker handles both on a 1200×400 canvas. For the wider process, see the signature maker guide.

What each method actually produces

Drawn. You move a mouse, finger or pen across the canvas and the tool records the path as strokes. You control stroke width and ink color, then export the result with transparency. The mark carries your hand’s speed, slant and small imperfections, which is exactly why it reads as personal. The export is a clean digital stroke rather than a scan of wet ink, so it looks more uniform than a pen on paper. It is still a drawing made in one sitting, and drawing the same name twice will not produce identical pixels.

Typed. You enter your name, pick a cursive font and adjust stroke and color. The output is a clean, repeatable rendering with consistent letter spacing and baseline. It is not your handwriting, and it should not be described as such. What it offers is speed and uniformity: the same name, the same proportions, every time.

Both methods end at the same place: a transparent PNG near 1200×400 pixels, saved locally. Neither method signs a PDF, verifies your identity or creates a certificate-based electronic signature. The image is a visual mark you can place into a document or form.

Consistency and legibility at small sizes

Consistency is the clearest split. A typed signature is identical on every export, which helps when your name appears on twenty invoices or a batch of routine forms. A drawn signature varies with the input device, the speed of your hand and the size of the canvas. That variation can look authentic, but it makes a drawn mark harder to standardize across a brand or a team.

Legibility does not follow the same rule. Method matters less than stroke weight and letter shapes. A thin 1px line on a 1200px-wide canvas becomes nearly invisible when the image is scaled down to a 140×60 form box. A 3px or 4px stroke survives reduction. Typed signatures fail in the opposite way: delicate script fonts with hairline joins can close up at small sizes, while heavier cursive faces stay readable. Always preview at the final display size, not at 100% on a large canvas.

CriterionDrawn signatureTyped signature
RepeatabilityVaries between attemptsIdentical every export
Small-size legibilityDepends on stroke weightDepends on font weight
Personal characterHighModerate
Input demandsSteady hand or pen tabletKeyboard only
EditingRedraw the strokeRetype or change font
Best fitOne-off, personal documentsRepeatable, high-volume use

A useful test is to export both versions, place them at the size they will actually appear, and view them on a phone. If the loops fill in or the ends disappear, adjust the stroke or choose a simpler font. Do not judge either version on the big canvas alone.

Style, accessibility and the human factor

Drawn signatures feel informal, personal and slightly imperfect. They suit a letter, a creative proposal or a document where the signature is part of the presentation. Typed signatures feel polished and consistent. They suit invoices, repeated authorizations and any workflow where speed matters more than flourish.

Accessibility cuts in favor of typing for many people. A mouse or trackpad makes smooth curves difficult, and a hand tremor turns an intended loop into a jagged line. Typing removes that barrier entirely. Some people also prefer a typed signature because it is easier to read. The counterpoint is that a recipient may specifically ask for a handwritten mark, and a typed name cannot satisfy that request. Check the instruction before choosing.

Color deserves a mention. Near-black ink reads best on white paper and survives photocopying. Navy is a common alternative that still looks formal. Very light gray, pastel colors and thin white strokes disappear on white backgrounds or in dark-mode viewers. Preview the signature on both a white and a dark surface before exporting, because a transparent PNG inherits whatever background it lands on.

Which method fits which job

Choose a drawn signature when the document is personal, when the recipient expects a handwritten mark, or when you want the signature to look distinctive. A lease addendum, a personal letter, a creative contract or a one-time consent form all fit. Drawing is also the better choice for initials in small boxes, where a short custom mark can be shaped to the space.

Choose a typed signature when you sign often, when the same file will be reused, or when small-size clarity matters more than personality. Freelancers sending monthly invoices, administrators processing routine forms and anyone with limited dexterity will get a more reliable result from a typed script. A hybrid approach works well: keep one typed signature for routine paperwork and draw a fresh one for documents that deserve more care.

Neither choice gives you a verified e-signature. If the recipient requires a platform with an audit trail, an identity check or a digital certificate, an image will not meet that requirement no matter how good it looks.

A practical workflow for both methods

Example 1: a typed signature for recurring invoices. Priya runs a small design studio and sends about thirty invoices a month. She types her name, picks a readable cursive font, sets the ink to a deep navy and the stroke to 3px, then previews the result on white and dark backgrounds. She exports a transparent PNG at 1200×400 and keeps it as her master file. Each invoice template places the same image at roughly 1.6 inches wide. She never redraws it, so every invoice looks consistent, and she keeps a second copy in a folder that is backed up with the rest of her business files.

Example 2: a drawn signature for a one-off lease addendum. Daniel uses a pen tablet to sign a single page. He draws with a 4px black stroke, checks that the loops are open at the size it will print, and exports the transparent PNG. In the PDF editor he places it on the signature line at about 1.8 inches wide, confirms it does not cover the printed text, and exports a flattened copy. He keeps the unsigned original and the exported PNG in case the landlord asks for a cleaner version.

  1. Pick the method that matches the document and the recipient’s instructions.
  2. Set a stroke width that survives the final size, usually 3px to 4px for a 1200×400 canvas.
  3. Preview on white and dark backgrounds, then check at the actual placement size.
  4. Export the transparent PNG and store the master file somewhere you can find it again.
  5. Place the image without stretching it, and keep the unsigned document separately.

If a portal or email system caps the file size, run the exported PNG through the image compressor and resize it to the required dimensions. For a deeper look at transparency and background behavior, read transparent signature PNG. If the signature is headed for a PDF, the placement notes in signature size for PDF will save a second export.

What the signature maker does not do

The tool draws or types one signature at a time and exports a PNG. It does not sign PDFs, issue certificates, verify identity or produce a legally qualified electronic signature. It cannot remove the background from an uploaded photograph, so a picture of a signature on paper will keep its paper texture unless you clean it in an image editor. It does not export SVG, which means the output is a fixed-resolution image rather than a scalable vector.

Those limits are fine for the job the tool is built for: making a clean image of your signature. They matter when someone asks for an authenticated signature. In that case, use the process the organization specifies rather than sending a PNG and hoping it is accepted. The electronic signature validity guide explains the difference in general terms.

Make your signature: open the signature maker, draw with a mouse, finger or pen or type your name in a cursive font, preview the transparent PNG, and download it. No upload and no account.

faqs.question: Is a typed signature as valid as a drawn one?
faqs.answer: It depends on the jurisdiction, the document and the recipient’s rules. Many electronic signature frameworks focus on intent, consent and record integrity rather than the look of the mark, but some documents require witnesses, notarization, a digital certificate or a qualified signature. Treat this as general information, not legal advice, and check the specific requirement before relying on either method.

faqs.question: Which style is more consistent across many documents?
faqs.answer: A typed signature, because the font renders the same shapes on every export. A drawn signature changes with your hand, the input device and the canvas size. If you sign the same invoice template every month, a typed master file gives you a repeatable result without redrawing anything.

faqs.question: Why does my signature disappear when I shrink it?
faqs.answer: Thin strokes become sub-pixel when a 1200px-wide image is scaled into a 140×60 form box. Increase the stroke to 3px or 4px and test at the final size. Typed signatures can fail the same way when a script font has hairline joins, so preview the actual placement rather than judging on the large canvas.

faqs.question: Can I use the exported PNG to sign a PDF?
faqs.answer: You can place it as an image in a PDF editor and then flatten or export the file. That produces a document with a picture of your signature, not a certificate-based signature with an audit trail. Many everyday agreements are handled this way, but high-value or regulated documents may require a specific e-signature service or digital signature.

faqs.question: Can I make a signature without a touchscreen or tablet?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can draw with a mouse or trackpad, though smooth curves take practice, or switch to the typed mode and choose a cursive font. Typing is also the easier option for anyone with a tremor or limited dexterity. Check whether the recipient accepts a typed mark before you commit to it.

faqs.question: Does the signature maker send my signature anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. The canvas runs locally in your browser, the image is generated on your device, and the download happens without an upload. Closing the tab clears the working session. The tool makes one signature at a time and does not keep an account-based library, so save the PNG somewhere safe.

title: How to Sign a PDF Without Printing: Image Method
description: Sign a PDF without a printer: export a transparent PNG signature, insert it as an image, place and scale it, then flatten and export the finished file.

toc.text: What you need before you start
Insert the image into the PDF

html:
The PDF is already in your inbox, the signature line is on page three, and the printer is out of toner. You do not need to print, sign and scan. You can place an image of your signature directly into the PDF, position it on the line, and export a finished copy. The result looks like a signed page, and for many everyday agreements that is enough.

It is not the same thing as a certificate-based electronic signature. This guide covers the image workflow end to end, then explains where that workflow stops. Make the image in the signature maker, and use the signature maker guide for the surrounding basics.

What you need before you start

Three things: a signature image with a transparent background, a PDF editor that can insert an image and export a flattened file, and the sender’s instructions. The instructions matter more than the software. Some organizations accept a visibly inserted signature, some require a specific e-signature platform, and some require a digital certificate. Read the request before you spend time on the file.

Most full PDF editors can add an image and then flatten annotations or print to a new PDF. Lightweight viewers may let you place a comment-style image but save it as a separate annotation that the recipient can move or delete. If the signature must be part of the page, look for “flatten”, “print to PDF” or an export option that merges annotations. Avoid any tool that asks you to upload the document to an unknown server unless the sender specifically approved that service.

Step 1: export a clean transparent PNG

Open the signature maker. Draw with a mouse, touch or pen, or switch to typing and choose a cursive font. Set the ink to near-black or deep navy and the stroke to 3px or 4px. Thin strokes vanish when the image is scaled down; heavy strokes can look clumsy on a form. Preview on white and dark backgrounds so you know the transparent area is actually clear.

Export the PNG at the full 1200×400 canvas and keep that master file. Do not crop it tightly unless you have a reason. The empty space around the mark gives you room to position it without clipping the ends of a loop. If you later need a smaller copy for a portal with a file-size cap, derive it from the master rather than redrawing.

Name the file clearly, for example signature-master.png, and keep it somewhere private. A signature image is easy to reuse, which is convenient for you and also the reason you should not leave it in a shared folder.

Step 2: insert the image into the PDF

Example 1: a three-page consulting NDA. The signature block sits on page three. Open the PDF in your editor, choose the add-image command, select signature-master.png, and click once on the signature line. The image may arrive at its natural size, which may be far too large for the page. Do not panic and do not drag the corner yet; first check that the page is not rotated and that you are on the correct copy of the document.

Place the image so the baseline of the signature sits just above the printed line. Leave the typed name and date below it visible. If the document has two signature blocks, place one image on each line rather than stretching a single image across both. For initials, a smaller copy of the same image is usually acceptable, but a dedicated initials mark looks cleaner.

If the PDF is a scan, the page may be slightly skewed. Align the signature visually with the printed line rather than with the page edge. At 100% zoom, check that the image does not cover a date field, a checkbox or a clause number.

Step 3: place and scale without distortion

Signature images are usually wider than they are tall. The 1200×400 canvas is a 3:1 ratio, so a signature placed 1.8 inches wide will be about 0.6 inches tall. Hold the Shift key, use the aspect-lock option or drag a corner handle to preserve that ratio. Dragging a side handle alone stretches the letters and makes the signature look fabricated.

A practical width is 1.5 to 2 inches for a full signature on a standard letter-size page. A form with a small box may need 1 inch or less. Judge the result at print size, not at 400% zoom. If the signature looks too light, increase the stroke and export again rather than applying a heavy shadow or outline in the PDF editor.

Example 2: a rental addendum with two initial boxes. The tenant needs to initial the top of page one and the bottom of page two. A full signature is too wide for the boxes, so scale one copy to about 0.5 inches wide, place it in the first box, then duplicate and place the second copy. Keep both copies at the same size and angle. Save the working file before flattening so you can fix a misplaced mark without starting over.

Do not scale the image up beyond its exported size. A 1200px-wide signature placed at 4 inches wide is being stretched, and the strokes will soften. If you need a larger mark, go back to the canvas and export at full size instead of enlarging a small file.

Step 4: flatten and export the finished PDF

Once the placement is right, flatten the annotations or print the document to a new PDF. Flattening merges the image into the page so the signature cannot be nudged out of place by the next person who opens the file. Check the exported copy at 100% zoom: the signature should be visible, the text should still be readable, and the page count should be unchanged.

Compare the file size before and after. A transparent PNG signature is usually small, but a print-to-PDF step can rasterize the whole page and inflate the file. If the result is unexpectedly large, try a different export path or compress the signature image first with the image compressor. Keep the unsigned original, the exported PNG and the signed PDF together in one folder so you can show exactly what changed if a question comes up.

Finally, name the file in a way the recipient can identify: nda-acme-signed-2026-10-22.pdf is easier to track than document-final-final.pdf. Send it through the channel the recipient requested, and avoid re-editing a flattened copy unless you intentionally want to add another mark.

Image signature vs certificate-based e-signature

An inserted image proves that a picture of a signature appears on the page. It does not prove who placed it, when it was placed or whether the page changed afterward. A certificate-based signature uses a private key and a digital certificate to bind an identity to the document, and it usually produces a tamper-evident audit trail. A qualified electronic signature adds a regulated identity check and a qualified certificate, and its recognition depends on the framework and the parties involved.

FeatureInserted image signatureCertificate-based e-signature
What it isA PNG placed on the pageA cryptographic signature tied to a certificate
Identity checkNone by itselfDepends on the provider and level
Tamper evidenceNone after flatteningDocument changes can invalidate the signature
Audit trailWhatever your email or file history showsOften includes timestamps, IP logs or signing events
Typical useEveryday internal forms and informal agreementsContracts, regulated filings and high-value transactions

None of this means an image signature is useless. Many day-to-day documents are handled with a scanned or inserted signature, and the parties accept that level of evidence. The mistake is assuming the image carries the same assurance as a digital certificate. If the sender asks for a DSC, a qualified signature or a specific platform, use that process. The electronic signature validity guide explains the general frameworks, and signature size for PDF covers placement dimensions in more detail.

Make the image first: open the signature maker, draw or type your signature, and download a transparent PNG. Then insert it in your PDF editor, place it on the line, and flatten the file. The signature is created on your device.

faqs.question: Does inserting an image count as signing a PDF?
faqs.answer: It produces a document with a visible signature image on the page, which many people treat as signed for everyday purposes. It is not a certificate-based signature and does not verify who inserted the image or whether the file changed later. Whether it satisfies a particular agreement or agency depends on the rules that apply, so check before using it for high-value or regulated documents.

faqs.question: How wide should the signature be on a letter-size page?
faqs.answer: About 1.5 to 2 inches for a full signature is a practical starting point. Because a 1200×400 image has a 3:1 ratio, a 1.8-inch width gives a height near 0.6 inches. Small form boxes may need 1 inch or less. Judge the result at print size and keep the aspect ratio locked so the letters do not stretch.

faqs.question: Do I need to flatten the signature after placing it?
faqs.answer: Flattening is safer if you want the mark to stay in place. An unflattened annotation can be moved or deleted by the next person who opens the PDF. Use the editor’s flatten command or print the document to a new PDF, then reopen the exported copy and check the signature at 100% zoom.

faqs.question: Can I sign a PDF on my phone?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your PDF editor supports adding an image on mobile. Create and download the PNG first, then use the editor’s image or annotation tool to place it. Small screens make precise alignment harder, so zoom in on the signature line and check the result at full size before sending. Keep a copy of the unsigned original.

faqs.question: Why is my signature image blurry in the PDF?
faqs.answer: The image was probably enlarged beyond its exported size, or the PDF was exported at a low resolution. A 1200px-wide PNG should be placed near 1.5 to 2 inches wide, not stretched across half the page. Export a fresh master at full canvas size and place it again rather than sharpening a stretched copy.

faqs.question: What is the difference between this and a digital signature?
faqs.answer: A digital signature uses cryptography and a certificate to bind an identity to the document contents and to reveal later changes. An inserted PNG is only a picture. Some workflows accept the picture, while others require a DSC, a qualified signature or a platform with an audit trail. The requirements come from the organization or the law that governs the document.

title: Signature Image for Email: Size, PNG and Alt Text
description: Put a signature image in an email footer: about 600×200 PNG, useful alt text, light file weight, and a dark-mode caveat. Not a full signature builder.

toc.text: Add the image to your footer

html:
An email footer with a signature image can look sharp and consistent across clients, or it can arrive as a giant blurry rectangle that pushes the message sideways. The difference is mostly preparation: a sensible canvas size, a transparent PNG, a display width that fits the footer, and alt text for the people whose email client blocks images.

This guide covers the image itself. The signature maker creates a transparent PNG; it does not build a complete email signature block with your job title, phone number, social icons and legal disclaimer. For the full signature workflow, start with the signature maker guide.

Why use an image instead of a signature font?

A font renders differently depending on the recipient’s device, and email clients are notoriously inconsistent about which fonts they load. An image renders the same shapes everywhere the message is displayed, as long as the client shows images at all. That consistency is useful when your signature is part of your brand, or when you want the exact slant and spacing you approved.

The tradeoff is that an image is a fixed block. It does not reflow like text, it may be blocked by default, and it can look wrong in dark mode. Text remains accessible and searchable; an image needs alt text to be understood when it does not load. Many footers combine both: a text block with name and contact details, and a small signature image for the personal mark.

Pick dimensions and format for the footer

A common target is about 600×200 pixels for the image file, displayed smaller inside the footer. The 3:1 shape matches a typical signature and leaves room for an underline or a short title if your design includes one. Start with a 1200×400 master, then save a 600×200 copy for the footer. Keeping the master means you can produce a larger version later without redrawing.

PNG is the right default because it preserves transparency and keeps thin strokes crisp. JPG is smaller but fills transparent areas with white, which produces a visible rectangle on any non-white background. If your footer already sits on a white card, a high-quality JPG can work, but PNG gives you more flexibility and avoids a surprise when the design changes.

PlacementSuggested image widthFormatNote
Standard email footer600 px file, displayed near 200 pxPNGTransparent background, dark ink
Narrow mobile footer480 px filePNGTest at the smallest width you support
White card or newsletter block600 pxJPG or PNGJPG loses transparency
High-resolution master1200 pxPNGExport source, then derive smaller copies

Do not use a 4000px phone photo as the footer image. It will be scaled down anyway, and the extra bytes make the message heavier for no visual gain. If you only have a large scan, resize and compress it before inserting it.

Export a footer-ready signature

Open the signature maker and draw with a mouse, touch or pen, or type your name in a cursive font. Use a stroke around 3px on the 1200×400 canvas and choose near-black or deep navy ink. Preview against white and dark surfaces, because a transparent PNG will sit on whatever background the email client provides.

Export the PNG at full size and save it as your master. Then create a 600×200 copy for the footer. If your email platform asks for a file under a certain size, run the copy through the image compressor and resize it to the exact dimensions rather than letting the email client squash a larger file. Keep the master untouched so you can make a light-ink variant for dark mode later.

Example 1: a consultant’s Gmail footer. Maya exports a 600×200 PNG with 3px dark navy ink, then inserts it in her Gmail signature settings at about 200px wide. She adds a plain-text line underneath with her role, email address and website. The text carries the contact details if images are blocked, and the image supplies the personal mark. She keeps a 1200×400 master in a private folder for future use.

Example 2: an Outlook footer for a small team. The team uses one shared signature image at 480px wide so it fits a narrow reading pane. Each person inserts the same PNG at the same display width, then edits the text lines with their own name and phone number. The shared image keeps the brand consistent, while the text block stays searchable and accessible.

Add the image to your email footer

In Gmail, open Settings, find the signature editor, and use the image button to insert the PNG. Set the display width so the signature does not dominate the message. In Outlook, the signature editor is under File, Options, Mail, Signatures; the insert-image control works similarly. Other clients have their own signature settings, but the pattern is the same: insert the file, set a width, add alt text if the editor exposes it, and send a test message to yourself.

Test the result in more than one client if you can. Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail and mobile apps all render images differently. Check the footer on a phone, where the available width is smaller, and confirm that the image does not force horizontal scrolling. If it does, reduce the display width or use a narrower crop.

Do not place the image inside a table cell that is narrower than the image’s display width. Many email templates use tables for layout, and an oversized image can break the column. Set the image width in the editor rather than dragging it to fill the space.

Alt text and the dark-mode caveat

Alt text describes the image when it cannot be displayed. Write something short and useful: alt="Signature of Maya Chen". Do not repeat your entire job history in the alt attribute. If the image contains your name and nothing else, the alt text can simply say whose signature it is. Some email editors hide the alt field, so add it in the HTML if you control the template.

Dark mode is the most common visual failure. A transparent PNG with dark ink can disappear against a dark background, and some clients invert or dim images unpredictably. There is no single fix that works everywhere. The practical approach is to export a second version with light ink for dark backgrounds, test it in the clients your recipients actually use, and consider placing the image on a light card if the design allows. Do not assume the client will preserve your intended colors.

A signature image is not a logo, and it does not need to be visible at every screen width. If the footer becomes crowded on mobile, let the text block carry the information and hide or shrink the image. The message should remain readable even when the image is blocked, inverted or stripped by a corporate mail gateway.

File weight, deliverability and what the tool does not build

Keep the image light. A footer image should be tens of kilobytes, not megabytes. Large images slow down loading, may be clipped by some clients and add unnecessary weight to every message in a thread. PNG line art at 600×200 is usually compact; if yours is not, check that you did not export a photo or a full-page scan. The image compressor can resize and re-encode a copy without touching the master.

The signature maker makes one signature image at a time. It does not generate an email-signature block, insert itself into Gmail or Outlook, add social icons, create a disclaimer or manage a team-wide template. Those parts belong in your email client or template editor. The tool also does not remove the background from a photographed signature, so start from a clean canvas rather than a picture of paper.

For the visual basics, see transparent signature PNG. If the same mark will also go on a PDF, signature size for PDF explains the placement dimensions. And if you are comparing a hand-drawn mark with a typed one, drawn vs typed signature walks through the tradeoffs.

Make a footer-ready mark: open the signature maker, draw or type your signature, preview it on light and dark backgrounds, and download a transparent PNG. Then insert it in your email signature settings at a width that fits.

faqs.question: What size should a signature image be for email?
faqs.answer: Start with a 1200×400 master and save a 600×200 copy for the footer, then display it around 200 pixels wide in the signature editor. The exact display width depends on your template and the reading pane. Test on a phone and in a narrow desktop pane so the image does not force horizontal scrolling.

faqs.question: Should I use PNG or JPG for an email signature image?
faqs.answer: PNG is the better default because it keeps transparency and crisp strokes. JPG fills transparent areas with white, which creates a visible rectangle on colored or dark backgrounds. Use JPG only when the footer sits on a white card and you have deliberately flattened the background.

faqs.question: How do I add the image to my Gmail or Outlook signature?
faqs.answer: In Gmail, open Settings, find the signature editor, and use the image button to insert the PNG. In Outlook, open File, Options, Mail, Signatures and use the insert-image control. Set a sensible display width, add alt text if the editor allows it, and send a test message to yourself before using it on real mail.

faqs.question: Why does my signature disappear in dark mode?
faqs.answer: A transparent PNG with dark ink can blend into a dark background, and some email clients invert or dim images. Export a light-ink version for dark backgrounds, test it in the clients your recipients use, or place the image on a light card if the design allows. There is no single setting that fixes every client.

faqs.question: Is this a complete email signature generator?
faqs.answer: No. The signature maker creates the image only. It does not build a block with your title, phone number, social icons or disclaimer, and it does not insert the image into Gmail or Outlook. Use your email client’s signature editor for the text and layout around the image.

faqs.question: Will a signature image hurt email deliverability?
faqs.answer: A small, clean image is unlikely to be the deciding factor, but large attachments and image-only messages are harder to read and slower to load. Keep the footer image to tens of kilobytes, include plain text for the important details, and avoid turning the entire signature into a single picture. Follow your organization’s email guidelines.

title: Electronic Signature Validity: ESIGN, eIDAS and India
description: How electronic signature validity works in general: intent, consent and record integrity under US ESIGN, EU eIDAS and India’s IT Act, with document caveats.
html:
“Is an electronic signature valid?” sounds like a yes-or-no question. In practice it depends on the framework that applies, the type of document, the intent of the people signing and the evidence that survives afterward. A typed name in an email, a signature image on a PDF and a qualified digital signature are all electronic in some sense, but they carry very different levels of assurance.

This is general information, not legal advice. The summary below covers the ideas shared by common frameworks, then the broad shape of US ESIGN, EU eIDAS and India’s IT Act. For the image side, see the signature maker guide. For a specific agreement, consult a qualified lawyer in the relevant jurisdiction.

Intent, consent and record integrity

Most electronic signature rules ask three practical questions. First, did the person intend to sign? A signature placed on a document is usually evidence of intent, but the surrounding facts matter. Second, did the parties agree to conduct the transaction electronically? Consumer protection rules often require clear consent and disclosures before electronic records replace paper. Third, can the record be retained and reproduced accurately? If the signed file cannot be shown later in a reliable form, the signature is hard to rely on.

A fourth idea sits underneath all three: attribution. Can you connect the mark to a particular person? An email account, a one-time code, a platform login or a digital certificate can support attribution. A transparent PNG on its own does not. That is why two documents can both look “signed” while carrying very different weight.

None of these elements is a magic checklist that makes a signature immune to challenge. They are the questions a court, regulator or counterparty is likely to ask when a signature is disputed.

United States: ESIGN and UETA

The federal Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act, usually called ESIGN, gives electronic signatures and records legal effect for many transactions in interstate or foreign commerce. It does not say every electronic mark is valid in every situation. The Act generally requires intent to sign, consent to electronic records, and a system that lets the parties retain and reproduce the record. State-level UETA rules follow a similar pattern.

ESIGN also excludes certain documents, and the list matters. Wills, codicils and testamentary trusts, family law matters, court orders and notices, and several consumer notices are outside its general coverage or subject to special rules. Some transactions involving utilities, insurance and foreclosure require specific consent or paper notices. The exact scope is technical, so do not assume that a signature image works for every agreement just because the parties are in the US.

For ordinary commercial contracts, a platform that records consent, identity checks, timestamps and the final document usually provides stronger evidence than a PNG pasted onto a page. The platform does not make a signature automatically enforceable, but it creates a record that is easier to explain if the document is challenged.

European Union: eIDAS levels

eIDAS is the EU regulation that gives a common framework for electronic identification and trust services. It describes three levels of electronic signature. A simple electronic signature is data in electronic form attached to or associated with other electronic data, used to sign. An advanced electronic signature is uniquely linked to the signer, capable of identifying the signer, created using data the signer controls and linked to the document so that later changes are detectable. A qualified electronic signature is an advanced signature created with a qualified certificate and a qualified signature creation device.

The practical difference is assurance. A simple signature may be enough for a low-risk internal approval, while a qualified signature is designed to carry a high level of identity assurance and is recognized across EU member states. Under eIDAS, a qualified electronic signature has the equivalent effect of a handwritten signature. That does not mean every document can be signed electronically; national rules still impose witnesses, notarization, registration or specific formalities for some transactions.

If a counterparty asks for a “qualified” signature, an image will not satisfy the request. The signature must come from a qualified trust service provider and meet the technical requirements of the framework.

India: the IT Act and digital signatures

India’s Information Technology Act, 2000 gives legal recognition to electronic records and electronic signatures, subject to the Act’s requirements. The framework includes digital signatures based on certificates issued by licensed certifying authorities, and it recognizes other electronic signature methods notified under the Act. Aadhaar-based eSign is widely used for routine digital paperwork, while a digital signature certificate, or DSC, is common for company filings, tax portals and other official submissions.

The IT Act also excludes certain documents from electronic signature treatment. The First Schedule includes negotiable instruments other than cheques, powers of attorney, trusts, wills and contracts for the sale or conveyance of immovable property. Those documents may still involve electronic processing, but the signature and formality rules are not solved by attaching a PNG. A sale deed, for example, typically involves stamp duty, witnesses and registration, and those requirements sit outside what an image signature can provide.

For a company filing that asks for a DSC, the portal is not asking for a picture of a signature. It is asking for a cryptographic credential tied to a certificate. Use the credential the portal specifies.

FrameworkCore ideaSignature levels or toolsWhat it does not remove
US ESIGN and UETAElectronic signatures and records can have legal effect when the rules are metBroad category, including simple electronic signaturesDocument exclusions, consumer consent and specific notices
EU eIDASCommon rules for electronic identification and trust servicesSimple, advanced and qualified electronic signaturesNational witness, notarization and registration rules
India IT ActLegal recognition for electronic records and specified signature methodsDSC, Aadhaar eSign and other notified methodsExcluded documents and formalities such as stamp duty or registration

Document caveats that override the signature type

Some documents need more than a signature, electronic or otherwise. A will may need witnesses. A property transfer may need a notarized or registered deed. A court filing may need a specific digital signature. A company registry may accept only a DSC. A cross-border contract may be governed by a law that imposes its own formalities. In those situations, the question is not “is an electronic signature valid?” but “what does this document require?”

Consent is another practical caveat. A consumer may be entitled to receive certain disclosures on paper or to withdraw consent to electronic delivery. An employee may be subject to an internal policy that requires a particular system. A counterparty may simply refuse to accept anything other than a named e-signature platform. Those are contractual and operational constraints, not just legal ones.

Example 1: a US freelance agreement. A designer in Texas sends an $1,800 project agreement through a platform that verifies the client’s email, records a timestamp and stores the final PDF. Both parties intend to sign and consent to electronic delivery. This is the kind of simple electronic signature that ESIGN and UETA are designed to accommodate, but the agreement’s terms, the consumer disclosures and any document-specific exceptions still matter.

Example 2: an Indian company filing. A Bengaluru startup submits an MCA form that requires a DSC. The founder attaches the company’s digital signature token and completes the portal flow. A PNG of the founder’s signature would not satisfy the portal, because the requirement is a cryptographic credential rather than a visual mark.

Where an image signature fits

An image signature is best understood as a visual mark, not as a complete trust system. It can show that a person intended to associate a mark with a document, and it can be perfectly adequate for an internal approval, a low-risk acknowledgment or an informal agreement where the parties are not disputing authenticity. The surrounding email thread, the file history and the conduct of the parties may supply context that the image itself does not.

It is a poor fit when identity assurance, tamper evidence or a regulated signature level is required. It is also a poor fit when the recipient has explicitly asked for a platform, a DSC or a qualified signature. In those cases, use the specified process. The signature maker can produce a clean transparent PNG for the visual mark, and the image compressor can resize a copy for a portal, but neither tool turns the image into a verified electronic signature.

Before signing anything important, read the instructions, identify the required signature type and keep a complete copy of the final record. If the document involves significant money, property, family law or a regulated filing, get advice from a qualified professional in the relevant jurisdiction. For the practical image workflow, see sign a PDF without printing. For the difference between a drawn and typed mark, see drawn vs typed signature.

Create the visual mark: open the signature maker to draw or type a signature and download a transparent PNG. Use it where a visual signature is appropriate, and use the process the document actually requires when assurance matters.

faqs.question: Is a picture of a signature legally valid?
faqs.answer: It can be evidence of intent in some situations, but it does not verify who placed it or whether the document changed afterward. Many frameworks allow simple electronic signatures, while others require a specific method, a witness, a notarized deed or a digital certificate. This is general information, not legal advice; check the rules for your document and jurisdiction.

faqs.question: What makes an electronic signature valid?
faqs.answer: Common frameworks look for intent to sign, consent to electronic records, a reliable way to retain and reproduce the record, and some link between the signature and the signer. The details vary by jurisdiction. A platform with identity checks and an audit trail usually provides stronger evidence than a pasted image, but it still does not override document-specific formalities.

faqs.question: What is a qualified electronic signature?
faqs.answer: Under EU eIDAS, a qualified electronic signature is an advanced signature created with a qualified certificate and a qualified signature creation device. It is designed to carry a high level of identity assurance and has the equivalent effect of a handwritten signature under the regulation. It is not the same thing as a signature image or a simple click-to-accept signature.

faqs.question: Does ESIGN cover every type of document?
faqs.answer: No. ESIGN and UETA exclude or treat separately certain documents such as wills, family law matters, court documents and some consumer notices. The exact scope is technical and fact-specific. For anything beyond an ordinary commercial agreement, check the applicable state and federal rules before relying on an electronic signature.

faqs.question: Can I use the signature maker for a contract?
faqs.answer: You can use it to create the visual mark, and many informal agreements are handled with an inserted signature image. That does not make the contract valid in every circumstance. If the contract is high-value, regulated or explicitly requires a platform, DSC or qualified signature, use the required process and get legal advice where appropriate.

faqs.question: Do I need a DSC for Indian government portals?
faqs.answer: Many Indian government and company filings require a digital signature certificate or Aadhaar eSign, and the portal will specify which method it accepts. A PNG signature image is not a substitute for a DSC. Check the filing instructions and use the credential the portal requests.

title: Signature for Exam Forms: 20-50KB and 140x60 Rules
description: Prepare a signature for exam forms: check the notification, resize to 140×60, then compress toward 20–50KB. Use a clean white background, not a screen photo.
html:
Exam and government application portals are strict about signatures in ways that feel arbitrary until you see the rejected upload notice. The box may demand exactly 140×60 pixels, a file between 20KB and 50KB, a plain white background and a format the portal accepts. A beautiful signature that misses one of those numbers is still rejected.

The reliable method is boring: read the notification, create a clean mark, resize to the required pixels first, then compress to the required file size. This guide walks through that order and the mistakes that cause most rejections. Make the mark in the signature maker and handle dimensions and bytes in the image compressor. For the broader workflow, see the signature maker guide.

Read the notification before you create anything

Find the official instructions for the current application cycle.
