Start with the ten pages that matter commercially, then add the supporting guides. For each source, list two to four targets and write the sentence that will carry the link. That sentence is the real work; the HTML is trivial.

For new posts, add the links before publishing, not after. For old posts, review the map quarterly and fix broken links, redirected targets and anchors that no longer describe the page. When a page is merged or retired, update every source row and redirect the old URL. A map that is not maintained becomes a list of 404s.

What to measure, and what the analyzer cannot do

Use crawl depth, orphan count and internal clicks to judge the map. Search Console's link report and a crawler can show which pages have few in-links; analytics can show whether readers follow the paths you built. Do not expect every link to earn clicks. Some exist for crawlers and for the reader who needs the next step, and a low click count is not automatically a failure.

The SEO analyzer checks on-page factors such as title, description, headings, density and links in the submitted content. It is not an internal-link crawler, so it will not discover orphan pages or draw your site graph. Pair it with a crawl for the structural view, and judge the two together.

Two fixes that change the graph

Example 1: an orphan pricing page

A 1,200-word pricing page is live and indexed, but no post links to it and it is missing from navigation. Four posts discuss plans, upgrades, costs and comparisons but never link. Add one contextual link in each: “pricing plans” from the plans post, “plan limits” from the upgrade post, “cost comparison” from the comparison post and “upgrade path” from the onboarding post. The page now has four relevant paths with four different anchors, and readers can reach it from the moment they need it.

Example 2: exact-match anchor stuffing

Twenty-two links across the blog all use “best CRM software”. The phrase is accurate for a few, awkward for most, and repetitive enough to look manipulative. Rewrite fifteen of them to match the sentence: “CRM for small teams”, “compare CRM pricing”, “CRM features” and “sales pipeline setup”. Keep the exact phrase where it genuinely fits. The link count stays the same; the context improves and the pattern stops looking automated.

Start with the 60-to-80 score rescue if the page itself is weak, and use sitemap splitting to keep large URL sets manageable. For AI citation structure, the GEO checklist shows how linked, self-contained passages help retrieval systems.

Audit the page, then map the links: run the draft through the SEO analyzer for on-page checks, then add two to four contextual links from pages that already discuss the topic. Start with the SEO publishing guide for the full sequence.

faqs.question: How many internal links should an article have?
faqs.answer: Two to four contextual body links is a practical range for most articles, not a fixed rule. A short post may need one and a long guide may justify more when each link answers a different next question. Judge by usefulness: if a reader would not want the target at that point, the link is decoration.

faqs.question: What is an orphan page?
faqs.answer: An orphan page has no internal links pointing to it, even if it appears in the sitemap. Orphans often appear after redesigns, removed categories or ad landing pages that were never added to the content plan. Find them by comparing the sitemap with a crawl's link graph, then add contextual links from pages that discuss the same topic.

faqs.question: Should I use exact-match anchor text?
faqs.answer: Use it sparingly and only when it fits the sentence naturally. Repeating one exact phrase across dozens of links looks engineered and reads poorly. Mix the page title, a close variant and a phrase from the surrounding sentence. The anchor should describe the target honestly, not repeat a keyword for its own sake.

faqs.question: Do breadcrumbs and navigation count as internal links?
faqs.answer: Yes. Breadcrumbs show hierarchy and give crawlers a consistent path, while navigation exposes core sections across the site. They are not a substitute for contextual body links, because sitewide links pass little topic-specific context. Use navigation for access and body links for relevance.

faqs.question: How do I audit internal links?
faqs.answer: Crawl the site to build a link graph, compare it with the sitemap to find orphans, and check crawl depth for important pages. Then list source URL, target URL, anchor and status in a spreadsheet. Review quarterly, fix redirects and 404s, and add links from relevant pages rather than relying on the footer.

faqs.question: Can the SEO analyzer find orphan pages?
faqs.answer: No. The SEO analyzer checks on-page factors in the content you submit, such as title, description, headings, density and links. It does not crawl your site or map the internal link graph. Use a crawler for that structural view, then use the analyzer to improve each page you decide to link.

title: Twitter/X Character Counter: What Actually Counts
description: What counts toward an X post: character weights, emoji and CJK variations, t.co link replacement, thread numbering and composer checks.
html:
A draft looks like it fits: 265 characters in the word counter, 42 words, no warnings. You paste it into X, add a link and a mention, and the composer says you are over. Nothing is broken. The word counter measures raw text; X applies its own counting rules, replaces links with a t.co URL and may give some characters more weight than others. The only reliable final check is the composer for the account you are using.

Part of the word counter guide. Draft and measure in the word counter, then verify the post in X before publishing.

What the word counter actually reports

The word counter reports characters with spaces, characters without spaces, words, sentences, paragraphs and estimated reading and speaking time. Those numbers are useful for drafting: they tell you whether a post is 180 characters or 420, and whether a thread is 600 words or 1,200. They do not calculate X's weighted length, thread numbering or link shortening.

Treat “characters with spaces” as a rough ceiling for plain English text. If the draft contains only Latin letters, digits and ordinary punctuation, the composer will often show a similar number. Once you add emoji, CJK characters, links or thread markers, the raw count and the composer can diverge. That is not a bug in either tool; they measure different things.

What X counts, and why the rules move

X counts most characters as one. Some emoji and some CJK characters can count as more than one, and the exact weighting is set by X, not by your text editor. A flag emoji, a skin-tone modifier or a character outside the Basic Latin range may consume more of the limit than its visual width suggests. Treat any “one emoji equals one character” rule as a simplification, not a guarantee.

The standard limit shown in the composer is 280 characters for most accounts at the time of writing, with different limits for some account types and features. Those rules can change. Do not hard-code a limit into a template or a social preview tool and assume it will stay correct. Check X's current help page and the composer for your account before a campaign that depends on a precise count.

Links are replaced, not counted as typed

X replaces links with a fixed-length t.co link. The raw URL in your draft is not what the composer counts, so a long UTM-tagged URL may cost less than its character count suggests, and a short link may still be wrapped. The replacement length is set by X and can change, so the only safe method is to paste the final URL into the composer and read the remaining count.

This matters for threads and replies. A link that fits in a standalone post may push a reply over the limit when combined with numbering and a mention. Build the post with the final link in place, then decide whether the link belongs in the first post, a reply or a follow-up. Shortening a URL for display can help readability, but it does not guarantee a particular counted length.

Link placement also changes the reading experience. A post that ends with a bare URL reads like an afterthought; a post that names the destination before the link gives people a reason to tap. If the link is essential, put it in the first post and keep the thread's promise visible. If it is supplementary, move it to a reply so the main post can stay short. The composer count follows the link wherever it goes, so decide placement before you finalize the numbering.

Threads, numbering and per-post limits

Thread numbering consumes characters in every post: “1/8”, “2/8” and so on. The word counter sees those characters as part of the draft, but it does not split the draft into posts or reserve room for the next number. If you write a 1,400-character thread, you still need to know how it divides at the composer's limit, not at the whole-draft total.

Plan the thread before drafting. Decide the number of posts, reserve space for the numbering and any link, then write each post to fit. A common workflow is to draft the thread in one document, split it into per-post blocks, count each block separately, and paste each one into the composer. Do not trust an auto-threader to preserve meaning or numbering; review the result post by post.

Hashtags and mentions count as typed. A mention such as @brand consumes characters in the post where it appears, and a hashtag consumes its letters and the hash. Neither is weighted like a link. Keep one or two hashtags, place the mention only where it is needed, and count the final text rather than the draft without them.

A manual counting workflow

  1. Draft without counting. Write the idea first; stopping every sentence to check a meter produces choppy posts.
  2. Measure the raw draft. Paste it into the word counter for characters and words. Use the with-spaces count as a rough ceiling, not a verdict.
  3. Split threads into posts. Number each post and count each block separately. Add a buffer for links, mentions and edits.
  4. Paste into the composer. Add the final link and any media. Read the remaining-character indicator for your account.
  5. Cut, do not cram. Remove a clause, move a detail to a reply or drop a hashtag. If the count still fails, the post is carrying too much.

Two posts measured

Example 1: a plain English post

A 38-word post has 240 characters including spaces and 203 without spaces. With only Latin letters, digits and periods, the composer will usually show a number close to 240. That leaves room under a 280-character limit for most accounts, but not enough for a long link and a mention. Paste the final version with the link before assuming it fits; the t.co replacement and the mention both change the count.

Example 2: a thread with weights

A six-post thread totals 1,500 characters in the word counter, with numbering and one link in the final post. The average is 250 characters per post, but averages hide the problem: one post contains a block of CJK text and an emoji, and the composer counts it higher than the raw text. Another post carries the link and the numbering. Count each post in the composer, keep a 20–30 character buffer, and rewrite the heavy post instead of trimming words at random.

ElementWord counterX composerWhat to do
Plain Latin textCounts each characterUsually counts each character as oneUse the raw count as a starting estimate
SpacesIncluded in the with-spaces countCountedDo not budget from the no-spaces number
EmojiCounts Unicode charactersSome count as more than oneVerify every emoji-heavy post in the composer
CJK charactersCounts each characterSome carry extra weightCheck the composer for the account
LinksCounts the full URLReplaced by a fixed-length t.co linkPaste the final URL before judging the count
Thread numberingCounts the charactersCounts them in each postReserve space per post, not for the thread total
Premium or other limitsNo special handlingAccount-dependentRead the composer for your plan

If the post is part of a longer article, the summarizing guide helps compress the source without losing the point, and grammar check before publish catches the errors that survive a character limit. The word counting guide explains the raw metrics in more detail.

Measure the draft, then verify in X: paste the text into the word counter for characters and words, split threads into posts, and check the final version in the composer. For the full set of text metrics, start with the word counter guide.

faqs.question: Does the word counter show the X character limit?
faqs.answer: No. The word counter shows raw characters with and without spaces, words, sentences, paragraphs and reading time. It does not apply X's character weights, thread numbering or t.co link replacement. Use it to size the draft, then read the remaining-character indicator in the X composer before publishing.

faqs.question: Do spaces count toward an X post?
faqs.answer: Yes, spaces count. The word counter shows them in the with-spaces figure, so budget from that number rather than the no-spaces total. For plain Latin text the composer usually matches the raw count closely, but links, emoji and thread markers can still change the result. Verify the final draft in the composer.

faqs.question: How do links count in an X post?
faqs.answer: X replaces links with a fixed-length t.co link, so the raw URL length is not what the composer counts. The replacement length is set by X and can change, which means you should paste the final URL into the composer instead of estimating. A long tracking URL may cost less than its raw count suggests.

faqs.question: Do emoji count as one character?
faqs.answer: Not always. Some emoji and some CJK characters can count as more than one, and the weighting is controlled by X. A flag or a skin-tone modifier may consume more of the limit than its visual width suggests. Treat one-emoji-one-character as a simplification and verify emoji-heavy posts in the composer.

faqs.question: How do I count characters in a thread?
faqs.answer: Count each post separately, not the whole thread total. Thread numbering such as 1/8 consumes characters in every post, and links or mentions may appear in only one. Draft the thread in one document, split it into blocks, add numbering to each block and check each block in the composer with a small buffer.

faqs.question: Is the X limit always 280 characters?
faqs.answer: Most accounts see a 280-character composer limit at the time of writing, but X can change limits and offers different limits for some account types and features. Do not treat any number as permanent. Check X's current help page and the composer for the account you are posting from before a campaign that depends on an exact count.

title: Pages per 1,000 Words: Formatting and Examples
description: How many pages 1,000 words takes: 250-300 words per double-spaced page, about 500 single-spaced, with font, margins and paragraph effects.
html:
A 1,000-word essay is often about 3.5 to 4 double-spaced pages. A 1,000-word report is about two single-spaced pages. Both statements are useful, and both are wrong without the formatting assumptions behind them. Page count depends on font, size, line spacing, margins, headings, paragraph spacing and bullet lists. The word count stays fixed; the pages move around it.

Part of the word counter guide. Measure the draft in the word counter, then check the page count in the document or PDF export.

Why page counts vary so much

A page is a physical container. Words are content. Change the container and the same content occupies more or fewer pages. A 12-point font with double spacing and one-inch margins holds far fewer words than an 11-point font with single spacing and narrow margins. Headings, blank lines between paragraphs, tables, images and bullet lists all consume vertical space that could have held text.

This is why “1,000 words equals four pages” is a planning heuristic, not a conversion factor. It describes a common academic manuscript format. It does not describe a business report, a newsletter, a screenplay or a web page. Always state the format when you quote a page count, and always check the actual document before submitting to a page limit.

The ranges also assume continuous body text. A title page, table of contents, figures, tables or appendices can extend a document well beyond the body estimate. Count only the sections the brief includes, and note in your style sheet whether front matter and back matter belong in the page limit.

The reference page: 12pt Times New Roman, double-spaced

The reference format for most page-count advice is a Word document with 12-point Times New Roman, double spacing, one-inch margins and 8.5-by-11-inch Letter paper. In that format, a full page of body text often runs about 250 to 300 words. At that density, 1,000 words is roughly 3.3 to 4 pages before headings, title blocks or a reference list.

Single-spaced 12-point Times New Roman holds about 500 words per page, so 1,000 words is roughly two pages. These are planning ranges, not exact counts. A page with many short paragraphs wastes space at the end of each paragraph; a page with long paragraphs uses more of the width. A heading near the top pushes body text down. A table can replace 200 words with a block that takes half a page.

Words per page by format

The table below gives practical ranges for common formats. Use the middle of the range for planning, then verify with the actual template.

FormatPlanning words per page1,000 words is aboutNotes
12pt Times New Roman, double-spaced, 1-inch margins250–3003.3–4 pagesThe standard academic manuscript range
12pt Times New Roman, single-spaced, 1-inch marginsAbout 500About 2 pagesDense body text with few headings
11pt Calibri, single-spaced, 1-inch margins450–5501.8–2.2 pagesCommon office report format
12pt Times New Roman, double-spaced, 1.25-inch margins220–2703.7–4.5 pagesWider margins reduce words per page
12pt font, 1.5 spacing, 1-inch margins330–4002.5–3 pagesBetween single and double spacing

Font, spacing, margins and furniture

Font choice changes density through character width and x-height. Times New Roman is relatively compact; Arial is wider at the same point size, and Calibri sits between the two depending on size. A 12-point Arial page holds fewer words than a 12-point Times New Roman page. Line spacing is the bigger lever: double spacing roughly halves the words per page compared with single spacing. Margins matter next; moving from one-inch to 1.25-inch margins removes roughly 8 percent of the text width.

Headings, paragraph spacing and lists add white space. A document with a heading every 150 words and a blank line between paragraphs will run longer than a wall of body text at the same word count. Tables and images can consume a full page with almost no words. If a page limit is strict, count the pages in the final format, not from a words-per-page average.

Paragraph style is a smaller but real variable. Indented first lines with no blank line between paragraphs pack more text onto a page than block paragraphs separated by a full blank line. Word processors also apply widow and orphan control, which can push a short paragraph to the next page and leave white space behind. Those settings are invisible in a word count, which is why the PDF page count is the final authority.

Two concrete examples

Example 1: a double-spaced academic essay

A 1,000-word essay in 12-point Times New Roman, double-spaced, with one-inch margins and a title block runs about 3.5 to 4 pages. Add a heading and a reference list and the document may reach 4.5 to 5 pages, even though the body still contains 1,000 words. Most academic word limits exclude the reference list, so check the rubric before trimming the argument to fit a page count.

Example 2: a single-spaced business report

A 1,000-word report in 11-point Calibri, single-spaced, with headings and bullet lists runs about 2 to 2.5 pages. Switch to 1.15 spacing and the same content may reach 2.5 to 3 pages. Add a title page and a table and it can pass 3 pages. The words did not change; the formatting and furniture did.

Turn page limits into word targets

Convert page limits to word targets with the range for your format. Five double-spaced pages at 250 to 300 words per page is roughly 1,250 to 1,500 words. Ten pages is roughly 2,500 to 3,000 words. Five single-spaced pages at about 500 words per page is roughly 2,500 words. Treat the result as a target band, then verify in the actual document.

Build a style sheet for recurring formats: font, size, spacing, margins, heading styles and whether the title page or references count. That sheet turns a vague page limit into a repeatable word target. For blog posts, page count matters less than scroll depth and readability; the blog length guide covers intent-based ranges, and the word counter reports reading time alongside words.

Paper size matters too. A4 is narrower and taller than US Letter, so the same margins and font can produce a different words-per-page count. If you are submitting across borders, confirm the required paper size before you convert a page limit into words. A document that fits four Letter pages may spill onto a fifth A4 page, or the reverse, without a single word changing.

Check the document in its final format

  1. Set the format first. Choose font, size, spacing and margins before writing, not after.
  2. Draft to a word target. Use the range for your format, then paste the draft into the word counter to confirm the count.
  3. Export to PDF. Page count in the editor can differ from the printed or submitted version, especially with tables and images.
  4. Check the pages that count. Confirm whether the title page, references and appendices are included in the limit.
  5. Adjust content or format, not filler. If the document is short, add evidence or examples. If it is long, cut repetition before shrinking the font.

For a broader view of length, the intent-based length guide explains why word counts are heuristics, and how to count words online covers the raw metrics. Readability is a separate question; the Flesch score guide explains why a page that fits can still be hard to read.

Count the words, then count the pages: paste the draft into the word counter for an exact word count, export the document in its final format, and compare the page count. Start with the word counter guide for the full method.

faqs.question: How many pages is 1,000 words?
faqs.answer: About four pages in 12-point Times New Roman, double-spaced, with one-inch margins, where a page often holds 250 to 300 words. Single-spaced, the same 1,000 words is about two pages. Font, size, spacing, margins, headings and paragraphing move the result, so treat these as planning ranges and check the actual document.

faqs.question: How many words are on a double-spaced page?
faqs.answer: A double-spaced page in 12-point Times New Roman with one-inch margins often holds about 250 to 300 words. Wider margins or larger fonts reduce that range; narrower margins or tighter paragraph spacing increase it. A page with headings, tables or images holds fewer words because those elements consume vertical space.

faqs.question: How many pages is 1,000 words single-spaced?
faqs.answer: About two pages in 12-point Times New Roman with one-inch margins, where a full page often holds about 500 words. An 11-point Calibri document may run slightly shorter, while 1.15 spacing or larger headings may push the count toward 2.5 pages. Verify in the final template rather than relying on the average.

faqs.question: Does font choice change the page count?
faqs.answer: Yes. Times New Roman is compact, while Arial and Calibri are wider at the same point size, so a 12-point page holds fewer words in the wider fonts. Line spacing and margins usually change the count more than the typeface alone. If a page limit is strict, set the font and spacing before drafting and check the export.

faqs.question: How do I convert a page limit into a word count?
faqs.answer: Multiply the page limit by the planning range for your format. Five double-spaced pages at 250 to 300 words per page is roughly 1,250 to 1,500 words; ten pages is roughly 2,500 to 3,000. Confirm whether the title page, references and appendices count, then verify the final document in its submitted format.

faqs.question: Why is my 1,000-word document five pages?
faqs.answer: Formatting is the likely cause: double spacing, wide margins, a large font, frequent headings, blank lines between paragraphs or a title page can push 1,000 words past four pages. Tables and images also consume space. Count the pages in the final PDF and check whether the limit includes the title page and references.

title: Format XML for Sitemaps, Feeds and Configs
description: Format XML sitemaps, feeds and config files, see how local parsing and minification work, and catch malformed markup before publishing.
html:
XML still carries sitemaps, RSS and Atom feeds, SVG files, SOAP payloads and a long tail of configuration formats. A single unclosed tag or unquoted attribute stops the whole document from parsing, and the failure often surfaces far from the mistake. A formatter gives you two things at once: a well-formedness check and an indented view of the hierarchy. This guide explains what the local XML formatter actually does, where its tokenizer can distort unusual markup, and how to prepare a sitemap or feed for publication.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. The tool runs entirely in the page, so internal config files never leave the machine. That privacy is useful, but it also means the tool has no schema service behind it: well-formed is not the same as valid against your XSD or business rules.

What the formatter checks

The input is parsed with the browser's DOMParser using the application/xml type. If the parser reports an error, the tool shows a generic invalid-XML message and refuses to produce partial output. Failing closed matters because a half-formatted document can look plausible while hiding the exact tag that broke. The input limit is 500,000 characters, close to 500 KB; anything larger is rejected before parsing.

This is a well-formedness check, not schema validation. The parser confirms that tags close, attributes are quoted, entities resolve and there is a single document element. It does not know whether a sitemap contains the required namespace, whether an RSS item has the fields your reader expects, or whether an order element follows your XSD. Those checks need a schema-aware validator or the receiving service.

The error message does not include a line and column number. If you need the exact location, open the file in an editor with XML support or check the browser console for the parser's own diagnostic. The value of the tool is the fast pass or fail and a readable tree once the document is accepted.

What changes when you press Format

Formatting is line-oriented. The serializer first normalizes the document, then a small tokenizer walks opening tags, closing tags, declarations, comments and text. Each opening tag increases the indent by two spaces, each closing tag decreases it, and self-closing tags stay on one line. The result is easy to scan:

<rss>
  <channel>
    <title>Example</title>
    <link>https://example.com/</link>
  </channel>
</rss>

Attributes are not reformatted or wrapped. A long attribute list stays on the element's line, which is fine for IDs and namespaces but unhelpful for dozens of attributes. Indentation is cosmetic; it does not add namespace declarations or repair missing closing tags.

Two edge cases deserve attention. Text nodes are trimmed, so mixed content such as <p>Hello <b>world</b></p> loses the space before the inline element when it is placed on its own line. Do not use the pretty output for XML where whitespace inside text is significant. Second, the tokenizer looks for the next > character, so an attribute value containing a literal greater-than sign can be split incorrectly. XML permits > in a quoted attribute, although escaping it is safer. Minify mode is the better choice for such documents.

CDATA sections can also confuse the line tokenizer when they contain > or look like tags. If a document uses CDATA for embedded HTML or SQL, format a copy and compare the text content before and after. For configuration files and sitemaps without CDATA, the output is predictable.

Minify mode and signed documents

Minify serializes the parsed document and collapses whitespace between adjacent tags with a simple replacement. It does not remove comments, change attribute order or rewrite namespaces. Elements that already sit next to each other stay unchanged, so the saving depends on how much indentation the source contains. A sitemap that is already machine-generated may shrink very little.

Never minify a document covered by an XML signature. XML digital signatures can include whitespace in the signed byte stream, and changing indentation or inter-tag spaces invalidates the signature even though the logical tree is identical. The same caution applies to files compared by checksum in a deployment pipeline. Keep the canonical byte-for-byte copy and use the formatter only on a scratch copy.

Minified output is still well-formed XML and is acceptable for sitemaps and feeds. Search engines do not require pretty indentation. What they require is a successful parse, the correct namespace and content that follows the sitemap protocol.

Sitemaps, feeds and namespaces

A sitemap is a small XML document with a specific namespace, a set of <url> entries and optional metadata. The formatter preserves namespace prefixes because the serializer keeps qualified names. After formatting, check that the root still declares the sitemap namespace and that every URL is absolute. The tool cannot check either condition for you. A sitemap may parse cleanly while pointing at relative paths that crawlers ignore.

Feed files have the same shape of risk. RSS and Atom are XML, so an unescaped ampersand in a title or a raw HTML fragment in a description will break the feed. Encode the text, or wrap markup in CDATA, then validate. If the feed is generated by a CMS, compare the generated file with a known-good sample rather than editing only the pretty output.

Sitemap protocol limits are separate from the parser. A single sitemap file is capped at 50,000 URLs and 50 MB uncompressed. Large sites should split into a sitemap index. None of that is enforced here; formatting a 60,000-URL file will succeed even though the file violates the protocol. Check the limits before submitting.

Where the tool stops

TaskSupported hereUse instead
Well-formednessYes, via the browser XML parserNothing else needed for a quick check
XSD or Relax NG validationNoA schema validator in your build or CI
Line and column errorsNoAn XML-aware editor or the browser console
Large documentsUp to 500,000 charactersSplit the file or use a command-line tool
Mixed content whitespaceTrimmed during pretty printKeep the source or use minify carefully
CDATA with angle bracketsCan be tokenized incorrectlyCompare content, or avoid pretty printing
Signed XMLNo signature awarenessKeep the canonical bytes untouched

The 500,000-character limit is a UI guard, not a statement about what XML can contain. Command-line parsers handle much larger files. If a sitemap is too large for the page, it is also a signal to split it, which is better for crawling and for error isolation.

A practical workflow

  1. Keep the original file in version control or a backup folder before pasting it anywhere.
  2. Format a copy first. If the tool rejects it, fix the first structural error and retry rather than rewriting the whole document.
  3. Inspect namespaces, the root element and the first few records after formatting.
  4. Check text values for accidental trimming, especially in mixed-content documents.
  5. Minify only if the receiving system benefits and the file is not signed or checksummed.
  6. Validate the final file against the protocol or schema that actually governs it before publishing.

A clean parse is necessary but not sufficient. For a sitemap, the next checks are URL count, absolute links, encoding and robots rules. For a feed, test in a reader and confirm that dates, GUIDs and enclosures survive. For a config file, deploy to staging and compare the parsed settings with the source of truth.

Check XML now: paste a sitemap, feed or config into the XML formatter, fix any parse failure, then copy the indented or minified result. For JSON payloads, use the JSON parse error guide; for form-encoded values, see URL encoding.

faqs.question: Does the XML formatter validate against a schema?
faqs.answer: No. It checks well-formedness with the browser XML parser. It can confirm that tags close and attributes are quoted, but it has no XSD, Relax NG or sitemap protocol knowledge. Use a schema validator or the receiving service for those checks.

faqs.question: Why is there no line number on the error?
faqs.answer: The page reports a generic parse failure and withholds output. Browsers expose richer parser diagnostics in the console, and desktop editors show line and column positions. If you need the exact location, open the source in one of those tools and compare the first broken element.

faqs.question: Can I minify a signed XML document?
faqs.answer: Do not. XML signatures can cover whitespace in the byte stream, so collapsing indentation can invalidate the signature even when the element tree is unchanged. Keep the signed copy untouched and format a separate working copy only.

faqs.question: Why did formatting change spaces in my text?
faqs.answer: Pretty printing trims text nodes and places them on their own lines. That is harmless for element-only data such as sitemaps, but it changes mixed content where a space between text and an inline element matters. Avoid pretty printing those documents or compare the text content before and after.

faqs.question: Is my XML uploaded anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. Parsing and serialization happen in the page. The tradeoff is that the tool cannot validate against a remote schema or call a server-side parser. Keep sensitive configuration files on a trusted machine and review the output before copying it into a deployment.

title: HTML Entities: Encode and Decode Without Breaking Markup
description: Learn when to escape ampersands, angle brackets and quotes, decode named or numeric entities, and avoid double-escaping in templates.
html:
An HTML entity is a short sequence that represents a character the parser would otherwise treat as markup. The ampersand starts an entity, the less-than sign starts a tag, and a quote can end an attribute. Encode the wrong one and a page shows raw code; encode twice and visitors see & in the middle of a sentence. This guide covers the rules, the exact behavior of the local HTML entities tool, and the contexts where HTML escaping is the wrong layer entirely.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. The tool handles text-level escaping in the page. It is not a template engine, a URL encoder or a JavaScript string escaper, and it does not know where the result will be inserted.

When escaping matters

In HTML text content, two characters are mandatory: & becomes & and < becomes <. The greater-than sign does not have to be escaped in text, but escaping it avoids confusion around sequences such as ]]>. In an attribute value, the quote that delimits the attribute must also be escaped. A double-quoted attribute needs "; a single-quoted attribute needs ' or '.

That distinction explains a common mistake. People paste text containing " and ' into an HTML encoder, see the quotes unchanged, and assume the tool is broken. It is not. In a text node, quotes need no escaping at all. The encoder is doing exactly what the browser's serializer does for text. If you are building an attribute string by hand, you need a different step that knows the delimiter.

There are also contexts where HTML entities do nothing useful. Inside a URL query value, a space must be percent-encoded, not turned into  . Inside a JavaScript string, a quote needs a backslash, not an entity, unless the string is itself inside an HTML attribute and the whole thing is decoded before the script runs. Inside JSON, entities are just text and should not be introduced. Match the escaping to the parser that will read the value next.

What the encoder and decoder actually do

Encode reads the input as text and serializes it back as HTML. In practice that means &, < and > are escaped, a non-breaking space becomes  , and ordinary punctuation and accented letters stay as they are. Quotes are not escaped because they are not special in a text node. The tool accepts up to 1,000,000 characters and reports an error above that limit.

Decode does the reverse: it parses the input as HTML fragment content and returns the text value. Named entities such as ©, decimal references such as © and hexadecimal references such as © all become the corresponding character. An unknown entity such as &unknown; is left as literal text by the browser rather than causing an error, so a successful decode does not prove that every entity was valid.

Neither direction is a sanitizer. Encoding makes text safe for display, but decoding an untrusted string and inserting the result with innerHTML would reintroduce markup. The tool returns text; where you put it is still your responsibility. Use textContent for plain text insertion, and a maintained sanitizer if you genuinely need to allow a subset of HTML.

Named, decimal and hexadecimal references

Named entities are easier to read, numeric references are more predictable across old documents.   is U+00A0, a non-breaking space that prevents a line break but is not an ordinary space for searching or wrapping. Replacing every space with it produces text that cannot wrap naturally. © is ©, — is an em dash, and ’ is a right single quotation mark. HTML5 recognizes a large set of names; XML without a DTD recognizes only a handful, which is why numeric references are safer in XML.

Names are case-sensitive. & and & both decode to an ampersand, but &Amp; is not recognized, and a missing semicolon can change how the parser consumes the following characters. Browsers are lenient with some legacy forms, but email clients and XML parsers are not. Always include the semicolon and prefer lowercase names from the HTML standard.

Hexadecimal references are useful for characters you cannot easily type. 😀 is a grinning face emoji, and ' is an apostrophe. Supplementary-plane characters can also be written as surrogate pairs, but a single code point reference is cleaner. Keep the x lowercase or uppercase consistently; both parse, but a style checker will thank you.

The attribute problem

Suppose you have a title and want to place it in title="...". If the title contains a double quote, the encoder leaves it alone because it treats the input as text. The attribute then ends early and the rest of the title becomes stray attributes. The correct workflow is to replace & first, then the delimiter quote, then the less-than sign if your framework requires it. Order matters: replacing & last would double-escape the ampersands introduced by the other replacements.

If you control the template, let the framework do this work. React, Vue, Svelte and server-side template engines escape interpolated values according to context. Raw HTML helpers exist precisely because escaping is context-sensitive. Hand-encoding a string and then passing it to a helper that escapes again is how visible entities end up on the page.

The same warning applies to URLs. An ampersand separating query parameters must become & in an HTML attribute, but the parameter values themselves need percent-encoding before that. Two layers, two encoders. The URL encoding guide covers the percent-encoding layer; this tool covers the HTML layer.

Recognizing double escaping

If a page displays &, the source probably contains &amp; or the value was encoded twice. If it displays <div> where a tag was intended, the content was encoded for display and then inserted as markup, or encoded before a template escaped it again. Decode once in a scratch copy and compare with the source of truth. Do not decode directly in a production database or CMS field unless you have a backup.

Round-tripping is a useful test. Encode a sample, decode the result, and compare it with the original. For plain text without non-breaking spaces, the result should match. If it does not, look for a second encoding step, a sanitizer that rewrote entities, or a rich-text editor that normalized the markup on save.

Email templates are a frequent offender. A marketing platform may escape merge tags, then an email client may decode them differently. Test the final received message, not just the preview in the editor. Transactional email should keep entities simple and avoid relying on named entities that older clients might not recognize.

A safe encode or decode checklist

  1. Identify the destination context: text node, attribute, URL, script or JSON.
  2. Use this tool only for HTML text. Use percent-encoding for URLs and a language-specific escaper for scripts.
  3. Encode a copy and paste the result into the smallest possible test page.
  4. Check quotes, ampersands and non-breaking spaces specifically; they are the usual suspects.
  5. Decode a sample back and compare it with the original before saving.
  6. Let the template engine handle dynamic values instead of pre-encoding them.
InputEncoded textNote
Tom & JerryTom & JerryThe ampersand is mandatory
<div><div>Shows markup as text
"quoted""quoted"Quotes stay in a text node
10 kg10 kgNon-breaking space is preserved
©© decoded to ©Named entity becomes a character
Encode or decode a snippet: paste it into the HTML entities tool, check the output in context, then copy it. For structured payloads, start with the JSON parse error guide.

faqs.question: Why does the encoder leave my quotes alone?
faqs.answer: Because quotes are not special in an HTML text node. The tool serializes the input as text, so only characters that would start markup or an entity are escaped. If the value will sit inside a quoted attribute, you must escape the delimiter quote separately.

faqs.question: Does decoding an unknown entity fail?
faqs.answer: No. Browsers leave an unrecognized named entity as literal text instead of raising an error. The decoder follows that behavior, so a clean-looking result can still contain a typo. Check unusual names against the HTML standard if the output looks wrong.

faqs.question: Is a non-breaking space the same as a normal space?
faqs.answer: No. A non-breaking space is U+00A0 and suppresses a line break at that point. Search, wrapping and string comparison can treat it differently from U+0020. Use it deliberately for units and labels, not as a replacement for every space.

faqs.question: Can I use the encoded output in an attribute?
faqs.answer: Only if you also escape the quote that delimits the attribute. The text encoder does not know the surrounding syntax. For attribute values, use a context-aware template helper or escape the matching quote before inserting the value.

faqs.question: Is decoding HTML entities safe for untrusted content?
faqs.answer: Decoding itself is just text conversion, but inserting the decoded result as HTML can reintroduce scripts and event handlers. Use textContent for plain text. If you need to allow markup, pass it through a maintained sanitizer rather than decoding and trusting it.

title: URL Slugs: Rules for Readable, Stable Links
description: Turn titles into clean URL slugs, understand transliteration and separator choices, and keep links stable after publication.
html:
A slug is the readable part of a URL that identifies a page: the url-slug-rules in /blog/json-formatter-guide/url-slug-rules. It is not a ranking trick, and it is not a place to repeat every keyword. It is a stable, human-readable address that should still make sense when the campaign, the season or the product name changes. The local slug generator handles the mechanical part, but the decisions that matter happen before and after the conversion.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. The tool turns one title per line into one slug per line, using either hyphens or underscores. It does not check whether a slug is already taken, whether it is too long, or whether the page will still exist next year.

What a slug does, and does not do

A good slug tells a person what the destination contains before they click. It also gives the page a stable identifier that can be shared, linked and printed. Search engines use the words in a URL as a weak relevance signal, but the page title, headings and content do far more work. Repeating a keyword five times in a slug looks spammy and makes the link harder to read.

The most important property is stability. Every change to a published slug breaks inbound links unless you add a redirect. A date in the slug becomes wrong when the article is updated. A campaign name becomes embarrassing when the campaign ends. A product code is stable only while the product exists. Choose the shortest phrase that describes the page's lasting topic, then leave it alone.

Slugs are also case-sensitive on many servers. Lowercase is the convention because it avoids duplicate URLs that differ only by capitalization. A URL ending in /Guide and one ending in /guide may resolve to the same page or may not, depending on the host. Pick lowercase and enforce it in the CMS.

The exact rules used by the generator

The generator normalizes each line with Unicode NFKD, removes combining marks in the U+0300 to U+036F range, lowercases the result, trims it and replaces every run of characters outside a-z and 0-9 with the chosen separator. Leading and trailing separators are removed. Empty lines are dropped, and the output keeps one slug per line.

The practical consequences are worth spelling out. Accented Latin letters usually survive as their base letters: Café becomes cafe. Punctuation, apostrophes, ampersands and emoji become separators, not deletions, so Tom & Jerry becomes tom-jerry rather than tomjerry. Consecutive punctuation collapses to one separator. A title written entirely in a non-Latin script may become empty because the tool does not transliterate Cyrillic, Arabic, Devanagari or CJK characters. Those titles need a manual slug.

The generator does not remove stopwords. How to Use the Tool becomes how-to-use-the-tool, including to and the. It does not enforce a maximum length, does not add a date, does not check for duplicates across pages and does not verify that the slug is unique within the current site. Those checks belong in your publishing workflow.

Example: Café déjà vu: 10 Tips & Tricks! becomes cafe-deja-vu-10-tips-tricks with hyphens. With underscores selected, it becomes cafe_deja_vu_10_tips_tricks. Both are valid URL path segments, but hyphens are the common convention for web pages and are treated as word separators by search engines.

SEO choices that the converter cannot make

Start with the primary topic, not the site name. /blog/url-slug-rules tells the reader more than /blog/tool4saas-post-2026-10-23. Remove filler words only when the result still reads naturally; a slug of three generic words may be shorter but less useful. Put the most specific noun near the front, because it survives when a link is truncated in a chat app or a search result.

Avoid changing slugs after launch. If a change is unavoidable, keep a permanent redirect from the old URL and update internal links. Redirect chains should be one hop, not five. If the page is substantially new content rather than a rename, create a new URL and leave the old page in place with a link to the successor.

Do not stuff synonyms into the slug. Pick the phrase people would use when describing the page, then use the title and body to cover related language. A slug like best-cheap-fast-reliable-tool-online-free reads like an advertisement and dates quickly. A slug like compare-json-formatters describes a durable comparison.

Canonical URLs and language versions add another layer. If the same page exists in several languages, keep the slug in the page's language where possible and use hreflang to connect the versions. If you transliterate a title for a Latin-script URL, do it once and document the mapping so future editors do not produce a second slug for the same page.

Unicode, accents and non-Latin titles

Unicode normalization matters because the same visual character can have more than one byte representation. NFKD splits accented letters into a base letter and a combining mark, and the generator then removes the mark. That is why é becomes e. It also means a character that has no canonical decomposition may disappear or become a separator. Always inspect the output for names and brands that use diacritics.

Non-Latin scripts require a decision. You can keep the original script in the URL, percent-encoded by the browser, or transliterate it into Latin characters. Keeping the original is more faithful but produces long, unreadable percent-encoded strings when copied. Transliteration improves readability but can be inconsistent, especially for names. Either way, do not let an automatic converter silently produce an empty slug; check it.

Symbols such as +, & and # have special meanings in URLs. The generator replaces them with separators, which is safer than leaving them raw. A literal # in a path would start a fragment; a literal ? would start a query. Replacing them avoids a whole class of broken links.

Bulk generation without creating a mess

Paste one working title per line, choose a separator, generate, then treat the output as a draft. Before publishing, check the list for duplicates, empty results, accidental dates and slugs that are too generic. Add a numeric suffix only when two pages genuinely need the same phrase, and make the suffix meaningful if possible.

Keep a small redirect map when migrating an existing site. A spreadsheet with old URL, new URL and status is enough for most teams. After the migration, crawl the site and check that internal links point to the new versions rather than bouncing through redirects. A redirect that works is still slower than a direct link.

TitleGenerated slugReview note
10 Tips for Faster JSON Parsing10-tips-for-faster-json-parsingClear and durable
Café déjà vu: 10 Tips & Tricks!cafe-deja-vu-10-tips-tricksAccents folded, symbols replaced
2026 Q4 Sale2026-q4-saleDate will age; keep only for a permanent archive
工具使用指南emptyNeeds manual transliteration
How to Use the Toolhow-to-use-the-toolStopwords are not removed

Before you publish

  1. Read the slug aloud. If it is awkward to say, it is awkward to share.
  2. Remove dates, campaign names and version numbers unless the page is explicitly archival.
  3. Check for duplicates in the CMS, including drafts and localized versions.
  4. Keep it lowercase and use one separator consistently across the site.
  5. Add a redirect before changing any slug that has already been indexed or shared.
  6. Update internal links so they point to the final URL directly.
Generate a batch now: paste your titles into the slug generator, choose hyphens, then review the list by hand. For the surrounding URL workflow, read URL encoding and the developer toolkit guide.

faqs.question: Does the slug generator remove stopwords?
faqs.answer: No. It keeps words such as to, the and for. You can delete them by hand after generating, but check that the remaining phrase still reads naturally. For short titles, keeping a stopword is often clearer than producing a three-word fragment.

faqs.question: What happens to Chinese or Arabic titles?
faqs.answer: The tool strips characters outside a-z and 0-9, so a title written only in a non-Latin script can produce an empty line. It does not transliterate. Write a Latin-script slug manually or use a transliteration service, then verify the result with a native speaker.

faqs.question: Should I use hyphens or underscores?
faqs.answer: Hyphens are the usual choice for page URLs and are treated as word separators by search engines. Underscores are common in some analytics and file naming conventions. Pick one and keep it consistent; the bigger risk is changing published URLs later.

faqs.question: Can I change a slug after publishing?
faqs.answer: You can, but add a permanent redirect from the old URL and update internal links in the same release. Repeated changes create redirect chains and dilute the value of inbound links. If the content is substantially different, publish a new page instead of renaming the old one.

faqs.question: Does the tool check for duplicate slugs?
faqs.answer: No. It converts each line independently and does not know what already exists on the site. Duplicate detection belongs in the CMS or a pre-publish script. Two pages with the same slug will collide on most static hosts.

title: MIME Types: What Content-Type Actually Controls
description: Look up common file extensions and MIME types, understand Content-Type headers, and fix the misconfigurations that break assets.
html:
A file extension is a naming convention. A MIME type is a declaration that tells the browser or the server how to interpret the bytes. When a stylesheet loads as text/plain, the browser may refuse to apply it. When an API response is labeled text/html, a fetch call can parse it as text or reject it. Most of the time the mapping is automatic, which is why the failures feel mysterious when it is not.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. Use the local MIME type lookup to move between common extensions and their registered types, then read the caveats below before treating the result as a server configuration.

What a MIME type actually contains

A MIME type has a top-level type and a subtype, separated by a slash: text/html, image/svg+xml, application/json. It can carry parameters such as charset=utf-8 or a multipart boundary. The Content-Type header on an HTTP response is the server's statement about the body. A <meta charset> tag or an HTML attribute can influence parsing, but the header usually wins for the initial response.

Type names are case-insensitive, although lowercase is conventional. The subtype can carry a structured-syntax suffix, as in application/ld+json or image/svg+xml. That suffix signals a structured syntax rather than a different top-level category. A server that does not recognize a suffix may still serve it correctly if the client understands the base type.

There is no universal registry lookup in the browser. The operating system, the web server, the framework and the CDN each carry their own table. That is why a file can have the right extension and still arrive with the wrong header. Diagnose the header, not just the file name.

How the lookup tool behaves

The tool contains a small built-in table of 44 common extensions and their types. It accepts an extension with or without a leading dot, lowercases the input and returns both sides of the mapping. It also accepts a MIME type and searches for the first matching extension. For example, json and .json both return application/json, while application/json returns .json.

Reverse lookup is not one-to-one. image/jpeg maps to both jpg and jpeg; the tool returns the first entry it encounters, which is jpg. text/javascript maps to js and mjs, and returns js. If you need a specific extension, use the extension-to-type direction instead of assuming the reverse is unique.

The table covers documents, images, audio, video, archives, fonts and a few application formats. It does not include every registered type, vendor-specific types, parameters such as charset, or structured suffixes beyond the ones in the table. An unknown value returns an informational no-match message. That is a limitation, not a statement that the type is invalid.

ExtensionTypeTypical use
.htmltext/htmlHTML documents
.csstext/cssStylesheets
.jstext/javascriptClassic and module scripts
.jsonapplication/jsonStructured API data
.svgimage/svg+xmlVector images, also executable in some contexts
.woff2font/woff2Web fonts
.webpimage/webpCompressed images
.wasmapplication/wasmWebAssembly modules

Serving assets with the right type

Static hosts usually infer the type from the extension. Dynamic frameworks may set it from a route handler or a file response helper. The failures cluster around a few patterns. A JavaScript module served as text/plain is blocked because module scripts require a JavaScript type. A CSS file served as text/html is ignored under strict MIME checking. A JSON endpoint served as text/html can still be read as text, but a client that expects JSON may parse it differently or reject it.

Fonts are another common case. A font served with the wrong type may fail to load, and a cross-origin font request also needs the right CORS headers. The MIME type alone does not grant permission. Check both the Content-Type and Access-Control-Allow-Origin values when a font or module fails only on a different origin.

SVG deserves separate treatment. It is an image type, but an SVG file is also XML and can contain scripts and external references. Served as image/svg+xml and loaded through <img>, scripts generally do not run. Inlined into the page or loaded as a document, the security model changes. Treat user-uploaded SVG as untrusted markup, not as a harmless picture.

Content-Type is not a security boundary

A browser may sniff the body and override a vague or missing type. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff disables that behavior for many responses and makes a wrong type fail loudly instead of being guessed. That is usually desirable for scripts and styles, but it raises the cost of misconfiguration. Set the header deliberately and test the site after enabling it.

On uploads, the client-supplied type is a hint, not proof. An attacker can name an HTML file photo.jpg and send image/jpeg as the type. Validate the actual bytes, re-encode images where possible, store uploads outside the web root or serve them with Content-Disposition: attachment when they are not meant to render. Never rely on the extension alone.

For APIs, declare application/json and reject unexpected content types on write endpoints. Accepting text/plain because a proxy rewrote the header hides a real configuration problem. Log the received type when debugging, but do not echo it back without validation.

Debugging a MIME problem

  1. Open the network panel and read the response Content-Type, not the file extension.
  2. Check the server or CDN rule that sets the header for that path or extension.
  3. Confirm the file is not being served by a fallback route that returns HTML for missing assets.
  4. Look for a proxy, service worker or build step that rewrites the response.
  5. Test with a direct request such as curl -I to separate browser behavior from server behavior.
  6. After changing the rule, purge the CDN cache and retest in a fresh tab.

A 404 disguised as a MIME error is common in single-page apps. The server returns the app shell with text/html for a missing script, and the browser reports a type mismatch. The real fix is the missing file or the route fallback, not the MIME table.

Limits of a small lookup table

The tool is a quick reference, not an authoritative registry. It will not resolve newer or vendor-specific types, and it does not tell you which type a particular server will send. Use it to check a familiar mapping, then verify the live header. For standards work, consult the IANA media types registry and your server's documentation. For a file you are about to publish, test the actual response from the actual host.

Look up a type now: enter an extension or MIME value in the MIME type lookup, then verify the live header on the deployed asset. For structured data, continue with the JSON parse error guide.

faqs.question: Is a MIME type the same as a file extension?
faqs.answer: No. The extension is part of the file name and helps software guess a type. The MIME type is a declaration sent with the content. A server can send any type it wants for a given extension, which is why the live header matters more than the file name.

faqs.question: Why does reverse lookup return only one extension?
faqs.answer: Several extensions can share a type, such as jpg and jpeg for image/jpeg. The tool returns the first match in its table. Use extension-to-type lookup when you need to confirm a specific extension, and do not treat the reverse result as the only valid name.

faqs.question: Where does charset belong?
faqs.answer: Charset is a parameter of the Content-Type header, as in text/html; charset=utf-8. The lookup table stores base types only. Set the charset in the server response or the document metadata, and keep the two consistent to avoid decoding errors.

faqs.question: Is image/svg+xml safe for uploads?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. SVG is XML and can contain scripts, event handlers and external references. Serving it as an image limits some behavior, but inlining it or opening it as a document changes the risk. Validate and sanitize untrusted SVG, and consider serving downloads as attachments.

faqs.question: What if the type is not in the table?
faqs.answer: The tool returns a no-match message. That does not prove the type is invalid; the table is intentionally small. Check the IANA registry or your platform documentation, then verify what the server actually sends for the file.

title: Inspect a CSV File Before You Import It
description: Preview pasted CSV data without Excel, handle quoted fields and formulas safely, and copy filtered rows as JSON for an import test.
html:
A CSV file looks simple until a field contains a comma, a quoted newline, a leading zero or a formula. Spreadsheet software hides those details behind formatting, and by the time an import fails the original file may already be open in three places. A quick table preview is a cheap way to see what the parser will actually see before the data reaches a database or a billing system.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. The local CSV viewer accepts pasted text rather than a file upload. That keeps the data in the page, but it also means the first step is opening the file in a text editor and copying its contents. For files that must stay on disk, use a desktop parser with the same review checklist.

Why a preview catches problems Excel hides

Spreadsheets interpret values as you open them. A product code of 00123 may display as 123. A date may be reordered according to the machine's locale. A long number may lose precision after the fifteenth digit. The file itself still contains the original text, but what you see on screen is a rendering, not the bytes. A plain-text preview shows the delimiters and quotes before any interpretation.

Formula injection is the other reason to inspect. A cell beginning with =, +, - or @ can be executed as a formula by some spreadsheet programs when the file is opened or re-exported. That is dangerous for exports built from user input. The viewer prefixes those cells with an apostrophe in its output so the leading character is visibly neutralized, but that is a display aid, not a complete security control for every downstream tool.

Encoding problems also surface early. A UTF-8 BOM at the start of the file can become part of the first header if a naive parser does not strip it. Windows line endings, stray blank lines and mixed quoting styles all change how rows are counted. Looking at the first few records in a neutral viewer is faster than debugging a failed import after the fact.

What the viewer does with pasted CSV

The input is capped at 500,000 characters, roughly 500 KB. Parsing is comma-only and follows the common quoting rules: a field wrapped in double quotes may contain commas and newlines, and a doubled quote inside a quoted field becomes one literal quote. Both LF and CRLF line endings are accepted. The first row becomes the header row.

Headers are cleaned before display. A blank header becomes Column 1, and duplicates get a numeric suffix such as name_1. Cell values are trimmed, null bytes are removed and each cell is capped at 10,000 characters. A cell that starts with a formula character is prefixed with an apostrophe in the parsed output. These transformations make the preview stable, but they also mean the copied JSON is not a byte-for-byte export of the original file.

The table shows at most 100 rows at a time, with a count of filtered rows and total rows above it. The filter is a case-insensitive substring match across every column of a row. Clicking a header sorts by that column: in ascending order, numeric values sort numerically and come before text, while text uses a locale-aware comparison that handles embedded numbers. Clicking the same header again reverses the direction.

The Copy as JSON button exports the currently filtered and sorted rows, not just the 100 visible ones. That is useful for a quick API fixture, but the output is an array of objects keyed by the cleaned headers. Nested structures, dates and numbers all become strings. If you need typed values, convert them after the copy rather than assuming the JSON preserves the original types.

Formula injection and the apostrophe prefix

A value such as =HYPERLINK("https://example.com","click") is data in a CSV file but a formula in a spreadsheet. Prefixing it with an apostrophe is a common spreadsheet convention that forces the cell to be treated as text. The viewer applies that prefix when it builds its rows, so the preview and the copied JSON show the neutralized form. It does not rewrite the source file, and it cannot guarantee that a different import tool will honor the apostrophe the same way.

If you are generating CSV for others, sanitize at the source: prefix dangerous leading characters, quote fields that contain delimiters, and document the expected encoding. If you are importing a file from an untrusted source, open it in a viewer or a text editor first, not in a spreadsheet with macros enabled. The viewer's transformation is one layer of defense, not a replacement for validating the data.

Leading zeros are a separate issue. The viewer keeps them as text, which is usually what you want for postal codes, account numbers and product IDs. A spreadsheet may drop them unless the column is explicitly formatted as text. When you export JSON for an application, keep those fields as strings to avoid the same loss.

Sorting and filtering quirks

The filter is a simple substring search, not a query language. It does not support column scoping, negation or regular expressions. A search for 2026 matches every row containing that sequence anywhere, including a product name or a note. Clear the filter before sorting if the row count looks wrong; the sort applies to the filtered set.

Numeric detection uses the browser's number parsing. Values such as 1e3 and 0x10 may be treated as numbers, and a value with a currency symbol is not. Mixed columns therefore produce an order where numeric-looking cells come first, followed by text. That is predictable once you know the rule, but it is not the same as a database sort with a declared type.

Duplicate headers are renamed rather than rejected. If the original file has two columns called email, the second becomes email_1. Any downstream mapping that expects the original duplicate name will need adjustment. This is a good reason to inspect headers before writing an import script.

What this viewer does not do

TaskViewer behaviorBetter tool
Open a file directlyPaste text onlyA desktop editor or a parser script
Detect delimitersComma onlyA CSV library with delimiter sniffing
Preserve raw bytesTrims cells and prefixes formulasA byte-level parser
Edit or export CSVNo editing; JSON copy onlyA spreadsheet or a data tool
Validate typesEverything is a stringSchema validation in your import pipeline
Large files500,000-character capStreaming parser or database import

Semicolon-separated and tab-separated files will appear as a single column because the parser expects commas. Replace the delimiter in a copy if the data is otherwise simple, or use a parser that accepts a delimiter option. Quoted commas are handled, but a stray quote that is never closed can swallow the rest of the file into one field; check the last row if the preview looks short.

A five-minute import check

  1. Open the file in a text editor and confirm it is really comma-separated.
  2. Copy the first few hundred lines into the viewer and check the header names.
  3. Filter for the values that usually break: leading zeros, long IDs, dates and formula characters.
  4. Sort by the column you plan to join on and look for unexpected blanks or duplicates.
  5. Copy the filtered JSON as a fixture, then validate it against the real import schema.
  6. Keep the original file unchanged and test the import in staging before production.

For a structured conversion rather than a preview, the JSON to CSV guide covers the reverse direction. For payload validation after the copy, see the JSON parse error guide.

Preview a CSV now: paste the text into the CSV viewer, sort and filter it, then copy the rows you need as JSON. Nothing is uploaded, and the original file stays untouched.

faqs.question: Can I upload a CSV file instead of pasting it?
faqs.answer: No. The viewer accepts pasted text only. Open the file in a text editor or terminal and copy the contents, or use a desktop parser if the data cannot leave the machine. The paste limit is 500,000 characters.

faqs.question: Does it support semicolon-separated files?
faqs.answer: No. The parser expects commas. A semicolon-separated file will appear as one column with the semicolons inside the values. Convert the delimiter in a copy or use a CSV library that accepts a delimiter option.

faqs.question: Why did my leading zeros disappear?
faqs.answer: The viewer keeps cells as text, so leading zeros should remain visible. A spreadsheet is more likely to drop them. When exporting JSON, keep ID and postal-code fields as strings, and check the import target's type coercion as well.

faqs.question: What does the apostrophe before a value mean?
faqs.answer: The viewer prefixes cells that start with a formula character to make them display as text. It is a preview-level neutralization, not a guarantee that every downstream spreadsheet will behave the same way. Sanitize untrusted exports at the source and open unknown files outside a macro-enabled spreadsheet.

faqs.question: Does Copy as JSON include the visible 100 rows only?
faqs.answer: No. It exports every row in the current filtered and sorted result, even though the table preview shows at most 100. All values are strings, and the headers are the cleaned versions shown in the table.

title: Minify CSS and JavaScript Without a Build Step
description: Beautify HTML and minify CSS or JavaScript in the browser, with clear limits on what a regex-based minifier can safely change.
html:
Minifying code removes characters that do not change behavior: indentation, comments, extra spaces and some optional punctuation. It is not compression. A gzip or Brotli response compresses the bytes on the wire and reverses them exactly; a minifier rewrites the text and does not restore the original. That distinction explains why a minified file can feel smaller in an editor yet travel at nearly the same compressed size, and why a bad minifier can break code that looked fine in the source.

Part of the developer toolkit guide. The local code formatter and minifier has three tabs. HTML can be beautified, while CSS and JavaScript can be beautified or minified. The implementation is deliberately lightweight, so this guide focuses on what it can safely change and when to use a full build tool instead.

What minification can and cannot remove

Whitespace between tokens is usually optional in CSS and JavaScript, but not always. A space can separate two identifiers, a newline can trigger automatic semicolon insertion, and a line break can end a single-line comment. A safe minifier has to understand strings, template literals, regular expressions and comments before it removes anything. A regex-based minifier can handle the common cases, but it cannot reason about the language.

Minification also does not rename variables, fold constants, remove dead branches or split bundles. Those are optimizations for a compiler or a bundler. The tool here only collapses whitespace and comments. That means the savings are modest compared with a production pipeline, and the risk is different: the output should remain readable enough to debug, but it may still break edge cases.

Always keep the source file. Commit the readable version and generate the minified artifact in a build step. If the minified file is the only copy, the next editor has to reverse-engineer formatting before making a change.

CSS: comments, strings and the license problem

The CSS tab formats with brace-based indentation and preserves comments in the formatted output. Minify does the opposite: it removes every /* ... */ comment, collapses whitespace runs and strips spaces around braces, colons, commas and semicolons. It also removes the final semicolon before a closing brace. For a typical rule set, the result is a compact one-line stylesheet.

Two limitations matter. First, the minifier does not protect quoted strings before applying its replacements. A declaration such as content: "a ; b"; can lose the spaces around the semicolon because the global semicolon rule runs inside the string too. The same applies to comment-like sequences inside a URL or a string. Review any CSS that contains generated content, data URIs or unusual quoting.

Second, all comments are removed, including license headers written as /*! ... */. If a license requires the notice to remain in the distributed file, do not use this minifier on that file, or restore the notice manually. A production CSS minifier usually has a setting to preserve important comments; this one does not.

The CSS tab has no explicit character cap in the component, unlike the JavaScript tab. Very large pasted stylesheets can still make the page sluggish on an older device. For a design system with tens of thousands of rules, use a command-line minifier and inspect the diff.

JavaScript: strings are protected, regexes are not

Beautify adds two-space indentation after opening braces and splits statements at semicolons. It temporarily replaces strings, template literals and comments with placeholders so braces inside them do not affect indentation. That is enough for small functions, but it is not a parser. Object literals, arrow functions and nested ternaries can still produce awkward line breaks.

Minify walks the source, removes line and block comments, protects quoted strings and template literals, then collapses whitespace and spaces around punctuation. The protected strings are restored at the end. The 500,000-character limit is enforced before either operation.

The gap is regular expressions. A regex literal is not tokenized as a string, so a pattern containing spaces, braces or comment-like sequences can be altered. Division and regex literals are also hard to distinguish without a parser. Test any code that uses complex patterns, and prefer a real JavaScript minifier for production bundles.

Automatic semicolon insertion is the other risk. Removing a newline can change meaning when the newline was significant:

function value() {
  return
  42;
}

This function returns undefined because the newline after return ends the statement. A minifier that joins the lines can turn it into return 42, silently changing the result. Similar hazards exist with a newline before ++ or --. The tool does not insert semicolons or analyze statement boundaries, so check the output before shipping it.

HTML is formatted, not minified

The HTML tab recognizes a list of void elements such as br, img, input and meta, and indents the rest by two spaces. It does not have a minify button, despite what a general “code minifier” label might suggest. That is a deliberate limitation of the page, not a hidden mode.

Formatting HTML with a token-based indenter can change rendering. Whitespace inside <pre>, <textarea> and inline elements is significant. A space between two inline elements can disappear when each is moved to its own line, and a newline can appear where none existed. Inline <script> and <style> content is also tokenized as text, so a < inside a JavaScript comparison can be mistaken for a tag. Use the HTML tab for a quick look at simple markup, not for a production template with inline scripts or preformatted content.

The same tokenizer caveat applies to attribute values containing a literal >. Escape it as > or avoid reformatting that element. A browser may accept the raw character, but the formatter's tag boundary can be wrong.

A safe minification workflow

  1. Start from a source file in version control, never from the minified artifact.
  2. Format first if you need to read the code; compare the formatted output with the original before minifying.
  3. Minify a copy and run the project's tests or a syntax check on the result.
  4. Open the page in a browser and exercise the code paths that use strings, regexes and automatic semicolons.
  5. Check license headers if the file is distributed to third parties.
  6. For production, use a maintained minifier such as esbuild, Terser or Lightning CSS, with source maps and a build pipeline.
TabFormatMinifyMain risk
HTMLTwo-space indentNot availableWhitespace-sensitive inline, pre and script content
CSSComments preservedAll comments removedStrings, data URIs and license notices
JavaScriptStrings and comments protectedComments removed, strings protectedRegex literals, ASI and complex expressions

If the minified output fails, compare it with the formatted source around the first changed line. A missing space, a removed newline or a comment that was part of a URL is more likely than a structural bug. Restore the source, fix the pattern, and retry with a narrower input.

Try it now: paste a small stylesheet or function into the code formatter and minifier, format it first, then minify a copy and test the result. For data payloads, the JSON parse error guide covers a different kind of syntax failure.

faqs.question: Does the tool minify HTML?
faqs.answer: No. The HTML tab only beautifies with two-space indentation. CSS and JavaScript each have Format and Minify buttons. If a label or a third-party description suggests otherwise, trust the controls on the page.

faqs.question: Why did my CSS content string change?
faqs.answer: The CSS minifier removes whitespace around punctuation without protecting quoted strings first. A value containing a semicolon, comma or brace and intentional spaces can be altered. Check generated content and data URIs, or use a parser-based minifier for that stylesheet.

faqs.question: Does it preserve license comments?
faqs.answer: No. Every CSS comment is removed, including important license headers. If the license requires the notice in the distributed file, keep the comment outside the minified output or use a minifier with a preserve-license option.

faqs.question: Is the minified JavaScript production-ready?
