faqs.answer: Treat it as a quick reduction, not a production build. It does not rename variables, analyze scope or protect regular expressions, and removing newlines can change automatic semicolon insertion. Run tests and use a maintained minifier for deployed bundles.

faqs.question: What is the input limit?
faqs.answer: The JavaScript tab enforces a 500,000-character limit before formatting or minifying. The CSS tab does not have the same explicit cap, so very large sheets may still tax the browser. Split large inputs or use a command-line tool.

title: Compare Two Texts Word by Word
description: Compare two drafts at word level, read the added and removed counts, and know when a line-based diff is the better tool.
html:
Two versions of a paragraph look identical until a comma moves, a number changes or a sentence disappears. Reading them side by side works for a short email and fails for a two-page proposal. A diff highlights what changed, but the unit of comparison matters: word-level tools catch small edits inside a sentence, while line-level tools are better for code and structured records. The local text diff compares words, and knowing that makes its output much easier to interpret.

Part of the word and text guide. The tool runs in the page and does not store either version. It has no account, no history and no export, so keep the original documents somewhere safe before pasting them.

What a word-level diff shows

The tool splits each version into words and whitespace, then finds the longest common subsequence between the middle sections. Text before the first difference and after the last one is treated as unchanged. The output colors removed words with a strikethrough and added words with a highlight, and reports a count of removed and added tokens.

That design makes small edits visible. Changing 30 days to 45 days highlights only the number. Reordering a clause shows the old words as removed and the new words as added, even though the meaning may be similar. Inserting a sentence produces a long green run, which is easy to spot.

Whitespace is part of the token stream. A changed space, a removed line break or a doubled space can appear as an added or removed token, and the counts include those tokens. That is why the numbers may be larger than the number of visible words you changed. It is not a bug; it is a consequence of comparing raw text.

Example: The plan costs 30 dollars per month. versus The plan costs 45 dollars per month. produces one removed token and one added token. The surrounding words stay unchanged. If the second version also changes the line wrapping, the whitespace tokens can add to the counts even though the prose is identical.

How the comparison works under the hood

After trimming the common prefix and suffix, the tool builds a dynamic-programming table over the remaining tokens. When the table is small enough, it reconstructs an ordered set of matches, deletions and additions. When the remaining block is very large, the table would be too expensive, so the tool skips the detailed alignment and shows the entire middle section as removed followed by added. That fallback is honest but coarse: it preserves the counts and the visible change, not the fine-grained pairing.

The practical threshold is a product of the two middle token counts. A large document with edits at both ends can trigger the fallback even if the changed middle is modest. If the output suddenly looks like two big blocks instead of interleaved words, shorten the input around the region you care about and compare that excerpt.

There is no option to ignore case, ignore punctuation or normalize whitespace. Total and total are different tokens. A curly apostrophe and a straight apostrophe are different characters. If those differences are noise for your task, normalize both versions in a text editor first, then paste the normalized copies.

Reading the counts and the colors

The red count is the number of removed tokens, and the green count is the number of added tokens. They are not a score, and they do not tell you whether the edit is good. A single changed digit can be more important than a rewritten paragraph. Use the counts to confirm that the diff actually ran and to estimate the size of the change, then read the highlighted passage.

Moved text is displayed as a removal in one place and an addition in another. The tool does not detect moves, so a paragraph that was relocated can look like a deletion and an unrelated insertion. For a contract, that difference matters: a moved clause may still be enforceable, while a deleted one may not. Read the context around both colors rather than relying on the summary.

Punctuation attached to a word stays attached. A changed comma may highlight the neighboring word, depending on where the token boundary falls. Numbers with thousands separators can split differently between versions. If the highlighting looks odd, compare the two source sentences directly and treat the diff as a pointer, not a verdict.

When word diff is the right tool

Use it for prose revisions: blog drafts, cover letters, policy summaries, product descriptions and translation checks. It is good at catching a changed date, a dropped negation or a swapped name. It is also useful when a collaborator says “I only made a few edits” and you want to verify that claim before publishing.

Do not use it as a code review tool. Code diffs need line numbers, context, syntax awareness and the ability to ignore whitespace. A word-level view of a JSON file or a function can be unreadable. Use version control for code, and use a line-based diff when you need to review configuration or structured text.

For legal redlines, a word diff is a starting point, not a replacement for a clause-by-clause review. It cannot tell you whether a change alters an obligation, and it does not track comments or authorship. Export the comparison or annotate the source document with a qualified reviewer.

A practical comparison workflow

  1. Save both versions with clear names before editing either one.
  2. Normalize obvious noise such as line endings or smart quotes if you do not want them in the diff.
  3. Paste the original on the left and the revision on the right.
  4. Read the first changed passage in context; do not start with the counts.
  5. Check names, numbers, dates and negations specifically, since a single token can change meaning.
  6. Copy the final approved text back into the source document, not from the diff view.
SituationWord diffBetter choice
Blog draft revisionGood fitThis tool
Contract clause reviewUseful pointerClause-level legal review
Code changesPoor fitGit diff or a code review tool
Translation QAGood for missing textA bilingual reviewer for meaning
Whitespace-only changesNoisyNormalize before comparing
Very large documentsFalls back to block viewCompare excerpts or use a desktop diff

The tool does not upload either document, which is useful for unpublished drafts and internal notes. It also does not save them, so closing the tab clears the comparison. If you need an audit trail, keep the versions in your document system and record which one was approved.

Compare two versions now: paste both into the text diff, read the highlighted passages in context, then copy the approved text back to your editor. For length checks on the result, use the word counter.

faqs.question: Does the diff ignore capitalization or punctuation?
faqs.answer: No. Every character is part of a token, so Total and total differ, and a changed comma can affect the surrounding token. Normalize the copies in an editor first if those differences are noise for your review.

faqs.question: Why do the counts include spaces?
faqs.answer: The tool splits on whitespace but keeps the separators as tokens. A changed line break or an extra space can therefore add to the added or removed count even when no visible word changed. Read the highlighted passages rather than treating the counts as a word count.

faqs.question: Why did a large document show two big blocks?
faqs.answer: When the changed middle is too large for the detailed alignment table, the tool falls back to showing the whole middle as removed followed by added. Compare a shorter excerpt around the section you care about to get word-level pairing again.

faqs.question: Can I use this for code reviews?
faqs.answer: It is a poor fit for code. Word-level highlighting loses line numbers, indentation context and syntax structure. Use Git or a line-based diff for source files, and keep this tool for prose and short documents.

faqs.question: Is either version uploaded?
faqs.answer: No. The comparison runs in the page and no history is stored. Closing the tab clears the input. Keep the originals in your document system if you need an audit trail or a record of the approved version.

title: Image to Base64: Data URLs in Practice
description: Turn images into Base64 data URLs, judge the size overhead, and avoid inlining where caching or email clients will punish it.
html:
A Base64 data URL lets an image travel inside a text document. Instead of a separate file request, the image bytes become a long string in the HTML, CSS or JSON. That can simplify a single-file demo or a small icon, and it can also bloat a page, break caching and leak metadata. The decision is less about whether the conversion works and more about whether inlining is appropriate for this particular image.

Part of the image optimization guide. The local image to Base64 tool converts a file into a data URL and previews a pasted data URL. It does not compress, resize or strip metadata, so it should not be the last step before publishing a photo.

What a data URL contains

The format is data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo.... The first part declares the media type, then comes the Base64 marker, then the encoded bytes. A browser can use that string directly as an image source. The payload is ordinary Base64, not encryption and not compression. Anyone who can read the page can decode it.

Base64 represents every three bytes as four text characters, so the encoded payload is about one third larger than the binary file. A 100 KB image becomes roughly 133 KB of text before the prefix. That overhead applies whether the image is a tiny icon or a photograph, and the text does not compress as well as the original binary in a gzip or Brotli response.

There is no file name, no separate cache key and no independent HTTP response. The image lives or dies with the document that contains it. Updating the image means updating the document, and every visitor downloads the full string again unless the document itself is cached aggressively.

What the converter accepts

Encode mode reads a local file through the browser's FileReader. The file must be 10 MB or smaller and one of five types: JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF or SVG. The result is a complete data URL, ready to copy. There is no resize, no quality setting, no EXIF removal and no dimension check. A 9000-pixel image that passes the size limit will still produce a very long string.

Decode mode expects a full image data URL, not raw Base64. It accepts a preview allowlist that includes PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG, BMP, AVIF and ICO, and it blocks obvious script and HTML payloads. The input is capped at 15,000,000 characters. Decoding shows a preview; it does not download a reconstructed file. To save the image, use the browser's image save command or decode the payload with a local script.

The asymmetry is intentional but easy to miss. The encoder accepts fewer types than the decoder can preview. If you have a BMP or AVIF file, convert it to PNG or WebP first. If you paste raw Base64 without the data:image/...;base64, prefix, the preview will reject it even though the characters are valid Base64.

OperationLimit or rule
Encode file size10 MB maximum
Encode typesJPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, SVG
Decode inputFull data URL, 15,000,000 characters maximum
Decode preview typesPNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG, BMP, AVIF, ICO
CompressionNone
Metadata removalNone
Download buttonNone; preview only

Doing the size math before you inline

A 10 KB icon becomes about 13.3 KB of text. A 100 KB illustration becomes about 133 KB. A 1 MB photo becomes about 1.33 MB. Add the prefix and the surrounding HTML, then compare that with a separate image request that can be cached, compressed and served from a CDN. For a single small icon used once, inlining can remove a request. For a photo used on every page, it usually makes the page heavier and less cacheable.

The break-even point depends on the connection, the cache hit rate and the number of pages that share the image. An image used once on a rarely visited page may be fine inline. An image used in a header on every page should be a separate file with a long cache lifetime. Measure the actual page weight rather than guessing from the file size alone.

Base64 also affects HTML parsing and memory. A very long attribute or text node is more expensive to parse than a URL, and editing a document with megabytes of encoded image is unpleasant. Keep inline images small, and move anything approaching a few hundred kilobytes to a normal file.

When inlining helps, and when it hurts

Good candidates are small SVG icons, a single-file HTML report, a tiny CSS background used on one page, or an email template that must survive a strict content security policy. Even then, test the final environment. Many email clients block or strip data URL images, and corporate gateways may rewrite them. A preview in one client is not proof that every recipient will see the image.

Poor candidates are photographs, hero images, product galleries and anything reused across pages. They benefit from separate requests, responsive sources, modern formats and CDN caching. Inlining also makes responsive images harder because you cannot use srcset with the same ease, and it can duplicate the payload if the same image appears in several components.

Content Security Policy adds another constraint. If the page uses a strict img-src directive, data URLs need to be allowed explicitly. Allowing data: broadly can weaken the policy, so scope it to images if possible. Test with the production policy, not just a local development server.

Metadata and SVG risks

Converting a photo to Base64 does not remove EXIF data. GPS coordinates, camera model, timestamps and orientation can all survive inside the encoded string. If the image is going public, strip metadata with an image editor or a dedicated EXIF tool before encoding. The converter's preview is not a privacy filter.

SVG is text and can contain scripts, event handlers and external references. The decoder's allowlist and the way an image is used affect the risk. An SVG loaded through an <img> element has a restricted scripting model, while SVG inlined into the page is part of the document. Treat user-supplied SVG as untrusted, and do not paste an unknown data URL into a context where it becomes active markup.

The converter checks the declared media type and blocks obvious script prefixes, but it does not sanitize the SVG contents. That is enough for a preview of your own file, not for a public upload pipeline.

A practical inlining workflow

  1. Resize and compress the image first; the converter does neither.
  2. Strip EXIF and other metadata if the image will be public.
  3. Encode the optimized file and check the resulting string length.
  4. Confirm the destination supports data URLs, especially if it is an email client or a CMS.
  5. Update the CSP if needed, scoped to images rather than all content.
  6. Measure the page before and after; remove the inline image if it makes the critical path heavier.

For a separate-file workflow, see the format comparison and the EXIF guide. For the text encoding layer, the Base64 modes guide explains why URL-safe alphabets differ from the standard one used in data URLs.

Convert an image now: choose a file in the image to Base64 tool, copy the data URL, and check its size before pasting it into a page. For large images, compress first with the image compressor.

faqs.question: Does the tool compress the image?
faqs.answer: No. It encodes the original bytes as Base64. Compress and resize first, then convert, or the data URL will carry the full original size along with the Base64 overhead. The image compressor is the right step before this one.

faqs.question: Can I paste raw Base64 without the data prefix?
faqs.answer: No. The decoder expects a complete data URL beginning with data:image/...;base64,. Raw Base64 has no media type, so the page cannot choose a preview format. Add the correct prefix if you know the image type.

faqs.question: Does the conversion remove EXIF data?
faqs.answer: No. The encoded bytes are unchanged, so camera metadata, timestamps and GPS coordinates can remain. Strip metadata with an editor or a dedicated tool before encoding an image that will be published.

faqs.question: Why do email clients hide data URL images?
faqs.answer: Support varies and many clients or gateways block data URLs for security, size or rendering reasons. Test the actual received message in the clients your audience uses. A normal hosted image is usually more reliable for email.

faqs.question: Can I download the decoded image?
faqs.answer: The decoder shows a preview but has no download button. Use the browser's save-image command on the preview, or decode the Base64 with a local script if you need the original file.

title: Monthly vs Yearly Compounding: The Real Gap
description: Compare monthly, quarterly and yearly compounding on the same nominal rate, including effective yield and the limits of a lump-sum model.
html:
Two deposits can both advertise 8% and pay different amounts. The difference is not a trick in the arithmetic; it is the compounding frequency. Interest added monthly starts earning interest a month earlier than interest added yearly. Over one year the gap is small. Over ten years it compounds into a meaningful sum, which is why the frequency belongs next to the rate in any comparison.

Part of the wealth and compounding guide. The local compound interest calculator models a single lump sum with yearly, half-yearly, quarterly or monthly compounding. It does not accept monthly contributions, taxes, fees or inflation. Those omissions are not flaws in the formula; they define what the result can and cannot tell you.

The formula behind the result

For a lump sum, the maturity value is A = P × (1 + r / n)^(n × t). P is the principal, r is the nominal annual rate as a decimal, n is the number of compounding periods per year and t is the time in years. The calculator offers four values of n: 1 for yearly, 2 for half-yearly, 4 for quarterly and 12 for monthly.

The interest earned is simply the maturity value minus the principal. The tool displays both, formatted in the selected currency. It accepts decimal years and uses the same formula, so a two-and-a-half-year projection is possible. It does not round each period separately, which means the displayed result can differ by a few cents from a bank's statement that rounds every credit.

Because the model has no payment field, it cannot represent a recurring deposit, a SIP or a loan with monthly installments. Adding contributions requires a different formula or a schedule of cash flows. Use the SIP calculator for monthly investments, and use an amortization calculator for a loan with payments.

A worked example: 10,000 at 8% for 10 years

Assume a nominal annual rate of 8%, a principal of 10,000 and a term of 10 years. Changing only the compounding frequency produces the following values, before tax and fees:

FrequencyPeriods per yearMaturity valueInterest earnedEffective annual rate
Yearly121,589.2511,589.258.00%
Half-yearly221,911.2311,911.238.16%
Quarterly422,080.4012,080.408.24%
Monthly1222,196.4012,196.408.30%

Monthly compounding adds 607.15 over yearly compounding on the same nominal rate, about 5.2% more interest. The maturity value is 2.8% higher. The gap is not free money: the nominal rate, the term and the absence of fees are all held constant. In a real product, a bank that compounds monthly may quote a lower nominal rate than one that compounds yearly, which can erase or reverse the difference.

Here is the same comparison for a principal of 500,000 at 7% for five years, useful when the currency is INR or another unit with a different scale: yearly gives 701,275.87, quarterly gives 707,389.10 and monthly gives 708,812.63. The absolute gap is smaller because the rate and term are smaller, but the direction is the same.

Nominal rate versus effective annual rate

The nominal rate is the quoted annual rate before compounding within the year. The effective annual rate, sometimes called the annual equivalent rate or effective yield, is what you actually earn over one year when the intra-year compounding is included. It is calculated as (1 + r / n)^n - 1. For an 8% nominal rate, monthly compounding produces an effective rate of about 8.30%.

This is the number to use when comparing products with different compounding schedules. Comparing an 8.30% effective yield with an 8.00% effective yield is meaningful; comparing a monthly-compounded 8.00% with a yearly-compounded 8.10% requires converting both to the same basis first. The calculator does not display the effective rate, but the maturity values already reflect it.

For loans, the same mathematics can work against the borrower. A higher compounding frequency at the same nominal rate can increase the effective cost, although most consumer loans quote an annual percentage rate that already accounts for fees and compounding. Do not compare a loan's nominal rate with a deposit's effective yield. They describe different cash flows.

Why the gap grows with time and rate

Compounding is exponential, so the difference between frequencies grows with both the rate and the term. At low rates and short terms, the gap is small enough to ignore for a rough estimate. At higher rates or longer horizons, it becomes visible. The monthly-versus-yearly gap on 10,000 at 8% is about 607 over ten years; at 12% over the same term it is much larger because the base grows faster.

The frequency also matters more when the term is long because each extra period's interest has more time to compound. A one-year comparison understates the long-run effect. If you are choosing between two multi-year products, compare the maturity values over the full term, not just the first-year yield.

Inflation is a separate subtraction. A maturity value that looks large in nominal terms may buy less after ten years. The real return guide covers that adjustment. Taxes and fees are also outside this model, and they can change the ranking of two products with different tax treatment.

What the result does not include

FactorIncluded?What to do
Recurring contributionsNoUse the SIP calculator or a cash-flow schedule
Tax on interestNoApply your marginal rate or the product's tax rule
Fees and chargesNoSubtract them from the maturity value or the rate
InflationNoConvert to real terms with the inflation calculator
Variable ratesNoRun scenarios for each rate path
Day-count conventionsNoUse the product's official statement for exact amounts

The calculator also assumes the rate stays constant for the entire term. A floating-rate deposit or a loan with a reset schedule needs a scenario analysis, not a single number. Run a low, middle and high case, and label them as scenarios rather than predictions.

Finally, the output is an illustration, not an offer. Banks may use a different day-count convention, credit interest at a different time or apply minimum-balance rules. Use the result to compare structures and to ask better questions, then confirm the actual terms in the product documents.

A clean comparison workflow

  1. Write down the nominal rate, the term and the compounding frequency for each option.
  2. Convert each option to an effective annual rate, or compare maturity values over the same term.
  3. Run the same principal through the calculator for each frequency.
  4. Subtract estimated tax and fees before comparing spendable amounts.
  5. Adjust for inflation if the goal is purchasing power rather than nominal balance.
  6. Stress-test the result with a lower rate and a shorter term before committing.

For a monthly investment rather than a lump sum, use the SIP calculator and the lump-sum versus frequency guide. For the retirement horizon, the retirement calculator adds contributions and withdrawals that this lump-sum model intentionally leaves out.

Compare frequencies now: enter the same principal, rate and term in the compound interest calculator, change only the frequency, and note the maturity difference. This is an educational estimate, not financial advice; confirm product terms with the provider.

faqs.question: Is monthly compounding always better than yearly?
faqs.answer: For a deposit at the same nominal rate and term, more frequent compounding produces a higher effective yield. But products rarely hold the nominal rate constant across schedules, and taxes and fees can reverse the ranking. Compare effective annual rates or full-term maturity values, not the frequency label alone.

faqs.question: Does the calculator support daily compounding?
faqs.answer: No. It offers yearly, half-yearly, quarterly and monthly. Daily compounding would use n equal to 365 and a slightly higher effective rate. The difference from monthly is usually small, but you need a calculator or a spreadsheet that supports the extra frequency.

faqs.question: Can I add monthly contributions?
faqs.answer: No. The model is a single lump sum. Adding a fixed amount every month changes the formula because each contribution has its own compounding period. Use the SIP calculator for recurring investments, and keep this tool for one-time deposits.

faqs.question: Why is my bank's maturity amount slightly different?
faqs.answer: Banks may round interest at each credit, use a different day-count convention, deduct tax at source or apply minimum-balance rules. The calculator uses one formula for the whole term and rounds only the display. Treat a small difference as a modeling convention, not an error.

faqs.question: Does the result include tax?
faqs.answer: No. Tax treatment depends on the product and jurisdiction, and it can change the effective return substantially. Apply the relevant tax rule to the interest earned, then compare the after-tax amounts. The result here is a pre-tax illustration.

title: Tip Calculator: How to Split a Bill Fairly
description: Use a tip calculator to apply a percentage, split the total by headcount and compare 15, 18 and 20 percent shares on the same bill.
html:
A restaurant bill is not one decision. You choose a gratuity rate, decide what amount the percentage applies to, and divide the result by the number of people. A tip calculator makes those steps visible, but only if you know what its fields do. The local tip calculator takes a bill amount, a whole-number percentage from 0 to 30, a headcount and one of seven currencies. It returns the tip, the total and an equal per-person share.

Part of the percentage calculator guide. The tool has no tax field, no service-charge detector and no custom split. Those limits are not hidden, but they matter when a receipt includes tax, a mandatory gratuity or a shared appetizer.

What the four fields actually change

The bill field is the base for the percentage. It accepts decimals and ignores negative values by falling back to zero. There is no separate sales-tax input, so the number you type is exactly the number the tip is calculated on. If you want to tip on the pre-tax subtotal, enter the subtotal. If you want to tip on the final charge, enter the final charge. The calculator will not infer either choice.

The tip slider runs from 0 to 30 in one-point steps. That means 15, 18 and 20 are available, while 18.5 is not. The value is stored as a whole number and the displayed label uses the same integer. A custom percentage would need a different tool or manual arithmetic.

The headcount field is parsed as an integer. A value such as 3.7 becomes 3, and a blank, zero or negative value becomes 1. The result is always an equal split; there is no way to assign a different share to one diner or to exclude someone from the total.

The currency menu lists USD, EUR, GBP, INR, JPY, CAD and AUD. Changing it changes the symbol and number formatting only. It does not convert the amount. A bill entered as 84.50 with EUR selected is still 84.50, now formatted as euros. JPY is displayed with no decimal places because of its normal currency formatting, so a per-person result can look more rounded than the same number in USD.

The formula behind the three results

The arithmetic is short enough to check by hand:

  • Tip = bill x rate / 100
  • Total = bill + tip
  • Per person = total / headcount

For an 84.50 bill at 18 percent with three people, the tip is 84.50 x 0.18 = 15.21. The total is 84.50 + 15.21 = 99.71. Each share is 99.71 / 3 = 33.2366..., displayed as 33.24. Raising the rate to 20 percent gives a 16.90 tip, a 101.40 total and a 33.80 share. The difference in the tip is 1.69, and the difference per person is 0.56.

Display rounding explains small inconsistencies. Three displayed shares of 33.24 add to 99.72, one cent more than the displayed 99.71 total. The underlying values are not rounded before division; the page rounds each formatted amount for display. If you are collecting cash, decide who absorbs the extra cent rather than treating the mismatch as a calculation error.

Here is the same 84.50 bill at four rates, with three diners:

RateTipTotalEach of 3
15%12.6897.1832.39
18%15.2199.7133.24
20%16.90101.4033.80
25%21.13105.6335.21

The 15 percent row shows the display effect clearly: 84.50 x 0.15 is 12.675, and 97.175 divided by three is 32.3916..., so the formatted values are 12.68, 97.18 and 32.39. The cents do not have to add back to the total after each line is rounded.

Pre-tax, post-tax and service charges

Sales tax is not part of the calculation. If an 84.50 subtotal is taxed at 8 percent, the post-tax charge is 91.26. An 18 percent tip on the subtotal is 15.21; the same rate on the post-tax charge is 16.43. That is a 1.22 difference. Neither answer is universally correct. Customs vary by country and city, and some people tip on the pre-tax base while others round up from the final charge. Choose the base deliberately and apply the same rule when you compare rates.

A mandatory service charge is a different problem. If the receipt already includes an 18 percent service charge, adding another 18 percent tip on the full charge pays twice for the same service. The calculator cannot detect a service charge, so read the bill before entering the number. Some restaurants print a service charge and leave the tip line blank; others include both a service charge and a discretionary gratuity. The tool can split a total, but it cannot tell you what the total represents.

Delivery orders and counter service can invert the usual assumptions. A delivery fee is not a tip, and a counter-service order may not expect one. The calculator stays neutral: it applies the rate you choose to the amount you enter. Etiquette is outside its scope.

Splitting the bill without false precision

Equal splitting is the only mode. For a 100 bill at 15 percent, the tip is 15, the total is 115 and each of three pays 38.333..., displayed as 38.33. At 18 percent, the total is 118 and each share is 39.33. At 20 percent, the total is 120 and each share is exactly 40. At 25 percent, the total is 125 and each share is 41.67.

If one person pays the whole card charge and the others reimburse in cash, use the total as the amount to collect, not the sum of the rounded shares. If everyone pays separately, the payment processor may split the exact total and ignore the display rounding. The correct reconciliation depends on who is paying, not on the calculator.

Shared items do not change the math once the bill total is known. The tool does not track who ordered what, so an uneven split needs a manual adjustment after the equal share is calculated. For example, if one diner owes 10 more for a shared bottle, add that amount to their share and subtract it from another. Do that outside the tool and keep a note of the adjustment.

A short workflow before you pay

  1. Read the receipt and separate the subtotal, tax, service charge and any delivery fee.
  2. Decide whether the tip applies to the pre-tax subtotal or the final charge.
  3. Enter that amount in the bill field.
  4. Move the slider to an available whole percentage and enter the number of people.
  5. Select the currency that matches the bill. Remember that this is formatting, not conversion.
  6. Compare two rates before committing, then use the total for payment and the per-person figure for reimbursement.

For a quick sanity check, 10 percent of 84.50 is 8.45. A 20 percent tip is double that, or 16.90. An 18 percent tip sits slightly below 20 percent, at 15.21. If the displayed tip is far from that range, check whether the bill field contains the subtotal or the post-tax total.

Split the next bill: open the tip calculator, enter the amount and headcount, and compare rates before paying. For the underlying percentage math, use the percentage calculator.

faqs.question: Does the calculator add sales tax?
faqs.answer: No. There is no tax field. It applies the selected percentage to the number in the bill field. Enter the pre-tax subtotal if you want to tip on that base, or the post-tax total if you prefer to tip on the final charge.

faqs.question: Can I enter 18.5 percent?
faqs.answer: No. The slider moves in one-point steps from 0 to 30, so 18 and 19 are available but 18.5 is not. Use the closest whole rate or calculate the exact gratuity separately.

faqs.question: Does it support an uneven split?
faqs.answer: No. The headcount field divides the total equally and truncates decimals in the headcount. Adjust individual shares outside the tool if one person owes more for a shared item.

faqs.question: Does changing the currency convert the amount?
faqs.answer: No. USD, EUR, GBP, INR, JPY, CAD and AUD change the symbol and formatting only. The numeric amount stays the same, so convert the bill first if you need a different currency.

faqs.question: Is the bill or result stored?
faqs.answer: No. The calculation runs in the page, with no account and no history. Closing the page clears the entries. Keep the receipt or a separate note if you need a record.

title: Sales Tax on a Price: Formula and Examples
description: Calculate sales tax from a subtotal and a combined rate, compare preset rates, and see why a register total can differ from a state-only estimate.
html:
Sales tax looks like one multiplication: price x rate. The hard part is finding the rate. A state rate is only the first layer. Counties, cities and special districts can add their own percentages, some products are exempt, and the rate that applies depends on where the buyer receives the goods. The US sales tax calculator keeps the arithmetic simple: enter a taxable subtotal, choose one of five presets or a custom rate, and read the tax and total.

Part of the percentage calculator guide. The tool is deliberately small. It does not look up a ZIP code, itemize local layers or decide whether an item is taxable. It applies one rate to one subtotal and displays the result in USD. Those constraints are useful if you use the tool for what it actually does.

The formula and two worked examples

Sales tax is a percentage of the taxable price:

  • Tax = taxable subtotal x rate / 100
  • Total = taxable subtotal + tax

A 100 dollar subtotal at 7.25 percent produces 7.25 in tax and 107.25 total. The same subtotal at 6.25 percent produces 6.25 and 106.25. At 8.875 percent, the tax is 8.875, displayed as 8.88, and the total is 108.875, displayed as 108.88. The unrounded value is used through the calculation; the display rounds to cents at the end.

Scaling up does not change the method. A 250 dollar subtotal at 7.25 percent produces 18.125 in tax, displayed as 18.13, and 268.125 total, displayed as 268.13. At 6.25 percent, the same cart produces 15.625 tax and 265.625 total, displayed as 15.63 and 265.63. If you are comparing two jurisdictions, use the same subtotal and the combined rate that actually applies to the ship-to address.

Here are the five presets on a 100 dollar taxable subtotal:

PresetRateTaxTotal
California7.25%7.25107.25
New York City8.875%8.88108.88
Texas6.25%6.25106.25
Florida6%6.00106.00
Washington10.35%10.35110.35

The presets are starting points, not a complete rate table. Rates change, and the local layers that apply to a particular delivery address are not included. Verify the current combined rate before quoting a customer or filing a return.

Why one combined rate is the right input

Suppose the state rate is 6.25 percent, the county adds 1 percent and the city adds 0.5 percent. The combined rate is 7.75 percent. On a 120 dollar taxable subtotal, the tax is 120 x 0.0775 = 9.30 and the total is 129.30. The calculator does not need to know the three layers separately; it needs the combined percentage. Select Custom and enter 7.75.

That is also the tool's main limitation. It does not itemize state, county, city and district components, and it cannot tell you whether the layers apply to a specific product or address. If a receipt shows a state rate, a county rate and a transit district rate, add them yourself from an official source, then enter the combined figure. Keep the component rates in your notes so you can explain the quote later.

Do not add percentages to a base more than once. A common error is to apply 6.25 percent, then apply 1 percent to the result, then apply another 0.5 percent to the new result. That is compounding, not stacking. Sales tax layers are normally combined into one rate and applied once to the taxable price. The difference is small at these rates, but it grows with the subtotal and makes reconciliation harder.

Start from the taxable subtotal

The calculator taxes every dollar you enter. It has no exemption checklist and no product categories. If a basket contains 100 dollars of goods and 20 dollars of exempt groceries, enter 80, not 100. At 7.25 percent, the tax on 80 is 5.80 and the total is 85.80. That is different from taxing the full 100 and then trying to subtract the tax on the exempt portion.

Shipping and delivery charges are another state-specific question. Some jurisdictions tax delivery when the goods are taxable, some do not, and some treat separately stated charges differently. The tool cannot resolve that. Decide whether the charge belongs in the taxable subtotal under the rules for the destination, then enter the adjusted amount.

Resale certificates, agricultural exemptions and occasional sales tax holidays add more exceptions. The calculator is not a compliance system. It is a way to apply a known rate to a known taxable base. If the base is wrong, the output will be wrong even when the multiplication is perfect.

Destination sourcing matters for remote sales. A seller may collect based on the ship-to location rather than the warehouse. The page has no address field, so it cannot implement that rule. Look up the destination rate, decide whether the product is taxable, and then use the chosen rate in Custom.

Comparing states without mixing bases

To compare two states, hold the taxable subtotal constant and change only the rate. A 250 dollar cart at 7.25 percent is 268.13; at 6.25 percent it is 265.63. The difference is 2.50, which is exactly 1 percentage point of 250. That is a useful sanity check: one percentage point on a 250 base is 2.50, before rounding.

A state-only comparison can mislead when local rates differ sharply. California's 7.25 percent preset excludes many local additions. The New York City preset at 8.875 percent is a combined state and city figure; the statewide base is lower and other localities differ. Washington's 10.35 percent is a high combined starting point, yet some jurisdictions produce a different figure. Treat each preset as a labeled assumption, not a quote for a specific address.

Use the same currency and the same subtotal for every comparison. The calculator displays USD only, which is appropriate for US sales tax but not for a cross-border VAT comparison. For a value-added tax, use the GST and VAT calculator instead of forcing a sales tax model onto an invoice.

A practical checkout workflow

  1. Build the taxable subtotal. Remove exempt items and add taxable delivery charges only when the destination rules require it.
  2. Find the combined rate for the ship-to location and product category from an official source.
  3. Choose the matching preset if it is close, or select Custom and enter the exact combined rate.
  4. Read the tax and total, then record the rate, the date and the source beside the quote.
  5. Recheck the rate when the address, product mix or tax authority guidance changes.

If the register total differs from the estimate, compare the taxable subtotal and the combined rate before assuming the calculator is broken. A missing local layer, an exempt item that was not removed or a delivery charge that was treated differently can explain the gap. The page shows one rate and two outputs, so there is no hidden district breakdown to inspect.

Apply a rate to a subtotal: open the US sales tax calculator, enter the taxable amount, and choose a preset or a combined custom rate. For percentage changes rather than tax, use the percentage calculator.

faqs.question: Does the calculator look up my rate by ZIP code?
faqs.answer: No. It has no address or ZIP field. It applies the selected preset or the custom rate you enter to the subtotal. Look up the combined rate from an official source before using it for a quote or return.

faqs.question: Which rates are preset?
faqs.answer: California at 7.25 percent, New York City at 8.875 percent, Texas at 6.25 percent, Florida at 6 percent and Washington at 10.35 percent. Choose Custom for another state or for a combined state, county and city rate.

faqs.question: Can I enter a combined local rate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select Custom and enter the combined percentage. The tool applies that single rate once. It does not itemize the state, county, city or district components.

faqs.question: Does it handle exemptions or shipping?
faqs.answer: No. It taxes the full subtotal you enter. Remove exempt items first, and include delivery charges only when the destination rules make them taxable. The calculator does not know product categories.

faqs.question: Is the result tax advice?
faqs.answer: No. It is arithmetic for planning. Rates, sourcing rules and product taxability vary by jurisdiction and change over time. Verify the current rule and consult a tax professional for filing or collection decisions.

title: Markdown Preview: Check Formatting Before Publishing
description: Preview Markdown before publishing, see which syntax this editor supports, and catch tables, lists and links that will not survive the export.
html:
Markdown is readable as plain text, which makes it easy to publish without checking how a renderer will treat it. A heading needs a space after the hashes. A blank line changes a paragraph break. A link with a relative path may be rejected. The Markdown editor shows a Write tab and a Preview tab, then lets you copy the generated HTML. It is a quick way to catch formatting mistakes before pasting content into a CMS.

Part of the word counter guide. The editor is not a full CommonMark implementation and it is not a split-pane live editor. Knowing the supported subset is more useful than expecting GitHub-flavored Markdown to work everywhere.

What the editor supports

The parser handles a narrow set of block and inline rules. It extracts fenced code blocks first, escapes the remaining HTML, then converts headings, blockquotes, unordered lists, inline code, links, bold and italic text. Paragraphs are split on blank lines, and single newlines inside a paragraph become line breaks.

FeatureSyntaxPreview result
Headings# through ###### plus a spaceh1 through h6
Bold**text**strong text
Italic*text*emphasized text
Inline codebackticks around textmonospace code
Link[label](https://example.com)new-tab link
Unordered list- item or * itembullet list
Blockquote> textindented quote
Code blocktriple backticks around linespreformatted block

Links are restricted to absolute http://, https:// and mailto: URLs. A relative path such as /contact becomes # in the generated HTML. That is a safety default, but it also means internal links need to be absolute before they survive this preview. The output adds target="_blank" and rel="noopener noreferrer" to every accepted link.

Raw HTML is escaped. A literal <strong> in the Write tab appears as text, not as bold markup. That is useful when you are documenting HTML, but it also means an embed, iframe or styled callout will not render here. Add those elements in the CMS after the Markdown step.

What does not render

The omissions are the practical source of surprises:

  • Tables. Pipe characters and separator rows stay as paragraph text. Use a CMS table block or build the table in HTML after export.
  • Ordered lists. Lines beginning with 1. are not converted into an ordered list. They remain paragraph lines, often separated by line breaks.
  • Images. Image syntax is not converted into a figure. It can appear as an exclamation mark followed by a sanitized link, not as an image.
  • Nested lists. Indentation is not used to build a hierarchy. Consecutive bullet lines become one flat unordered list.
  • Task lists, footnotes and strikethrough. None of these extensions are parsed.
  • Syntax highlighting. A language label after the opening fence is kept as the first line of the code block rather than used to color the code.

A table is a good test case. Paste a two-column table into the editor and switch to Preview. If the pipes are still visible in a paragraph, the parser did not recognize the table and the CMS will need to handle it. The same applies to an ordered procedure: if the numbers remain plain text, convert the steps to bullets here or rebuild the ordered list in the publishing tool.

Fenced blocks need a closing fence. The parser extracts a complete block only when it finds an opening and closing set of triple backticks. An unclosed fence can produce a confusing mix of code and paragraph text. Close the fence, then check that the language label is acceptable as a first code line or remove it.

A preview-first publishing workflow

  1. Write or paste the draft in the Write tab.
  2. Add a blank line between paragraphs and keep a space after heading hashes.
  3. Switch to Preview and check headings, bullet structure, links and code blocks.
  4. Open the generated HTML details if you need to confirm the exact tags before copying.
  5. Use Copy HTML, then paste into the CMS in text or code mode rather than visual mode.
  6. Check the published page in the CMS theme, because the editor's preview styles are not exported with the HTML.

The tab switch matters. The preview is recalculated when the source changes, but you only see it on the Preview tab. There is no side-by-side view, so keep the draft short enough to compare sections without scrolling far. For a long article, preview one section at a time or paste the final HTML into a local page for a second check.

Copy HTML exports the generated fragment, not a complete document. It does not include the editor's fonts, spacing, dark code background or responsive layout. A CMS may strip tags it does not allow, especially links with target attributes or raw code blocks. That is another reason to inspect the published result instead of trusting the preview alone.

Size, storage and privacy limits

The editor has a 512,000-character guard labeled as 500 KB. If a paste exceeds it, the page truncates the input and shows a size error. That is large enough for most articles but not for a full documentation export. Split a long document before previewing, or use a desktop editor for the complete file.

Nothing is uploaded or saved by the page. Refreshing clears the draft, and there is no account, history or download button. Copy the HTML or keep the Markdown source somewhere else before closing the tab. The Clear button empties the editor, while Reset example restores the built-in sample.

The safety rules are useful but not a publishing policy. Raw HTML is escaped and unsafe link protocols are rejected, yet the CMS still owns the final sanitization, canonical URLs and accessibility checks. Treat the preview as a formatting check, not as a security review.

Preview before publishing: open the Markdown editor, paste the draft, and compare the Write and Preview tabs. Use the word counter for length and the grammar checker for a final language pass.

faqs.question: Does the editor show a split-screen preview?
faqs.answer: No. It has separate Write and Preview tabs. The HTML is recalculated as the source changes, but you must switch tabs to see the result.

faqs.question: Does it support Markdown tables?
faqs.answer: No. Pipe tables are not parsed and remain paragraph text. Use a CMS table block or add the table as HTML after copying the rest of the draft.

faqs.question: Can I use relative links?
faqs.answer: No. Only absolute http, https and mailto URLs are accepted. A relative path such as /contact becomes # in the generated HTML, so use a full URL or fix the link in the CMS.

faqs.question: Is the Markdown or HTML saved?
faqs.answer: No. Everything runs in the page with no account or history. Refreshing clears the draft, so copy the HTML or keep the source elsewhere.

faqs.question: Why does my code block show a language name?
faqs.answer: The parser keeps the text after the opening fence as part of the code. It does not use that label for syntax highlighting. Remove the label if you do not want it on the first line.

title: WCAG Contrast Checker: Pass AA and AAA
description: Check a text and background pair against WCAG AA and AAA contrast thresholds, read the ratio correctly, and see which checks the tool cannot perform.

toc.text: What the checker cannot tell you

html:
Contrast is not a matter of taste. WCAG compares the relative luminance of text and background, then expresses the result as a ratio from 1:1 to 21:1. A ratio of 1:1 means no difference; 21:1 is black on white. The color contrast checker accepts two hex colors, shows the ratio and reports three pass or fail badges. It is a quick check for a color pair, not a complete accessibility audit.

Part of the image and design guide. The tool checks text contrast only. It does not inspect icons, focus rings, charts, disabled controls or text placed over a photograph. Those need separate checks.

How the ratio is calculated

Each color is converted from hex to red, green and blue values. Every channel is divided by 255, linearized with a gamma correction, and combined into a relative luminance using the coefficients 0.2126, 0.7152 and 0.0722. The lighter luminance and the darker luminance are then inserted into (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). The order of the two colors does not matter because the formula always puts the lighter value on top.

TextBackgroundRatioWhat it means
#1a1a1a#ffffff17.40:1Passes AAA for normal text
#595959#ffffff7.00:1Meets the AAA normal-text threshold exactly
#767676#ffffff4.54:1Passes AA normal text, fails AAA normal text
#999999#ffffff2.85:1Fails AA normal text and AA large text
#ff5733#ffffff3.15:1Passes AA large only, not AA normal
#c2410c#ffffff5.18:1Passes AA normal text
#14b8a6#ffffff2.49:1Fails all three badges
#0f766e#ffffff5.47:1Passes AA normal text
#1e3a5f#f8fafc10.99:1Strong contrast without pure black or white
#334155#f8fafc9.90:1Passes AAA for normal text

The exact numbers matter at the boundaries. A ratio of 4.50 passes AA normal text, while 4.49 does not. The page displays two decimal places but compares the unrounded ratio, so rounding can hide a value just below a threshold. A displayed 4.50 is close enough that you should darken or lighten the pair slightly instead of relying on the display.

The calculation assumes opaque colors. A hex value has no alpha channel, so a translucent overlay must be composited against its real background before it is checked. A 50 percent black overlay on white is not the same as #808080 in every rendering context; compute the resulting solid color first, then enter that color here.

The three badges and the missing fourth check

WCAG sets different thresholds for different text sizes and levels:

LevelNormal textLarge text
AA4.5:13:1
AAA7:14.5:1

The tool shows AA normal at 4.5, AA large at 3 and AAA normal at 7. It does not show a separate AAA large badge. That is a real limitation, not a claim that AAA large does not exist. If you need AAA for large text, compare the ratio manually against 4.5.

Large text is generally at least 18 point regular or 14 point bold, which is about 24 pixels regular or 18.66 pixels bold. The tool does not know the font size, so the AA large badge is only a hint until you confirm the rendered size. A 16-pixel paragraph does not become large text because the badge says AA large passes.

The threshold also depends on what is being tested. Normal body copy needs the full 4.5 ratio at AA. Icons, borders and focus indicators are non-text elements with a different requirement, and the checker does not evaluate them. Placeholder text, error messages and link text inside a paragraph are text, so check them with their actual colors rather than assuming the surrounding body style covers them.

Reading a failed result

Start with the contrast ratio and identify which badge fails. A 3.15 ratio passes AA large but fails AA normal. That might be acceptable for a 24-pixel headline and unacceptable for a 16-pixel paragraph. The same color pair can be right for one role and wrong for another.

Do not automatically jump to pure black or pure white. The navy and off-white pair at 10.99:1 is easier on the eyes than 21:1 and still clears AAA for normal text. A gray such as #767676 is a common compromise at 4.54:1: it passes AA normal but fails AAA. A darker gray such as #595959 reaches 7.00:1 and clears AAA normal, but it may look heavier in a minimal interface.

For a brand color, change lightness before changing hue. Orange #ff5733 fails AA normal at 3.15:1, while a darker burnt orange such as #c2410c reaches 5.18:1 and passes. Teal #14b8a6 fails all three badges, while #0f766e reaches 5.47:1. The darker versions keep the hue family and give the text enough separation from white.

Test the actual pair, not the intended pair. A button may have a gradient, a hover overlay or a semi-transparent border that changes the effective background. A card may sit on an image. If the text lands on a photograph, sample the lightest and darkest areas or add a solid scrim; the checker can only evaluate two solid colors.

A short contrast workflow

  1. Enter the actual text color and background color as three- or six-digit hex values.
  2. Read the ratio and the three badges. Ignore the AA large badge until you know the rendered font size and weight.
  3. Identify the target: AA normal for body copy, AA large for confirmed large text, AAA normal for stricter body copy.
  4. Adjust one color at a time, usually by darkening the text or lightening the background, and recheck.
  5. Test hover, focus, visited, disabled and dark-mode variants separately.
  6. Check icons, borders and focus rings with a non-text contrast review after the text pair passes.

A useful habit is to record the ratio beside the design token. For example, body text on a page background might be 14.48:1, while secondary text on the same background might be 7.00:1. Naming the pair and its ratio makes later changes easier to review than a screenshot alone.

What the checker cannot tell you

It does not simulate color vision deficiency, measure perceived readability, inspect font weight or evaluate text over images. It does not save a palette, export a report or pick a color from the screen. The three-digit shorthand is expanded to six digits, so #fff and #ffffff produce the same result. Invalid hex input produces no numeric ratio and the preview falls back to a safe color.

Passing a ratio is necessary but not sufficient. A page can meet contrast thresholds and still be hard to read because of tiny type, tight spacing, long lines, motion or poor focus states. Use the checker as one gate in a broader accessibility review, not as a substitute for testing with real content and assistive technology.

Check a pair now: open the WCAG contrast checker, enter the text and background hex values, and confirm the intended text size before accepting a badge. Use the color converter when you need HEX, RGB or HSL values.

faqs.question: Does the tool check AAA for large text?
faqs.answer: No. It shows AA normal, AA large and AAA normal. AAA large requires 4.5:1, so compare the displayed ratio against 4.5 manually if that is your target.

faqs.question: Does color order matter?
faqs.answer: No. The formula always uses the lighter luminance first, so swapping text and background produces the same ratio.

faqs.question: Can it check transparent colors?
faqs.answer: No. Only three- and six-digit hex values are accepted. Composite transparency against the final background first, then enter the resulting solid color.

faqs.question: Does it check text over an image?
faqs.answer: No. It evaluates two solid colors. For text over a photo or gradient, test the lightest and darkest effective background areas or add a solid scrim and check that color.

faqs.question: Is passing AA enough for accessibility?
faqs.answer: No. Contrast is one requirement. Font size, spacing, focus visibility, motion, semantics and assistive-technology behavior still need separate review.

title: Estimate AI Token Cost Before Sending a Prompt
description: Estimate input tokens from characters, compare model costs per million tokens, and see why a heuristic is not a provider tokenizer or a final bill.
html:
AI providers bill by tokens, not by words or characters. That makes a long prompt feel cheaper than it is: a 10,000-word document can be tens of thousands of tokens before the model writes a single sentence. The AI token counter estimates input tokens from the pasted text, compares a few default model prices and shows an editable cost table. It is a planning aid, not a billing statement.

Part of the JSON formatter guide. The connection is practical: prompts often carry JSON, code and structured examples, and those characters do not tokenize like ordinary English. The tool is input-only. It does not estimate the model's reply, reserve space for a system prompt or enforce a context window.

How the estimate is produced

The page normalizes the text to Unicode NFC, counts Unicode code points as characters, counts runs of non-whitespace as words, and applies a simple ratio:

  • Base estimate = characters / 4
  • Code estimate = base x 1.15 when the text looks code-like
  • Displayed tokens = rounded up to the next whole token

The code boost triggers on three or more characters from a punctuation set, in a row, that includes braces, brackets, parentheses, semicolons, equals signs, angle brackets, colons, slashes and backslashes, or on keywords such as function, const, import, def and class. It is a single multiplier, not a syntax-aware parser. A string of nested braces or array brackets can trigger the boost, while a plain English paragraph with one colon usually does not. Many ordinary JSON payloads will not trigger it, so the estimate can land low for structured data.

For 4,000 characters of prose, the base estimate is 1,000 tokens. If the same length looks code-like, the estimate becomes 1,150. A 2,000-word article is often around 10,000 to 13,000 characters, which puts the rough range near 2,500 to 3,250 tokens. That is close enough for a budget estimate and far enough from exact to matter when you are near a hard limit.

Characters are counted as Unicode code points, so a simple emoji is one character. A multi-person emoji built from several code points can count as more than one. This is one reason the estimate should be treated as a range rather than a precise count.

Turning tokens into a cost

The cost formula is straightforward:

Input cost = estimated tokens / 1,000,000 x price per million input tokens

The default table uses GPT-4o at 2.50 dollars per million input tokens, Claude Sonnet at 3.00 and Gemini Flash at 0.35. Those are editable starting values, not a live price list. Provider pricing changes, and the same family can have different prices for input, cached input, output, batch processing and long-context tiers.

Input tokensGPT-4o at $2.50Claude Sonnet at $3.00Gemini Flash at $0.35
1,000$0.002500$0.003000$0.000350
10,000$0.025000$0.030000$0.003500
50,000$0.125000$0.150000$0.017500
100,000$0.250000$0.300000$0.035000
1,000,000$2.500000$3.000000$0.350000

At 100,000 input tokens, GPT-4o is 0.25 dollars, Claude Sonnet is 0.30 and Gemini Flash is 0.035 on these assumptions. The cheapest model is roughly seven times cheaper for the input portion. That does not automatically make it the best choice: output quality, latency, context limits and output prices can reverse the decision.

The table displays six decimal places. Very small jobs can round to 0.000000 even when the real cost is a tiny fraction of a cent. For a one-off prompt that is harmless; for a high-volume workload, export the token count and calculate against current prices in a spreadsheet instead of reading a rounded display.

What the estimate leaves out

The biggest omission is output. Many providers charge a different, often higher, rate for generated tokens. A prompt with 2,000 input tokens and a 1,000-token response has two billable components, and this page estimates only the first. Add the expected output separately using the provider's output price.

A real request also includes more than the text you paste. System instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool definitions, images and formatting can all consume input tokens. Conversation history grows with every turn, so the tenth message can be far more expensive than the first even when the new question is short. The tool has one text area and no notion of turns.

Context limits are separate from cost. A model may accept a large context but charge more above a threshold, or reject the request when input and reserved output together exceed the window. The counter does not know the selected model's actual context size, does not count the system prompt and does not reserve room for a reply. Check the provider's limit before sending a long document.

Caching, batch discounts, free tiers and reasoning-token billing are not modeled. Those can change the real bill by a large factor. The estimate is most useful for comparing prompt drafts and spotting runaway length before you call an API.

Why a tokenizer still matters

Production tokenizers use byte-pair encoding or a similar scheme. They split common words into single tokens, rare words into pieces, punctuation into separate tokens and code according to learned patterns. Four characters per token is an average for English prose, not a rule. The same 1,000 characters can produce very different counts in English, Chinese, Python, minified JSON or a block of emoji.

Use the page to choose a model and budget a draft. Use the provider's tokenizer or the usage field in an API response when the number affects billing, truncation or a hard limit. If the two disagree by more than a few percent, trust the provider's count for the request you actually send.

Normalization also creates small differences. NFC combines some accented characters, which can change the character count before the ratio is applied. That is reasonable for text comparison, but a provider may tokenize the original byte sequence differently. Keep a margin near limits rather than tuning a prompt to the last estimated token.

A practical prompt-budget workflow

  1. Paste the exact prompt or document, not a summary of it.
  2. Read the character, word and estimated-token figures together. A high word count with a low token estimate is a signal to check the text, not a guarantee.
  3. Replace the default prices with the current input price for the models you are considering.
  4. Compare the input cost first, then add the expected output cost from the provider's separate output rate.
  5. Add room for system instructions, history and retrieved context, and confirm the total fits the context window.
  6. Copy the summary for your notes, then verify the first real request against the provider's usage report.

When a prompt is too expensive, shorten it before changing models. Remove duplicated instructions, replace pasted reference material with a short excerpt, summarize earlier turns, and send structured data in a compact format. The JSON formatter can help you inspect a payload, and the word counter gives a second view of length. Neither replaces a tokenizer, but both make waste easier to see.

The text stays in the page. There is no account, upload or saved history, and the input is capped at 500,000 characters for performance. That cap is a guardrail, not a context-window recommendation; many models accept far less, and some accept more.

Estimate before you send: open the AI token counter, paste the prompt, and edit the per-million prices to match your provider. For structured prompts, clean the payload with the JSON formatter first.

faqs.question: Is this an exact token count?
faqs.answer: No. It uses about four characters per token, with a 1.15 multiplier for code-like text. Provider tokenizers split text differently, so use the API usage report when the exact number matters.

faqs.question: Does it estimate output tokens?
faqs.answer: No. It counts the pasted input only. Add the expected response length separately at the provider's output price, and reserve context space for it.

faqs.question: Why does code cost more in the estimate?
faqs.answer: The heuristic applies a 1.15 multiplier when it detects code-like punctuation or keywords. Code and JSON often tokenize less efficiently than plain English, so the boost is a rough adjustment rather than a syntax-aware count.

faqs.question: Are the model prices live?
faqs.answer: No. GPT-4o at 2.50, Claude Sonnet at 3.00 and Gemini Flash at 0.35 per million input tokens are editable defaults. Replace them with current provider prices before relying on a cost.

faqs.question: Is my prompt uploaded?
faqs.answer: No. The estimate runs in the page and nothing is saved. The input is capped at 500,000 characters, and refreshing clears the text.
